### 1.2.2 Performance Measures of the Online Learning Algorithms

By viewing the cognitive user as a player or agent, and the channels as arms the player can choose so as to maximize the long‐term accumulated reward, the network model described can be cast as a restless multi‐armed bandit (RMAB) problem, which is a generalization of the classic multi‐armed bandit (MAB) problem (Gittins, [1979](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0037); Lai and Robbins, [1985](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0050); Anantharam et al., [1987](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0004)). In the classic MAB problem, the states of passive arms remain frozen, which is not suitable to model cognitive radio networks, where the channel states (used for transmission or not) change dynamically. In contrast, in the RMAB setting, the state of each arm (active or passive) can change. Thus, the class of RMAB problems considered here has been studied in recent years in the context of cognitive radio networks in (Tekin and Liu, [2012](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0075); Liu et al., [2013](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0055); Gafni and Cohen, [2018b, a](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0034)).

The RMAB problem under the Bayesian formulation with known Markovian dynamics has been shown to be P‐SPACE hard in general (Papadimitriou and Tsitsiklis, [1999](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0070)). Nevertheless, there are a number of studies that obtained optimal solutions for some special cases of RMAB models. In particular, the myopic strategy was shown to be optimal in the case of positively correlated two‐state Markovian arms with a unit reward for good state and zero reward for bad state (Zhao et al., [2008](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0096); Ahmad et al., [2009](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0002); Ahmad and Liu, [2009](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0001)). In (Liu and Zhao, [2010](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0056); Liu et al., [2011](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0057)), the indexability of a special classes of RMAB has been established. In (Wang and Chen, [2012](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0079); Wang et al., [2014](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0080)), the myopic strategy was shown to be optimal for a family of regular reward functions that satisfy axioms of symmetry, monotonicity and decomposability. In our previous work, optimality conditions of a myopic policy have been derived under arm‐activation constraints (Cohen et al., [2014](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0029)).

Although optimal solutions have been obtained for some special cases of RMAB models as detailed, solving RMAB problems directly is intractable in general (Papadimitriou and Tsitsiklis, [1999](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0070)). Thus, instead of looking for optimal strategies, it is often desired to develop asymptotically optimal strategies with time. Specifically, a widely used performance measure of an algorithm is the *regret*, defined as the reward loss with respect to a player with side information on the model. An algorithm that achieves a sublinear scaling rate of the regret with time is thus asymptotically optimal in terms of approaching the performance of the player with the side information as time increases. The challenge is to design an algorithm that achieves the best sublinear scaling of the regret with time by learning the side information effectively.

In (Auer et al., [2002b](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0006)), regret was defined as the reward loss of an algorithm with respect to a player that knows the expected reward of all arms and always plays the arm with the highest expected reward. Since this strategy is known to be optimal in the classic MAB under i.i.d. or rested Markovian rewards (up to an additional constant term (Anantharam et al., [1987](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0004))), it is commonly used in RMAB with unknown dynamic settings that allows measuring the algorithm performance in a tractable manner. This approach was used later in (Tekin and Liu, [2012](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0075); Liu et al., [2013](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0055); Gafni and Cohen, [2018b, a](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0034)) to design effective learning strategies for DSA. In this chapter, we focus on this definition of regret.

 

### 1.2.3 The Objective

As explained in [Section 1.2.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0005), we define the regret ![images](images/c01-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>&#966;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> for policy ![images](images/c01-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow></math> as the difference between the expected total reward that can be obtained by using the channel with the highest reward mean, and the expected total reward obtained from using policy ![images](images/c01-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow></math> up to time ![images](images/c01-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>:

(1.3)![equation](images/c01-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>r</mi> <mi>&#966;</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>t</mi> <msub> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mrow> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> <mi>&#966;</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The objective is to find a policy that minimizes the growth rate of the regret with time. Achieving this goal requires designing a strategy that effectively addresses the well‐known exploration versus exploitation dilemma in online learning problems. On the one hand, the cognitive user should explore all channels to learn their unknown states. On the other hand, it should exploit the inference outcome to use the channel with the highest mean. Since the wireless channels are restless (i.e. both active and passive arms are restless in the context of the RMAB model), the designed strategy should learn the Markovian reward statistics consecutively for a period of time (i.e. epoch). This will avoid the potential reward loss due to the transient effect as compared to steady state when switching channels.

 

### 1.2.4 Random and Deterministic Approaches

In this subsection, we overview two algorithms that were developed in recent years to achieve the objective just described. The first uses random epoch lengths, dubbed the regenerative cycle algorithm (RCA) (Tekin and Liu, [2012](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0075)); and the second uses deterministic epoch lengths, dubbed the deterministic sequencing of exploration and exploitation (DSEE) algorithm (Liu et al., [2013](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0055)). The idea of the RCA algorithm is to catch predefined channel states each time the algorithm enters a transmission epoch when using a channel. These catching times are called *regenerative cycles* and are defined by random hitting times. The channel selection is based on the upper confidence bound (UCB) index (Auer et al., [2002a](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0005)). The authors showed that RCA achieves a logarithmic scaling of the regret with time. However, since RCA performs a random regenerative cycle at each epoch, the scaling with the mean hitting time ![images](images/c01-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> is of order ![images](images/c01-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

The DSEE algorithm overcomes this issue by avoiding the execution of random regenerative cycles at each epoch. Instead, the idea behind DSEE is to use deterministic sequencing of exploration and exploitation epochs. It has been shown that by judiciously designing these deterministic epochs, a logarithmic regret with time is obtained. However, the design of these deterministic epochs by DSEE requires oversampling bad channels for transmission to achieve the desired logarithmic regret. This oversampling results in a scaling order of ![images](images/c01-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msqrt><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c01-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> is the number of channels and ![images](images/c01-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> is a known lower bound on the square difference between the highest reward mean ![images](images/c01-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and the second‐highest reward mean ![images](images/c01-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.

When the channel state space increases, or when the probability of switching between channel states decreases, then the mean hitting times of catching predefined channel states increases, which decreases performance under the RCA algorithm. On the other hand, increasing the number of channels ![images](images/c01-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> when ![images](images/c01-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is small as compared to the differences between ![images](images/c01-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and the reward means of other channels decreases performance under the DSEE algorithm. We next overview a very recent algorithm that we developed to overcome these issues.

 

### 1.2.5 The Adaptive Sequencing Rules Approach

In (Gafni and Cohen, [2018b,a](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0034)), we developed the Adaptive Sequencing Rules (ASR) algorithm for solving the RMAB problem for DSA. The basic idea of ASR is to estimate the desired (unknown) exploration rate of each channel online during the algorithm to achieve efficient learning. This approach avoids oversampling bad channels as in DSEE, and at the same time it significantly reduces the total amount of regenerative cycles as required by RCA. Specifically, we show in (Gafni and Cohen, [2018b,a](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0034)) that we must explore a bad channel ![images](images/c01-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c01-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>, at least ![images](images/c01-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> times, where

[(1.4)](#c01.xhtml#c01-R_disp-0004)![equation](images/c01-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>D</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8796;</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mn>4</mn> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mrow> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The intuition is that the smaller the difference between the channel reward means, the more samples we must take to infer which one is better with sufficient accuracy. Since the channel reward means are unknown, however, we replace ![images](images/c01-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></math> with its estimate value, which allows us to estimate ![images](images/c01-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Then, we can use the estimate of ![images](images/c01-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> (which is updated dynamically during time and controlled by the estimate channel reward means) to design an adaptive sequencing rule for sampling channel ![images](images/c01-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>. The designed sequencing rules decide whether to enter an exploration epoch or an exploitation epoch, and are adaptive in the sense that they are updated dynamically and controlled by the current estimated reward means in a closed‐loop manner. Interestingly, we found that the size of the exploitation epochs is deterministic and the size of the exploration epochs is random under ASR.

In (Gafni and Cohen, [2018b,a](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0034)), we showed that ASR achieves a logarithmic scaling of the regret with time as achieved by RCA and DSEE. The scaling with the mean hitting time ![images](images/c01-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> under ASR, however, is significantly better than the scaling under RCA. Specifically, ASR achieves a scaling order of ![images](images/c01-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> as compared to ![images](images/c01-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> under RCA. We also showed that scaling with the number of channels and ![images](images/c01-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math> under ASR is significantly better than scaling under DSEE. Specifically, ASR achieves a scaling order of ![images](images/c01-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msqrt><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math> as compared to ![images](images/c01-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msqrt><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></msqrt></mrow></mfrac><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math> under DSEE. Extensive simulation results support the theoretical analysis and demonstrate significant performance gains of ASR over RCA and DSEE. We omit the analysis in this chapter and focus on the description of the algorithm.

 

#### 1.2.5.1 Structure of Transmission Epochs

As discussed earlier, the designed strategy should use the channels in a consecutive manner for a period of time to learn the restless Markovian reward statistics. The RCA algorithm selects channels based on UCB and uses the channel for a random period of time that depends on hitting times used to catch predefined channel states, while the DSEE algorithm uses channels for a deterministic period of time that grows geometrically with time. The ASR algorithm uses hybrid random/deterministic transmission epoch lengths, while determining the exploration rate for each channel according to judiciously designed adaptive sequencing rules, as discussed later. This approach allows ASR to achieve significant performance improvements both theoretically and numerically.

[Figure 1.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0002) illustrates the structure of the time horizon, which consists of exploration and exploitation epochs. The adaptive sequencing rules decide whether to enter exploration epoch and which channel to explore. The design of the adaptive sequencing rules is discussed later. We define ![images](images/c01-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> as the number of exploration epochs in which channel ![images](images/c01-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> was used at time ![images](images/c01-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. The exploitation epochs are used to select the channel with the highest sample reward mean, whenever exploration is not being performed. We define ![images](images/c01-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> as the number of exploitation epochs at time ![images](images/c01-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>.

![Figure 1.2 An illustration of the exploration and exploitation epochs as implemented by the ASR algorithm. During exploitation epoch, the cognitive user uses the same channel that had the highest sample reward mean at the beginning of the epoch. An exploration epoch is divided into a random‐size sub‐block SB1 and a deterministic (geometrically growing) size sub‐block SB2. SB1 of a channel (say images, as in the figure) is random and used to catch the last channel state images observed in the previous exploration epoch. The ASR's selection rule decides which epoch to play at each time. The exploration epoch is illustrated for channel images only. In general, an interleaving of exploration epochs for all channels with exploitation epochs (for the channel with the highest sample reward mean) is performed.](images/c01f002.jpg)

[Figure 1.2](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0002) An illustration of the exploration and exploitation epochs as implemented by the ASR algorithm. During exploitation epoch, the cognitive user uses the same channel that had the highest sample reward mean at the beginning of the epoch. An exploration epoch is divided into a random‐size sub‐block SB1 and a deterministic (geometrically growing) size sub‐block SB2. SB1 of a channel (say ![images](images/c01-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, as in the figure) is random and used to catch the last channel state ![images](images/c01-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#947;</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></math> observed in the previous exploration epoch. The ASR's selection rule decides which epoch to play at each time. The exploration epoch is illustrated for channel ![images](images/c01-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> only. In general, an interleaving of exploration epochs for all channels with exploitation epochs (for the channel with the highest sample reward mean) is performed.

**The structure of exploration epoch:** As illustrated in [Figure 1.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0002), when entering the ![images](images/c01-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> exploration epoch, the cognitive user starts by using channel ![images](images/c01-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> for a random period of time until observing ![images](images/c01-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#947;</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> (i.e. a random hitting time). This random period of time is denoted by sub‐block 1 (SB1). After completing SB1, the cognitive user uses the channel for a deterministic period of time with length of ![images](images/c01-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mn>4</mn><mrow><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. This deterministic period of time is denoted by sub‐block 2 (SB2). The cognitive user stores the last reward state ![images](images/c01-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#947;</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>O</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> observed at the current ![images](images/c01-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>n</mi><mi>O</mi><mi>i</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> exploration epoch, and so on. The set of time instants during SB2 epochs is denoted by ![images](images/c01-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">V</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

**The structure of exploitation epoch:** The sample reward mean of channel ![images](images/c01-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> when entering the ![images](images/c01-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> exploitation epoch is denoted by ![images](images/c01-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Then, the cognitive user uses the channel with the highest sample reward mean ![images](images/c01-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> for a deterministic period of time with length ![images](images/c01-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#183;</mo><msup><mn>4</mn><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> (note that the cognitive user does not switch between channels inside epochs). The set of time instants in exploitation epochs is denoted by ![images](images/c01-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">W</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. The cognitive user computes the sample reward mean ![images](images/c01-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> for each channel based on observations taken at times ![images](images/c01-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">V</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c01-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">W</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Observations that have been obtained at the SB1 period are discarded to ensure the consistency of the estimators.

 

#### 1.2.5.2 Selection Rule under the ASR Algorithm

We next describe the selection rule that the cognitive user applies when deciding whether to explore the channels, or whether to exploit the channel with the highest sample reward mean. Let ![images](images/c01-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> be the sample reward mean of channel ![images](images/c01-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> that the user computes based on observations taken from ![images](images/c01-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">V</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> only at time ![images](images/c01-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. Let

(1.5)![equation](images/c01-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>D</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8796;</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mn>4</mn> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>s</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>s</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#949;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c01-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> is a known lower bound on ![images](images/c01-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c01-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> is a fixed tuning parameter (we discuss the implementation details later). We also define:

(1.6)![equation](images/c01-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>I</mi> <mo>&#8796;</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msup> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>&#183;</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>n</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <mn>192</mn> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>r</mi> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>x</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

As explained earlier, the user must take at least ![images](images/c01-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> samples from each bad channel (![images](images/c01-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is given in Eq. ([1.4](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0004))) to compute the sample means ![images](images/c01-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> with sufficient reliability. Therefore, the user replaces the unknown value ![images](images/c01-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> with its overestimate ![images](images/c01-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Furthermore, since ![images](images/c01-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a random variable, we need to guarantee that the desired property holds with a sufficiently high probability. ![images](images/c01-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow></math> can be viewed as the minimal rate function of the estimates among all channels and used to guarantee the desired property. Specifically, let ![images](images/c01-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">V</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> be the set of all time instants during the SB2 period at time ![images](images/c01-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. Then, if there exists a channel (say ![images](images/c01-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>) such that the following condition holds

[(1.7)](#c01.xhtml#c01-R_disp-0007)![equation](images/c01-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script">V</mi> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>D</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mfrac> <mn>2</mn> <mi>I</mi> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#183;</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mi>t</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

the cognitive user enters an exploration epoch for channel ![images](images/c01-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>. Otherwise, it enters an exploitation epoch (for the channel with the highest sample reward mean). Note that the selection rule for each channel that determines the channel sequencing policy is adaptive in the sense that it is updated dynamically with time and controlled by the random sample reward mean in a closed‐loop manner.

 

#### 1.2.5.3 High‐Level Pseudocode and Implementation Discussion

To summarize the discussion, the cognitive user applies the following algorithm:

1.  For all ![images](images/c01-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> channels, execute an exploration epoch where a single observation is taken from each channel.
2.  If condition Eq. ([1.7](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0007)) holds for some channel (say ![images](images/c01-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>), then execute an exploration epoch for channel ![images](images/c01-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>; and, when completing the exploration epoch, go to Step 2 again. Otherwise, go to Step 3.
3.  Execute an exploitation epoch. When completing the exploitation epoch, go to Step 2.

To achieve the theoretical performance, the ASR and DSEE algorithms require the same knowledge of the system parameters. The knowledge of the parameter ![images](images/c01-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math>, however, is not needed under the RCA algorithm. In terms of practical implementations, it is well known that there is often a gap between the sufficient conditions required by theoretical analysis and actual performance. In practice, ![images](images/c01-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math> is not needed, and the parameters can be estimated on the fly. Extensive simulation results demonstrated strong performance when estimating ![images](images/c01-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> directly by setting ![images](images/c01-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8592;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mn>4</mn><mi>L</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>s</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>. An example is given in [Figure 1.3](#c01.xhtml#c01-fig-0003), where we executed ASR without knowing ![images](images/c01-i0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi></mrow></math> and by setting ![images](images/c01-i0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> to to zero. ![images](images/c01-i0123.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>D</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> was estimated on the fly. It can be seen that ASR significantly outperforms both DSEE and RCA. Additional numerical experiments can be found in (Gafni and Cohen, [2018b,a](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0034)).

 

## 1.3 Learning Algorithms for Channel Allocation

In this section, we consider the more general case where multiple users share the spectrum, and the goal is to effectively allocate channels to users in a distributed manner with the goal of maximizing a certain objective. Since the focus in this section is on the interaction among users (and not between the cognitive user and external processes as discussed in the previous section), we do not assume that there are primary and secondary users in the networks (e.g. as in the open sharing model for DSA (Zhao and Sadler, [2007](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0094))). Nevertheless, the model can be extended by adding external processes that are not affected by other users' actions to model the coexistence of primary users in the network.

![Figure 1.3 The regret (normalized by images) for the RMAB channel model with eight Markovian channels under ASR, DSEE, and RCA as a function of time. Each channel has two states, good and bad, with rewards 1, 0.1, respectively. The transition probability vectors from good state to bad state and from bad state to good state are \[0.09,0.9,0.08,0.7,0.06,0.5,0.04,0.3\] and \[0.01,0.1,0.02,0.3,0.04,0.5,0.06,0.7\], respectively.](images/c01f003.jpg)

[Figure 1.3](#c01.xhtml#R_c01-fig-0003) The regret (normalized by ![images](images/c01-i0124.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>) for the RMAB channel model with eight Markovian channels under ASR, DSEE, and RCA as a function of time. Each channel has two states, good and bad, with rewards 1, 0.1, respectively. The transition probability vectors from good state to bad state and from bad state to good state are \[0.09,0.9,0.08,0.7,0.06,0.5,0.04,0.3\] and \[0.01,0.1,0.02,0.3,0.04,0.5,0.06,0.7\], respectively.

 

### 1.3.1 The Network Model

Consider a wireless network consisting of a set ![images](images/c01-i0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math> of users and a set ![images](images/c01-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math> of shared orthogonal channels. The users transmit their data on the shared channels using a random access protocol. We mainly focus on Aloha‐type narrowband transmission, in which at each time slot, each user is allowed to choose a single channel for transmission with a certain transmission probability. In [Section 1.3.2](#c01.xhtml#c01-sec-0014), we discuss other types of communication protocols. We assume that users are backlogged, i.e. all users always have packets to transmit. Transmission on channel ![images](images/c01-i0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is successful if only a single user transmits over channel ![images](images/c01-i0128.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> in a given time slot. Otherwise, a collision occurs. Note that in the case where ![images](images/c01-i0129.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>, it is possible that all users transmit at the same time without collisions. Otherwise, a certain transmission schedule should be applied to reduce the number of collisions. Each user receives an acknowledgement signal (ACK) after transmission to indicate whether its packet was successfully delivered. The ACK signal at time slot ![images](images/c01-i0130.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> is denoted by the binary observation ![images](images/c01-i0131.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c01-i0132.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> indicates successful transmission and ![images](images/c01-i0133.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> indicates that the transmission has failed (i.e. a collision occurred).

The action for user ![images](images/c01-i0134.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> at time slot ![images](images/c01-i0135.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> is denoted by ![images](images/c01-i0136.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math>. We say that ![images](images/c01-i0137.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> when user ![images](images/c01-i0138.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> does not transmit a packet at time slot ![images](images/c01-i0139.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c01-i0140.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c01-i0141.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>, when user ![images](images/c01-i0142.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> transmits a packet on channel ![images](images/c01-i0143.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> at time slot ![images](images/c01-i0144.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. Note that the actions ![images](images/c01-i0145.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c01-i0146.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, which are taken by other users, are unknown to user ![images](images/c01-i0147.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. As a result, the network state (i.e. the entire action profile of all users) at time ![images](images/c01-i0148.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> is only partially observed by user ![images](images/c01-i0149.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> through the local signal ![images](images/c01-i0150.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, which makes the problem of obtaining efficient DSA strategies among users challenging. Let ![images](images/c01-i0151.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">H</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>o</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math> be the history of user ![images](images/c01-i0152.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> at time slot ![images](images/c01-i0153.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, which is the set of all its past actions and observations. ### 1.3.2 Distributed Learning, Game‐Theoretic, and Matching Approaches

In this subsection, we discuss related works that use game‐theoretic models, distributed optimization and learning, and matching techniques, and that were proposed in past and recent years for related models. Very recent developments based on deep learning will be discussed later.

**Aloha‐Based Protocols and Cross‐Layer Optimization**. Aloha‐based protocols have been widely used for spectrum access primarily because of their easy implementation and random nature. Related work on Aloha‐based protocols can be found in (Pountourakis and Sykas, [1992](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0071); MacKenzie and Wicker, [2001](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0059); Jin and Kesidis, [2002](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0046); Shen and Li, [2002](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0073); Altman et al., [2004](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0003); Bai and Zhang, [2006](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0011); Menache and Shimkin, [2008](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0062); To and Choi, [2010](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0076); Cohen et al., [2012, 2013](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0028); Cohen and Leshem, [2013, 2016](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0024); Wu et al., [2013](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0088)) for fully connected networks, where all users interfere with each other, and in (Kar et al., [2004](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0048); Wang and Kar, [2006](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0085); Baccelli et al., [2006](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0009); Kauffmann et al., [2007](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0049); Baccelli et al., [2009](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0010); Gupta and Stolyar, [2012](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0038); Chen and Huang, [2013](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0018); Hou and Gupta, [2014](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0043); Cohen et al., [2015, 2017](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0031)) for spatially connected networks, where each user interferes with its neighbors only. Opportunistic Aloha schemes that use cross‐layer techniques, in which the design of the medium access control (MAC) layer is integrated with physical layer (PHY) channel information to improve spectral efficiency, have been studied under both the single‐channel (Bai and Zhang, [2006](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0011); Menache and Shimkin, [2008](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0062); Baccelli et al., [2009](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0010)) and multi‐channel (Bai and Zhang, [2006](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0011); To and Choi, [2010](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0076); Cohen et al., [2012, 2013](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0028); Cohen and Leshem, [2013, 2016](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0024)) cases. Other recent related studies considered opportunistic carrier sensing in a cross‐layer design to exploit the channel diversity to optimize a certain objective (e.g. maximizing the data rate, minimizing the invested energy) (Cohen and Leshem, [2009, 2010b,a, 2011](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0022); Leshem et al., [2012](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0051)).

**Game‐Theoretic Analysis and Distributed Learning.** The question of how multiple users can effectively interact and converge to good strategies when applying Aloha‐based access has attracted much attention in past and recent years under various network models. A convenient way to address this question is to use game‐theoretic analysis in the development of algorithms and convergence analysis because it provides useful tools for modeling and analyzing the multi‐user dynamics. Since users in a wireless network are active entities that take actions, modeling the users as players as in a game‐theoretic framework allows one to develop game‐theoretic tools to establish design principles for the algorithm and to gain insights about its operating points under different objective functions. In (Jin and Kesidis, [2002](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0046); Menache and Shimkin, [2008](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0062)), the authors considered multiple users that access a single channel using an Aloha‐based protocol under a target rate demand for each user (assuming that the demands are feasible), and equilibria analysis has been successfully established. In (Baccelli et al., [2006, 2009](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0010)), spatial single‐channel Aloha networks have been studied under interference channels using stochastic geometry. More recently, the case where multiple users access multiple channels using an Aloha‐based protocol as in OFDMA systems, was considered in (Chen and Huang, [2013](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0018)) and our previous works (Cohen et al., [2012, 2013](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0028); Cohen and Leshem, [2013, 2016](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0024)). In (Chen and Huang, [2013](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0018)), the authors have developed a distributed algorithm in which a mixed strategy was applied to obtain local information in a spatially distributed network. In (Cohen et al., [2012, 2013](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0028); Cohen and Leshem, [2013, 2016](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0024)), pure strategies were applied, where the local information was obtained by sensing the spectrum in a fully connected network.

A number of studies have considered the problem of achieving proportionally fair rates in spatial random access networks. This problem has been studied under the cases where multiple users access a single channel in (Kar et al., [2004](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0048); Wang and Kar, [2006](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0085); Gupta and Stolyar, [2012](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0038)) and multiple channels in (Hou and Gupta, [2014](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0043); Cohen et al., [2015, 2017](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0031)) using Aloha‐based protocols. It was shown that by using altruistic plus selfish components in the algorithm design when users update their strategies, proportional fairness can be attained (asymptotically with time). Practically, such algorithms require a small number of message exchanges between users. Furthermore, convergence to the optimal solution requires the judicious application of log‐linear learning techniques (see (Young, [1998](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0090); Marden and Shamma, [2012](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0061)) for more details on the theory of log‐linear learning). Other related studies that use log‐linear learning, and altruistic plus selfish components in the algorithm design under different spectrum‐access models and objectives, can be found in (Xu et al., [2012](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0089); Herzen et al., [2013](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0041); Singh and Chen, [2013](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0074); Jang et al., [2014](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0045); Herzen et al., [2015](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0042)).

Cooperative game‐theoretic optimization has been studied under frequency‐flat interference channels in the single‐input and single‐output (SISO) (Leshem and Zehavi, [2006](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0052); Boche et al., [2007](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0014)), multiple‐input and single‐output (MISO) (Jorswieck and Larsson, [2008](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0047); Gao et al., [2008](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0036)) and multiple‐input and multiple‐output (MIMO) cases (Nokleby et al., [2007](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0068)). The frequency‐selective interference channels case has been studied in (Han et al., [2005](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0039); Leshem and Zehavi, [2008](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0053)). The collision channels case has been studied under a fully connected network and without information sharing between users in (Cohen and Leshem, [2016](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0024)), where the global optimum was attained under the asymptotic regime (i.e. as the number of users ![images](images/c01-i0184.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> approaches infinity) and the i.i.d assumption on the channel quality. Other related game‐theoretic models have been used in cellular, OFDMA, and 5G systems (Scutari et al., [2006](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0072); El‐Hajj et al., [2012](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0033); Zhao et al., [2014](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0093); Zhang et al., [2014](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0092); Wang et al., [2016](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0084)). In (Scutari et al., [2006](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0072)), the authors modeled and analyzed the problem of power control using potential game theory. Potential games have been used in (Wang et al., [2016](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0084); Zhao et al., [2014](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0093)) as well to analyze effective channel allocation strategies for the downlink operation of multicell networks. In (El‐Hajj et al., [2012](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0033)), the problem of channel allocation in OFDMA systems has been investigated using a two‐sided stable matching game formulation. In (Zhang et al., [2014](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0092)), the authors investigated channel utilization via a distributed matching approach.

**Spectrum Access as Matching, and Graph‐Coloring Problems**. Another set of related works is concerned with modeling spectrum access problem as a matching problem between channels and users. In (Naparstek and Leshem, [2014](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0066)), the authors developed a fully distributed auction algorithm for optimal channel assignment in terms of maximizing the user sum rate. The expected time complexity was analyzed in (Naparstek and Leshem, [2016](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0067)). A low‐complexity distributed algorithm has been developed in (Leshem et al., [2012](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0051)) that attains a stable matching solution, where the achievable data rates were assumed known. In (Bistritz and Leshem, [2018a, b](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0013); Avner and Mannor, [2016, 2018](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0008)), channel‐assignment algorithms have been developed under partial observation models using distributed learning. Another related approach models the spectrum‐access problem as a graph‐coloring problem, in which users and channels are represented by vertices and colors, respectively. Thus, coloring vertices such that two adjacent vertices do not share the same color is equivalent to allocating channels such that interference between neighbors is avoided (see (Wang and Liu, [2005](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0083); Wang et al., [2009](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0078); Checco and Leith, [2013, 2014](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0017)) and references therein for related works). However, generally, spectrum‐access problems are more involved when the number of users is much larger than the number of channels (thus, coloring the graph may be infeasible). Furthermore, users may select more than one channel, and may prefer some channels over others, as well as optimize their rates with respect to the attempt probability.

 

### 1.3.3 Deep Reinforcement Learning for DSA

The spectrum‐access algorithms that we discussed in the previous section mainly focused on model‐ and objective‐dependent problem settings, often requiring more complex implementations (e.g. carrier sensing, wideband monitoring), and thus the solutions cannot effectively adapt in general for handling more complex real‐world models. Therefore, in this section we overview the very recent developments of a deep learning based approach to overcome these issues. Specifically, we now focus on model‐free distributed learning algorithms to solve ([1.9](#c01.xhtml#c01-disp-0009)) that can effectively adapt to changes in network topology, objective functions, time horizons (in which solving dynamic programming becomes very challenging, or often impossible for large ![images](images/c01-i0185.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>), etc. Obtaining an optimal solution for the spectrum‐access problem considered here, however, is a combinatorial optimization problem with a partially observed network state that is mathematically intractable as the network size increases (Zhao et al., [2007](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0095)). Therefore, in this section we overview methods that use a deep reinforcement learning (DRL) approach, due to its capability to provide good approximate solutions while dealing with a very large state and action spaces. We first describe the basic idea of Q‐learning and DRL. We then overview recent developments of DRL to solve the DSA problem.

 

#### 1.3.3.1 Background on Q‐learning and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL):

Q‐learning is a reinforcement learning method that aims at finding good policies for dynamic programming problems. It has been widely applied in various decision‐making problems, primarily because of its ability to evaluate the expected utility from among available actions without requiring prior knowledge about the system model, and its ability to adapt when stochastic transitions occur (Watkins and Dayan, [1992](#c01.xhtml#c01-bib-0087)). The algorithm was originally designed for a single agent who interacts with a fully observable Markovian environment (in which convergence to the optimal solution is guaranteed under some regularity conditions in this case). It has been widely applied to more involved settings as well (e.g. multi‐agent, non‐Markovian environments) and demonstrated strong performance, although convergence to the optimal solution is open in general under these settings. Assume that we can encode the entire history of the process up to time ![images](images/c01-i0186.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> to a state ![images](images/c01-i0187.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> that is observed by the system. By applying Q‐learning to our setting, the algorithm updates a Q‐value at each time ![images](images/c01-i0188.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> for each action‐state pair as follows:
