where ![images](images/c02-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math> is the maximum distortion (equal to the variance of the synthetic Gaussian source).

On the other hand, the channel‐induced distortion ![images](images/c02-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> is due to errors introduced during transmission over the wireless channel that cannot be corrected by the error‐correction mechanism. When assuming that these errors are concealed by replacing the erred source samples with their expected value, the channel‐induced distortion is a constant equal to the variance of the source samples. The impact of ![images](images/c02-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> on the end‐to‐end distortion is determined by the probability that an uncorrectable transmission error occurs, which we denote by ![images](images/c02-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>Pr</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>. Furthermore, ![images](images/c02-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>Pr</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> depends on both the channel SINR ![images](images/c02-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and the channel coding rate ![images](images/c02-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, which determine the strength of the channel coding. Also, it is worth noting that given a channel throughput ![images](images/c02-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and a fixed channel‐coding rate ![images](images/c02-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, the best‐effort source‐encoding rate can be determined as ![images](images/c02-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><msubsup><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>. Considering all these observations, the end‐to‐end distortion can be expressed as a function of the parameters ![images](images/c02-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> in the following form:

[(2.6)](#c02.xhtml#c02-R_disp-0006)![equation](images/c02-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>D</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>&#947;</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>r</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>R</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>D</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>c</mi> </mrow> </msubsup> <mi>Pr</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi>r</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <msup> <mn>2</mn> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi>r</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi>R</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>Pr</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi>r</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Note from Eqs. ([2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0002)) and ([2.4](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0004)) that ![images](images/c02-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c02-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> are jointly determined by the transmit powers of all the SUs, i.e. ![images](images/c02-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></mrow></math>. Therefore, Eq. ([2.6](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0006)) can be rewritten as

[(2.7)](#c02.xhtml#c02-R_disp-0007)![equation](images/c02-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>D</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi>r</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>D</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>c</mi> </mrow> </msubsup> <mi>Pr</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi>r</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#951;</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi>r</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>Pr</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi>r</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The goal of each SU will be to perform resource allocation so as to minimize the expected end‐to‐end distortion during transmission of its real‐time multimedia source. Note that this involves a cross‐layer approach, since the resources to be allocated by each SU are ![images](images/c02-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, with the goal of minimizing the expected end‐to‐end distortion, which depends on parameters from multiple layers. Due to the distributed nature of the SN in a practical scenario, we focus on finding for the SUs a decentralized resource‐allocation mechanism. In other words, an individual transmitting SU ![images](images/c02-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> independently searches for its optimal cross‐layer choice of power and channel‐coding rate that minimizes end‐to‐end distortion while keeping the information exchange with the other SUs at a minimum. Here, the requirement of minimum information exchange is due to both the limited signaling capability over a non‐dedicated channel and the privacy concerns of revealing local transmitting parameters (e.g. channel‐coding parameters) to peer devices. We note that such a limit will cause difficulty coordinating among the SUs. As noted in (Han et al. ([2012](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0007))), the simple best response‐based strategy searching scheme will end up in an arms race, where each SU keeps increasing its transmit power and consequently causes interference to both other SUs and the PU to increase, finally exceeding the SINR limits. This suggests that it is necessary to introduce repeated play among the SUs to help them out of the trap of the prisoner dilemma‐like equilibrium. Therefore, considering the strategy coupling between SUs, it is natural to establish our cross‐layer strategy‐searching scheme based on the framework of reinforcement learning as presented in the following.

Without loss of generality, we consider that both the power level and the channel‐coding rate of an SU are selected from a discrete set. Assume that the parameter sets of each SU are the same and are denoted by ![images](images/c02-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">P</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c02-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>. Then we can map the problem of transmitting‐strategy searching into a general reinforcement learning (RL) process, which consists of three major elements: a set of system state ![images](images/c02-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math>, a set of system actions ![images](images/c02-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow></math>, and a vector of individual cost functions ![images](images/c02-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">c</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>c</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mo>&#8868;</mo></msup></mrow></math>, which measures the instantaneous quality of a local action given the other SUs' choices and the current system state. Specifically, given the current system state ![images](images/c02-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>, the transition to a new system state is (probabilistically) determined by the joint actions of all the SUs. Meanwhile, each SU relies on its own observation of the state changes and the evaluated cost level (i.e. feedback) to guide its further selection of transmitting actions.

To avoid explicitly coordinating the power allocation upon the interference conditions given in Eqs. ([2.1](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0001)) and ([2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0002)), we define the system state at a discrete time interval ![images](images/c02-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> as ![images](images/c02-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c02-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> reflects whether the interference condition of an individual SU ![images](images/c02-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is satisfied as per Eq. ([2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0002)), and ![images](images/c02-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> reflects whether the interference condition of the PU is satisfied according to the underlay DSA approach. Namely,

[(2.8)](#c02.xhtml#c02-R_disp-0008)![equation](images/c02-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.4em"/> <mtext>if</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msubsup> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.4em"/> <mtext>otherwise</mtext> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> 

and

[(2.9)](#c02.xhtml#c02-R_disp-0009)![equation](images/c02-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>L</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.4em"/> <mtext>if</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msubsup> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mrow> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>P</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.4em"/> <mtext>otherwise</mtext> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c02-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c02-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> are given in Eqs. ([2.1](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0001)) and ([2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0002)), respectively. The action of SU ![images](images/c02-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is defined by ![images](images/c02-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. By Eq. ([2.7](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0007)), we define the cost function of SU ![images](images/c02-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> at time instance ![images](images/c02-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> as follows:

[(2.10)](#c02.xhtml#c02-R_disp-0010)![equation](images/c02-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left left"> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mi>C</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mtext>if</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msub> <mi>L</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>&#62;</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <msub> <mi>D</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msubsup> <mi>P</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi>r</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mtext>otherwise</mtext> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c02-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is an arbitrarily large constant (larger than the maximum possible valuable for ![images](images/c02-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>) indicating a failure for a secondary transmission to meet the target SINR or the violation of the DSA rule for the PU. Also, ![images](images/c02-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> follows from Eq. ([2.7](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0007)).

With the system state, SU actions, and individual cost functions defined by Eqs. ([2.8](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0008)) through ([2.10](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0010)), we are ready to approximate the decentralized strategy‐searching process by a group of standard single‐agent Q‐learning processes (Sutton and Barto ([2011](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0018)), Wang et al. ([2016](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0019))). Here, by approximation, we assume that the SUs do not observe the joint SU actions and are unaware of their effect on state transitions. Namely, each SU treats the other SUs as if they are part of the stationary environment. Let ![images](images/c02-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> denote the probability of SU ![images](images/c02-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> selecting action ![images](images/c02-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow></math> given the observed state ![images](images/c02-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. We consider that SU ![images](images/c02-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> repeatedly adjusts its strategy ![images](images/c02-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> in order to finally obtain an optimal strategy that minimizes the state value, i.e. the expected sum of costs over time with a discounting factor ![images](images/c02-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> (![images](images/c02-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>):

(2.11)![equation](images/c02-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mi>V</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#960;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>E</mi> <mi>&#960;</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>V</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#960;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> ![](images/c02-gra-0001.png)

According to Bellman's principle of optimality, the solution for finding the optimal state value can be obtained in a recursive manner. Namely, it can be obtained by taking the current optimal action, provided that the optimal strategies thereafter are available:

[(2.12)](#c02.xhtml#c02-R_disp-0012)![equation](images/c02-math-0012.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>V</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>&#960;</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mi>min</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script">A</mi> </mrow> </munder> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>c</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <munder> <mo>&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msubsup> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script">S</mi> </mrow> </munder> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msubsup> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">|</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msubsup> <mi>V</mi> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>&#960;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> </mrow> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msubsup> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where we remove the time instance suffixes ![images](images/c02-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> or ![images](images/c02-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> to unclutter the notation. In Eq. ([2.12](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0012)), we denote ![images](images/c02-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> as the optimal strategy of SU ![images](images/c02-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c02-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> as the state transition probability from ![images](images/c02-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> to ![images](images/c02-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> given the chosen action ![images](images/c02-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Observing Eqs. ([2.8](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0008)) and ([2.9](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0009)), we note that the system state at the next time instance depends only on the joint actions of the SUs. Therefore, by assuming that Eq. ([2.12](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0012)) holds, we are able to apply the standard, single‐agent Q‐learning scheme for approximately finding the optimal deterministic strategy of each SU. Then, letting ![images](images/c02-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> denote the Q‐value (i.e. the estimated state‐action value) of SU ![images](images/c02-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> in its strategy‐updating process, we can update the Q‐values with the iterative scheme of state‐action value backups as follows:

(2.13)![equation](images/c02-math-0013.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>Q</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8592;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msub> <mi>Q</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msubsup> <mi>Q</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msubsup> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c02-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the learning rate, ![images](images/c02-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c02-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> is SU ![images](images/c02-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>'s minimum Q‐value at stage ![images](images/c02-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>:

[(2.14)](#c02.xhtml#c02-R_disp-0014)![equation](images/c02-math-0014.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>Q</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mi>min</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script">A</mi> </mrow> </munder> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>Q</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>s</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

which approximates the optimal state‐action value after the state is updated to ![images](images/c02-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. The corresponding action ![images](images/c02-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> in Eq. ([2.14](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0014)) also provides the action update at the next time instance ![images](images/c02-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. Then, the basic strategy‐learning scheme based on the standard, single‐agent Q‐learning scheme can be summarized in Algorithm 1.

It is worth noting that the standard off‐policy Q‐learning algorithm has an exponential time complexity. Therefore, Algorithm 1 is only computationally tractable when the state‐action space of each SU is sufficiently small. Consider that by ignoring the interaction between SUs and assuming the underlying state‐transitions of the SUs are stationary, the basic individual learning scheme in Algorithm 1 only provides an approximated process of optimal strategy searching. Moreover, a coarse discrete state‐action space with actions represented in relatively small sets may severely undermine the representativeness of the considered model for optimal strategy searching. As a result, the use of Q‐learning faces the challenge that large state or action spaces lead to long convergence times. This is already a challenge in many wireless resource allocation scenarios but could become exacerbated in cross‐layer approaches due to states and actions depending on more variables. This issue will be revisited over the following sections of this chapter.

 

## 2.2 Deep Q‐Learning and Resource Allocation

We now expand the ongoing discussion on resource allocation along multiple dimensions. The first such dimension follows on the note at the end of the previous section, where we said that a challenge encountered with Q‐learning is the long convergence time. With a table‐based algorithm (referred to this way because it estimates the Q‐values for each possible pair ![images](images/c02-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>), such as Algorithm 1, one reason for the slow convergence is that it estimates each Q‐value for each possible pair of a state and an action through an stochastic gradient descent method. An alternative approach is to estimate together the action‐value function (also called the *Q‐function*) that maps the Q‐values as a function of the (state, action) pair of variables. To follow this approach, neural networks can be used as function approximators (of the action‐value function) and compensate for the limitations seen with the standard table‐based Q‐learning algorithm in terms of generalization and function approximation capability. A *deep Q‐network* (DQN) is an emerging class of deep reinforcement learning algorithms that is capable of combining the process of RL with a class of neural networks known as *deep neural networks* to approximate the action‐value function. The team at Google DeepMind pioneered the use of this technique and demonstrated superhuman performance for a single learning agent playing Go and video games (Mnih et al. ([2015](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0011)), Silver et al. ([2016](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0017))).

A second dimension of the resource‐allocation problem we will expand upon pertains to new foci in network design that are brought about by the development of 5G wireless systems. The evolution of wireless communications toward the 5G era involves a transformation in network design and evaluation that aims at placing the end user at the center of any decision. As a result, resource management techniques for 5G networks need to be based on quality of experience (QoE) performance assessment (Wu et al. ([2014](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0020))). The shift in performance assessment from objective QoS metrics to subjective end user QoE metrics has been aided by a number of studies in multimedia quality assessment that have contributed techniques to estimate the QoE from objective measurements while retaining high correlation with the subjective perception of quality. Among these techniques, mean opinion score (MOS), a metric rating from 1 (bad) to 5 (excellent), is the most widely used QoE metric (Chen et al. ([2015](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0002))).

As a third dimension to delve deeper into the resource‐allocation problem, we will consider that different SN links may be carrying different types of traffic. For example, one link may be carrying delay‐sensitive real‐time video, while another link may be seeing regular data traffic. In the context of distributed resource allocation, the challenge in this case is that, because SUs are interacting through actions taken on their shared wireless environment, the rewards or cost functions that is seen by the SUs has to share a common yardstick for all the different types of traffic. Importantly, by providing a single common measuring scale for different types of traffic, the MOS metric provides the means to perform this integrated seamless traffic management and resource allocation across traffic of dissimilar characteristics (Dobrijevic et al. ([2014](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0003))).

To advance in the presentation along these dimensions, we will continue to assume the same network setup described earlier in this chapter. We will further assume that all primary and secondary links in the network transmit using adaptive modulation and coding (AMC). In AMC, the modulation scheme and channel coding rate are adapted according to the state of the transmission link, usually measured in terms of SINR. Under this assumption, SUs can infer the state of the primary link and maintain their caused interference to the PN below a tolerable threshold (Mohammadi and Kwasinski ([2018](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0013))). When using AMC, from (Qiu and Chawla ([1999](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0015))), the relation between transmit bit rate and the SU threshold SINR is

[(2.15)](#c02.xhtml#c02-R_disp-0015)![equation](images/c02-math-0015.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>R</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mi>W</mi> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mi>k</mi> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>&#946;</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c02-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>k</mi><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is in fact the number of bits per modulation symbol (and thus, in practice, takes only a small number of integer values) and ![images](images/c02-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1.5</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>5</mn><mi>B</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> is a constant that depends on a target maximum transmit bit error rate (BER) requirement. For the underlay DSA scheme, the SUs will perform resource allocation by selecting their target SINRs ![images](images/c02-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#947;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, with the goal of meeting the SINR constraints in Eqs. ([2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0002)) and ([2.1](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0001)). Under the present transmission settings, the selection of ![images](images/c02-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is equivalent to the selection of modulation scheme, channel‐coding rate and ![images](images/c02-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>.

As mentioned earlier, QoE‐based performance assessment is gaining significant attention as we move toward the 5G era. Consequently, we will now use QoE as the network performance metric to assess the quality of the delivered traffic. Among the metrics used to model QoE, we chose MOS because of its popularity and widespread use. Thus, resource allocation will be carried on for all types of traffic using a reward function that is based on average QoE. Since we will concentrate on real‐time video and regular data traffic, we summarize next for this type of traffic how MOS metrics are derived from QoS measurements:

*   **Data MOS model:**
    
    From (Dobrijevic et al. ([2014](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0003))), the MOS ![images](images/c02-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow></math> for data traffic is calculated as
    
    (2.16)![equation](images/c02-math-0016.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>Q</mi> <mi>D</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mn>10</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>b</mi> <msubsup> <mi>R</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mrow> <mi>e</mi> <mn>2</mn> <mi>e</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 
    
    where ![images](images/c02-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c02-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mn>2</mn><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are the data traffic MOS and end‐to‐end packet loss probability, respectively. The parameters ![images](images/c02-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c02-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> are calculated using the maximum and minimum perceived data quality by the end user. If the transmit rate of a user is ![images](images/c02-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and the effective receive rate is also ![images](images/c02-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, the packet loss rate is zero, and the quality perceived by the end‐user when measured in terms of MOS should be maximum (that is, 5). The minimum MOS value of 1 is assigned to the minimum transmission rate. In this chapter ![images](images/c02-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1.3619</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c02-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.6780</mn></mrow></math>.
    
*   **Video MOS model:**
    
    The peak signal‐to‐noise ratio (PSNR) is commonly accepted as an objective video quality assessment metric to measure, for example, coding performance. However, it is known that PSNR does not accurately reflect subjective human perception of video quality (Sheikh et al. ([2006](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0016))). A wide variety of techniques have been proposed to estimate user satisfaction for video applications, among which (Khan et al. ([2007](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0009))) proposed a simple linear mapping between PSNR and MOS, as shown in [Figure 2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0002). The work in (Piamrat et al. ([2009](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0014))) presented the heuristic mappings from PSNR to MOS, as shown in [Table 2.1](#c02.xhtml#c02-tbl-0001), while, according to the recommendation ITU‐R BT.500‐13 (Assembly ([2003](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0001))), the relationship between MOS and an objective measure of picture distortion have a sigmoid shape. Consequently, (Hanhart and Ebrahimi ([2014](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0008))) claimed that if picture distortion is measured with an objective metric, e.g. PSNR (dB), then a logistic function can be used to characterize the relation between MOS and PSNR, as follows:
    
    [(2.17)](#c02.xhtml#c02-R_disp-0017)![equation](images/c02-math-0017.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>Q</mi> <mi>V</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mi>c</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <mi>e</mi> <mi>x</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>P</mi> <mi>S</mi> <mi>N</mi> <mi>R</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 
    
    where ![images](images/c02-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>V</mi></msub></mrow></math> denotes the MOS for video, and ![images](images/c02-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c02-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c02-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> are the parameters of the logistic function. In this chapter, we selected the logistic function to evaluate the quality of video traffic.
    
    To compute the parameters of the logistic function in Eq. ([2.17](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0017)), a set of PSNRs and their corresponding MOS values is needed, while at the same time we would like to relate the PSNR to the bit rate ![images](images/c02-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> so that Eq. ([2.17](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0017)) itself characterizes the video MOS as a function of the QoS variable of bit rate. To first obtain the PSNR‐bit rate function representative of video sequences with different resolutions and levels of activity, we averaged over the PSNR‐bit rate functions for multiple MPEG‐4 coded video sequences at different resolutions (240p, 360p, and 480p), which were combined in the proportions of 39% (240p), 32% (360p), and 28% (480p) so as to follow the mix of resolutions seen in actual traffic (Mobile ([2011](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0012))). The video sequences used were “Flowervase” and “Race Horses,” at 30 frames per second (fps) and resolution 480p, while for resolution 360p, “Tennis” and “Park Scene” at 24 fps were selected. As a result, it was observed that a function of the form ![images](images/c02-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>S</mi><mi>N</mi><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>k</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><msubsup><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> can be used to very closely approximate the average PSNR‐bit rate curve, where ![images](images/c02-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10.4</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c02-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>28.7221</mn></mrow></math> are constants. Next, to obtain the parameters of the logistic function in Eq. ([2.17](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0017)), we computed PSNR values using the PSNR‐bit rate curve for bit rates obtained from Eq. ([2.15](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0015)) for all candidate resource allocation actions. To get the MOS values that correspond to the computed PSNR values, we used the average of the linear mapping in [Figure 2.2](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0002) and the conversion in [Table 2.1](#c02.xhtml#c02-tbl-0001). After obtaining the MOS‐PSNR pairs, the resulting parameters in Eq. ([2.17](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0017)) were ![images](images/c02-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>6.6431</mn></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c02-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>0.1344</mn></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c02-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>30.4264</mn></mrow></math>.
    

In the present case, following the user‐centric approach, each SU will perform resource allocation aimed at maximizing its QoE, measured as MOS for all traffic types. For the reasons discussed earlier, resource allocation is done through a Q‐learning process. However, in order to reduce the convergence time, in this case we will follow a DQN approach instead of table‐based Q‐learning. Nevertheless, as in any Q‐learning process, we first need to design the state space, action space, and the cost or reward function. Because the network setup has not changed from the previous section, the states are still defined as ![images](images/c02-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> following Eqs. ([2.9](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0009)) and ([2.8](#c02.xhtml#c02-disp-0008)). Since the goal now is to maximize MOS, the Q‐learning process is designed with a reward given by

(2.18)![equation](images/c02-math-0018.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mi>M</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mtext>if</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msub> <mi>L</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>&#62;</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <msubsup> <mi>Q</mi> <mi>D</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mtext>or</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msubsup> <mi>Q</mi> <mi>V</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mtext>otherwise</mtext> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c02-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> is a constant smaller than the minimum MOS. As can be seen, the MOS for either video (![images](images/c02-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>V</mi></msub></mrow></math>) or data (![images](images/c02-i0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>D</mi></msub></mrow></math>) traffic is the reward obtained when satisfying the interference constraints, and is sent from the SU receiver to its transmitter through the AMC feedback channel. Finally, for the action space, each SU conducts a search into the finite discrete space of candidate target SINRs, ![images](images/c02-i0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>. At the same time, when choosing one strategy from ![images](images/c02-i0123.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow></math>, each SU adapts its transmit power as well as its modulation and channel coding rate, which, in turn, determines ![images](images/c02-i0124.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>.

![Figure 2.2 MOS versus PSNR.](images/c02f002.jpg)

[Figure 2.2](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0002) MOS versus PSNR.

![ Table 2.1  PSNR to MOS conversion from (Piamrat et al. (2009)).](images/c02-i0109.png)

 [Table 2.1](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-tbl-0001)  PSNR to MOS conversion from (Piamrat et al. ([2009](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0014))).

As previously indicated, in the DQN approach, a function estimator is used to estimate the optimal action‐value function, with a neural network being used as an efficient nonlinear approximator to estimate action‐value function ![images](images/c02-i0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8776;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> (Mnih et al. ([2015](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0011))), where the notation of the bivariate function ![images](images/c02-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> has now been expanded to include the parameters (the internal weights) ![images](images/c02-i0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> of the neural network (which was designed as a fully connected feed‐forward multilayer perceptron \[MLP\] network). Moreover, the design of the DQN includes a technique known as *experience replay* to improve learning performance. In experience replay, at each time step, the experience of each agent with the environment is stored as the tuple ![images](images/c02-i0128.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> into a replay memory ![images](images/c02-i0129.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8230;</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#62;</mo></mrow></math> for the ![images](images/c02-i0130.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th agent. Also, each agent utilizes two separate MLP networks as Q‐function approximators: one as action‐value function approximator ![images](images/c02-i0131.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and another as target action‐value function approximator ![images](images/c02-i0132.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>Q</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. At each time step of DQN learning, the parameters ![images](images/c02-i0133.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> of each agent's action‐value function approximator are updated through a mini‐batch of random samples of experience entries from the replay memory ![images](images/c02-i0134.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> following a gradient descent backpropagation algorithm based on the cost function,

Algorithm 2 summarizes the steps that need to be taken by each SU in order to implement the multi‐agent DQN mechanism. It should be noted that the action selection procedure in Algorithm 2 follows the ![images](images/c02-i0138.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐greedy policy, which means that an action is randomly chosen from the action set ![images](images/c02-i0139.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow></math> with probability ![images](images/c02-i0140.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>; otherwise, an action with the highest action‐value is chosen.

 

## 2.3 Cooperative Learning and Resource Allocation

The cognitive SUs seen in this chapter perform resource allocation after learning about the wireless environment and the rewards/penalties of the different actions by running a Q‐learning algorithm. Whether the algorithm is the Q‐table based or the DQN approach, we can think with a broad perspective that the function of these algorithms is to learn the relation between actions and the wireless environment, a relation that gets represented with more accuracy as the learning algorithm progresses. This relation is represented either as the Q values stored in the Q‐table or as the neural network parameters that characterize the Q function in the DQN. Because part of the wireless environment involves background noise and the interference created by each SU to the rest of the system, the Q‐table or the DQN parameters will reflect both the individual local wireless environment for each SU and the collective interrelation between the system components. It is, therefore, worthwhile to study the differences and similarities between how different SUs represent the relation between actions and the environment.

![](images/c02-gra-0002.png)

For the Q‐table approach to Q‐learning, [Figure 2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0003) shows a comparison between Q‐tables from two SUs as a function of the distance between them. The Q‐tables are compared by calculating the average of the relative difference between elements of Q‐tables corresponding to the same action. The comparison was done over 10,000 runs of the Q‐learning algorithm for a network with 16 SUs, each run corresponding to a different random location of SUs (further network setup details will be presented next). Results are presented in the form of statistical frequency values for the average relative differences. The figure shows the somewhat expected result that Q‐tables become more similar as SUs become closer. For distances less than 100 meters, the probability of Q‐tables differing on average by less than 10% is close to 50%. Even more interesting, the figure shows that even for SUs separated by large distances, the probability of their Q‐tables differing on average by 10% or less is still significant. This is because the Q‐tables incorporate information not only about each SU's local environment, but also about the interaction of all network components.

For the DQN approach to Q‐learning, [Figure 2.4](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0004) compares through the mean squared error (MSE) the DQN parameters ![images](images/c02-i0141.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> of the action‐value function of SUs separated by different distances (we selected one node as a reference SU, and consider different distances by comparing it to the its nearest SU, its second nearest, and its farthest other SU). The comparison was done over 4000 runs of the DQN learning algorithm for a network with 4 SUs, each run corresponding to a different random location of SUs. The statistical frequency of different MSE results in the figure shows that parameters of the Q action‐value function are very similar between nearby SUs, and that the similarity decreases as the distance between SU increases but not to a level that makes the DQNs in two SUs remarkably different.

![Figure 2.3 Differences and similarities between how different SUs represent the relation between actions and the environment: distribution of the average relative difference between Q‐tables of SUs separated by a given distance.](images/c02f003.jpg)

[Figure 2.3](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0003) Differences and similarities between how different SUs represent the relation between actions and the environment: distribution of the average relative difference between Q‐tables of SUs separated by a given distance.

![Figure 2.4 Differences and similarities between how different SUs represent the relation between actions and the environment: distribution of the MSE of the action‐value function parameters images between a first SU and other SUs in a secondary network of four links.](images/c02f004.jpg)

[Figure 2.4](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0004) Differences and similarities between how different SUs represent the relation between actions and the environment: distribution of the MSE of the action‐value function parameters ![images](images/c02-i0142.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#952;</mi></mrow></math> between a first SU and other SUs in a secondary network of four links.

Reflecting on [Figures 2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0003) and [2.4](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0004), it is clear that the sharing of the wireless environment leads the SUs to experience significant similarities in how the learned effect of actions on the environment are represented. In a practical scenario, nodes do not join a network all at the same time. Usually, the network will be initially formed by a few nodes, and then other nodes join at a relatively slow time scale. In the case of a new SU joining an existing SN, it makes sense for the newcomer node to avoid learning from scratch (experiencing the complete convergence time for Q‐learning) and leverage the experience already learned by the nodes that have been active in the network and have encoded this experience as converged Q‐tables. Therefore, [Figures 2.3](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0003) and [2.4](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0004) indicates that learning complexity and the time for Q‐learning to converge can be reduced by collaboratively sharing learned experience between nodes. In the rest of this chapter, we discuss how to realize this idea for the two Q‐learning approaches discussed earlier.

![](images/c02-gra-0003.png)

In the case of table‐based Q‐learning, the exploration of actions by a newcomer SU can be significantly sped up by resorting to the paradigm of *docitive radio* (Giupponi et al. ([2010](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0004))), where the Q‐table is no longer initialized at random, but instead uses the average of the Q‐tables from the other nodes in the network that have already completed their learning process. The implementation of this idea is described in Algorithm 3 (which assumes the availability of a low bit‐rate control channel used by SUs when a newcomer join the network to share the Q‐tables).

[Figures 2.5](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0005) and [2.6](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0006) illustrate the performance of the table‐based Q‐learning algorithm for cross‐layer resource allocation and the performance impact when implementing cooperative learning. The figures compare the results from simulations of three different systems: a system performing joint cross‐layer CR adaptation, called *individual learning*; a system called *docitive* that also performs joint cross‐layer CR adaptation but considers a SU joining the network that learns through the cross‐layer docitive approach implemented in Algorithm 3; and a system identified as *physical layer only*, which is identical to the individual learning system except that it does not implements cross‐layer CR, as it only adapts the transmit bit rate. The simulations, based on the Monte Carlo method, were set up for a system with bandwidth 10MHz and system noise power equal to ‐60 dBm. The PU limited SINR to 10 dB and had a transmit power of 10 dBm. The PU and SUs were placed randomly around their respective base stations within a circle of radius 250 m. Channel gains followed a log‐distance path‐loss model with path‐loss exponent equal to 2.8.
