![Figure 2.5 Average distortion as a function of the number of SUs in the network.](images/c02f005.jpg)

[Figure 2.5](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0005) Average distortion as a function of the number of SUs in the network.

![Figure 2.6 Average number of iterations to achieve convergence (lower plot is a detailed version focused on a small number of iterations).](images/c02f006.jpg)

[Figure 2.6](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0006) Average number of iterations to achieve convergence (lower plot is a detailed version focused on a small number of iterations).

[Figure 2.5](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0005) shows the average distortion that the SUs achieve as a function of the number of SUs in the network. It can be seen how with cross‐layer resource allocation, the average network distortion is significantly reduced when compared to the physical‐layer‐only scheme. Moreover, the cross‐layer approach exhibits an increase in distortion that is smoother than the physical‐layer‐only scheme. [Figure 2.6](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0006) shows the average number of iterations to achieve convergence using table‐based Q‐learning. The result shows first how the implementation of a cross‐layer CR approach, as in the individual learning case, increases the number of iterations necessary to learn compared to the physical‐layer‐only scheme. However, it can also be seen how the cooperative teaching of SUs already in the network allows the initialization of a newcomer SU with such an accurate sharing of experience that the number of iterations needed to achieve convergence is reduced by as much as 30 times (and more than approximately 10 times in all cases). The docitive approach even achieves a number of iterations that is always less than the physical‐layer‐only scheme, even when the latter scheme has an action space 13 times smaller. Even more, because the docitive approach benefits from the knowledge of experienced SUs, the number of iterations actually decreases when the number of SUs in the network increases. Importantly, [Figures 2.5](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0005) and [2.6](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0006) show how cooperation during learning speeds up the learning process without a sacrifice in performance.

![](images/c02-gra-0004.png)

In the case of DQN, cooperative learning when a newcomer SU joins the network takes the form of the well‐known technique in ML called *transfer learning*. Transfer learning refers to the mechanism where what has been learned in one setting is exploited in order to improve the learning process and generalization in another setting (Goodfellow et al. ([2016](#c02.xhtml#c02-bib-0006))). In the present case, transfer learning is realized by having the newcomer SU initialize the parameters of its action‐value function neural network approximator with the same parameters of the nearest node. Note that the technique exposes another advantage of using MOS as performance (and reward) metric because the choice of the node from where to transfer the DQN parameters is based on the distance to the newcomer SU but not based on the traffic type being carried by either node. As such, the common yardstick for all types of traffic presented by MOS allows such a seamless integration of dissimilar traffic that experience can be transferred between nodes even when their traffic type is different. This technique is shown in Algorithm 4.

[Figure 2.7](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0007) illustrates the effect of applying transfer learning to the DQN cognitive engine of a newcomer SU through the results obtained from 500 Monte Carlo simulation runs. The setup for the simulations consisted of a single‐link primary network accessing a single channel. The target SINR for the PU was set at 1 dB. The Gaussian noise power and the transmit power of PU were set to be ‐60 dBm and 10 dBm, respectively. All SUs and PUs were distributed randomly around their respective base stations within a circle of radius 300 m. The distance between the primary base station and the secondary base station was 2 km. Channel gains followed a log‐distance path loss model with path loss exponent equal to 2.8. For a single SU, its target SINR could be chosen from the finite discrete set ![images](images/c02-i0162.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>12</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> dB. Regarding to the learning algorithm, the same learning rate ![images](images/c02-i0163.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow></math> and discounting factor ![images](images/c02-i0164.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow></math> were assumed for all SUs. In the ![images](images/c02-i0165.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐greedy exploration, ![images](images/c02-i0166.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> is initially set to be 0.8, as the number of iteration increases it decreases to a value of 0. As action‐value function and target action‐value function approximators, we used two separate feed‐forward neural networks for each SU. Each neural network was configured with two fully connected hidden layers with three and two neurons. The capacity of replay memory and mini‐patch was set to 100 and 10, respectively. The input layer consisted of three nodes representing the state and the selected action to be taken. The output layer had one neuron.

The simulation results in [Figure 2.7](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0007) compare three resource allocation algorithms in terms of the MOS and the average number of learning steps necessary to achieve convergence. All three algorithms consider the scenario when one newcomer SU joins the network while the rest of the SUs have already finished learning through individually running the DQN algorithm. The three algorithms considered are: *DQN‐Newcomer Individual Learning*, where all SUs perform Algorithm 2 and a newcomer SU initializes its action‐value function parameters randomly; *DQN‐Newcomer Transfer Learning*, which exploits the transfer learning mechanism for the newcomer SU; and *Q‐learning Newcomer Individual Learning*, which implements standard table‐based Q‐learning for all SUs and initializes the Q‐table of new joined SU with zeros. The right side of [Figure 2.7](#c02.xhtml#c02-fig-0007) shows how the DQN approach performs faster learning than the table‐based Q‐learning and how transfer learning accelerates learning in the DQN approach without negative effects on the MOS performance.

![Figure 2.7 (Left): Average MOS in the secondary network. (Right): Average number of learning steps to achieve convergence.](images/c02f007.jpg)

[Figure 2.7](#c02.xhtml#R_c02-fig-0007) (Left): Average MOS in the secondary network. (Right): Average number of learning steps to achieve convergence.

 

## 2.4 Conclusions

In this chapter, we have discussed the use of ML to perform resource allocation in cognitive radio networks. We framed the presentation within a scenario consisting of a number of CRs that establish wireless links by sharing through underlay DSA a portion of the radio spectrum with an incumbent primary network. The chapter focuses on reinforcement learning because it is a machine learning technique that displays the advantages of alignment with the cognition cycle approach, it is flexible for the implementation of cross‐layer resource allocation, and there is no need for prior knowledge of a system model.

We first explained the use of table‐based Q‐learning, a popular implementation of RL, to allocate resources following a cross‐layer approach in a CRN; following this, we noted that if left unaddressed, this approach is at risk of exhibiting long convergence times. We then expanded the presentation in various directions. We explained how a current approach to address the long convergence time in table‐based Q‐learning is to approximate the correspondence of Q‐values (expected rewards) as a function of the actions and environment states variables. The approximation of this Q‐function is done through an artificial neural network called a deep Q‐network. We also explored resource allocation following the tenets in fifth‐generation wireless systems development, which place the end user at the center of design. With this approach, resource allocation is based on the quality of experience as a performance metric. We highlighted that adopting the mean opinion score as a QoE metric enables seamless integration of dissimilar traffic during distributed resource allocation.

In the later part of the chapter, we revisited the question of how to accelerate learning. We noted that in a wireless network, it is rare to see all nodes join the network at the same (initial) moment; instead, nodes enter and leave the network individually at different times. It is then expected that when a node joins a network, it will find other nodes that are already operating and, for CRs, have already gone through the learning process, making them experienced agents. Then, we explained how the learning of CRs that join a network can be accelerated by having those CRs already in the network act as teachers by sharing their experience. This idea takes the form of the described cooperative learning and transfer learning techniques.

Concluding with a broader perspective, we remark that many of the recent developments in CRs leverage significant new advances in ML that are often applied to technical domains that are outside wireless communications. Visible examples are autonomous vehicles, computer vision, and natural language processing. However, the application of these new ML techniques to CRs presents the interest and challenges that are uniquely distinct for the environment in this case, i.e. the wireless network. Particular to a wireless networking environment are how the agents are coupled through the interference they create on each other, and that agents seek to and become able to communicate with each other. Exploring how these unique features of the environment affect ML techniques is where the challenge, potential, and appeal reside for studying the application of ML in this unique environment.

# 3  
Machine Learning for Spectrum Sharing in Millimeter‐Wave Cellular Networks

*Hadi Ghauch¹, Hossein Shokri‐Ghadikolaei², Gabor Fodor³, Carlo Fischione², and Mikael Skoglund⁴*

¹*COMELEC Department, Telecom ParisTech, Paris, France*

²*Division of Network and Systems Engineering, Royal Institute of Technology, KTH, Stockholm, Sweden*

³*Division of Decision and Control Systems, Royal Institute of Technology, KTH, Stockholm, Sweden*

⁴*Division of Information Science and Engineering, Royal Institute of Technology, KTH, Stockholm, Sweden*

 

This chapter is devoted to the use of machine learning (ML) tools to address the spectrum‐sharing problem in cellular networks. The emphasis is on a hybrid approach that combines the traditional model‐based approach with a (ML) data‐driven approach. Taking millimeter‐wave cellular network as an application case, the theoretical analyses and experiments presented in this chapter show that the proposed hybrid approach is a very promising solution in dealing with the key technical aspects of spectrum sharing: the choice of beamforming, the level of information exchange for coordination and association, and the sharing architecture.

This chapter is organized into the following four sections. [Section 3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0002) focuses on motivation and background related to spectrum sharing. [Section 3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0008) presents the system model and problem formulation, the focus of [Section 3.3](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0025) is on all technical aspects of the proposed hybrid approach. Finally, [Section 3.4](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0034) discusses further issues and conclusions.

 

## 3.1 Background and Motivation

 

### 3.1.1 Review of Cellular Network Evolution

The evolution of cellular networks and their enabling technologies is driven by the insatiable demand for mobile broadband and machine‐type communication services. This unprecedented growth in data traffic is fueled by the rapidly increasing number of mobile data subscriptions along with a continuous increase in the average data volume per subscription. On average, more than 1 million new mobile broadband subscribers will be added every day up to the end of 2022, resulting in 8.5 billion mobile broadband subscriptions and 6.2 billion unique mobile subscribers worldwide by 2023 (5G Americas White Paper, [2018](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0001)).

According to Ericsson, overall worldwide data traffic grew by 55% between 2016 and 2017. Data traffic is forecast to grow at a compounded annual rate of 42% from 8.8 exabytes to 71 exabytes between 2016 and 2022, and it is expected that 75% of the worlds mobile data traffic will be video by 2020. In 2017, mobile technologies and services generated 4.5% of the global gross domestic products and will reach 4.6 trillion USD (Ericsson, [2018](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0008)).

To a large extent, this tremendous growth in mobile data traffic has been enabled by the globally harmonized specifications and technologies developed by the Third Generation Partnership Project (3GPP), which has brought together the entire mobile industry and enabled a worldwide ecosystem of infrastructure, devices, and services. Due to this harmonized global ecosystem, the global uptake of long‐Term evolution (LTE) networks by the 3GPP reached a milestone of 3 billion out of the total of 8 billion total cellular connections worldwide at the end of the first quarter of 2018 and will continue to 4 billion by the end of 2019.

As the demand for wireless data traffic in terms of higher subscriber density, higher throughput, and data capacity continues to grow, the research and standardization communities have started to define the enabling technologies for the next generation of wireless and cellular networks: 5G. 5G networks, founded on a new set of physical and higher‐layer specifications commonly referred to as *3GPP new radio* (NR), are designed to meet the demands set by mobile broadband services as well as new vertical markets, including massive machine‐type communications, ultra‐reliable low latency communication, and a broad range of Internet of Things (IoT) applications (Jiang et al., [2018](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0011)).

In terms of enabling technology components, NR incorporates scalable orthogonal frequency division modulation, where transmission time intervals are optimized for wide bandwidths and fast beam‐switching, beam‐steering, and beam‐tracking to focus energy on highly mobile users. These technologies enable directional communications not only to ensure high signal‐to‐noise ratios at the desired users, but to also eliminate undesired signals (interference) at the non‐intended receivers. Indeed, directional three‐dimensional antenna arrays hosting massive multiple‐input and multiple‐output (MIMO) techniques are key to increasing both the coverage and capacity of 5G networks (Fodor et al., [2016](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0009)); these systems have been demonstrated to boost coverage and capacity in diverse spectrum bands, including low‐bands (![images](images/c03-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#60;</mo></mrow></math> 1 GHz), mid‐bands (1 to 6 GHz), and high‐bands (above 30 GHz, millimeter‐wave).

 

### 3.1.2 Millimeter‐Wave and Large‐Scale Antenna Systems

Although 5G research and standards development are underway to achieve the throughput rates of multiple Gbps, radio carriers of at least 1 GHz will be required, according to the ITU. Such bandwidths are typically only available at frequencies above 6 GHz. Thus, high‐frequency spectrum options will be important to 5G, including both centimeter‐wave frequencies of 3–30 GHz and millimeter wave (mmWave) frequencies of 30–300 GHz.

Recognizing the need for exploiting mmWave bands, the World Radio Conference 2015 (WRC‐15) approved the study of 11 high‐band spectrum allocations for WRC‐19. It can be expected that many governments will follow similar polices. For example, the 2016 allocation by the FCC in the United States of 28 GHz, 37 GHz, and 39 GHz licensed spectrum for 5G is the first important high‐band licensed spectrum for 5G in North America (5G Americas White Paper, [2018](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0001)). By means of these technologies, including the 3GPP specifications for 5G NR and capitalizing on mmWave bands, 5G is expected to serve as a unified connectivity platform for future innovation and to embrace the evolving cellular ecosystem of diverse services, devices, deployments, and spectrum.

Large‐scale antenna systems – sometimes referred to as full‐dimension MIMO systems – boost the coverage and capacity of 4G networks deployed in the low‐bands and are key enablers of deploying 5G networks in the mid‐ and high‐bands. Indeed, it is expected that in the mmWave bands, a large number of transmit and receive antennas will be deployed at cellular BSs, which will enable directional communications using very narrow beams. Narrow beams are effective for ensuring proper coverage by boosting the link budget in mmWave bands, and they also minimize interference at unintended receivers.

It is therefore clear that mmWave MIMO – enabling highly directional beamforming – is a critical solution for many operators facing the challenges of meeting increasing traffic demands and serving vertical industries. mmWave MIMO channels are characterized by a small number of eigenmodes (represented by a sparsity in the eigenvalues), a high percentage of blockage/penetration loss, and severe pathloss. *Highly directional communications*, consisting of beamforming and combining at base stations (BS) and user equipment (UE), are a prevalent design, to counteract the severe pathloss attenuation with array gain. Additionally, the large number of BS and UE antennas is made possible by using a reduced number of radio frequency (RF) chains, thus reducing the complexity and power consumption of the system. These ideas gave rise to the so‐called hybrid analog‐digital architecture, where the precoding and combining are performed by separate analog and digital stages (Ardah et al., [2018](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0003)).

 

### 3.1.3 Review of Spectrum Sharing

As discussed, mmWave communications are an essential part of 5G networks, due to their potential to support extremely high data rates and low‐latency services. Although mmWave bands offer a much wider spectrum than the commonly used low‐and mid‐bands, achieving high spectral efficiency and high spectrum utilization by making the best use of licensed and unlicensed spectrum is important due to the large capacity demands and high user densities in many deployment scenarios. Spectrum sharing addresses this goal by allowing multiple service providers and mobile network operators to access the same spectrum band for the same or different sets of services. At the same time, the newly opened bands for 5G services, including the 37 GHz and 57–71 GHz bands, present an opportunity to improve spectrum utilization by sharing valuable spectrum resources.

A precursor to sharing spectrum among multiple mobile network operators is the 3GPP‐defined NR‐based license‐assisted access. It enables the deployment of cellular networks in unlicensed spectrum that co‐exist with non‐3GPP technologies, thereby facilitating spectrum sharing between multiple radio access technologies. However, extending spectrum sharing facilitated by license‐assisted access to sharing even licensed bands opens up new paradigms that are particularly suitable for mmWave deployments exploiting the spatial domain. This new paradigm can be built on the key observation that in mmWave networks, large antenna arrays, directional communications, and the unique propagation environment substantially simplify the problem of managing interference in shared spectrum; see (S. Ghadikolaei et al., [2016](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0015)), (Boccardi et al., [2016](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0006)).

Over‐the‐air demonstrations of 5G NR spectrum‐sharing technologies have already been performed. The use of 5G spectrum sharing technologies is expected to improve the performance of mobile broadband and IoT services using unlicensed and shared mmWave spectrum (Tehrani et al., [2016](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0019)).

The early research reveals that four prominent aspects have a major impact on the performance and feasibility of spectrum‐sharing schemes: the choice of beamforming, the amount of information exchange (coordination), the amount of spectrum shared, and the sharing architecture:

*   Beamforming and directional communications at both the transmitter and the receiver are the key technology enabler of spectrum sharing in mmWave networks. Digital, analog, and hybrid beamforming are key enablers to realize directional communications. The appropriate beamforming technique depends on the required flexibility in beam formation, processing and constraints on power consumption, cost, and channel state information acquisition.
*   The level of coordination among different mobile network operators (inter‐operator coordination) has a substantial influence on the feasibility and effectiveness of spectrum sharing. Without any coordination, spectrum sharing may not even be beneficial, especially in traditional sub‐6 GHz networks. Full coordination may bring substantial performance gains in terms of throughput, especially because it enables complementary techniques such as joint precoding and load balancing. From a technical perspective, the challenge is the high overhead of channel estimation and the complexity in the core networks in a multi‐operator scenario.
*   The amount of spectrum that is shared among the operators is a factor because increasing the bandwidth may improve the achievable capacity by a prelog factor (that is, a factor outside the log function of the achievable data‐rate), but usually reduces the signal‐to‐interference‐plus‐noise ratio, due to higher noise and interference powers. Spectrum sharing is beneficial if the contribution of the prelog factor outweighs the resulting SINR reduction.
*   The supporting architecture is another aspect that affects the performance of spectrum sharing. Infrastructure sharing is an example of an architecture that increases the gain of spectrum sharing. In general, the trade‐off between performance gain and protocol overhead determines whether spectrum sharing is beneficial. Reference (Boccardi et al., [2016](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0006)) discusses various supporting architectures for spectrum sharing in mmWave networks, including interfaces at the radio access networks and at the core network.

 

### 3.1.4 Model‐Based vs. Data‐Driven Approaches

Although the problem of spectrum sharing in millimeter‐wave MIMO cellular networks is well‐motivated, it is essentially open due to the signaling and computational complexities. Indeed, similar problems such as coordination in cellular networks and multi‐cell beamforming have been traditionally addressed using *model‐based approaches*. However, these approaches always suffer from elevated signaling and computational complexity, thereby hindering their implementation in practical cellular networks. We will show in [Section 3.2.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0020) that the problem considered here is intractable using these model‐based approaches.

Although model‐based approaches serve as the foundations of communication systems (Tse and Viswanath, [2005](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0020)), the simplified models and multiple approximations often required for the mathematical tractability may lead to protocols that do not work well in practice (Ghadikolaei et al., [2018](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0010)). On the other hand, data‐driven approaches address this disadvantage by learning and optimizing from the data – usually acquired by measurements – and making minimal assumptions about the system model. These approaches, however, may need a large number of training samples to perform well, which are not available in most wireless networks due to their time variations (Sevakula et al., [2015](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0017)).

Recognizing the strengths and limitations of model‐based and data‐driven approaches, in this chapter we present the use of a hybrid approach, in which the *model‐based component* operates on a small time scale, while the *data‐driven component* operates on a coarser time scale and refines the models used in the model‐based part. We apply this approach to the important (but complicated‐to‐solve) problem of spectrum sharing in a multi‐operator cellular network. As seen in this chapter, the paradigm of hybrid (model‐based and data‐driven) approaches is applicable to a plethora of problems in the area of ML for wireless communication. We note that a similar conclusion was put forth by Recht ([2018](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0014)), namely that a hybrid approach may still give many of the benefits of a pure model‐based approach in the area of optimal control.

## 3.2 System Model and Problem Formulation

The model presented here is generic and embraces distinct model elements for the network, the association scheme, the antenna and channel models, and models for beamforming and coordination.

 

### 3.2.1 Models

 

#### 3.2.1.1 Network Model

We consider a general multi‐user, multi‐cell, multi‐operator network. The network consists of ![images](images/c03-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Z</mi></mrow></math> operators, each operating a (sub)set ![images](images/c03-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> B</mi></mrow><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></math> of the BSs in the network, where it is assumed that each BS belongs to an operator, and no BS is shared among operators. The set of all UEs is denoted by ![images](images/c03-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c03-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the set of all UEs of operator ![images](images/c03-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math>. Finally, we let ![images](images/c03-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> be the total bandwidth available in the network and ![images](images/c03-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></math> be that of operator ![images](images/c03-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math>. We further assume universal frequency reuse.

 

#### 3.2.1.2 Association Model

We let ![images](images/c03-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> model that UE ![images](images/c03-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow></math> is served by (or associated with) BS ![images](images/c03-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> B</mi></mrow></math>. Moreover, we denote by ![images](images/c03-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></math> the ![images](images/c03-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> B</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></math> the *binary association matrix* of operator ![images](images/c03-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math>, namely, ![images](images/c03-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> if ![images](images/c03-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c03-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. We also define the aggregate association matrix ![images](images/c03-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> as ![images](images/c03-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>Z</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></math>. We assume that no national roaming is allowed, i.e. each BS servers UEs of one operator; see (S. Ghadikolaei et al., [2018](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0016)), where this assumption is relaxed. For simplicity, let us define ![images](images/c03-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> F</mi></mrow><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math> as the set of feasible assignments for ![images](images/c03-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>. Simply stated, ![images](images/c03-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> F</mi></mrow><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math> encodes constraints that each UE is associated with a single BS (since no joint transmission is assumed), that each BS is serving no more than ![images](images/c03-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></math> users simultaneously (for the sake of load balancing), and that the UEs of operator ![images](images/c03-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math> can be only served by BSs of the same operator, thereby preventing national roaming.

An association period is defined as a succession of *coherence intervals (CIs)* during which the association matrix is essentially constant; see [Figure 3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0001). In that sense, we assume that association is done over a longer time period (many CIs) compared to beamforming, which has to be done during each CI. Such an assumption is natural due to the high overhead incurred by reassociation. After finding the optimal ![images](images/c03-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></math> for each operator, each BS and UE recalculates its beamforming vectors every CI. To simplify the presentation, we further assume that each BS can simultaneously serve all of its associated users (in multi‐user MIMO fashion).

 

#### 3.2.1.3 Antenna and Channel Model

Each BS (resp. UE) is equipped with ![images](images/c03-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>BS</mtext></msub></mrow></math> (resp. ![images](images/c03-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>UE</mtext></msub></mrow></math>) antennas, assumed to be uniform linear arrays for simplicity. The ![images](images/c03-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>UE</mtext></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>BS</mtext></msub></mrow></math> MIMO channel between BS ![images](images/c03-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and UE ![images](images/c03-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> is denoted as ![images](images/c03-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. #### 3.2.1.4 Beamforming and Coordination Models

 

##### *Analog Combiners*

We assume that each UE has a single RF chain, where combiners at the UE consist of phase shifters only. This design is commonly used in mmWave literature due to its simple implementation. Letting ![images](images/c03-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow><mi>u</mi><mtext>UE</mtext></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>UE</mtext></msub></mrow></msup></mrow></math> denote the combining vector of UE ![images](images/c03-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>, each combiner is designed to maximize the link budget (Ayach et al., [2012](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0004)) to its serving BS. Formally, ![images](images/c03-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow><mi>u</mi><mtext>UE</mtext></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mtext>UE</mtext></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#952;</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi><msup><mi>n</mi><mo>&#9733;</mo></msup></mrow><mtext>UE</mtext></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c03-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mo>&#9733;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mi><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>g</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></math>, i.e. the combiner is matched to the receive array response having the highest path gain. Evidently, this design assumes that channel gains and angles of arrival (AoAs) are available at each UE.

 

##### *Precoders*

We assume that each BS uses fully digital precoding, without loss of generality. Furthermore, the UEs associated with each BS are simultaneously served with multi‐user MIMO. Moreover, we employ *regularized zero‐forcing (RZF)* precoding, as it directly minimizes intra‐BS interference (within and among different operators).[1](#c03a.xhtml#c03-note-0001) Let ![images](images/c03-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow><mtext>BS</mtext></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>BS</mtext></msub></mrow></msup></mrow></math> be the precoding vector that BS ![images](images/c03-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> uses for user ![images](images/c03-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>. Using RZF, the precoding vector of UE ![images](images/c03-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> is

(3.1)![equation](images/c03-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>b</mi> <mi>u</mi> </mrow> <mtext>BS</mtext> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>&#955;</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>b</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <msub> <mrow> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>b</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#948;</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mo>&#8224;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>u</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mn>0</mn> <mo>&#60;</mo> <mi>&#948;</mi> <mo>&#8810;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c03-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the effective channel for BS ![images](images/c03-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> (see [Section 3.2.1.5](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0018)), and ![images](images/c03-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></math> is a normalization to satisfy a maximum transmit power at each BS. The assumption of fully digital precoding is in no way limiting. The precoding method presented here can be applied to the co‐called hybrid analog‐digital architecture, prevalent in mmWave literature; see (S. Ghadikolaei et al., [2018](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0016)).

 

#### 3.2.1.5 Coordination Model

Given the precoding/combining method, we let ![images](images/c03-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mi>u</mi><mtext>UE</mtext></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mi mathvariant="sans-serif">H</mi></msup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> be the effective channel between BS ![images](images/c03-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> B</mi></mrow></math> and UE ![images](images/c03-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>, i.e. a cascade of the actual channel, ![images](images/c03-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, and the combiner, ![images](images/c03-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow><mi>u</mi><mtext>UE</mtext></msubsup></mrow></math> (not to be confused with ![images](images/c03-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></math>). We let ![images](images/c03-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> B</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> be the *binary coordination matrix*, where ![images](images/c03-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> denotes BS ![images](images/c03-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> B</mi></mrow></math> estimating the effective channel ![images](images/c03-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. We define the effective channel ![images](images/c03-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi><mrow><msub><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mi>u</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>BS</mtext></msub></mrow></msup></mrow></math> as a matrix whose rows correspond to the effective channels ![images](images/c03-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> for ![images](images/c03-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8739;</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>. In this, ![images](images/c03-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> (resp. ![images](images/c03-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>) denotes the index of the serving (resp. coordinating) BS.

Note that acquiring this effective channel incurs a lower cost when two BSs belong to the same operator than when they belong to different operators. In view of modeling this asymmetry in the usage of the network resources and promoting an efficient use of the backhaul, we include a penalty (cost) for coordination. More specifically, we let ![images](images/c03-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> denote the penalty/cost of BS ![images](images/c03-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> estimating the (effective) channel of UE ![images](images/c03-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>, corresponding to element ![images](images/c03-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> of the coordination matrix. To keep the exposition simple, we consider hereafter a constant penalty matrix ![images](images/c03-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math>, i.e. having equal entries. In practice, however, the penalty should be a function of distance, operator load, number of antennas, and operators (reflecting various billing policies), etc.; see [Section 3.3.3.3](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0033) for specific instantiations of the penalty matrix.

Note that ![images](images/c03-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math> will depend on ![images](images/c03-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>, since the cost of coordination depends on assignment of UEs to BSs. We express this dependence in general form (concrete choices are discussed in [Section 3.3.3.3](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0033)),

where ![images](images/c03-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is affine in its argument. Ultimately, we aim to find an optimal coordination policy, i.e. one that maximizes the sum‐rate of the network while satisfying the coordination budget.

 

### 3.2.2 Problem Formulation

Here, we first show that a pure model‐based approach to optimize beamforming/ combining, association, and coordination is computationally intractable, using the models developed in [Section 3.2](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0008). Moreover, after reformulating the problem as a multi‐armed bandit, we highlight the massive signaling overhead of a pure data‐driven method.

![Figure 3.2 An example topology with two operators, gray and black. BSs and UEs are marked by squares and circles, respectively. Black lines show association. Gray lines show coordination.](images/c03f002.jpg)

[Figure 3.2](#c03.xhtml#R_c03-fig-0002) An example topology with two operators, gray and black. BSs and UEs are marked by squares and circles, respectively. Black lines show association. Gray lines show coordination.

 

#### 3.2.2.1 Rate Models

The SINR of each UE in the network is a function of the desired signal from its serving BS, ![images](images/c03-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow><mtext>Rx</mtext></msubsup></mrow></math>; intra‐cell interference, ![images](images/c03-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> (signals transmitted to other UEs by the same BS); inter‐cell interference, ![images](images/c03-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>I</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> (interference from the signals transmitted by other BSs of the same network operator); inter‐operator interference, ![images](images/c03-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> (interference from the signals transmitted by all BSs of other operators toward their own UEs); and noise power spectral density. We will skip over the exact expressions and refer the reader to (S. Ghadikolaei et al., [2018](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0016)).

With that in mind, the average rate achieved by UE ![images](images/c03-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>,

where the expectation is over all random channel gains. Moreover, the assignment variable are taken from the feasible set, i.e. ![images](images/c03-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> F</mi></mrow><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

 

### 3.2.3 Model‐based Approach

Here we present a (pure) model‐based approach to the spectrum sharing. When the association and coordination matrices are given, each BS estimates the effective channel to its UEs, computes the precoding and combining vectors (see [Section 3.2.1.4](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0014)), and computes the average rate for each of the UEs it is serving from Eq. ([3.4](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0005)). A cloud server (logical controller) collects ![images](images/c03-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> from all the BSs, computes the coordination cost per CI from Eq. ([3.3](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0003)), and evaluates a network utility ![images](images/c03-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> for operator ![images](images/c03-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi></mrow></math>. While Eq. ([3.5b](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0007)) denotes the feasible set for ![images](images/c03-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c03-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mrow></math>, constraint Eq. ([3.5d](#c03.xhtml#c03-disp-0009)) ensures that the coordination cost does not exceed a maximum budget predetermined as ![images](images/c03-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>z</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> for each operator.

In the following, we discuss why a direct solution of ![images](images/c03-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> P</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> would be infeasible with the signaling and time limitations of the current radio access and core networks. Solving ![images](images/c03-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> P</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> implies that each BS in the network sends (or receives) pilot signals to each UE in the network (including other operators) and exchanges a huge amount of information with a central controller, which then proceeds to solve ![images](images/c03-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> P</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math>. Moreover, the complexity and signaling overhead grows with the number of BSs and UEs, and becomes overwhelming for mmWave networks with dense BS deployment. Additionally, there is the large burden of *inter‐operator signaling* to compute ![images](images/c03-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>. Furthermore, *channel aging* may render the exchanged information outdated before it serves its purpose. This is particularly problematic for mmWave channels due to their inherently low coherence time. While earlier approaches dealt with these issues by neglecting interference and assuming noise‐limited systems, recent works have shown that a few links may observe strong interference (Park and Gopalakrishnan, [2009](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0012)). These limitations have hindered the application of optimal spectrum sharing to wireless systems. Nonetheless, the solution of ![images](images/c03-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> P</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> is interesting since it gives a theoretical upper bound for the performance of spectrum sharing (a *benchmark*).

 

### 3.2.4 Data‐driven Approach

*Data‐driven approaches* are attractive because they do not need the models to be accurate reflections of the corresponding physical processes. We refer the reader to (S. Ghadikolaei et al., [2018](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0016)), where the authors reformulate the spectrum‐sharing problem using the MAB framework. In particular, an *agent* (decision maker) explores an unknown *environment* by taking different *actions* (each action corresponding to a choice of the beamforming vectors, association, and coordination) and observes the corresponding *rewards* (the sum‐rate). The aim is to find the optimal set of actions that maximizes the collected reward; see Appendix A.1 for an overview of reinforcement learning.

While this purely data‐driven approach offers the distinct advantage of relying on minimal assumptions regarding the model, it is practically infeasible due to the huge dimensions of the action space (which grows exponentially with ![images](images/c03-i0156.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c03-i0157.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mrow></math>, and the number of choices of precoding/combining vectors), as well as the time constraints on the network. More specifically, the number of pilots for CSI acquisition should be limited to a few per CI, which is much lower than what is needed to efficiently run a multi‐armed bandit; see (S. Ghadikolaei et al., [2018](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0016)).

 

## 3.3 Hybrid Solution Approach

We have argued so far regarding the practical limitations of a purely model‐based approach (i.e. a direct solution to ![images](images/c03-i0158.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> P</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math>), due to the massive complexity, signaling overhead, and lack of CSI. On the other hand, the curse of dimensionality prevents the pure data‐driven approach from finding the optimal coordination and association decisions given the limited time available for the learning task. In the proposed hybrid approach, the learning task continuously refines the rate model of every UE rather than optimizing the decision variables. The model‐based part then uses the updated rate models to find the optimal association and coordination strategies.

![Figure 3.4 Overview of the hybrid solution. Channel estimation and precoding/combining are used to update the rate measurements (per CI). These measurements are in turn used to update the rate models during each training frame.](images/c03f004.jpg)

[Figure 3.4](#c03.xhtml#R_c03-fig-0004) Overview of the hybrid solution. Channel estimation and precoding/combining are used to update the rate measurements (per CI). These measurements are in turn used to update the rate models during each training frame.

The so‐called hybrid approach consists of two frame types: training and operation frames designed to balance the trade‐off between exploration and exploitation. During a *training frame*, the BSs and UEs use a randomized policy to explore the space of feasible solutions for ![images](images/c03-i0159.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and improve the rate models (see [Section 3.3.2.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0028)). During an *operation frame*, the operators apply a previously found good solution to protect the UE's performance from potential degradation due to a candidate ![images](images/c03-i0160.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. The solutions are only updated after passing a predefined confidence bound on their rate performance, measured over several training frames; see the illustration in [Figure 3.4](#c03.xhtml#c03-fig-0004).

 

### 3.3.1 Data‐Driven Component

Developing an efficient solution for ![images](images/c03-i0161.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> P</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> is challenging. First, the lack of closed‐form solutions implies that iterative approaches are needed: the objective function must be evaluated for several values of associations/coordination matrix, until convergence. This results in sending additional pilots to evaluate the updated combining vectors at the UEs and estimate some new channels. These additional pilot transmissions and channel estimations can be very expensive, as we may need many iterations until convergence, and we may end up estimating almost all the channels; clearly this is impractical in a mmWave cellular network. Moreover, only parts of ![images](images/c03-i0162.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c03-i0163.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> for which the respective entry of ![images](images/c03-i0164.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mrow></math> is 1 can be computed. Consequently, the cloud is not able compute either ![images](images/c03-i0165.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> nor ![images](images/c03-i0166.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, and therefore the objective function.

The *data‐driven component* of the hybrid solution takes as input the network topology (i.e. location/number of BSs and UEs, ![images](images/c03-i0167.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>BS</mtext></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c03-i0168.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>UE</mtext></msub></mrow></math>, etc.), the association matrix ![images](images/c03-i0169.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>, the coordination matrix ![images](images/c03-i0170.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mrow></math>, and the effective channels ![images](images/c03-i0171.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and outputs an approximation of the rate of UE ![images](images/c03-i0172.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math>, denoted by ![images](images/c03-i0173.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>u</mi></msub></mrow></math>. More specifically, it consists of a dataset and a learning method. The entries of the dataset are ![images](images/c03-i0174.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></math>,![images](images/c03-i0175.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and the learning method approximates the rate function. The dataset is maintained at at the cloud and updated before/after each training frame; see [Section 3.3.3.1](#c03.xhtml#c03-sec-0031).

BS ![images](images/c03-i0176.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> measures ![images](images/c03-i0177.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>u</mi></msub></mrow></math> for each of its associated UEs, during each CI, via feedback from the UEs of its rate in this CI. These values are collected at BS ![images](images/c03-i0178.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> and reported to the cloud before each training frame. The dataset and the mapping, ![images](images/c03-i0179.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> for all ![images](images/c03-i0180.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow></math>, are updated at the cloud, and the next tuple ![images](images/c03-i0181.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> to be tested in the following training frame is computed (using the EXPLORE function in Algorithm 1). Then, the cloud updates the dataset and the rate models, and subsequently decides whether the new association and coordination solutions should be applied in subsequent operation frames. The cloud server then gradually updates these models with any new entry in the dataset through the UPDATE procedure. The other functions of this algorithm available to all operators are outlined in Algorithm 1, as follows.

![](images/c03-gra-0001.png) 

### 3.3.2 Model‐Based Component

Given the updated rate models, the cloud formulates a variant of ![images](images/c03-i0182.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> P</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and finds the new association and coordination solutions. Here we state the optimization problem and outline the solution method.

Every operator proceeds to approximate the rate of its UEs (via the DOWNLOAD function in Algorithm 1) and constructs an approximation of ![images](images/c03-i0183.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, denoted by ![images](images/c03-i0184.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>z</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c03-i0185.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>z</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>u</mi></msub></mrow></math>. The modified optimization problem is written as

(3.6a)![equation](images/c03-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtable columnalign="left"><mtr><mtd/><mtd><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="-2.27621pt"/><mo>:</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mspace width="-3.69885pt"/><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mrow></munder><munderover><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>Z</mi></munderover><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>z</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd><mspace width="3em"/><mtext>s.t.&#160;</mtext><mtext>Eq</mtext><mo>.</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3.5</mn><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mtext>Eq</mtext><mo>.</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3.5</mn><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mtext>Eq</mtext><mo>.</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>3.5</mn><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math> 

Note that solving ![images](images/c03-i0186.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is quite complex, since ![images](images/c03-i0187.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></math> generally is not jointly convex in ![images](images/c03-i0188.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c03-i0189.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mrow></math>, and the feasible set is combinatorial. To circumvent such limitations, we leverage the block‐coordinate descent (BCD) framework (also known as *alternating optimization*). The BCD method (Razaviyayn et al., [2013](#c03a.xhtml#c03-bib-0013)) consists of splitting ![images](images/c03-i0190.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> P</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> into two subproblems (steps) that are iteratively updated. In the A‐step, ![images](images/c03-i0191.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> is optimized for a given/known ![images](images/c03-i0192.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mrow></math> matrix. Then, in the C‐step, ![images](images/c03-i0193.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mrow></math> is optimized for a given/known ![images](images/c03-i0194.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> matrix. Letting ![images](images/c03-i0195.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c03-i0196.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> be the values for ![images](images/c03-i0197.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c03-i0198.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi></mrow></math> at iteration ![images](images/c03-i0199.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, the two steps are formalized as

(A‐step)

![equation](images/c03-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtable columnalign="left"><mtr><mtd/><mtd><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><munder><mtext>argmax</mtext><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> F</mi></mrow><mi>A</mi></msub></mrow></munder><munderover><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>Z</mi></munderover><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>z</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="2.22198pt"/><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd><mspace stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow><mi>z</mi></msub></mrow></munder><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mi>z</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msubsup><mspace width="2.22198pt"/><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mo>&#8704;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>Z</mi><mspace width="2.22198pt"/><mo>,</mo></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math> 

(C‐step)

![equation](images/c03-math-0012.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtable columnalign="left"><mtr><mtd/><mtd><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><munder><mtext>argmax</mtext><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">C</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> B</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>Z</mi></munderover><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>z</mi></msub><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>z</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mrow><mo
