As shown in Ide et al. ([2016](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0016)), RSRP and RSRQ can be exploited for deriving estimations for the SINR if the modem does not explicitly report this indicator. The resulting transmission probability is shown in [Figure 8.4](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0004).

 

### 8.2.2 Groundwork: Predictive CAT

While the immediate channel properties of single measurements are highly dynamic in the mobile scenario, their behaviors often follow a general trend as the distance to the respective base station is either decreasing or increasing. Therefore, if the current channel quality decreases, it will likely decrease further in the near future before it will increase again, e.g. due to a cellular handover. In order to pay attention to this phenomenon, CAT was extended to pCAT by introducing a *temporal lookahead* ![images](images/c08-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> in order to proactively detect low channel‐quality periods. The extended transmissions scheme sends data early if it expects the channel quality to decrease and late if the channel quality is anticipated to improve. The prediction is based on the previous measurements that have been performed on the same track.

![Figure 8.3 Example comparison of straightforward periodic data transfer and SINR‐based CAT.](images/c08f003.jpg)

[Figure 8.3](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0003) Example comparison of straightforward periodic data transfer and SINR‐based CAT.

The resulting transmission probability for pCAT is shown in [Figure 8.5](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0005). It can be observed that pCAT formally meets the defined tasks: transmissions are delayed if the channel quality is expected to improve and performed early if a decrease is anticipated. Further results of empirical evaluations are described in Pillmann et al. ([2017](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0020)).

### 8.2.3 ML‐based CAT

Due to the highly dynamic channel characteristics, the channel properties are likely changing during ongoing transmissions. Therefore, the meaningfulness of the channel assessment is limited, especially for larger packet sizes. Moreover, even for high channel coherence times, the resulting data rate is impacted by transport‐layer interdependencies such as the slow start of the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP). Although the complexity of these factors exceeds the limits of analytical system descriptions, ML is able to uncover the hidden interdependencies between the different types of context information. Apart from the SINR, LTE offers further network quality indicators such as RSRP, RSRQ, and CQI that can be used to achieve a better channel quality assessment. Therefore, CAT can be extended to ML‐CAT, which uses ML‐based data‐rate prediction as a transmission metric.

In the first step, the probabilistic transmission scheme of CAT is generalized, as for CAT and pCAT the metric calculation is implicitly normed to the value range of the SINR. Therefore, an abstract metric ![images](images/c08-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi></mrow></math> is introduced, for which the value range is specified with defined values for ![images](images/c08-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mrow><mi>min</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c08-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mrow><mi>max</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Each measured value ![images](images/c08-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is converted in a *normed current metric* ![images](images/c08-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> with

(8.6)![equation](images/c08-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="left"> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mi>min</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mi>max</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mi>min</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

The resulting transmission probability ![images](images/c08-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is then computed as

(8.7)![equation](images/c08-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="right"> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mo>:</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mi>min</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mi>&#945;</mi> </msup> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mo>:</mo> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mi>min</mi> </msub> <mo>&#60;</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#60;</mo> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mi>max</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mo>:</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#62;</mo> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mi>max</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd/> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

The performance of different ML models for uplink data‐rate prediction in vehicular scenarios is further analyzed in Sliwa et al. ([2018b](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0028)). The analysis shows that for all considered models, the M5 regression tree is able provide the highest prediction accuracy while still being able to be implemented in a very resource‐efficient manner for online execution on embedded devices.

Based on these observations, the processing pipeline for the context information is derived in [Figure 8.6](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0006). The prediction features are the channel context parameters RSRP, RSRQ, SINR, and CQI. Further information is added by the current vehicle speed and the payload size of the data packet. During the training phase, the resulting data rate of active transmission provides the label for the prediction.

[Figure 8.7](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0007) shows an example of the temporal behavior of the proposed data‐rate prediction mechanism in a real‐world evaluation. It can be seen that the payload size has a severe impact on the overall performance, as the anticipated data rate significantly decreases after each transmission, which clears the current transmission buffer. For low payload sizes, the slow start of TCP has a dominant impact; for very high payload sizes, the channel dynamics become the major influence on overall behavior.

![Figure 8.6 Learning pipeline for M5‐based data‐rate prediction using different types of context parameters.](images/c08f006.jpg)

[Figure 8.6](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0006) Learning pipeline for M5‐based data‐rate prediction using different types of context parameters.

![Figure 8.7 Example temporal behavior of the uplink data‐rate prediction of a real‐world drive test.](images/c08f007.jpg)

[Figure 8.7](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0007) Example temporal behavior of the uplink data‐rate prediction of a real‐world drive test.

The resulting prediction accuracy for suburban and highway scenarios is shown in [Figure 8.8](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0008). It can be observed that although both tracks have different velocity statistics, the prediction itself shows a similar behavior. It should be noted that, from an application perspective, prediction failures in the upper‐left triangle region – referred to as *underestimations* – are not problematic for the considered use case as the end‐to‐end data rate is even higher than anticipated.

Although the focus of this work is on using ML‐based data‐rate prediction as a metric, the abstract definition of ![images](images/c08-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#920;</mi></mrow></math> allows the extension of ML‐CAT for flexible use of other metrics as well, e.g. directly using the passive downlink indicators for scheduling the transmission decision. Furthermore, it enables the transfer of the proposed method to different communication technologies, e.g. for IEEE 802.11p‐based vehicle‐to‐infrastructure communication (Sliwa et al. ([2018d](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0030))).

[Figure 8.9](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0009) shows the trained and pruned M5 regression tree used for the data‐rate prediction. Since it only consists of threshold decisions and a small number of linear regression models, it can be implemented in a very resource‐efficient manner using a sequence of `if/else`‐statements and executed in real time.

![Figure 8.8 Performance of M5 regression tree data‐rate predictions on real‐world measurement data.](images/c08f008.jpg)

[Figure 8.8](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0008) Performance of M5 regression tree data‐rate predictions on real‐world measurement data.

![Figure 8.9 Trained and pruned M5 regression tree model for data‐rate prediction, consisting of seven linear regression models.](images/c08f009.jpg)

[Figure 8.9](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0009) Trained and pruned M5 regression tree model for data‐rate prediction, consisting of seven linear regression models.

 

### 8.2.4 ML‐based pCAT

Finally, ML‐pCAT brings together the ideas of pCAT and ML‐CAT for context‐predictive and ML‐based sensor data transmission.

A blueprint for the composition and implementation of the different components is illustrated by the architecture model in [Figure 8.10](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0010) In order to allow the estimation of the future channel context for all considered network quality indicators, all vehicles manage a *multi‐layer connectivity map* that stores aggregated information of previous indicator measurements in a cellular structure. Based on the measured mobility context parameters, vehicles derive their future location by *mobility prediction*. The estimated future channel context is then derived as a lookup operation for the predicted cell within the connectivity map. In Sliwa et al. ([2018a](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0027)), different methods for predicting future vehicle locations and their effects on the accuracy of the obtained context information from connectivity maps are discussed in detail. In the following evaluations, only the trajectory‐aware mobility prediction approach is applied, as it is able to provide precise and turn‐robust predictions.

While the connectivity map can be generated in a decentralized manner by using only measurements of the respective UE, the approach highly benefits from large‐scale, crowdsensing‐based map generation. A reasonable approach for data synchronization would be to use a non‐cellular data connection whenever it is available.

[Figure 8.11](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0011) shows an example excerpt of the derived connectivity map within the overall evaluation scenario. Although the different indicators characterize larger road segments similarly, intensity and variance are significantly different. The transmission probability relies on the metric abstraction from [Section 8.2.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-sec-0008) and is calculated as

## 8.3 Methodology for Real‐World Performance Evaluation

In this section, the methodological setup for the real‐world performance evaluation is presented. Furthermore, the process for the power consumption analysis is described.

 

### 8.3.1 Evaluation Scenario

The measurements are performed with off‐the‐self Android‐based UE, which executes the CAT application and performs the online ML‐based data‐rate prediction. Further information about the framework has been published in Sliwa et al. ([2018c](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0029)). A virtual sensor application generates a fixed amount of sensor data per second, which is stored in a local buffer. The probabilistic transmission schemes assess the channel each ![images](images/c08-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> and compute a transmission probability for the whole buffer. All raw measurements (Sliwa ([2018](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0025))) and the developed measurement application are provided in an open source way (available at [https://github.com/BenSliwa/MTCApp](https://github.com/BenSliwa/MTCApp)). In total, the data set consists of more than 7500 transmissions, which were performed within a driving range of more than 2000 km.

The transmission schemes are evaluated in a real‐world scenario using the public cellular network infrastructure. [Figure 8.11](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0011) shows a map of the evaluation scenario. Drive tests are performed on different track types (suburban and highway) with different velocity characteristics.

[Table 8.1](#c08.xhtml#c08-tbl-0001) shows the parameters of the considered evaluation scenario. ![images](images/c08-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mtext>SINR</mtext></msub></mrow></math> represents the transmission metrics of CAT and pCAT. ![images](images/c08-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mtext>ML</mtext></msub></mrow></math> is applied for ML‐CAT and ML‐pCAT. The required information for the creation of the connectivity map is based on the data obtained from the experiments in Sliwa et al. ([2018b](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0028)).

 

### 8.3.2 Power Consumption Analysis

Apart from transmission efficiency, which is represented by the achieved data rate in the following section, the changed transmission behavior is likely having a severe impact on energy efficiency. While the communication‐related battery drain is nearly negligible for cars, it has a crucial impact on the flight‐time potential of small‐scale aerial vehicles. As these types of vehicles are becoming more and more integrated into road traffic scenarios (Menouar et al. ([2017](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0019))), the application of CAT‐based data transfer for UAV‐based data provisioning is a promising option for increasing the possible flight time.

![ Table 8.1  Parameters of the evaluation scenario.](images/c08-i0025.png)

 [Table 8.1](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-tbl-0001)  Parameters of the evaluation scenario.

Measuring the impact of data transmissions on power consumption of a mobile device is a nontrivial task, as it involves the isolation of the running process from the rest of the system. For evaluating the energy efficiency of the considered transmission schemes, we therefore rely on a sequential process that is executed in a post‐processing step:

*   **ML‐based estimation of transmission power**: The model of Falkenberg et al. ([2018](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0013)) is utilized to predict the applied value of ![images](images/c08-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>X</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> for each performed transmission from the passive downlink indicators, analogously to the process described in [Section 8.2.3](#c08.xhtml#c08-sec-0008). As ![images](images/c08-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>X</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> has a strong correlation with the distance to the base station, the RSRP provides a meaningful indicator for the learning process.
*   **Determination of device‐specific characteristics**: The relationship between ![images](images/c08-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>X</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and the actual power consumption is highly specific for the UE and depends on its different power amplifiers. Therefore, this dependency is captured by controlled variation of ![images](images/c08-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>T</mi><mi>X</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in a laboratory environment (Falkenberg et al. ([2017b](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0012))).
*   **Model‐based analysis**: Finally, the state‐based context‐aware power consumption model (CoPoMo) (Dusza et al. ([2013](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0008))) is applied to compute the average power consumption of the UE with respect to the different possible transmission states.

 

## 8.4 Results of the Real‐World Performance Evaluation

In this section, the results of the empirical performance evaluation are presented and discussed. First, the behavior of the measured network quality indicators is discussed. Afterward, the results of the considered transmissions schemes are analyzed, and finally, an overall summary is provided.

 

### 8.4.1 Statistical Properties of the Network Quality Indicators

[Figure 8.12](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0012) shows the statistical distributions of the measured channel context parameters during the real‐world measurements. It can be observed that the reported values have different dynamics and allow the derivation of different conclusions about the channel quality. The RSRP has a clear Gaussian distribution around the center value of 90 dBm. For the RSRQ, higher values are more frequently reported than lower values. The empirical results of the channel quality indicator (CQI) show a peak for the amount of CQI reports for the value 2. Since this indicator is not standardized, its definition and implementation are specified by the modem manufacturer. Therefore, it can be assumed that the CQI is less significant than the other indicators, which is confirmed by the small CQI coefficients shown in [Figure 8.9](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0009).

 

### 8.4.2 Comparison of the Transmission Schemes

[Figure 8.13](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0013) shows the resulting data rate for the different considered transmission schemes. Three characteristic areas can be identified: periodic data transfer, SINR‐based approaches, and ML approaches. The lowest data rate is achieved by the straightforward approach, which sends the data periodically, regardless of the channel conditions. With the opportunistic approach, SINR‐based schemes CAT and pCAT are able to increase the data rate significantly. The probabilistic and channel‐aware method is applied for exploiting channel‐quality knowledge.

Finally, the highest values are achieved by the ML‐based transmission schemes ML‐CAT and ML‐pCAT. The predicted data rate provides a better metric for channel quality assessment than pure SINR measurements. In particular, the integration of the payload size information allows the implicit consideration of hidden interdependencies of the network quality indicators in their significance for different channel coherence times. For both variants, additional benefits are achieved by the context‐lookahead of the pCAT approach.

![Figure 8.12 Statistics of real‐world measurements for the considered channel context parameters.](images/c08f012.jpg)

[Figure 8.12](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0012) Statistics of real‐world measurements for the considered channel context parameters.

![Figure 8.13 Comparison of the resulting data rate for the considered transmission schemes.](images/c08f013.jpg)

[Figure 8.13](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0013) Comparison of the resulting data rate for the considered transmission schemes.

The empirical cumulative distribution function (ECDF) for the age of the sensor information contained in the transmitted packets is shown in [Figure 8.14](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0014). As expected, the curve of the periodic approach is very steep due to the fixed interval. Rare deviations from the mean are related to scheduling effects and the need for data retransmissions and cellular handovers. For pCAT, the average age of information is even lower as transmissions are performed more frequently. As the vehicle moves forward on its trajectory, the channel lookahead ![images](images/c08-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> behaves like a moving window. This behavior is intensified by the dynamics of the SINR metric, resulting in a high probability of experiencing SINR‐peaks during the transmission evaluation.

![Figure 8.14 Comparison of the resulting age of information for the considered transmission schemes.](images/c08f014.jpg)

[Figure 8.14](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0014) Comparison of the resulting age of information for the considered transmission schemes.

Although generally, ML‐pCAT is equal to pCAT with a different channel assessment metric, their behaviors show significant differences for the data age. The M5 tree‐based prediction is far less dynamic than the SINR assessment (c.f. [Figure 8.7](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0007)). Therefore, it is less influenced by short‐term influences (e.g. multipath propagation) that only have a minor significance in the considered scenario, as the vehicle will likely have moved to a different location when the transmission has been initialized. Since the payload size has a severe impact on the achievable data rate, the ML‐based approach waits longer until a minimum transmission buffer size is achieved. CAT and ML‐CAT, which only rely on the current channel quality measurements, show a similar behavior.

The impact of the optimized transmission behavior on the power consumption of the mobile device is shown in [Figure 8.15](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0015). Here, a similar behavior as for the data‐rate evaluations can be observed. The energy efficiency benefits from the improved transmission behavior in multiple ways. As transmissions are performed during better channel‐quality periods, less transmission power needs to be applied in order to deliver the data, which is the most dominant factor for overall power consumption (Dusza et al. ([2013](#c08.xhtml#c08-bib-0008))). In addition, as the transmissions are performed with higher data rates, the transmission duration itself is reduced, and the modem is able to stay in the `IDLE` state for longer time periods. As a result, ML‐CAT reduces the average power consumption of the UE by 49.51 % and ML‐pCAT by 58.29 %.

 

### 8.4.3 Summary

[Figure 8.16](#c08.xhtml#c08-fig-0016) summarizes the key results of the considered transmission schemes in the domain's data rate, energy efficiency, and data freshness. Overall, it can be seen that there is a trade‐off among gains in data rate, power consumption, and additional buffering delay. The flexible definition of the proposed scheme allows its behavior to be configured with respect to application requirements.

The great benefit of using ML for assessing channel quality in comparison to traditional approaches (e.g. SINR measurements) is the implicit consideration of hidden effects that have a strong influence on the overall behavior but are too complicated to be covered by a closed analytical description. As the proposed approach integrates the payload size and the velocity of the vehicle into the data‐rate prediction, it implicitly considers payload versus overhead ratio, slow start of TCP, and the dependency on the channel coherence time.

![Figure 8.15 Comparison of the resulting power consumption efficiency for the considered transmission schemes.](images/c08f015.jpg)

[Figure 8.15](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0015) Comparison of the resulting power consumption efficiency for the considered transmission schemes.

 

## 8.5 Conclusion

In this chapter, we presented a ML‐based approach for anticipatory data transmission for using mobile sensor nodes. Since the spectrum resources are highly limited and the medium is shared between different cell users, the overall goal is to improve transmission efficiency by freeing occupied resources as early as possible.

The presented ML‐pCAT approach relies on context‐predictive data transmission and the exploitation of favorable channel conditions in order to boost the resulting transmission efficiency. Through anticipatory and opportunistic data transfer, the existing network is utilized in a more efficient way for both individual UE and the network as a whole. As a side effect, the average power consumption of the UE is significantly reduced, which increases the operation lifetime of the mobile device.

The presented approach also shows how communication engineering and ML can benefit from each other to achieve better results. While the foundation of the proposed transmission scheme relies on analytical modeling and exploitation of expert knowledge, the integration of ML allows the consideration of hidden interdependencies between the variables, which are too complex to be described in an analytical way.

![Figure 8.16 Summarizing comparison of the considered transmission schemes in the domain's data rate, energy efficiency, and data freshness. The scales for sensor data age and power consumption are inverted such that a large footprint means better performance.](images/c08f016.jpg)

[Figure 8.16](#c08.xhtml#R_c08-fig-0016) Summarizing comparison of the considered transmission schemes in the domain's data rate, energy efficiency, and data freshness. The scales for sensor data age and power consumption are inverted such that a large footprint means better performance.

In future work, we will investigate the applicability of ML‐pCAT for multi‐interface communication with heterogeneous network technologies. In addition, the data‐rate prediction will be improved by considering information about the cell load obtained from passive probing of the LTE control channels.

#  Part II  
Transmission Intelligence and Adaptive Baseband Processing

# 9  
Machine Learning–Based Adaptive Modulation and Coding Design

*Lin Zhang¹, and Zhiqiang Wu²*

¹*School of Electronics and Information Technology, Sun Yat‐sen University, Guangzhou, China*

²*Department of Electrical Engineering, Wright State University, Dayton, Ohio, USA*

 

## 9.1 Introduction and Motivation

Adaptive modulation and coding (AMC) technologies have been widely used in wired and wireless communication systems in order to adapt to the variations of channel conditions. AMC schemes can help communication systems to achieve higher spectrum efficiency and a better trade‐off between data rate and reliability via adjusting the modulation order and/or coding rate according to real‐time channel conditions. Since wireless channels are usually more dramatically time‐variant than wired channels, most standards for wireless communication, such as the Wi‐Fi standards IEEE 802.11n and IEEE 802.11ac, propose to employ AMC for improving spectrum efficiency in order to meet user demands. In order to further improve spectrum efficiency and reliability, AMC schemes have been combined with multiple‐input and multiple‐output (MIMO) and orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM). Owing to the enhanced reliability, these AMC‐aided systems allow reduced overhead and latency, while meeting the upper‐layer demand for real‐time transmissions.

However, due to the complicated operational scenarios and time‐varying nature of wireless channels, in wireless communication systems such as IEEE 802.11n‐based wireless networks, the physical layer configuration/link adaptation is difficult to implement in practice. Consequently, optimal physical layer configurations have rarely been achieved in practice (Iera et al., [2005](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0008); Daniels et al., [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0007)), making the AMC schemes not well adapted to the channel's states, and thereby yielding performance degradation.

In addition, when AMC schemes are combined with MIMO and OFDM, modeling the joint effect of OFDM modulation, convolutional coding, and MIMO processing is highly challenging due to the following issues. First, in a practical system, there are various imperfections, such as nonlinear distortion of power amplifiers, quantization error of the analog‐digital converters (ADCs), and non‐Gaussian additive noise. In this case, accurate modeling of a complete telecommunication system is difficult. Second, in the design of communication systems, it is the convention to split the signal processing into multiple independent blocks, with each executing a specific and isolated function. Consequently, jointly optimizing these components leads to computationally complex systems (OShea and Hoydis, [2017](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0019)). For the reasons as above‐mentioned, existing AMC implementations are either inaccurate due to the model‐based approximations or cumbersome due to the large‐size lookup tables (Peng et al., [2007](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0021); Jensen et al., [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0009)). Therefore, in order to save the computation expense as well as to avoid making impractical approximations, such as the Gaussian approximation of non‐Gaussian distributions, a concise approach is desired to enable AMC schemes to be operated with mathematical models that need as few assumptions as possible.

On the other side, machine learning (ML), or “the programming of computers to optimize a performance criterion using example data” (Alpaydin, [2009](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0003)), has the potential to jointly optimize the rigid modular blocks using a unified nonlinear framework. Hence, it may serve as a good candidate for the optimization of AMC‐aided wireless systems having specific hardware configurations, when communicating over wireless channels.

Based on these considerations, in this chapter, we apply ML techniques to AMC‐aided wireless systems to allow them to adapt to the variations of channels. We introduce and analyze two types of ML‐assisted AMC schemes in the context of the MIMO and OFDM scenarios, where the conflicting demands for high date rate and high reliability are met by adjusting the modulation order and coding rate. Specifically, a supervised learning approach and a reinforcement learning approach are considered.

Here we first provide an overview of the ML‐assisted AMC.

 

### 9.1.1 Overview of ML‐Assisted AMC

Supervised learning (SL) approaches have the following advantages to facilitate their applications in AMC. First, during the operation of the communication network, training data can be collected online for updating the dataset. Second, there are abundant training datasets, including cyclic redundancy checks (CRCs), channel state information (CSI), the associated modulation and coding scheme (MCS), etc. These data can be used to update the training set for learning AMC in a specific wireless network, or be reused for training in other networks via transfer learning (Pan et al., [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0020)). Lastly, non‐ideal operations that are often approximated or neglected in the model‐based approach, such as nonlinear amplifications and finite resolutions in the analog circuit components (Daniels et al., [2008](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006)), are welcomed by the SL techniques when performing link adaptation, thanks to the black box approach.

One drawback of the SL approaches is that the sample data obtained can hardly represent accurately all the situations that signals may experience, including time‐varying wireless channel conditions, nonlinear behavior of the amplifier, non‐Gaussian distributed noises and interference, etc. (Leite et al., [2012](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0014)). Hence, SL approaches may be infeasible for online learning, where the feature set could be inconstant and collecting large number of training examples could be impractical.

By contrast, reinforcement learning (RL) and Markov decision process (MDP) methods are able to directly learn from the environment, which thus provides solutions for the online learning required by communication systems. Unlike SL approaches, which learn from examples given by external supervisors, RL methods have the capability to learn online. Recently, (Jiang et al., [2017](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0010)) has introduced RL to the field of wireless communications (Jiang et al., [2017](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0010)). In (Leite et al., [2012](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0014)), a Q‐learning‐based framework has been proposed for selecting the best MCS at a given signal‐to‐noise ratio (SNR). In (Melián‐Gutiérrez et al., [2015](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0016)), the authors have proposed an algorithm based on a hybrid hidden Markov decision and upper confidence bound (UCB), which is used to optimize the performance of secondary users in cognitive radios. However, a main drawback of using this technique in AMC is that the interacting time with the environment might be too long for it to select the preferable MCS. This is explicitly undesirable for operation in time‐variant wireless channels. In order to mitigate this problem, some offline training may be required.

As we know, ML‐assisted AMC has so far mainly been implemented in the context of SL or RL. Although unsupervised learning, like principal component analysis (PCA), has been used in (Daniels et al., [2008](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006)) to reduce the feature dimensions, its final decision is still accomplished with the aid of the ![images](images/c09-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐nearest neighbor(![images](images/c09-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN) algorithm, which is a SL method. The reason is that unsupervised learning is mainly suitable for data preprocessing, but not suitable for decision‐making, such as in AMC.

Considering SL, the most widely used learning algorithms include support vector machines (SVMs), decision trees, ![images](images/c09-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN, neural networks, and so on. All these algorithms require labeled data. They can all be operated as classifiers after appropriate training. Therefore, without loss of generality, in the following sections, we will only consider ![images](images/c09-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN and SVM as our two examples, in order to show the applications of SL in AMC. For RL, we will address Q‐learning, since it has been widely investigated in literature (Venkatraman et al., [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0025); Oksanen et al., [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0018); Leite et al., [2012](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0014)).

In the following sections, we will first present the principles of both SL‐assisted and RL‐assisted AMC. Then the performance of the AMC schemes is investigated. In our investigation, the specifications and parameters defined in the IEEE 802.11n standards are used. Note that IEEE 802.11n is the underlying protocol of the Wi‐Fi Alliance, which is the first Wi‐Fi protocol to support MIMO‐OFDM transmissions.

The rest of this chapter is organized as follows. [Section 9.1.2](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0003) provides a brief overview of the AMC schemes specified in the IEEE 802.11n, and gives details of the modulation types and coding rates used in the standards. Then, [Section 9.2](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0004) is devoted to SL‐assisted AMC, where both the ![images](images/c09-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN and SVM approaches are considered. In [Section 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0014), the RL‐ and MDP‐based AMC schemes are addressed. Corresponding simulation results and analyses are provided at the end of [Section 9.2](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0004) and [Section 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0014), respectively. The last section of this chapter provides some further discussion and observations.

 

### 9.1.2 MCS Schemes Specified by IEEE 802.11n

In this subsection, we briefly introduce the MCS schemes specified by the IEEE 802.11n standards. Part of the MCS specifications are shown in [Table 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0001), where ![images](images/c09-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>MCS</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> indicates the ![images](images/c09-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> MCS, and Nss represents the number of spatial streams that may be transmitted simultaneously via the corresponding air interfaces of IEEE 801.11n transceivers. As shown in [Table 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0001), the modulation types include binary phase shift keying (BPSK) and quadrature phase shift keying (QPSK), which transmit, respectively, one bit and two bits per symbol by modulating information using two phase states and four phase states. The 16 quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) and 64QAM transmit respectively 4 bits and 6 bits per symbol, with the aid of 16 constellation points and 64 constellation points uniformly distributed on the corresponding constellation maps. In [Table 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0001), the ratio of the number of information bits and the number of coded bits input to modulate is defined as the *coding rate*. The modulation level and coding rate determine the data rate of the system, expressed as the number of bits per second (bps).

![ Table 9.1  List of modulation images coding schemes defined in IEEE 802.11n.](images/c09-i0006.png)

 [Table 9.1](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-tbl-0001)  List of modulation ![images](images/c09-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#38;</mi></mrow></math> coding schemes defined in IEEE 802.11n.

Note that, in the IEEE 802.11n standards, MCSs are indexed from 0–31, corresponding to different MCSs and hence different data rates. In [Table 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0001), we only list the parameters of the MCSs with indexes from 0–15. Explicitly, the data rate achieved by these MCSs ranges from 6.5–130 Mbps. In general, when a higher order of modulation type and/or higher coding rate are employed, and/or two spatial streams instead of one are employed, the system can achieve a higher date rate.

Therefore, in practice, when a wireless channel is time‐variant, the system may adapt to the corresponding communications situation by employing an appropriate MCS via activating a corresponding MCS index, in order to attain the best possible trade‐off between data rate and reliability. However, identifying a near‐optimum MCS in responding to time‐varying wireless channels is not an easy task. In the following sections, we will introduce a range of AMC schemes based on the SL and RL methods.

 

## 9.2 SL‐Assisted AMC

In the principle of ML, a SL algorithm aided by some training data generates an inferred function, which is thereby used for mapping new examples. In SL, labeled training data are constituted by a set of training examples, each of which contains an input object and its desired output value. The set of training examples is used to produce an inferred function.

Naturally, it is expected that the class of labels can be correctly determined for the unknown instances by the learning algorithm. Hence, it is required that the learning algorithm is able to adapt to unknown situations by using the training data intelligently and reasonably. In supervised ML, the most widely used learning algorithms include SVM, decision trees, the ![images](images/c09-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm, neural networks, and so on. Here, we will consider ![images](images/c09-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN and SVM as two examples to illustrate their applications in AMC schemes.

 

### 9.2.1 ![images](images/c09-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN‐Assisted AMC

With the objective to maximize throughput under the constraint of a given packet error rate (PER), the link adaptation relying on AMC is required to measure a specific feature set in order to determine the near‐optimal AMC parameters – the modulation order and coding rate – as defined in [Table 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0001). In literature, PER has often been selected as the performance metric to determine an MCS index (Kant et al., [2007](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0011)), which may be formulated as:

[(9.1)](#c09.xhtml#c09-R_disp-0001)![equation](images/c09-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">argmax</mi> <mi>i</mi> </munder> <mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo> <msub> <mi>R</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>:</mo> <mi>P</mi> <mi>E</mi> <msub> <mi>R</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>P</mi> <mi>E</mi> <msub> <mi>R</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mi>g</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c09-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></math> represents the near‐optimal MCS index identified by solving this optimization problem, and the index ![images](images/c09-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> corresponding to ![images](images/c09-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>MCS</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is defined by the IEEE 802.11n standards as shown in [Table 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0001). ![images](images/c09-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the throughput when ![images](images/c09-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>MCS</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is used, ![images](images/c09-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>PER</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the corresponding PER, and ![images](images/c09-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>E</mi><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>target</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the constraint on PER. Therefore, if ![images](images/c09-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>E</mi><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the largest PER that is less than or equal to ![images](images/c09-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>E</mi><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> for a given channel realization, then ![images](images/c09-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>MCS</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is selected for data transmission.

When ![images](images/c09-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN‐assisted AMC is considered, the previous optimization problem is transformed into a classification problem, which is then solved using the ![images](images/c09-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm (Daniels et al., [2008](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006); YİĞİT and Kavak, [2013](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0028)). Note that ![images](images/c09-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN is a non‐parametric SL algorithm that can be used for both classification and regression, which is detailed as follows.

 

#### 9.2.1.1 Algorithm for ![images](images/c09-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN‐Assisted AMC

From the previous discussion, we know that AMC in wireless communication is a typical classification problem. In order to fulfill the classification for a desired MCS, the feature set for training should be extracted first. We assume that there are ![images](images/c09-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> distinct realizations in the training set, expressed as ![images](images/c09-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> W</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mi>W</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>. Then, after the training of the ![images](images/c09-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN system, each realization ![images](images/c09-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> W</mi></mrow></math> is assigned to a class, i.e. a MCS, ![images](images/c09-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> I</mi></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c09-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> I</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mi>I</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> by solving the problem of Eq. ([9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0001)).

To be more explicit, let ![images](images/c09-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>&#969;</mi></msub></mrow></math> represent the feature set obtained from training, using the realization of ![images](images/c09-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> W</mi></mrow></math> that can be expressed as

(9.2)![equation](images/c09-math-0002.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>z</mi> <mi>&#969;</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8658;</mo> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mi>&#969;</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c09-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mspace width="0.1em"/><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mi>&#969;</mi></mfenced></mrow></math> is the class ![images](images/c09-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>MCS</mtext><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> obtained from the realization of ![images](images/c09-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#969;</mi></mrow></math>. Thus, after training, a mapping table between the feature set and its corresponding MCSs can be obtained. With the aid of this table, once a new ![images](images/c09-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>&#969;</mi></msub></mrow></math>, corresponding to a communication situation, is observed, the ![images](images/c09-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm can determine a corresponding MCS scheme to achieve AMC transmission. It is worth pointing out that in practical AMC classification applications, the ![images](images/c09-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm has been improved to enhance training efficiency in (Daniels et al., [2008](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006)).

Algorithm 1 summarizes the ![images](images/c09-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm for AMC by using a feature query ![images](images/c09-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow></math>. In this algorithm, ![images](images/c09-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> nearest neighbors ![images](images/c09-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></math> ![images](images/c09-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are listed first. Then, the classes that occur most often among ![images](images/c09-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> are selected. Finally, the class having the smallest ![images](images/c09-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, which leads to the lowest throughput ![images](images/c09-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is chosen, in order to guarantee the required PER.

![](images/c09-gra-0001.png)

As an example, [Figure 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0001) illustrates the ![images](images/c09-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm for AMC, where ![images](images/c09-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> is assumed. According to Algorithm 1, the first five nearest neighbors are identified, as shown by the five points together with their labels inside the circle in [Figure 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0001). Then, the classes that occur most often among the feature query ![images](images/c09-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi></mrow></math> are identified. In this example, the query is represented by the black‐filled square. As shown by the classes in the circle, there are two neighbors with ![images](images/c09-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>MCS</mtext><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> (![images](images/c09-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>), two neighbors with ![images](images/c09-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>MCS</mtext><mn>8</mn></msub></mrow></math> (![images](images/c09-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math>), and one neighbor with ![images](images/c09-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>MCS</mtext><mn>4</mn></msub></mrow></math> (![images](images/c09-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>). Hence, the selected classes are ![images](images/c09-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c09-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math>. Finally, the class indexed by the smallest ![images](images/c09-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is chosen, which fields the smallest throughput ![images](images/c09-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> to guarantee the required PER. In this specific example, the throughput ![images](images/c09-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mn>8</mn></msub></mrow></math>, as shown in [Table 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0001), but this is not necessarily true.

![Figure 9.1 Illustration of MCS class selection in a 5‐NN algorithm.](images/c09f001.jpg)

[Figure 9.1](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0001) Illustration of MCS class selection in a 5‐NN algorithm.

Additionally, as shown in [Table 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0001), there are classes ![images](images/c09-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, but the throughput ![images](images/c09-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. In this case, although classes ![images](images/c09-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> are selected from the first step, class ![images](images/c09-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is chosen as the last. In other words, given a selected class set ![images](images/c09-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>, the final class selected is the class generating the lowest throughput. This is because the lowest throughput yields the highest reliability. Therefore, the previous selection rule could guarantee the required reliability.

 

### 9.2.2 Performance Analysis of ![images](images/c09-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN‐Assisted AMC System

In the MIMO‐OFDM‐based IEEE 802.11n wireless systems (Daniels et al., [2008](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006); YİĞİT and Kavak, [2013](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0028)) with ![images](images/c09-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> transmit antennas and ![images](images/c09-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> receive antennas, after the discrete Fourier transform (DFT), the signal received from the ![images](images/c09-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> ![images](images/c09-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> subcarrier can be represented as:

(9.3)![equation](images/c09-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msqrt> <mrow> <msub> <mi>E</mi> <mi>s</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msqrt> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c09-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> is the DFT size and also the number of subcarriers; ![images](images/c09-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the transmit symbol vector; ![images](images/c09-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi>C</mi><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the additive complex Gaussian noise vector, with each element having a zero mean and a variance of ![images](images/c09-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>; ![images](images/c09-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> represents the ![images](images/c09-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> channel matrix of the ![images](images/c09-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> subcarrier; and ![images](images/c09-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> represents the expected total received signal energy. Therefore, we have ![images](images/c09-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> ![images](images/c09-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>.

In the performance analysis, we assume that the wireless channel ![images](images/c09-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> undergoes quasi‐static block fading, meaning the channel states remain constant across all OFDM symbols within one packet, but are independent for different packets. In addition to this assumption, the following assumptions (Daniels et al., [2008](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006)) are also employed in our analysis:

*   *Fixed packet length*: All packets are set to 128 bytes. Hence, for a given bit error rate, all packets have the same expected PER.
*   *Perfect synchronization*: All packets are synchronized perfectly in both the time domain and frequency domain. Therefore, any time and frequency offsets can be ignored.
*   *Estimation*: Unlike (Daniels et al., [2008](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006)), we assume that the noise power and channels estimation are estimated at receivers. Corresponding to IEEE 802.11n, legacy long training field (L‐LTF) symbols are used to estimate the noise power, while the high‐throughput long training field (HT‐LTF) is used to estimate the channel state.
*   *Linear equalization*: A linear zero‐forcing (ZF) equalizer is employed at the receiver to combat inter‐symbol interference (ISI).

As described in Algorithm 1, the feature set is required to be extracted first, and is then used to calculate the distances between the input query and the data in the training set so that we can determine the ![images](images/c09-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐nearest neighbors. More explicitly, for the considered MIMO‐OFDM AMC system, specifically at the receiver, after post‐processing, a link quality metric (LQM) to describe the performance of the link can be evaluated based on ![images](images/c09-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c09-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c09-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>. This LQM is regarded as the feature set extracted from ![images](images/c09-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c09-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c09-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>.

Specifically, when the ZF post‐processing is employed, for each of the spatial streams of ![images](images/c09-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c09-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the number of spatial streams and ![images](images/c09-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> (Daniels et al., [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0007)), the SNR of subcarrier ![images](images/c09-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> is given by (YİĞİT and Kavak, [2013](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0028)):

[(9.4)](#c09.xhtml#c09-R_disp-0004)![equation](images/c09-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>a</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>n</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mi>E</mi> <mi>s</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <munderover> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msup> <mi>a</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>s</mi> </msub> </mrow> </munderover> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">G</mi> <mrow> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>F</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>a</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>a</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c09-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">G</mi><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>H</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>H</mi></msubsup></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c09-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mo>&#183;</mo></mfenced></mrow><mo>&#8224;</mo></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c09-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mo>&#183;</mo></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> denote the pseudo‐inverse Hermitian transpose and inverse operation, respectively. Note that the SNR dimension for each subcarrier is equal to its spatial stream number.

According to Eq. ([9.4](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0004)), for each subcarrier, we can obtain a feature query from the SNR of each spatial stream. However, as described in (Daniels et al., [2008](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006)), a clear‐implementation MIMO‐OFDM AMC methodology is highly desired. In order to simplify the AMC system, in the following analysis, each packet will only produce one feature query instead of producing a feature query for each subcarrier. Moreover, each subcarrier of a packet will also apply the same MCS according to the feature query. In the following, we will discuss situations for frequency‐flat fading and frequency‐selective fading, since the way to extract a feature query from a packet is different for these two fading channels.

For transmissions over frequency‐flat fading channels, all subcarriers share the same channel state. Therefore, post‐processing SNR averaged over all subcarriers is available as the feature query. Then we can obtain a one‐dimensional feature set for MCS 0‐7 with one spatial stream and a two‐dimensional feature set for MCS 8‐15 with two spatial steams, according to Eq. ([9.4](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0004)). Since there are two feature sets with different dimensions, we perform Algorithm 1 in each feature set. Once we obtain the suggested MCS for each feature set, the MCS with the highest rate is selected.

However, for transmissions over frequency‐selective fading channels, average post‐processing SNR cannot effectively reflect the variations of channel conditions, which are uniquely determined by the channel matrix, signal energy, and noise variance. In this case, the feature space of the training set might include ![images](images/c09-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c09-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c09-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>, which leads to a higher feature space dimension. On the other hand, due to the curse of dimensionality in SL, dimensions on order of ![images](images/c09-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> require exceedingly large training sets even for typical values of ![images](images/c09-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c09-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c09-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>.

In order to reduce the dimension of the feature space, a subcarrier ordering method is proposed in (Daniels et al., [2008](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0006)). In this method, under the assumption that subcarrier position does not affect total packet performance, the packet performance can be determined by analysis of the per‐subcarrier post‐processing SNR distribution. According to this method, define ![images](images/c09-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>N</mi><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> as the post‐processing SNR for the spatial stream ![images](images/c09-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> for the subcarrier ![images](images/c09-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c09-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the number of the data‐bearing subcarrier and ![images](images/c09-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>52</mn></mrow></math> for 20MHz channel bandwidth. All of the SNRs can compose a SNR set, which is expressed as:

(9.5)![equation](images/c09-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mrow> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <msubsup> <mrow> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>S</mi> <mi>N</mi> <msubsup> <mi>R</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mrow> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>F</mi> </mrow> </msubsup> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mi>n</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>a</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>s</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </msubsup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Then define ![images](images/c09-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>N</mi><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#951;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> to be the ![images](images/c09-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math>th smallest element in the set, where ![images](images/c09-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>. Inspired by empirical observations in IEEE 802.11n channels, this method proposes that ![images](images/c09-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mi>N</mi><msubsup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#951;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>Z</mi><mi>F</mi></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> for a few values of ![images](images/c09-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math> often determines packet performance and can work as the feature query. In order to obtain appropriate values of ![images](images/c09-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow></math>, extensive computer searches are utilized, and a four‐dimension feature query with ![images](images/c09-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>26</mn></mrow></math> is discovered to be necessary for MCS 0‐7 and MCS 8‐15‐based IEEE 802.11n systems over frequency selective fading channels, which are given by:

(9.6)![equation](images/c09-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold">q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>S</mi> <mi>N</mi> <msubsup> <mi>R</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>F</mi> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mi>N</mi> <msubsup> <mi>R</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>F</mi> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mi>N</mi> <msubsup> <mi>R</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>6</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>F</mi> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mi>N</mi> <msubsup> <mi>R</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>26</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>F</mi> </mrow> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Finally, Algorithm 1 is performed in the feature set consisting of these four‐dimension feature queries and the suggested MCS is selected.

 

### 9.2.3 SVM‐Assisted AMC

The ![images](images/c09-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN‐assisted AMC can effectively help the system to adapt to channel variations and enhance system performance. However, similar to other conventional SL algorithms, this method cannot explicitly construct class boundaries. Additionally, the ![images](images/c09-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN method has high computational complexity and requires a large offline database for training, which prevents its efficient use in AMC.

To elaborate a bit further, the conventional methods use an offline database with the PER subjected to different fixed‐channel realizations. However, the offline database is usually too large to implement online AMC. Thus we have to collect the training data in an online way instead of constructing an offline database. Since a large amount of PER data for each channel should be collected to decrease the variance of the PER and improve the accuracy of the estimation, how to reduce the required PER training data has attracted a lot of research interest. A good representative in this direction is an online AMC scheme proposed in (Daniels and Heath, [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0004)), which could achieve a fast AMC by using a support vector machine as given in the following subsections.

 

#### 9.2.3.1 SVM Algorithm

The SVM‐aided algorithm uses a single measurement of the frame like the success/failure and the measurements of current channel states to train SVM classifiers (Daniels and Heath, [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0004)). Compared with other fast online AMC algorithms based on the nearest neighbor classification (Daniels and Heath, [2009](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0005)), the SVM‐based fast online AMC algorithm can achieve the same performance with fewer excessive memory and processing requirements.
