In addition, the researchers have presented that the SVM‐based fast online AMC algorithm has much lower complexity than the nearest neighborhood classification–based online AMC algorithm. Moreover, the SVM‐based fast online AMC algorithm has further been improved to enhance performance, like using kernel functions to construct the nonlinear boundary, selecting appropriate training set and feature set to balance performance and the complexity, and so on.

In this subsection, we discuss how to apply the SVM to learn channel condition variations, with the aim to provide a reliable solution for fast AMC (Xu and Lu, [2006](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0027); Yun and Caramanis, [2009](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0029)). For building binary online AMC classifiers, SVM can significantly discriminate complex nonlinear class region boundaries with lower complexity than many other SL algorithms, including the neural network‐based ones. Moreover, the implementation of SVM also alleviates the issues of optimization, overfitting, and interpretation (Daniels and Heath, [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0004)), which benefit from the dual representations of SVM.

The SVM algorithm maximizes the margin between different classes in the training set, and also places the label ![images](images/c09-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> on the feature set realizations according to the distance from different margin boundaries of each class. That is to say, the SVM constructs the maximum margin classifier to determine the class region of each feature set. When we apply SVM for AMC, the class regions correspond to the success or failure of transmissions. Namely, they represent whether frame decoding at the receiver is successful or not. Usually, success/failure classes are denoted by ![images](images/c09-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c09-i0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, respectively. For the feature set realization ![images](images/c09-i0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>p</mi></msup></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c09-i0123.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> is the dimension of the feature vector and ![images](images/c09-i0124.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math> is the set of real numbers, the margin of SVM is defined by the inference function ![images](images/c09-i0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c09-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math> can be defined as a linear discriminant vector for training, ![images](images/c09-i0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the SVM feature transformation performing on the feature set to generate the SVM feature set, and ![images](images/c09-i0128.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is denoted as the margin bias.

Then the result of the inference function acts as the input to the discriminant function ![images](images/c09-i0129.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, which is the compound function of ![images](images/c09-i0130.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> defined as ![images](images/c09-i0131.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> when ![images](images/c09-i0132.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c09-i0133.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> when ![images](images/c09-i0134.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. Each SVM provides the binary classification, so ![images](images/c09-i0135.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> SVMs are needed to distinguish ![images](images/c09-i0136.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> modulation and coding scheme classes. The classifiers are defined as one‐versus‐none classifiers (Daniels and Heath, [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0004)). The ![images](images/c09-i0137.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>th classifier is used to select the appropriate one among the class ![images](images/c09-i0138.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>. When the PER constraint ![images](images/c09-i0139.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>PER</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> is not met, where ![images](images/c09-i0140.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi></mrow></math> is the threshold of PER, no class is selected. When a frame encoded with MCS ![images](images/c09-i0141.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is chosen by the classifier as a successful transmission, the classifier is reinforced to choose MCS ![images](images/c09-i0142.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>. Otherwise, when a frame transmission is considered a failure transmission, the classifier is reinforced to choose no MCS classes. Thus, the appropriate MCS for the frame transmission can be selected from ![images](images/c09-i0143.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> MCS classes after applying the ![images](images/c09-i0144.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> one‐versus‐none classifiers.

As a matter of fact, one‐versus‐none classification cannot address the PER constraint. In order to fit in with the change of PER of training sets, the training data from training sets are equally weighted. The discriminant functions with PER regression are replaced with regression functions and are respectively set with different MCS classes so as to calculate the posterior probability of each class. Then the regression functions are set as ![images](images/c09-i0145.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, which differs depending on ![images](images/c09-i0146.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>.

Therefore, the SVM‐based algorithm used for online AMC to classify different feature‐set realizations ![images](images/c09-i0147.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> with a two‐stage classifier framework – one‐versus‐none classifiers and regression functions – can be defined as follows (Daniels and Heath, [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0004)):

1.  Compute ![images](images/c09-i0148.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> according to the training data.
2.  Compute ![images](images/c09-i0149.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> according to ![images](images/c09-i0150.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and the training data.
3.  Map ![images](images/c09-i0151.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![images](images/c09-i0152.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>.
4.  Find the optimized ![images](images/c09-i0153.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">arg&#160;min</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>.
5.  If the number of appropriate ![images](images/c09-i0154.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></math> is equal to 1, ![images](images/c09-i0155.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>&#8592;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">arg&#160;min</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.
6.  If the best ![images](images/c09-i0156.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></math> is not found, randomly choose one.

where ![images](images/c09-i0157.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the time consumed to transmit the data bits with MCS ![images](images/c09-i0158.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>. Steps 5 and 6 guarantee that only one optimal ![images](images/c09-i0159.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>m</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></math> is chosen for the transmission. Steps 3–6 are used to find the most appropriate MCS for an unknown channel realization. It can be concluded from Step 4 that ![images](images/c09-i0160.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> also provides an estimate of ![images](images/c09-i0161.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>PER</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. It is worth pointing out that there is no need to complete steps 1–2 for each new frame observation since regression and inference functions need not be evaluated frequently.

Specifically, the ![images](images/c09-i0162.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>th element of the ![images](images/c09-i0163.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>th classifier's dataset is ![images](images/c09-i0164.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>. The subscript ![images](images/c09-i0165.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> can be omitted since the SVM optimization is done with the aid of each of the ![images](images/c09-i0166.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> binary classifiers separately.

In the SVM algorithm, the geometric margin for each ![images](images/c09-i0167.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> is defined as

(9.7)![equation](images/c09-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mfrac> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mi>b</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The geometric margin of ![images](images/c09-i0168.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> corresponding to the training set is the smallest margin of geometric margins on ![images](images/c09-i0169.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>, which can be defined as

(9.8)![equation](images/c09-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The objective of the SVM algorithm is to maximize the geometric margin, which can be denoted as

(9.9)![equation](images/c09-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="right left"> <mtr> <mtd> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi> <mi>P</mi> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi> </mrow> </munder> <mspace width="1em"/> </mtd> <mtd> <mfrac> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mtext>subject to</mtext> <mspace width="1em"/> </mtd> <mtd> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c09-i0170.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c09-i0171.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> is the functional margin. Considering that ![images](images/c09-i0172.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c09-i0173.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> can be added with an arbitrary scaling constraint: here we use the scaling constraint, which means the functional margin ![images](images/c09-i0174.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> of ![images](images/c09-i0175.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> can be set as 1, i.e. ![images](images/c09-i0176.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.

Therefore, the previous optimization problem can be transformed as

(9.10)![equation](images/c09-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="right left"> <mtr> <mtd> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi> <mi>P</mi> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi> </mrow> </munder> <mspace width="1em"/> </mtd> <mtd> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mtext>subject to</mtext> <mspace width="1em"/> </mtd> <mtd> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

Let ![images](images/c09-i0177.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> denote the penalty for the feature‐set realization requiring ![images](images/c09-i0178.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> to solve the non‐separable case. Then the optimization problem can be rewritten as

(9.11)![equation](images/c09-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="right left"> <mtr> <mtd> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi> <mi>P</mi> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi> </mrow> </munder> <mspace width="1em"/> </mtd> <mtd> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mi>C</mi> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mtext>subject to</mtext> <mspace width="1em"/> </mtd> <mtd> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> </mrow> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

The one‐versus‐none classifier will become non‐separable when the feature space realizations cannot lead to the deterministic class outcomes. Hence ![images](images/c09-i0179.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> acts as the parameter to optimize the performance of the classifier and minimize the probability of choosing the wrong MCS class.

To remove the non‐separable classifier and reduce the dimension of the feature set, the kernel function can be applied to transform the feature set. The kernel function for the SVM classifier can be defined as ![images](images/c09-i0180.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><msup><mrow/><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>&#966;</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><msup><mrow/><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. In addition, defining ![images](images/c09-i0181.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> where ![images](images/c09-i0182.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><msup><mrow/><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><msup><mrow/><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><msup><mrow/><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, with the help of Lagrangian dual and the Karush‐Kuhn‐Tucker (KKT) conditions, the maximum margin can be constructed by

(9.12)![equation](images/c09-math-0012.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="right left"> <mtr> <mtd> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mrow> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi> <mi>N</mi> </msup> </mrow> </munder> <mspace width="1em"/> </mtd> <mtd> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mrow> <msup> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </msub> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mrow> <msup> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </msub> <msubsup> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msubsup> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mrow> <msup> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mtext>subject to</mtext> <mspace width="1em"/> </mtd> <mtd> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd> <mn>0</mn> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>C</mi> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

Then, using the kernel function, the term ![images](images/c09-i0183.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><msup><mrow/><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> can be updated as ![images](images/c09-i0184.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><msup><mrow/><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and the previous equation becomes

(9.13)![equation](images/c09-math-0013.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="right left"> <mtr> <mtd> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mrow> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi> <mi>N</mi> </msup> </mrow> </munder> <mspace width="1em"/> </mtd> <mtd> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <msup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">Q</mi> <mi>&#945;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mtext>subject to</mtext> <mspace width="1em"/> </mtd> <mtd> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd> <mn>0</mn> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>C</mi> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c09-i0185.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mrow></math> is a vector with all elements being “1”, ![images](images/c09-i0186.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the ![images](images/c09-i0187.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>th element in the vector ![images](images/c09-i0188.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#945;</mi></mrow></math>, and the inference function becomes ![images](images/c09-i0189.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><msup><mrow/><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>. The kernel function generalizes the boundary shape between classes. The most frequently used kernels, such as the linear kernel ![images](images/c09-i0190.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><msup><mrow/><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>, the polynomial kernel ![images](images/c09-i0191.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>l</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><msup><mrow/><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></math> where ![images](images/c09-i0192.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> is the polynomial dimension, and the Gaussian kernel ![images](images/c09-i0193.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mrow><mi>g</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>u</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><msup><mrow/><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><msup><mrow/><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></math> where ![images](images/c09-i0194.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> defines the boundaries according to the exponentially scaled Euclidean distance (Daniels and Heath, [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0004)), can provide different kinds of class boundaries.

Notably, in the dual formulation, the dual‐optimization variable ![images](images/c09-i0195.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> reveals the concept of the support vector, whose value has three cases. When ![images](images/c09-i0196.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c09-i0197.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> is not the support vector and does not contribute to the inference function. When ![images](images/c09-i0198.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c09-i0199.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the support vector lying on the margin. When ![images](images/c09-i0200.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c09-i0201.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> is also a support vector, but lies inside the margin.

In the SVM‐based fast online algorithm, the regression function ![images](images/c09-i0202.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, wherein ![images](images/c09-i0203.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the inference function, is applied on ![images](images/c09-i0204.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> MCS classes to address the PER constraint for each one‐versus‐none classifier. The prior probabilities of the normally distributed inference function outputs can be expressed in the sigmoid form as (Daniels and Heath, [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0004))

(9.14)![equation](images/c09-math-0014.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>Pr</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mi>h</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mn>3</mn> </msub> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c09-i0205.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c09-i0206.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c09-i0207.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mn>3</mn></msub></mrow></math> are constants.

Considering that the quadratic function is non‐monotonic, the inference output can be simplified, and the corresponding prior probabilities can be described as

[(9.15)](#c09.xhtml#c09-R_disp-0015)![equation](images/c09-math-0015.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <mi mathvariant="bold">Pr</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>B</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>B</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c09-i0208.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c09-i0209.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> are constants (Platt et al., [1999](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0022)). The output of the SVM classifier provides reasonable and accurate results of choosing the MCS class with the fitting function given in Eq. ([9.15](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0015)) (Niculescu‐Mizil and Caruana, [2005](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0017); Keerthi et al., [2001](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0012)). Thus for each one‐versus‐none classifier, the regression function to address the PER constraint can be denoted as

(9.16)![equation](images/c09-math-0016.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <msub> <mi>r</mi> <mi>m</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>h</mi> <mi>m</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>B</mi> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>m</mi> </mrow> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>h</mi> <mi>m</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>B</mi> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>m</mi> </mrow> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

where optimized parameters ![images](images/c09-i0210.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c09-i0211.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> can be calculated by the fitting algorithm according to the result of Eq. ([9.15](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0015)). Moreover, the subscript ![images](images/c09-i0212.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> can be omitted, since the fitting could be implemented with each MCS.

In order to achieve ![images](images/c09-i0213.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c09-i0214.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, the cost function can be constructed and optimized, and then ![images](images/c09-i0215.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c09-i0216.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> are defined as

(9.17)![equation](images/c09-math-0017.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo> <msubsup> The optimization for choosing the best ![images](images/c09-i0220.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c09-i0221.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>B</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> can be efficiently implemented by the Newton algorithm that can converge quickly to the optimal value (Lin et al., [2007](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0015)).

Furthermore, [Table 9.2](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0002) compares the complexity of SL‐based AMC schemes. It can be observed that the complexity of the SVM‐based fast online AMC algorithm with a linear kernel has the lowest processing complexity and memory cost. Since training data far from the margin should be maintained for the following optimizations, the SVM‐based AMC with a Gaussian kernel and ![images](images/c09-i0242.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN will consume much more processing resources.

 

#### 9.2.3.2 Simulation and Results

 

##### *System Parameters*

Similar to the discussions in [Section 9.2.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-sec-0005), the simulations are provided to investigate the performance of SVM‐based AMC systems following the IEEE 802.11n standard (802, [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0001)). The simulation parameter settings are given as follows (Daniels and Heath, [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0004)): the channel bandwidth is 20 MHz, the number of receive antennas and transmit antennas is 2, the number of available MCS classes is 16 from MCS0–MCS15, the PER constraint is 0.1, and the frame length is 128 bytes. In the simulations, we assume that the synchronization and channel estimation at the receiver are performed perfectly, and that the zero‐forcing algorithm is used for equalizations. In addition, the simulated online AMC algorithm is based on the SVM that uses linear or Gaussian kernels and nearest neighbor classifiers with ![images](images/c09-i0243.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> (Daniels and Heath, [2009](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0005)). The post‐processing SNR feature sets are well ordered (Daniels et al., [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0007)), 32000 channel realizations with SNRs ranging from 0–30dB are applied, and 4‐tap Gaussian channels are employed with severe frequency selectivity and uniform power‐delay profiles. The parameters of ![images](images/c09-i0244.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> SVM classifiers are determined by the empirical results of the cross‐validation set: hereby we set ![images](images/c09-i0245.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> for both the linear and Gaussian kernels, and we set ![images](images/c09-i0246.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.005</mn></mrow></math> for the Gaussian kernel. Moreover, it is noticeable that according to (Daniels and Heath, [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0004)), when the number of training examples is set to ![images](images/c09-i0247.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></math>, the classifier can provide robust performances with no need to increase the training sample number.

 

##### *Results*

[Figure 9.2](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0002) describes the relationship between the throughput and the average SNR over all preset channels, while [Figure 9.3](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0003) provides the result of the PER at different SNRs. From these two figures, we can see that SL‐based AMC can help the wireless communication system reach a good compromise between high data rate and high reliability by using experience information originated from labeled training data. When ![images](images/c09-i0248.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> increases, the throughput increases, but the PER also increases. When ![images](images/c09-i0249.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> is small and SNR is large, the SVM‐based algorithm achieves higher throughput than the ![images](images/c09-i0250.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN‐based algorithm. Hence, using the linear kernel can provide satisfactory performances for the system, and we do not need to pay extra to use the Gaussian kernel.

It is worth pointing out that the performance of the ![images](images/c09-i0251.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm‐based AMC scheme is deeply dependent on the selection of the sampled data and ![images](images/c09-i0252.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, since in the ![images](images/c09-i0253.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm, the ![images](images/c09-i0254.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐nearest neighbor is determined by calculating the distance between the unlabeled object and all labeled objects. Thus, compared with the SVM‐based AMC scheme, the robustness of the ![images](images/c09-i0255.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN algorithm‐based AMC scheme is worse.

## 9.3 RL‐Assisted AMC

In this section, we introduce the RL algorithm and address how to apply it in AMC. As mentioned earlier, unlike the SL method, the RL approach can directly interact with the environment, which means an agent can choose its actions according to the interactions and rewards obtained from the environment (Sutton et al., [1998](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0024)). Specifically, the RL approach does not require an external supervisor, since the learning examples are obtained from interactions with the environment. When applying the RL approach to AMC, an agent can learn and formulate the best modulation and coding scheme by using past experiences obtained in real time and channel states, with minimal assumptions about the communication scenario. Accordingly, with the objective of maximizing spectrum efficiency, a Markov decision process is constructed to decide which modulation and coding scheme should be used (Leite et al., [2012](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0014)). Notably, the RL‐aided AMC does not require offline training that needs to consider all possible situations the physical transmissions may experience, and thus this type of AMC can provide more adaptive services than SL‐aided AMC.

 

### 9.3.1 Markov Decision Process

As mentioned at the beginning of this chapter, the RL approach can be represented by the theory of MDP (Puterman, [2014](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0023)). There are four key elements in a MDP problem: the states ![images](images/c09-i0256.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi></mrow></math>, the actions ![images](images/c09-i0257.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math>, the transition function ![images](images/c09-i0258.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>, and the reward ![images](images/c09-i0259.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>. Specifically, ![images](images/c09-i0260.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> denotes the set of ![images](images/c09-i0261.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> possible states, which describes the dynamic variations of the environment; ![images](images/c09-i0262.png)<math stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> denotes the set of ![images](images/c09-i0263.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>: ![images](images/c09-i0265.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi></mrow></math> ![images](images/c09-i0266.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#215;</mo></mrow></math> ![images](images/c09-i0267.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> ![images](images/c09-i0268.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#215;</mo></mrow></math> ![images](images/c09-i0269.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi></mrow></math> ![images](images/c09-i0270.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8594;</mo></mrow></math> \[0, 1\] is a transition probability function in which ![images](images/c09-i0272.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi></mrow></math> to state ![images](images/c09-i0273.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi
