display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> is a reward function, where ![images](images/c09-i0276.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the immediate reward of the environment when taking action ![images](images/c09-i0277.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> at state ![images](images/c09-i0278.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>.

At the ![images](images/c09-i0279.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> stage of the learning process, the agent performs an action ![images](images/c09-i0280.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> at the observed state ![images](images/c09-i0281.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi></mrow></math>. At the next stage, before the state changes to ![images](images/c09-i0282.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi></mrow></math> with probability ![images](images/c09-i0283.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>(![images](images/c09-i0284.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>,![images](images/c09-i0285.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>,![images](images/c09-i0286.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>), the agent receive the reward ![images](images/c09-i0287.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>(![images](images/c09-i0288.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>,![images](images/c09-i0289.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>) generated by the environment. Later on, a similar process is carried out, and the agent receives a series of subsequent rewards ![images](images/c09-i0290.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c09-i0291.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c09-i0292.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>,… from the environment.

The aim of the agent is to find a policy ![images](images/c09-i0293.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></math> that defines the behavior of the mapping from the states to the actions – ![images](images/c09-i0294.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi></mrow></math>: ![images](images/c09-i0295.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi></mrow></math> ![images](images/c09-i0296.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8594;</mo></mrow></math> ![images](images/c09-i0297.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> – to obtain the discounted accumulative reward as much as possible. Denoting ![images](images/c09-i0298.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#960;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> as the action that the agent takes at state ![images](images/c09-i0299.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>, then the accumulative reward is a function related to the state values, which can be calculated by

[(9.19)](#c09.xhtml#c09-R_disp-0019)![equation](images/c09-math-0019.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="right left"> <mtr> <mtd> <msup> <mi>V</mi> <mi>&#960;</mi> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mtd> <mtd> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mi>&#8734;</mi> </munderover> <msup> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msup> <msub> <mi>R</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#960;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd> <mo>=</mo> <mi>R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#960;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#947;</mi> <munder> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msup> <mi>s</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi> </mrow> </munder> <mi>P</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>s</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#960;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msup> <mi>V</mi> <mi>&#960;</mi> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>s</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c09-i0300.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> is a discount factor used for weighting the long‐term accumulative rewards. The discount factor determines how much the future reward will contribute to the accumulative reward function.

As time goes by, the future reward becomes less reliable and predictable, and hence the future reward is less important than the current reward such that ![images](images/c09-i0301.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. More concretely, if the discount factor is close to 0, the agent thinks highly of the current reward and almost neglects the future rewards, while higher values of ![images](images/c09-i0302.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> make the agent attach more importance to the long‐term future reward.

As given by Eq. ([9.19](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0019)), once the state of the environment at time ![images](images/c09-i0303.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> is given, the reward only depends on the action taken by the agent. Therefore, for each ![images](images/c09-i0304.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>, the agent needs to find an optimal policy ![images](images/c09-i0305.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#960;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi></mrow></math> to maximize the accumulative reward as defined in Eq. ([9.19](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0019)). To be more specific, the objective of the agent is to find a policy ![images](images/c09-i0306.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> such that ![images](images/c09-i0307.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>V</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>&#960;</mi></msub><msup><mi>V</mi><mi>&#960;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

 

### 9.3.2 Solution for the Markov Decision

In the MDP model, the policy iteration and value iteration dynamic programming (Sutton et al., [1998](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0024)) methods are two well‐known methods to obtain the optimal policy. However, these two methods both require prior knowledge of the environmental dynamics, which is hard to estimate beforehand in a practical view. In other words, we can hardly obtain prior knowledge of ![images](images/c09-i0308.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c09-i0309.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> in the AMC scenario. In this case, exploration of the state‐action‐reward relationship is required to query the environment. To accomplish this task, Q‐learning stands out as an outstanding reinforcement technique due to its simplicity and low computational cost (Watkins and Dayan, [1992](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0026)).

In the Q‐learning method, the state‐action value function (Q‐function) is used to characterize policies. Specifically, the Q‐function represents fitness to perform action ![images](images/c09-i0310.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> when in state ![images](images/c09-i0311.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>. It starts from a given state and then accumulates its value according to the rewards that the agent received when taking a series of actions following the policy thereafter. The Q‐function is defined as

(9.20)![equation](images/c09-math-0020.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi>Q</mi> <mi>&#960;</mi> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>E</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8734;</mi> </mrow> </munderover> <msup> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msup> <msub> <mi>R</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi>a</mi> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> 

The optimal Q‐function, ![images](images/c09-i0312.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, is the one that maximizes the discounted cumulative rewards, namely ![images](images/c09-i0313.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mi>&#960;</mi></munder><msup><mi>Q</mi><mi>&#960;</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. According to Bellman's optimality principle, a greedy policy can be used to solve this optimization problem. In the greedy policy, an action with the largest Q‐value is selected at each state. This means that for each state ![images](images/c09-i0314.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi></mrow></math>, once ![images](images/c09-i0315.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is known, the optimal policy is to take action ![images](images/c09-i0316.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> with the highest ![images](images/c09-i0317.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> value, i.e.

(9.21)![equation](images/c09-math-0021.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi>&#960;</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mrow> <mi>a</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> </mrow> </munder> <msup> <mi>Q</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Moreover, in the Q‐learning algorithm, ![images](images/c09-i0318.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is updated recursively using the current state ![images](images/c09-i0319.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>, the next state ![images](images/c09-i0320.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>s</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math>, action ![images](images/c09-i0321.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> taken at ![images](images/c09-i0322.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>, and reward ![images](images/c09-i0323.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> obtained from the environment due to taking ![images](images/c09-i0324.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> at the current state. The updating formula is given as

[(9.22)](#c09.xhtml#c09-R_disp-0022)![equation](images/c09-math-0022.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>Q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8592;</mo> <mi>Q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>R</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#947;</mi> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mi>a</mi> </munder> <mi>Q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>s</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>Q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c09-i0325.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> is the learning rate.

As can be inferred from the previous discussions, the RL algorithm has an exploration versus exploitation dilemma. *Exploration* means collecting informative data about the environment by taking new actions for the given state space. *Exploitation* means preserving the process well enough according to the available knowledge obtained previously. To balance the need for exploration and exploitation, two commonly adopted strategies are the ![images](images/c09-i0326.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐greedy search and the softmax action‐selection method (Sutton et al., [1998](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0024)).

  ![images](images/c09-i0327.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐greedy search 

In the ![images](images/c09-i0328.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐greedy search, the agent uses the probability ![images](images/c09-i0329.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> to decide whether to exploit the Q‐table or explore the new choices. Since ![images](images/c09-i0330.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> is usually small, the agent tends to select the action that satisfies ![images](images/c09-i0331.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mi>a</mi></munder><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. On rare occasions, with probability ![images](images/c09-i0332.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>, the agent takes a random action for the purpose of experiencing as many actions and effects as possible.

 softmax action‐selection 

Due to the small probability of random selection, the ![images](images/c09-i0333.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>‐greedy search can only attain a suboptimal policy. To solve this problem, random selection is abandoned in the softmax action‐selection method. Instead, the action ![images](images/c09-i0334.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> taken at state ![images](images/c09-i0335.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> is chosen with probability ![images](images/c09-i0336.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> given by

[(9.23)](#c09.xhtml#c09-R_disp-0023)![equation](images/c09-math-0023.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>P</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mi>Q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mi>&#964;</mi> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> <mrow> <msubsup> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>m</mi> </msubsup> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mi>Q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mi>&#964;</mi> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c09-i0337.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> determines the selection trend. As can be inferred from Eq. ([9.23](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0023)), if ![images](images/c09-i0338.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> is close to 0, the agent prefers choosing actions with the highest Q‐value. If ![images](images/c09-i0339.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> becomes larger, the policy trends toward random selection, as all actions tend to have the same probability of being chosen.

 

### 9.3.3 Actions, States, and Rewards

Using the Markov process, ML‐assisted AMC systems can take actions based on the collected environment states and rewards to adapt to dynamically changing channel conditions. More details about the actions, states, and rewards are given as follows.

  Actions 

The target of AMC is to maximize throughput for a given state of the environment by adopting the modulation and coding schemes. In practical protocols such as IEEE 802.11n, there are only a finite number of modulation and coding schemes. Each scheme is considered an action, and the agent selects the optimal scheme based on past experiences just before packet transmission.

 States 

The link establishment has enabled the agent to collect environment information including the past and the current channel states, extracted network features, and so on. Although the environment state can be determined by various features, as an example of one possible solution, the received SNR averaged over all subcarriers is used to determine the state of the environment (Leite et al., [2012](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0014)). Due to the constraint that the state value should belong to a finite set, we consider SNR values in the range from ‐2–20 dB with step of 1 dB to avoid dealing with an infinite number of states. As a result, a total of ![images](images/c09-i0340.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>23</mn></mrow></math> states are used to determine the environment. At each single state ![images](images/c09-i0341.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>, the agent chooses one action from a finite action set, and different actions lead to different expected rewards. Since the channel link may be time‐varying, the agent must continually track and update the value of ![images](images/c09-i0342.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, embodying the real‐time compatibility of the RL approach. To maximize the achievable throughput, the agent must search and find the optimal MCS for a given state of the channel environment.

 Rewards 

To ensure the effectiveness of applying the RL approach to a practical problem, the reward function ![images](images/c09-i0343.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> must be defined appropriately in a specific context. Given the link‐adaptation scenario, the throughput achieved by taking action ![images](images/c09-i0344.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> at state ![images](images/c09-i0345.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> is used to define the reward function ![images](images/c09-i0346.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>, namely

(9.24)![equation](images/c09-math-0024.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mi>o</mi> <msub> <mi>g</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>M</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msub> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mi>a</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>P</mi> <mi>E</mi> <mi>R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c09-i0347.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>M</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></math> denotes the modulation order of action ![images](images/c09-i0348.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c09-i0349.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#961;</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the coding rate when taking action ![images](images/c09-i0350.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c09-i0351.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>E</mi><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the packet error rate when taking action ![images](images/c09-i0352.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi></mrow></math> at channel state ![images](images/c09-i0353.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>. Using the CRC field in each packet, the receiver can detect packets with errors, and the PER can be estimated by the error packet measurements. This information is then fed back to the transmitter to update the learning algorithm in order to increase spectrum efficiency.

 

### 9.3.4 Performance Analysis and Simulations

Due to the exploration, the RL framework is not as powerful as SL. Next, we perform simulations to investigate the performance of RL‐aided AMC.

In the simulations, we only consider the combination of ![images](images/c09-i0354.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> modulation and coding with ![images](images/c09-i0355.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, as given in [Table 9.1](#c09.xhtml#c09-tbl-0001). Unless stated otherwise, we have set ![images](images/c09-i0356.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.4</mn></mrow></math> on the softmax action‐selection method given by Eq. ([9.23](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0023)). Similarly, the learning rate of the Q‐learning algorithm, given by Eq. ([9.22](#c09.xhtml#c09-disp-0022)), is set to ![images](images/c09-i0357.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.4</mn></mrow></math> by default. These settings will be further discussed as follows.

[Figures 9.4](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0004) and [9.5](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0005) investigate the effects of tuning parameters, including the softmax parameter and the learning rate, on the convergence behavior of the algorithm. To indicate the differences among the RL policies and different modulation and coding for a given SNR, the mean square error (MSE) is calculated over the frame numbers.

From [Figure 9.4](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0004), we can see that the lower the value of the softmax parameter, the faster the convergence. The reason is that for ![images](images/c09-i0358.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, actions with a higher Q‐value are preferred. However, low ![images](images/c09-i0359.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> can lead to bad system performance because the learning procedure finishes its exploration too early. For example, ![images](images/c09-i0360.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.2</mn></mrow></math> leads to a MSE of about ![images](images/c09-i0361.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mi>d</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, which is larger than that of the scenario ![images](images/c09-i0362.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.4</mn></mrow></math> or ![images](images/c09-i0363.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.8</mn></mrow></math>.

Moreover, it can be observed from [Figure 9.5](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0005) that when the learning rate ![images](images/c09-i0364.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> has a larger value, the learning engine can get more immediate rewards than the accumulated rewards and vice versa. Hence, the learning rate can be used for the balance of the exploitation and exploration, and the optimal learning rate depends on specific systems. For example, the simulated system performs best when ![images](images/c09-i0365.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.4</mn></mrow></math>.

Next we compare system performance using the RL engine with that using the lookup table approach, which is also known as RawBER mapping (Jensen et al., [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0009)) used for link adaptations. In RawBER mapping, the probability of uncoded bit errors at each subcarrier is used to calculate the LQM. Specifically, the relationship between RawBER and PER can be determined by a regression generated by simulations performed over the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel, which can be prepared beforehand (Lamarca and Rey, [2005](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0013)).

![Figure 9.4 Influence of the softmax parameter images on the convergence of the RL algorithm for images.](images/c09f004.jpg)

[Figure 9.4](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0004) Influence of the softmax parameter ![images](images/c09-i0366.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> on the convergence of the RL algorithm for ![images](images/c09-i0367.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.4</mn></mrow></math>.

![Figure 9.5 Influence of the learning rate images on the convergence of the RL algorithm for images.](images/c09f005.jpg)

[Figure 9.5](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0005) Influence of the learning rate ![images](images/c09-i0368.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> on the convergence of the RL algorithm for ![images](images/c09-i0369.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.4</mn></mrow></math>.

The drawback of the lookup table approach is that it requires a large amount of memory and simulation time for each scenario. For example, in some scenarios, the Gaussian assumption – i.e. the interference along with the Gaussian noise can be regarded as a single Gaussian distribution – may be unreasonable (Aljuaid and Yanikomeroglu, [2010](#c09.xhtml#c09-bib-0002)). Hence, one kind of generated data cannot guarantee to cover all possible situations. Consequently, lookup tables can potentially lead to suboptimal solutions.

Let us consider the scenario where the channel SNR can be ideally obtained. [Figure 9.6](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0006) shows that the spectrum efficiency is a function of the average SNR in this scenario. It can be observed that the RL approach achieves lower throughput as compared to the lookup table approach, since the latter approach is optimized in the specific channel, while the RL gradually adapts to the environment.

By contrast, as shown in [Figure 9.7](#c09.xhtml#c09-fig-0007), when the channel SNR cannot be ideally obtained due to the estimation error, which is a more common scenario in practical communication systems, the proposed RL scheme can outperform the lookup table approach. This is because RL is able to learn from the environment and adapts to the environment, including the SNR estimation error, while the lookup table approach must be optimized in a specific environment. Moreover, RL can operate in online mode, and hence it does not require an expert or extensive simulations to adapt to different scenarios. The best MCS selection does not require an exhaustive trial‐and‐error procedure but a small amount of programming effort to build the system.

![Figure 9.6 Average spectrum efficiency of the lookup table and the RL technique over an AWGN channel with ideal SNR estimation.](images/c09f006.jpg)

[Figure 9.6](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0006) Average spectrum efficiency of the lookup table and the RL technique over an AWGN channel with ideal SNR estimation.

![Figure 9.7 Average spectrum efficiency of the lookup table and the RL technique over an AWGN channel with SNR estimation error.](images/c09f007.jpg)

[Figure 9.7](#c09.xhtml#R_c09-fig-0007) Average spectrum efficiency of the lookup table and the RL technique over an AWGN channel with SNR estimation error.

It can be seen from the simulation results and analyses that the RL framework can provide a promising solution for the AMC problem. In this method, the maximization of spectral efficiency is regarded as a Markov decision process, and the mean SNR is used to determine the channel state of the radio link. A relation between the SNR values and modulation and coding schemes can be determined by adopting Q‐learning for solving the problem of the Markov decision process. From the simulations, we can further see that RL‐aided AMC can be used for online radio link establishment, since offline training is not required by RL. Moreover, this method is adaptive to changes of the radio environment. Thus, with the aid of RL, AMC can dynamically adjust the parameters and provide services for users with higher efficiencies and reliability.

 

## 9.4 Further Discussion and Conclusions

In this chapter, we have presented three ML‐assisted AMC schemes for wireless communication systems to adapt to variations in channel conditions with fewer model‐based approximations and potentially higher accuracy than traditional adaptive modulation and coding schemes. Two of them are SL‐based approaches, and the other is implemented by RL. Notably, although there are many SL algorithms such as SVM, decision trees, ![images](images/c09-i0370.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN, neural networks, and so on, they have similar mechanisms, such as the requirement of labeled data and the analogy to classifiers after training has been done. Therefore, without a loss of generality, we have only taken ![images](images/c09-i0371.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐NN and SVM as examples to show the application of SL in AMC. For the RL approach in AMC, we have taken Q‐learning as an example, since it represents the primary mechanisms of RL and has been widely used due to its conciseness.

To verify the practicability and effectiveness of applying these learning algorithms to AMC, simulations with parameter settings referring to the IEEE 802.11n standard have been done to compare the presented ML‐assisted AMC schemes with traditional approaches. It is worth pointing out that SL‐based AMC schemes are suitable for the scenario where training examples are representative of all the situations the transmitter might be exposed to. By contrast, the RL algorithm can directly learn from the interacting environment and can gradually achieve satisfactory performance with no offline training as required by SL. Therefore, these two types of learning mechanisms can be selected according to whether training is performed offline or online based on different user demands in different application scenarios.

Thanks to training and learning mechanisms, ML‐aided AMC approaches have achieved intelligent and outstanding reliability in wireless systems. Future research directions may include the combination of RL and SL, how to enhance the robustness of ML‐assisted AMC systems, and how to achieve better trade‐offs between complexity and system performance, with the objective of providing more adaptive, intelligent, and better services for end users.
