# 10  
Machine Learning–Based Nonlinear MIMO Detector

*Song‐Nam Hong and Seonho Kim*

*Electrical and Computer Engineering, Ajou University, Suwon, South Korea*

 

## 10.1 Introduction

Wireless systems make it possible to provide communication links with Gbps data rates by using a massive antenna array (Swindlehurst et al., [2014](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0023)) and/or by using wide (possibly multi‐gigahertz) bandwidth (Pi and Khan, [2011](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0018)). The common weakness of both approaches is significant power consumption at the receiver, caused by high‐precision (e.g. 8![images](images/c10-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8764;</mo></mrow></math>14‐bit precision) analog‐to‐digital converters (ADCs), because total power consumed by ADCs scales linearly with the number of precision levels, bandwidth, and the number of the ADCs (Murmann; Walden, [1999](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0024); Mezghani et al., [2010](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0011)). For example, power consumption of ADCs is shown to be proportional to both the number of precision levels and the bandwidth, under Nyquist rate sampling (Mezghani et al., [2010](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0011)). Therefore, the use of high‐precision ADCs at the receiver becomes impractical when a massive antenna array and/or wide bandwidth are used.

Low‐resolution (e.g. 1![images](images/c10-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8764;</mo></mrow></math>3‐bit precision) ADCs have been regarded as a cost‐effective solution to reduce power consumption of future wireless systems that include massive multiple‐input and multiple‐output (MIMO) systems and wideband communication systems (Nossek and Ivrlač, [2006](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0017); Singh et al., [2009](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0022); Dabeer and Madhow, [2010](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0002); Mo and Heath, [2015](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0012)). In spite of the benefits, the use of low‐resolution ADCs gives rise to numerous challenges. One challenge is that it is difficult to obtain accurate channel‐state information at the receiver (CSIR) with conventional pilot‐based channel estimation techniques. In addition, conventional data‐detection methods, developed for linear MIMO systems, provide poor detection performance due to the nonlinearity at the ADCs.

Extensive research has been performed to resolve the channel‐estimation and data‐detection problems in uplink massive MIMO systems with one‐bit ADCs Jacobsson et al. ([2015](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0004),[2017](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0005)), Risi et al. ([2014](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0019)), Choi et al. ([2016](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0001)), Li et al. ([2017](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0009)), Mollén et al. ([2016](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0013),[2017](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0014)), Wang et al. ([2015](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0025)), Liang and Zhang ([2016](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0010)), Wen et al. ([2016](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0026)). For the channel‐estimation problem in such systems, numerous methods have been developed to improve the accuracy of CSIR. The developed methods include a least‐squares (LS)‐based method (Risi et al., [2014](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0019)), a maximum‐likelihood–based method (Choi et al., [2016](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0001)), and a method using Bussgang decomposition (Li et al., [2017](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0009)). For the data‐detection problem, optimal maximum‐likelihood detection (MLD) has been introduced in (Choi et al., [2016](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0001)), and some other low‐complexity methods have also been developed in (Mollén et al., [2016](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0013),[2017](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0014); Jeon et al., [2018a](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0006)).

These works can be extended into a multihop MIMO system, called a *distributed uplink MIMO system*, where an end‐to‐end channel transfer function between ![images](images/c10-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> sources and the data center is highly nonlinear. Thus, it is extremely challenging to estimate such a channel transfer function with a limited number of quantized pilot signals. This motivates the consideration of a data‐driven supervised learning (SL) based detector where pilot signals (or training data) are exploited to directly learn a MIMO detector, rather than estimating a complex channel transfer function. In this chapter, we will explain various SL‐based detectors for nonlinear multihop MIMO communication systems.

The rest of this chapter is organized as follows. [Section 10.2](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0002) is devoted to the problem formulation and system model of a multihop MIMO system with one‐bit ADCs. [Section 10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0003) explains MIMO detectors with regard to SL Learning for considered system. In this section, these detectors are described as being in two categories: non‐parametric learning and parametric learning. [Section 10.4](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0006) introduces a low‐complexity SL detector that applies clustering algorithms on SL detectors with parametric learning. [Section 10.5](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0007) shows the performance of introduced SL detectors via simulation. [Section 10.6](#c10.xhtml#c10-sec-0008) will offer some further discussion and conclusions.

 

## 10.2 A Multihop MIMO Channel Model

As shown in [Figure 10.1](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0001), let us consider a multihop distributed uplink MIMO system in which ![images](images/c10-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> sources transmit independent messages to one data center with the aid of intermediate relays. Also, the data center is equipped with ![images](images/c10-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></msub><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> receive antennas with one‐bit ADCs in the uplink system.

Let ![images](images/c10-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> denote the source ![images](images/c10-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>'s message for ![images](images/c10-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>, each of which contains ![images](images/c10-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> information bits. We also denote the ![images](images/c10-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>‐ary constellation set by ![images](images/c10-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> with power constraint ![images](images/c10-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mi>m</mi></mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>s</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">t</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Let ![images](images/c10-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>sign</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="-0.31em"/><mo>:</mo><mi>R</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> represent the one‐bit ADC quantizer function with ![images](images/c10-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>sign</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> if ![images](images/c10-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c10-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>sign</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, otherwise. Then the transmitted symbol of source ![images](images/c10-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c10-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>, is obtained by a modulation function ![images](images/c10-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><mi>W</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> S</mi></mrow></math> as ![images](images/c10-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> S</mi></mrow></math>.

Then, from real and imaginary parts, the data center observes

[(10.1)](#c10.xhtml#c10-R_disp-0001)![equation](images/c10-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mtext>sign</mtext> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> ![Figure 10.1 Description of a distributed multihop MIMO system with low‐resolution ADCs.](images/c10f001.jpg)

[Figure 10.1](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0001) Description of a distributed multihop MIMO system with low‐resolution ADCs.

where ![images](images/c10-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>N</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">r</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c10-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> represents a complex nonlinear function (called an *end‐to‐end channel transfer function*) and ![images](images/c10-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">z</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow></math> denotes the noise vector whose elements are independently identically distributed as circularly symmetric complex Gaussian random variables with zero mean and unit variance: in other words, ![images](images/c10-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>z</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mi>z</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Note that ![images](images/c10-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> captures all the intermediate relays' operations and all the local wireless channels in the network. For example, each local channel in the multihop can be assumed as Rayleigh fading. It is remarkable that the channel model in Eq. ([10.1](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0001)) is quite general, including an uplink MIMO system with one‐bit ADCs.

The communication framework consists of training and data‐transmission phases (see [Figure 10.2](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0002)). Note that while undergoing these two phases, the channel is assumed to be fixed within the coherence time:

*   *Training phase*: During this phase, ![images](images/c10-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> sources transmits “known” sequences (i.e. pilot signals) so that the data center can learn a nonlinear function ![images](images/c10-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. From a machine learning (ML) perspective, the data center collects the data and the corresponding labels. Let ![images](images/c10-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mi>K</mi></msup></mrow></math> denote the set of all possible messages of the ![images](images/c10-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> sources. For each class ![images](images/c10-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi></mrow></math>, the ![images](images/c10-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> sources transmit ![images](images/c10-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> pilot signals ![images](images/c10-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> for ![images](images/c10-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>. In other words, ![images](images/c10-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> is the number of repetitions of a signal according to each message(class) ![images](images/c10-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>. From Eq. ([10.1](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0001)), the data center can collect the labelled data set ![images](images/c10-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow></math> as [(10.2)](#c10.xhtml#c10-R_disp-0002)![equation](images/c10-math-0002.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <msubsup> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msubsup> <mspace width="-0.21em"/> <mo>:</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>&#8230;</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>T</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> where ![images](images/c10-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>c</mi></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow></math>. After sending the pilot signals in Eq. ([10.2](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0002)), the receiver creates empirical conditional probability mass functions (PMFs) by using the received signals observed during the pilot transmission. An empirical conditional PMF for each message (class) ![images](images/c10-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is given by [(10.3)](#c10.xhtml#c10-R_disp-0003)![equation](images/c10-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>r</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>T</mi> </mfrac> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="bold">1</mtext> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo> <mi>r</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo> </mrow> </msub> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mtext>for</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi>c</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> where ![images](images/c10-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext mathvariant="bold">1</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is an indicator function that equals 1 if an event A is true and zero otherwise.
*   *Data‐transmission phase*: Given the ![images](images/c10-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow></math> and a new observation ![images](images/c10-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi></mrow></math>, the data center detects the class of ![images](images/c10-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi></mrow></math> (i.e. users' messages ![images](images/c10-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#373;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#373;</mi><mi>K</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>) as [(10.4)](#c10.xhtml#c10-R_disp-0004)![equation](images/c10-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#936;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> which will be introduced in the next sections.

![Figure 10.2 Illustration of the training and data‐transmission phases within the coherence time.](images/c10f002.jpg)

[Figure 10.2](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0002) Illustration of the training and data‐transmission phases within the coherence time.

 

## 10.3 Supervised‐Learning‐based MIMO Detector

From a ML perspective, the detection problem in Eq. ([10.4](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0004)) (a.k.a. the *supervised learning problem*) can be classified into two approaches (Robert, [2014](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0020)): non‐parametric learning and parametric learning. Non‐parametric learning – such as ![images](images/c10-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>‐nearest neighbor (kNN), decision trees, and support vector machines (SVMs) – does not require a priori knowledge of a data set ![images](images/c10-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow></math> (e.g. a distribution of data). On the other hand, in parametric learning – such as logistic regression, naive Bayes, and neural networks – data is assumed to be generated from a given probabilistic model with some parameters (e.g. Gaussian model); then, the parameters are optimized using the given data set ![images](images/c10-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow></math>. Therefore, it is very important to choose a proper probabilistic model using a priori knowledge (or domain knowledge) about the data set ![images](images/c10-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow></math>.

With this classification, we will briefly explain the existing (parametric or non‐parametric) SL detectors. Note that they can be immediately applied to a multihop MIMO system, since SL detectors do not rely on a specific system model.

 

### 10.3.1 Non‐Parametric Learning

According to (Jeon et al., [2018a](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0006)), non‐parametric learning characterizes empirical conditional probability mass function (PMF) based on a training data set. Non‐parametric learning is categorized into empirical‐maximum‐likelihood detection and minimum‐mean‐distance detection, as follows:

1) *Empirical‐maximum‐likelihood detection (eMLD)*: The key idea is the selection of an index for the input symbol vector that maximizes the empirical conditional PMF in Eq. ([10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0003)) as follows:

(10.5)![equation](images/c10-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#265;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">argmax</mi> <mrow> <mi>c</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo> </mrow> </munder> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>r</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

When training repetitions ![images](images/c10-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> increases to infinity, this detection is equivalent to the optimal maximum‐likelihood detection method, since the empirical distribution converges to the corresponding true distribution by the law of large numbers. When ![images](images/c10-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> is insufficient, however, the empirical distribution cannot represent the true distribution, resulting in detection errors. More specifically, there is a non‐zero probability ![images](images/c10-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8713;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow></math>, leading to ![images](images/c10-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>p</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> for all messages ![images](images/c10-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi></mrow></math>. To solve this problem, the receiver finds ![images](images/c10-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow></math> that are the closest vectors to ![images](images/c10-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi></mrow></math>. Let ![images](images/c10-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> be the set of these closest vectors. Then, the eMLD method ![images](images/c10-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#936;</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo>:</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is given by

(10.6)![equation](images/c10-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#936;</mi> <mrow> <mi>e</mi> <mi>M</mi> <mi>L</mi> <mi>D</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>r</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">argmax</mi> <mrow> <mi>r</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> N</mi> </mrow> </munder> <munder> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>r</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> N</mi> </mrow> </munder> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi>r</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

As in [Figure 10.3](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0003), this is similar to the kNN classifier in the sense that they simply compare the number of neighbor labels. One notable difference is that eMLD uses the neighbor set of elements that are equidistant from the received vector.

2) *Minimum‐mean‐distance detection (MMD)*: The drawback of eMLD is partially using the empirical conditional PMFs, because the set is limited to the nearest neighbors (![images](images/c10-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> N</mi></mrow></math>) only. Therefore, to fully exploit the empirical PMFs, we introduce an alternative detection method: MMD. As illustrated in [Figure 10.4](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0004), the MMD method, ![images](images/c10-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#936;</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>D</mi></mrow></msub><mo>:</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>, selects the index of the symbol vector that yields the conditional minimum mean distance, i.e.

(10.7)![equation](images/c10-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#936;</mi> <mrow> <mi>M</mi> <mi>M</mi> <mi>D</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>r</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">argmin</mi> <mrow> <mi>c</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>r</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>r</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>r</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">argmin</mi> <mrow> <mi>c</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi> </mrow> </munder> <munder> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>r</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>r</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>r</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mover accent="true"> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>r</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

MMD finds the message that minimizes the weighted sum of the empirical PMFs, where the weights are the distance between the received vector and the trained vector, ![images](images/c10-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>r</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>. Although the optimality of MMD is not guaranteed, it may perform better than eMLD when ![images](images/c10-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> is insufficient, because MMD additionally uses reliability information captured by the distance between the received signal and the trained signal.

![Figure 10.3 Empirical‐maximum‐likelihood detection (eMLD).](images/c10f003.jpg)

[Figure 10.3](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0003) Empirical‐maximum‐likelihood detection (eMLD).

![Figure 10.4 Minimum‐mean‐distance detection (MMD).](images/c10f004.jpg)

[Figure 10.4](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0004) Minimum‐mean‐distance detection (MMD).

 

### 10.3.2 Parametric Learning

The weakness of non‐parametric approaches (eMLD, MMD) is that they cause high computational complexity. In both methods, the receiver should compute all distances in the training set (![images](images/c10-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></math>). In particular, when the size of ![images](images/c10-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow></math> is large (e.g. ![images](images/c10-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi><mo>&#8811;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>), a non‐parametric approach is intractable in practical systems. Therefore, by learning parameters during the training phase, we can alleviate the complexity significantly.

1) *SL based on a Gaussian model (SLGM)*: In this approach, it is very important to identify a proper probabilistic model for a given data set ![images](images/c10-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow></math>. A Gaussian model is the most widely used (Jeon et al., [2018a](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0006); Robert, [2014](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0020)) where the data ![images](images/c10-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow></math> is assumed to be generated from the following probability distribution: ![images](images/c10-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> N</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#931;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math> where ![images](images/c10-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi></mrow></math> denotes the class (or message) of the ![images](images/c10-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> sources and ![images](images/c10-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></math> represents the parameter vector for the class ![images](images/c10-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>. Using the given data ![images](images/c10-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>c</mi></msubsup><mspace width="-0.21em"/><mo>:</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>, we can optimize ![images](images/c10-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#931;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>c</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> via maximum likelihood estimation as

(10.8)![equation](images/c10-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>T</mi> </mfrac> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </munderover> <msubsup> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msubsup> </mrow> </math> [(10.9)](#c10.xhtml#c10-R_disp-0009)![equation](images/c10-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#931;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>T</mi> </mfrac> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msubsup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mi>c</mi> </msubsup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c10-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c10-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#931;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></math> represent the mean and covariance of the training data corresponding to class ![images](images/c10-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>, respectively. As in [Figure 10.5](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0005), ![images](images/c10-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></math> could be considered representative vectors according to each class ![images](images/c10-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>. When the training data is not sufficient, the covariance matrix tends to be rank‐deficient and ill‐conditioned. This problem can be resolved with a shrinkage estimator Schäfer and Strimmer ([2005](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0021)). Given ![images](images/c10-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#931;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>c</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, the optimal maximum‐likelihood detector is derived as

[(10.10)](#c10.xhtml#c10-R_disp-0010)![equation](images/c10-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#936;</mi> <mrow> <mi>P</mi> <mi>G</mi> <mi>D</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">argmin</mi> <mrow> <mi>c</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi> </mrow> </munder> <mspace width="2.77695pt"/> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <msubsup> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#931;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>c</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>c</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

In particular, the distance measure in this detector is referred to as *Mahalanobis distance*, and the inverse matrix of ![images](images/c10-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#931;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>c</mi></msub></mrow></math> in Eq. ([10.9](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0009)) is called a *precision matrix*. When ![images](images/c10-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#931;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></mrow></math> for all ![images](images/c10-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math>, as a special case, the resulting detector is equivalent to the minimum‐centered‐distance (MCD) detector proposed in Jeon et al. ([2018b](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0007)). In Jeon et al. ([2018b](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0007)), it was shown that, among the previously discussed SL detectors, MCD and eMLD detectors yield the best performance. Since the complexity of eMLD is higher than MCD, the latter was highly recommended. However, one can argue that the Gaussian model in Eq. ([10.10](#c10.xhtml#c10-disp-0010)) may not be appropriate as the probability distribution of binary data ![images](images/c10-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow></math>. This motivates the development of a SL detector using a novel probabilistic model that is suitable for binary data.

![Figure 10.5 Description of a parametric learning.](images/c10f005.jpg)

[Figure 10.5](#c10.xhtml#R_c10-fig-0005) Description of a parametric learning.

2) *SL based on a Bernoulli‐like model (SLBM)*: A SL detector based on a Bernoulli‐like model is introduced. Here, data are assumed to be generated from the following probability distribution:

[(10.11)](#c10.xhtml#c10-R_disp-0011)![equation](images/c10-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>P</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8719;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>&#949;</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">c</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">i</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="bold">1</mtext> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo> <msub> <mi>r</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8800;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mrow> <mi>c</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </msubsup> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mrow> <mi>c</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mtext mathvariant="bold">1</mtext> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo> <msub> <mi>r</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mrow> <mi>c</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c10-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#952;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow></math> for all ![images](images/c10-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c10-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></math> denotes an indicator function with ![images](images/c10-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext mathvariant="bold">1</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> A</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> if ![images](images/c10-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext mathvariant="bold">1</mtext><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> A</mi><mo When one‐bit ADCs are employed at receivers, it is shown that SLBM outperforms SLGM since the former is developed for and more proper to the treatment of binary data.

The principle of parametric learning is very close to that of a nearest‐centroid classifier (NCC), which is a simple solution of the classification problem in SL. NCC assigns the class label of an unlabelled observed vector by using the centroid vectors that represent their classes. Similarly, in parametric learning, the SL detector works by selecting a message that has the minimum distance from the conditional mean vector of the pilot signals. This resemblance is a good example to show an interesting connection between a data‐detection problem in wireless communications and a classification problem in SL.

 

## 10.4 Low‐Complexity SL (LCSL) Detector

Although a parametric learning detector requires lower complexity than a non‐parametric learning detector, the computational complexity is prohibitive as the size of search‐space (e.g. ![images](images/c10-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>m</mi><mi>K</mi></msup></mrow></math>) grows exponentially with ![images](images/c10-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>. Thus, as in conventional MIMO systems, sphere decoding, which efficiently finds a reduced search space, can be considered. However, the conventional sphere decoding in Hassibi and Vikalo ([2005](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0003)) cannot be used directly due to the nonlinearity of the considered channel models. So‐called one‐bit sphere decodings (OSDs), which are suitable for one‐bit quantizations, have been proposed in Jeon et al. ([2018b](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0007)), Kim et al. ([2017](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0008)). In this section, OSD based on a hierarchical clustering forest (OSD‐HCF) is introduced, which can yield a higher‐quality reduced search space. In this method, a fast binary nearest neighbor search algorithm (flann) Muja and Lowe ([2012](#c10.xhtml#c10-bib-0015)) is used, which finds a reduced search space efficiently by exploiting hierarchical clustering structures. Combining with the SL detector, it is called a low‐complexity SL (LCSL) detector. The overall procedures of the LCSL detector are provided as follows:

1.  First decompose the (binary) Hamming space hierarchically so as to build a tree structure. It starts with choosing ![images](images/c10-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>J</mi></mrow></math> elements from ![images](images/c10-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> randomly, which act as ![images](images/c10-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>J</mi></mrow></math> cluster centroids.
2.  The previous step forms the ![images](images/c10-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>J</mi></mrow></math> clusters around these centroids, and the decomposition process is repeated recursively (see Algorithm 1).
3.  This process is performed ![images](images/c10-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> times to construct ![images](images/c10-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> T</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> T</mi></mrow><mi>W</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> trees.

The resulting trees in will be used in the data‐transmission phase to efficiently reduce the search space according to a new observation ![images](images/c10-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi></mrow></math>. It is noticeable that the algorithm constructs multiple hierarchical trees having possibly different decomposition structures, and thus is able to improve the quality of a resulting reduced search space.

As you see [Figure 10.6](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0006), we explain this process (Algorithm 1) by giving a simple example (![images](images/c10-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>16</mn></mrow></math>) in the case of a single tree. The decomposition procedure is applied into binary space (in this case, 16 ![images](images/c10-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>) hierarchically until the cluster size is less than ![images](images/c10-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>J</mi></mrow></math>, which is called the size of the leaf node. (A cluster size at the last hierarchical level can be called the size of the leaf node because the output structure of this process can be viewed as a tree: [Figure 10.7](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0007).) Also, the leaf node size equals branch factor ![images](images/c10-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>J</mi></mrow></math>. This is due to the reduction of the number of parameters and the calculation of approximate complexity. However, we skip this as it is not the main point of this section. If we operate this process multiple times, several distinctive trees (forest) are constructed.

**Data‐transmission phase:** Given a current observation ![images](images/c10-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi></mrow></math>, the search algorithm begins with traversing multiple trees in parallel (see Algorithm 2). Note that ![images](images/c10-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> multiple trees share a single priority queue (![images](images/c10-i0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> Q</mi></mrow></math>), and the nodes in the priority queue are arranged in order of shortest hamming distance with regard to the observation ![images](images/c10-i0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi></mrow></math>. In order to help you understand Algorithm 2, we provide a simple example ([Figure 10.8](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0008)) that finds a reduced search space based on the structure built in the prior example ([Figure 10.6](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0006)). During the first search, the observation continues selecting the closest centroid at each level until it reaches a leaf node. The elements included in the leaf node are returned into the reduced search space (![images](images/c10-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> S</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>). Moreover, the unselected centroids are put into the priority queue that sorts centroids in such an order that makes an efficient nearest‐neighbor search possible. For the second search, the same search method begins from the first node in the priority queue. This algorithm ends when it satisfies the predetermined size of the reduced search space (![images](images/c10-i0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> S</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></math>).

In [Figure 10.9](#c10.xhtml#c10-fig-0009), the search starts by going down from the root node to a leaf node simultaneously at each tree along the closest centroid to ![images](images/c10-i0130.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi></mrow></math> at each level. The search stops when it reaches a leaf node and it obtains approximately ![images](images/c10-i0132.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>J</mi></mrow></math> ![images](images/c10-i0133.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> contained in the leaf node of each tree. In the next step, the search starts from the first node of the shared priority queue in the same way. ## 10.5 Numerical Results

In this section, we evaluate the average bit‐error rate (BER) performances of the introduced SLGM and SLBM detectors. Furthermore, it is shown that the LCSL detector can achieve the original performance with much lower complexity for a large‐scale distributed MIMO system. For the simulations, a Rayleigh fading channel is considered for local wireless channels where each element of a channel matrix is drawn from an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) circularly symmetric complex Gaussian random variable with zero mean and unit variance. In addition, the relays' operations are assumed to be amplify‐and‐forward (AF), and QPSK modulation is assumed. However, it is remarkable that performance trends are kept for other relays' operations. Note that each relay is equipped with a single antenna. When training overhead is small (e.g. ![images](images/c10-i0135.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>T</mi></mrow></math> is small), an empirical error probability (e.g. ![images](images/c10-i0136.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#949;</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>) can be underestimated as zero, although it is actually not. This can cause a severe error‐floor problem. To prevent this, we assign a minimum value of ![images](images/c10-i0137.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>c</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> as ![images](images/c10-i0138.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>.

## 10.6 Conclusions

In this chapter, promising SL detectors were described for distributed multihop MIMO systems, especially when receivers are equipped with one‐bit ADCs. The SL detectors can be categorized as non‐parametric or parametric. The former have the benefit of a large training set (e.g. a large number of pilot signals) since the resulting empirical conditional probability distribution approaches a true one. However, this approach suffers from extremely high complexity. Parametric SL detectors can reduce this complexity by estimating representative vectors (called codewords) corresponding to each class (message) during the training phase. Furthermore, by combining them with one‐bit sphere decodings, they can perform very well with reasonable complexity. Thus, the SL‐based detectors produced in this chapter can be considered cutting‐edge for a nonlinear communication system.

# 11  
Adaptive Learning for Symbol Detection: A Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Space Approach

*Daniyal Amir Awan¹, Renato Luis Garrido Cavalcante², Masahario Yukawa³, and Slawomir Stanczak²*

¹*Network Information Theory Group, Technical University of Berlin, Berlin, Germany*

²*Wireless Communications and Networks, Fraunhofer Heinrich Hertz Institute & Network Information Theory Group, Technical University of Berlin, Berlin, Germany*

³*Department of Electronics and Electrical Engineering, Keio University, Yokohama, Japan*

 

## 11.1 Introduction

Solutions to problems in wireless communications are typically based on models that require, for example, channel state information, knowledge of interference patterns, and information about the phase of desired signals, to name a few. As a result, before sending any information over the wireless channel, transceivers traditionally estimate many model parameters. However, this approach has two major drawbacks that can severely impair the performance of communication systems. First, perfect estimation of parameters is impossible in general because of the presence of noise and the limitations of the algorithms being used. Second, the models themselves are only idealizations, and it is often unclear how well they can capture the true behavior of real systems.

To mitigate these handicaps of purely model‐based approaches, researchers have been proposing alternatives based on data‐driven approaches including machine learning. The idea is to replace some building blocks of model‐based transceivers with learning algorithms, with the intent to drastically reduce the number of assumptions about the models and the need for complex estimation techniques. However, this reduction in model knowledge brings many technical challenges, especially in the physical layer of the communication stack. In particular, some state‐of‐the‐art learning tools require large training sets and a long training time. However, in the physical layer, the environment (channel and user distribution, etc.) can be considered roughly constant only for a very short time, which can be all the time available to collect a training set based on pilots, train a machine, and perform the communication task. If this temporal aspect is not taken into account, then by the time enough samples are available to train existing learning algorithms, the propagation environment may have changed so drastically as to render the training set useless for the current propagation conditions, even if we assume that training can be performed instantaneously.

Against this background, this chapter introduces a novel machine learning algorithm for symbol detection in multiuser environments. We consider a challenging multiuser uplink scenario in which the number of antennas available at the base station may be smaller than the number of active users. More specifically, the proposed method is an adaptive (nonlinear) receive filter that learns to detect symbols from data directly, without performing any intermediate estimation tasks (e.g. channel estimation). Furthermore, the method is robust against abrupt changes of the wireless environment. We build upon recent adaptive learning methods in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) that have already been successfully applied to the *robust nonlinear beamforming* problem in Theodoridis et al. ([2011](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0007)), Slavakis et al. ([2009](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0005)). In contrast to these studies, rather than assuming knowledge of the angle of arrivals or channels of the desired user, we provide our algorithm with additional robustness against the vagaries of the wireless environment by considering partially linear filters, as proposed in Yukawa ([2015a](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0009)) in the context of a different application.

The rest of this chapter is organized as follows. We present the relevant mathematical background in [Section 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0002). After presenting our system model in [Section 11.3](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0008), we present our symbol‐detection method in detail in [Section 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0011). Simulations are presented in [Section 11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0018), and [Section 11.6](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0019) summarizes the chapter.

By ![images](images/c11-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8741;</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>&#183;</mo><mspace width="0.1em"/><msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> we denote the conventional Euclidean norm in ![images](images/c11-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></math>. If ![images](images/c11-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#954;</mi><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math> is a function of two variables, we denote the function of a single variable obtained by keeping the second argument fixed to ![images](images/c11-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow></math> by ![images](images/c11-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8614;</mo><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

 

### 11.2.1 Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces

The proposed algorithms for symbol detection are based on the theory of reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs), which have been extensively used in diverse fields such as statistics, probability, signal processing, and machine learning, among others Berlinet and Thomas‐Agnan ([2004](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0002)), Theodoridis et al. ([2011](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0007)), Slavakis et al. ([2009](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0005)), Yukawa ([2015a](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0009)). These spaces can be formally defined as follows:[1](#c11a.xhtml#c11-note-0001)

For readers who are not familiar with these particular Hilbert spaces, [Definition 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-fea-0002) may not give any hints about the functions ![images](images/c11-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#954;</mi><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math> that qualify as reproducing kernels or an intuition on the functions ![images](images/c11-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math> in an RKHS. Therefore, it may be enlightening to construct inner product spaces (or pre‐Hilbert spaces) for which RKHSs emerge as their completion (this construction can be seen as part of the Moore‐Aronszajn theorem Aronszajn ([1950](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0001))(Berlinet and Thomas‐Agnan, [2004](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0002), Ch. 1)). For this purpose, we now introduce the concept of *positive definite kernels*, which we later show to be equivalent to the concept of reproducing kernels:

We emphasize that this definition requires no structure on the set ![images](images/c11-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow></math>. However, in the application considered in this chapter, we focus on the case ![images](images/c11-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo>&#8834;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></math>. We also note that the *positivity* property in the definition is equivalent to the following property: for arbitrary ![images](images/c11-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c11-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow><mi>M</mi></msup></mrow></math>, the matrix ![images](images/c11-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">K</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> with the element in the ![images](images/c11-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th row and ![images](images/c11-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>th column given by ![images](images/c11-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">K</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi></mrow></msub><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> has to be positive semi‐definite. Note that kernels can be further categorized into positive definite kernels and positive semi‐definite kernels depending on whether ![images](images/c11-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">K</mi></mrow></math> is always positive definite or only positive semi‐definite for distinct vectors ![images](images/c11-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow><mi>M</mi></msup></mrow></math>. However, in this study we do not make this distinction.

To construct a pre‐Hilbert space of functions associated with a given positive definite kernel ![images](images/c11-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, we define the following vector space of functions ![images](images/c11-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math>:
