stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, which is the Hilbert space denoted by ![images](images/c11-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, satisfies both: (i) ![images](images/c11-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow></math> and (ii) ![images](images/c11-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. As a result, ![images](images/c11-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is a RKHS. Furthermore, positive definite functions are reproducing kernels, and the converse can also be shown to be valid. The Moore‐Aronszajn theorem also states that, given a positive definite kernel ![images](images/c11-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#954;</mi></mrow></math>, there is only one Hilbert space for which ![images](images/c11-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#954;</mi></mrow></math> is the reproducing kernel.

 

### 11.2.2 Sum Spaces of Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces

We now briefly summarize the ideas originally proposed in Yukawa ([2015a](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0009)). Suppose that we have the task of learning an unknown nonlinear function ![images](images/c11-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math> (where ![images](images/c11-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo>&#8834;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>d</mi></msup></mrow></math>) that can be decomposed into the sum of ![images](images/c11-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> distinct components, such as high‐ and low‐frequency components, linear and nonlinear components, and periodic and aperiodic components. Assume that each of these components belongs to one of ![images](images/c11-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math> RKHSs ![images](images/c11-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi>Q</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> of functions mapping ![images](images/c11-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow></math> to the real line. In this case, the unknown function ![images](images/c11-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> is a member of the *sum space* defined by

![equation](images/c11-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><munder><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> Q</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi mathvariant="script"> Q</mi><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>Q</mi></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> 

For fixed (strictly) positive weights ![images](images/c11-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow></math>, we can equip the space ![images](images/c11-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></math> with the (weighted) norm

(11.2)![equation](images/c11-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>&#8704;</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> </mrow> <mo>+</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mspace width="1em"/> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <mi>f</mi> <msubsup> <mrow> <mo>&#8741;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> </mrow> <mo>+</mo> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>:</mo> <mspace width="-0.1em"/> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <munder> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>q</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> Q</mi> </mrow> </munder> <msubsup> <mi>w</mi> <mi>q</mi> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <msubsup> <mrow> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>q</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8741;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> </mrow> <mi>q</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi>f</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>q</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> Q</mi> </mrow> </munder> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>q</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>&#8704;</mo> <mi>q</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> Q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>q</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> </mrow> <mi>q</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

and it can be shown that the resulting normed vector space ![images](images/c11-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8741;</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>&#183;</mo><mspace width="0.1em"/><msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is also the RKHS ![images](images/c11-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> associated with the reproducing kernel ![images](images/c11-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#954;</mi><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><msub><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> Q</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math> (Berlinet and Thomas‐Agnan, [2004](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0002), p. 24)Aronszajn ([1950](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0001)).

If no additional structure is imposed on ![images](images/c11-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, then, for a given function ![images](images/c11-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mo>+</mo></msup></mrow></math>, the decomposition ![images](images/c11-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> Q</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c11-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>q</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> Q</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>q</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math> is not necessarily unique, which in turn makes the computation of the norm in Eq. ([11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0005)) a particularly challenging task in general. One notable exception for the non‐uniqueness of the decomposition is shown here:

From a practical perspective, with a sum space satisfying the assumption in [Remark 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-fea-0006), algorithms can perform many operations by simply considering the Hilbert spaces ![images](images/c11-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>,…, ![images](images/c11-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi>Q</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> separately and by summing the results, as done in Eqs. ([11.3](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0006)) and ([11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0007)), for example. By doing so, hard‐to‐solve optimization problems, such as those required for the evaluation of norms in Eq. ([11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0005)), are avoided. The algorithms described later in this chapter use a sum space of this type.

 

## 11.3 System Model

We now turn our attention to the adaptive learning method for symbol detection in multiuser environments. For brevity, in the following we focus on the uplink of a wireless network, but we emphasize that the proposed approaches can also be used in the downlink.

![Figure 11.1 Multiuser uplink: The received baseband signal images consists of the desired signal and noise plus interference from users in the same cell and also from users from other cells.](images/c11f001.jpg)

[Figure 11.1](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-fig-0001) Multiuser uplink: The received baseband signal ![images](images/c11-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> consists of the desired signal and noise plus interference from users in the same cell and also from users from other cells.

 

### 11.3.1 Symbol Detection in Multiuser Environments

Consider the uplink in [Figure 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0001), where a base station with ![images](images/c11-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math> antennas receives a noisy superposition of signals from ![images](images/c11-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math> users, each of which is equipped with a single antenna. The receive baseband signal at the base station at time ![images](images/c11-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math> is given by

(11.5)![equation](images/c11-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>K</mi> </munderover> <msqrt> <mrow> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msqrt> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi> <mi>M</mi> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c11-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c11-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c11-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi><mi>M</mi></msup></mrow></math> are the power, the modulation symbol, and the channel, respectively, for user ![images](images/c11-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math>, and where ![images](images/c11-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi><mi>M</mi></msup></mrow></math> denotes noise. As is common in the literature, we assume that the channels between the users and the base station undergo *Rayleigh block fading*. Under this assumption, the channels remain constant for a block of complex‐valued channel symbols known as the *coherence block*. More precisely, let ![images](images/c11-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![images](images/c11-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math> denote the start of the coherence block ![images](images/c11-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c11-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>block</mtext></msub></mrow></math> is the coherence block size. Then, ![images](images/c11-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![images](images/c11-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8707;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi><mi>M</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![images](images/c11-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup></mrow></math>; i.e., ![images](images/c11-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>b</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> is the fixed channel of user ![images](images/c11-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, lasting from ![images](images/c11-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>b</mi></msub></mrow></math> to ![images](images/c11-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, for the coherence block ![images](images/c11-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>.

Now, we introduce the general idea of the proposed learning algorithm from a high‐level perspective. Without any loss of generality, we outline the learning process for detecting the data symbols of user 1 in Eq. ([11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0008)). In mathematical terms, the algorithm should ideally learn a function ![images](images/c11-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi><mi>M</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></mrow></math> such that ![images](images/c11-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.[2](#c11a.xhtml#c11-note-0002) To this end, in each coherence block ![images](images/c11-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math>, user 1 transmits a sequence of pilot symbols ![images](images/c11-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c11-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>block</mtext></msub></mrow></math>. The pilots are also known to the base station, and it uses them, along with the corresponding received signals ![images](images/c11-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, to learn ![images](images/c11-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math>. Unlike traditional batch learning methods, the proposed algorithm improves its estimate of ![images](images/c11-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> sequentially with each incoming training sample; i.e. it operates in an *online* fashion and does not wait for the acquisition of the entire batch ![images](images/c11-i0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> S</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to start the learning process. The detection can therefore, in principle, be performed without any delay starting at ![images](images/c11-i0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub></mrow></math>, which is important in high‐data‐rate systems. Denoting the latest estimate (at ![images](images/c11-i0123.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>) of ![images](images/c11-i0124.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> by ![images](images/c11-i0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>:</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi><mi>M</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></mrow></math>, we use ![images](images/c11-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>f</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></msub></mrow></math> as the estimate of the information symbols ![images](images/c11-i0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>train</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mrow><mi>b</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></msub></mrow></math>.

 

### 11.3.2 Detection of Complex‐Valued Symbols in Real Hilbert Spaces

Before proceeding with the description of the learning algorithm for symbol detection, we need to make a brief technical detour. The reason is that the theory presented in [Section 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0002) involves vector spaces of functions mapping members of an abstract set ![images](images/c11-i0131.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow></math> (see [Definition 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-fea-0004)) to real numbers. However, in the problem described in [Section 11.3.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0009), we have to learn a function mapping complex‐valued vectors in ![images](images/c11-i0132.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi><mi>M</mi></msup></mrow></math> \[the input signals ![images](images/c11-i0133.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>\] to complex numbers \[the symbols ![images](images/c11-i0134.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>\]. We could naturally define ![images](images/c11-i0135.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi><mi>M</mi></msup></mrow></math> because there are no restrictions imposed on ![images](images/c11-i0136.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow></math>, but the co‐domain of the functions being learned requires special attention because we are working with real RKHSs. To deal with this issue, we use the approach described in Slavakis et al. ([2009](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0005)), Yukawa et al. ([2013](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0011)), which exploits the trivial bijection between ![images](images/c11-i0137.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c11-i0138.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> for arbitrary ![images](images/c11-i0139.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math> to enable the estimation of complex‐valued symbols with real RKHSs. In more detail, we define ![images](images/c11-i0140.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, and, for each ![images](images/c11-i0141.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math>, we split ![images](images/c11-i0142.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> in Eq. ([11.5](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0008)) into two ![images](images/c11-i0143.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>‐dimensional vectors given by ![images](images/c11-i0144.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><mi>&#8476;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi>&#8465;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8890;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c11-i0145.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><mi>&#8465;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#8476;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8890;</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Similarly, the complex‐valued symbols ![images](images/c11-i0146.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are mapped to vectors ![images](images/c11-i0147.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><mi>&#8476;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi>&#8465;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>b</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>. Our task is now to learn a function ![images](images/c11-i0148.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math> that operates on ![images](images/c11-i0149.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c11-i0150.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> separately, as depicted in [Figure 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0002). The relation between ![images](images/c11-i0151.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> and the ideal complex‐valued function ![images](images/c11-i0152.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math> is given by ![images](images/c11-i0153.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![images](images/c11-i0154.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>i</mi><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c11-i0155.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> is the solution to the equation ![images](images/c11-i0156.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.

In the remainder of this chapter, to align our terminology with that of previous studies Slavakis et al. ([2009](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0005)), Theodoridis et al. ([2011](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0007)), we will use the words *filter* and *function* interchangeably when referring to the function ![images](images/c11-i0166.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> and its estimates.

 

## 11.4 The Proposed Learning Algorithm

Two important properties of an ideal receive filter are *high spatial resolution* and *robustness* against changes in the environment. In Slavakis et al. ([2009](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0005)), the authors design a high‐resolution nonlinear receive filter (which they refer to as a *nonlinear beamformer*) in an infinite‐dimensional RKHS associated with the Gaussian kernel. It has been shown that this receive filter outperforms the *linearly constrained minimum variance* receive filter Bourgeois and Minker ([2009](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0003)). However, when compared to linear filters, one of the main drawbacks of nonlinear filters is that they are in general less robust against changes in the environment. For instance, in the case of linear filtering, if a user leaves the system, the signal‐to‐interference‐plus‐noise ratios (SINRs) of the remaining users improve. However, this property cannot be ensured in general with nonlinear filters; performance may in fact deteriorate.

To achieve a good trade‐off between the robustness of conventional linear filters and the high resolution of nonlinear filters, we incorporate linear and nonlinear components in our filter design by considering the theory in [Section 11.2.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0006). In particular, we propose to work in the sum space of a linear kernel and a Gaussian kernel, defined as ![images](images/c11-i0167.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![images](images/c11-i0168.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c11-i0169.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo>&#8741;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">u</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi><msubsup><mo>&#8741;</mo><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math>, respectively. It is known that ![images](images/c11-i0170.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c11-i0171.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub></mrow></math> are reproducing kernels associated with RKHSs, which we denote by ![images](images/c11-i0172.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>[3](#c11a.xhtml#c11-note-0003) and ![images](images/c11-i0178.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""><mrow><mo>&#183;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, respectively. By defining ![images](images/c11-i0179.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub></mrow></math>, we construct the sum RKHS associated with the kernel ![images](images/c11-i0180.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#954;</mi><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c11-i0181.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> are fixed weights. ### 11.4.1 The Canonical Iteration

We now proceed to pose the learning problem as a special case of the *convex feasibility problem* involving (possibly) countably infinitely many sets. This problem is then solved with a particular version of the *adaptive projected subgradient method* Yamada and Ogura ([2005](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0008)). To simplify the exposition, we assume that all transmitted symbols are pilots, and the coherence block size ![images](images/c11-i0192.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>block</mtext></msub></mrow></math> is infinite. By doing so, we highlight that the computational complexity during training is kept at low levels even if the number of pilots is very large, and later we show that the resulting algorithm has good performance with few pilots.

By recalling that an ideal filter ![images](images/c11-i0193.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow></math> should satisfy the equalities in Eq. ([11.6](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0009)), we can expect that reasonable estimates of an ideal filter should belong to closed convex sets ![images](images/c11-i0194.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> given by

(11.7)![equation](images/c11-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>&#8704;</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>:</mo> <mspace width="-0.1em"/> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>h</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> <mo>:</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>h</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#954;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mo>&#183;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>s</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>&#949;</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c11-i0195.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi>&#8734;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo></mrow></math> is a relaxation parameter used to, for example, combat erroneous assumptions and the detrimental effects of noise in measurements. With these sets, similarly to the problems in Theodoridis et al. ([2011](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0007)), we pose the learning problem as follows:

(11.8)![equation](images/c11-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext>For some</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mtext>find</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msup> <mi>f</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> <mtext>such that</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <msup> <mi>f</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <munder> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8898;</mo> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where we assume that ![images](images/c11-i0196.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mo>&#8898;</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>&#8709;</mi></mrow></math>. Briefly, we seek filters that belong to all but finitely many sets in Eq. ([11.7](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0010)). Removing a finite number of sets from the intersection in Eq. ([11.8](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0011)) enables us to derive computationally simple learning algorithms based on the adaptive projected subgradient method Yamada and Ogura ([2005](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0008)) (note, however, that the solution to Eq. ([11.8](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0011)) belongs to infinitely many sets in ![images](images/c11-i0197.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>). In particular, with some mild technical assumptions, the problem in Eq. ([11.8](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0011)) can be solved with a particular case of the adaptive projected subgradient method Yamada and Ogura ([2005](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0008)), which we now describe.

Denote by ![images](images/c11-i0198.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> J</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8834;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math> the indices of the sets in ![images](images/c11-i0199.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> that we intend to process at iteration ![images](images/c11-i0200.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math> of the training procedure. In particular, note that ![images](images/c11-i0201.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> J</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> can be changed at every iteration ![images](images/c11-i0202.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, which is useful to process the sets in ![images](images/c11-i0203.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> as soon as they become available, or to adjust the computation complexity of the algorithm according to the hardware capabilities of the receiver, or both. Starting from ![images](images/c11-i0204.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, the canonical training procedure produces a sequence of filters ![images](images/c11-i0205.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> in ![images](images/c11-i0206.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow></math> with the iterations given by

(11.9)![equation](images/c11-math-0012.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>&#8704;</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>j</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> J</mi> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mrow> </munder> <msubsup> <mi>q</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>P</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c11-i0207.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the projection of ![images](images/c11-i0208.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> onto the set ![images](images/c11-i0209.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c11-i0210.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#946;</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> given by

and where ![images](images/c11-i0211.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> J</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are non‐negative weights satisfying ![images](images/c11-i0212.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> J</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub><msubsup><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. Note that the iterates produced by this algorithm are steered toward the sets with proportionally large weights, which is a feature that can be useful in scenarios where some sets are known to be more reliable than others.

In particular, the iteration in Eq. ([11.9](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0012)) has the following desirable property. If ![images](images/c11-i0213.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8713;</mo><msub><mrow><mo>&#8745;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> J</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></msub><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>, then (Yamada and Ogura, [2005](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0008), Theorem 2)

![equation](images/c11-math-0014.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>&#9733;</mo></msup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mo>&#8745;</mo><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>&#9733;</mo></msup><msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><mo>&#8741;</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>&#9733;</mo></msup><msub><mo>&#8741;</mo><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow></msub><mo>;</mo></mrow></math> 

i.e. the recursion in Eq. ([11.9](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0012)) at time ![images](images/c11-i0214.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is guaranteed to move ![images](images/c11-i0215.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> to a point closer to the solution to problem Eq. ([11.8](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0011)). For other properties of the algorithm, including its convergence, we refer readers to Yamada and Ogura ([2005](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0008))

 

### 11.4.2 Practical Issues

Next, we look at issues related to the implementation of Eq. ([11.9](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0012)). The first issue is the selection of an appropriate set ![images](images/c11-i0216.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> J</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>. A reasonable and simple way of selecting ![images](images/c11-i0217.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> J</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> is to include the ![images](images/c11-i0218.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math> most recent training samples. More precisely, at time ![images](images/c11-i0219.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math>, we define ![images](images/c11-i0220.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> J</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> as the set given by ![images](images/c11-i0221.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> J</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>W</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math> if ![images](images/c11-i0222.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mi>W</mi></mrow></math>, or ![images](images/c11-i0223.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> J</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math> otherwise. The window size ![images](images/c11-i0224.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>W</mi></mrow></math> is a design parameter chosen according to the available computational power. Larger sizes typically improve the performance at the cost of increased computational complexity.

The second issue pertains to the memory requirement and the complexity of the learning framework. To understand the main challenges, let us look at how the canonical algorithm in Eq. ([11.9](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0012)) proceeds. At time ![images](images/c11-i0225.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math>, we can show that the filter estimate generated by Eq. ([11.9](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0012)) is given by ![images](images/c11-i0226.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c11-i0227.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mover accent="true"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are real coefficients that depend on the sets ![images](images/c11-i0228.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> Theodoridis et al. ([2011](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0007)). Since ![images](images/c11-i0229.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> is expressed as a linear combination of the elements in the set ![images](images/c11-i0230.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>,

![equation](images/c11-math-0015.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>span</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8834;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> 

Note that ![images](images/c11-i0231.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is also a Hilbert space if equipped with the same inner product of the sum RKHS ![images](images/c11-i0232.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow></math>. In the following, we will refer to ![images](images/c11-i0233.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> as the *learning dictionary*. At each iteration ![images](images/c11-i0234.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math> of the algorithm, a new element ![images](images/c11-i0235.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is admitted, and the dictionary is extended to ![images](images/c11-i0236.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8746;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>. It follows that ![images](images/c11-i0237.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8834;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8834;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow></math>, and the extended space ![images](images/c11-i0238.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> is spanned by ![images](images/c11-i0239.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Therefore, to evaluate ![images](images/c11-i0240.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![images](images/c11-i0241.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> (by using the reproducing property discussed in [Section 11.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0002)), we need to store ![images](images/c11-i0242.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi><mtext>mem</mtext></msubsup><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> along with the coefficients ![images](images/c11-i0243.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> in the memory of the receiver (note: ![images](images/c11-i0244.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>&#8834;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow></math> can be trivially recovered from ![images](images/c11-i0245.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi><mtext>mem</mtext></msubsup><mo>&#8834;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>). Moreover, the coefficients ![images](images/c11-i0246.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, the number of which increases with ![images](images/c11-i0247.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>, are required at each iteration ![images](images/c11-i0248.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> by the projections ![images](images/c11-i0249.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> J</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> ![images](images/c11-i0250.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> in Eq. ([11.9](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0012)). This fact shows that the memory requirements and the computational complexity may become prohibitive when ![images](images/c11-i0251.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> becomes sufficiently large. To keep the complexity and the memory requirements of the learning algorithm at manageable levels, we use online dictionary learning techniques, as explained next.

 

### 11.4.3 Online Dictionary Learning

It follows from [Section 11.2.2](#c11.xhtml#c11-sec-0006) that the filter estimate ![images](images/c11-i0252.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> at time ![images](images/c11-i0253.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></math> can be uniquely decomposed as the sum of its linear and Gaussian components as follows:
