To curb the growth of the dictionaries ![images](images/c11-i0259.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c11-i0260.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> as a function of ![images](images/c11-i0261.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> in such a way as to have a minor impact on the performance of the filter ![images](images/c11-i0262.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>, we use *dictionary sparsification*, as explained next.

Dictionary sparsification has its origins in the seminal work in Engel et al. ([2004](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0004)), but here we use an approach similar to that proposed in Yukawa ([2015b](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0010)), which handles the linear and Gaussian components of the sequence ![images](images/c11-i0263.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">N</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> of filters separately. In the proposed approach, we use admission control to verify whether the most recent inputs ![images](images/c11-i0264.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c11-i0265.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> should be added to the dictionaries ![images](images/c11-i0266.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c11-i0267.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, respectively. Briefly, the idea is to check if ![images](images/c11-i0268.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c11-i0269.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> can be approximated (in some sense) by a linear combination of elements previously admitted in dictionaries ![images](images/c11-i0270.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c11-i0271.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Newly arriving elements are added to the dictionary only if such an approximation is not possible. The particular techniques for dictionary sparsification of the linear and Gaussian components of the proposed filter are described in the next two subsections.

 

#### 11.4.3.1 Dictionary for the Linear Component

Admission control for the linear part can be easily done as follows. Since ![images](images/c11-i0272.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub></mrow></math> is nothing but the Euclidean space ![images](images/c11-i0273.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, it is spanned by the Euclidean basis ![images](images/c11-i0274.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c11-i0275.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is a vector having a one at the ![images](images/c11-i0276.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>th index and zeros elsewhere. So, every ![images](images/c11-i0277.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> can be written in terms of a linear combination given by ![images](images/c11-i0278.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi></mrow></msubsup><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi><mi>m</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c11-i0279.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> the ![images](images/c11-i0280.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>th entry of ![images](images/c11-i0281.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>. #### 11.4.3.2 Dictionary for the Gaussian Component

The proposed sparsification technique for the dictionary ![images](images/c11-i0293.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is based on the studies in Engel et al. ([2004](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0004)), Slavakis and Theodoridis ([2008](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0006)), and it can be summarized as follows. Suppose that we start with the dictionary ![images](images/c11-i0294.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>&#954;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>. At time ![images](images/c11-i0295.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>, we have the dictionary ![images](images/c11-i0296.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, and the objective is to determine whether the newly arriving element ![images](images/c11-i0297.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> should be added to ![images](images/c11-i0298.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to construct ![images](images/c11-i0299.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Informally, if ![images](images/c11-i0300.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> can be “well approximated” by any vector in the subspace ![images](images/c11-i0301.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>span</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi ![images](images/c11-i0302.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>span</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> can also be “well approximated” by functions in ![images](images/c11-i0303.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>span</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi ## 11.5 Simulation

For the simulation, we consider ![images](images/c11-i0323.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> users and a single base station with ![images](images/c11-i0324.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> antennas. The modulation scheme is quadrature phase‐shift keying (QPSK). The simulation parameters are shown in [Table 11.1](#c11.xhtml#c11-tbl-0001). The average user performance is shown in terms of the averaged gray coded bit error rate (BER). We simulate two Rayleigh channel blocks, each consisting of ![images](images/c11-i0325.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>block</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>500</mn></mrow></math> complex channel symbols, and we average results over 100 channel realizations. To show the online learning progress of Eq. ([11.10](#c11.xhtml#c11-disp-0018)), we evaluate the detection performance for every 100 training samples.

In the following, we denote our proposed method by *PLAF*. [Figure 11.3](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0003) compares the performance of *PLAF* against the *minimum mean squared error* (MMSE) receive filter with symbol‐level *successive interference cancellation* (SIC), commonly referred to as the symbol‐level *MMSE‐SIC* receiver. We assume perfect channel knowledge for the *MMSE‐SIC*, which is an unrealistic assumption in practice, but it highlights the advantages of the proposed method (which does not require channel knowledge explicitly). To demonstrate that *PLAF* has a high resolution, we are interested in the number of users that we can detect, with a certain average user BER, for a fixed number of antennas at the base station. [Figure 11.3](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0003) shows that *PLAF* is able to support a larger number of users than the *MMSE‐SIC*‐based receiver.

![ Table 11.1  Simulation parameters.](images/c11-i0326.png)

 [Table 11.1](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-tbl-0001)  Simulation parameters.

![Figure 11.3 Comparison between PLAF and MMSE‐SIC for images.](images/c11f003.jpg)

[Figure 11.3](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-fig-0003) Comparison between PLAF and MMSE‐SIC for ![images](images/c11-i0343.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.

![Figure 11.4 Comparison between PLAF and NLAF for images.](images/c11f004.jpg)

[Figure 11.4](#c11.xhtml#R_c11-fig-0004) Comparison between PLAF and NLAF for ![images](images/c11-i0344.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>.

In addition to *MMSE‐SIC*, we also compare the proposed method with the purely nonlinear adaptive receive filter, which we denote by *NLAF*. The difference between *PLAF* and *NLAF* is that *NLAF* employs a Gaussian kernel only. With this comparison, we demonstrate that *PLAF* is more robust than *NLAF* against changes in the environment. Specifically, at the start of each block, we change user channels and the user activity. We denote by ![images](images/c11-i0342.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mspace width="0.3em"/><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> the probability with which all users are active during a block. After 500 channel symbols, the channel and user activity are changed, which is a common scenario in communication systems. It is clear from [Figure 11.4](#c11.xhtml#c11-fig-0004) that *PLAF* is more robust against changes in the environment than *NLAF*.

 

## 11.6 Conclusion

In this chapter, we showed that the theory of RKHS in sum spaces can be applied in the design of robust receive filters for symbol detection. In more detail, we used a particular version of the adaptive projected subgradient method to generate a sequence of filters that can be uniquely decomposed into a linear component and a nonlinear component constructed with a Gaussian kernel. By doing so, we equipped the resulting algorithm with the robustness of linear filters and the high performance of nonlinear filters. Simulations have shown that the learning algorithm is able to cope with small training sets and abrupt changes in the environment. In the simulated scenario, the proposed method outperformed, in particular, the traditional MMSE‐SIC with perfect channel knowledge.

[(A.1)](#c11a.xhtml#c11-R_disp-0019)![equation](images/c11-math-0019.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold">P</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#954;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mo>&#183;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>S</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </munderover> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#950;</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>l</mi> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </msubsup> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold">&#936;</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c11-i0365.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#950;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is given by ![images](images/c11-i0366.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#950;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">K</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#958;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow></math>; the vector ![images](images/c11-i0367.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#958;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> is given as

![equation](images/c11-math-0020.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#958;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><mtable columnalign="left"><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#936;</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mi>&#8942;</mi></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><msub><mrow><mfenced open="&#9001;" close="&#9002;" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">&#936;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>S</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> 

Suppose now that ![images](images/c11-i0368.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">K</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> is given; then the distance of ![images](images/c11-i0369.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> from ![images](images/c11-i0370.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the solution to Slavakis and Theodoridis ([2008](#c11a.xhtml#c11-bib-0006))

![equation](images/c11-math-0021.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#958;</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#950;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> 

Given ![images](images/c11-i0371.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c11-i0372.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#958;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#950;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow></math>, the inverse ![images](images/c11-i0375.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> to ![images](images/c11-i0376.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">K</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, which further enables us to calculate ![images](images/c11-i0377.png)<math In more detail, we initialize the inverse by ![images](images/c11-i0380.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">K</mi></mrow><mrow><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. For ![images](images/c11-i0381.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> if ![images](images/c11-i0382.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is admitted to the dictionary, i.e. if ![images](images/c11-i0383.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> D</mi></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#8746;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>&#954;</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">G</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>, then

![equation](images/c11-math-0022.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">K</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>:</mo><mspace width="-0.1em"/><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><mtable columnalign="left"><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">K</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#950;</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#950;</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfrac></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#950;</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfrac></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd columnalign="center"><mo>&#8722;</mo><mfrac><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#950;</mi><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mo>&#8890;</mo></msup></mrow><mrow><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfrac></mtd><mtd columnalign="center"><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msubsup><mi>d</mi><mi>n</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></mfrac></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></mfenced><mo>,</mo></mrow></math>

# 12  
Machine Learning for Joint Channel Equalization and Signal Detection

*Lin Zhang¹, and Lie‐Liang Yang²*

¹*School of Electronics and Information Technology, Sun Yat‐sen University, Guangzhou, China*

²*School of Electronics and Computer Science, University of Southampton, Southampton, UK*

 

## 12.1 Introduction

Over the last two decades, wireless communication has faced the demand to provide services anywhere. One of the vital technical challenges to achieve this is to support high reliability and high‐data‐rate communication in communication environments where signals experience severe inter‐symbol interference (ISI) caused by multipath signal propagation embedded in broadband signal transmissions (Ranhotra et al., [2017](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0046)). Another technical challenge is the mitigation of nonlinear signal distortions caused by imperfect design of wireless transceivers (Olmos et al., [2010](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0033)).

In wireless communications, channel equalization is the main technique to combat the effect of ISI (Rappaport, [2002](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0047)). Various equalizers have been proposed and implemented, which can be used to mitigate ISI and even to exploit the dispersive nature of wireless signals, in order to improve reliability. Among the family of channel equalization, adaptive equalizers have been proposed and applied to track the time‐varying characteristics of wireless mobile channels.

Adaptive equalization typically includes a training phase and a tracking phase. During the training phase, a given training sequence is sent by a transmitter to a receiver in order to implement a proper setting for the equalizer in the receiver. After training, user data can then be sent. During this stage, the adaptive equalizer may further estimate the channel statistics and use the information to update the adaptive filter's coefficients, in order for the adaptive filter to adapt to time‐varying communication environments.

In general, equalization techniques can be classified into two categories – linear and nonlinear equalization – depending on whether the output of an adaptive equalizer is fed back for performance enhancement (Chiu and Chao, [1996](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0013)). Specifically, in the family of linear equalization, the most commonly used are zero‐forcing (ZF) and minimum mean‐square error (MMSE) equalizers (Haykin, [1986](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0026)). In applications where channel distortion is too severe to be handled by linear equalizers, nonlinear equalizers are usually introduced, which can achieve higher reliability than linear equalization, but usually with high complexity. In the family of nonlinear equalization, there are typically three types of nonlinear methods developed: the decision feedback equalizer (DFE), the maximum likelihood symbol detection (MLSD) assisted equalizer, and the maximum likelihood sequence estimation (MLSE) assisted equalizer (Uesugi et al., [1989](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0055)). Among these three, the MLSE equalizer is optimal in the sense that it minimizes the probability of sequence errors. However, the classic MLSE equalizer requires that the channel statistics are known to the receiver. Furthermore, the MLSE equalizer's complexity grows exponentially with the number of taps of the channel impulse response (CIR) (Patwary and Rapajic, [2005](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0041)).

Conventional equalizers deconvolve received signals to combat distortions induced by channels and, ultimately, to recover the received message. Therefore, conventional equalizers can be viewed as inverse filters, and the joint response function of a channel and the corresponding equalizer should be close to an ideal delay function (Lee and Messerschmitt, [1994](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0029)). Accordingly, the complexity of equalization is dependent on the channels and may be very high in practical communication environments, where multiple reflections, multiple refractions and scattering, etc. exist.

In order to reduce the computational cost of traditional equalizers, machine learning (ML) based equalizers have been proposed for ISI suppression. In channel equalization, typical ML methods include multilayer perceptron (MLP) (Peng et al., [1991](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0042)), radial basis functions (RBFs) (Guha and Patra, [2009](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0025)), recurrent RBFs (Cid‐Sueiro and Figueiras‐Vidal, [1993](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0014)), and Pao networks (Arcens et al., [1992](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0002)). In these ML‐based equalizers, in principle, each class is defined by the possible output of the symbol alphabet and a proper nonlinear boundary found in a higher dimensional space. Hence, ML‐based channel equalization can be viewed as a problem of pattern recognition. Consequently, the complexity of ML‐based equalization is mainly determined by the symbol number and the size of the constructed space, but is not determined by the CIRs. In addition to those previously mentioned, other benefits of ML‐based channel equalizers include their intelligent and adaptive signal‐processing capabilities, which enable them to operate in dynamic and time‐varying wireless communication environments.

In this chapter, our focus is on ML‐based channel equalization and data detection, which utilize deep learning neural networks (NNs) to learn and formulate the feature sets of time‐varying wireless channels in order for them to be efficiently operated in highly dynamic wireless channels.

The rest of this chapter is organized as follows. After a brief overview of ML‐based equalizers in [Section 12.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0002), in [Section 12.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0011) we describe three classic equalization algorithms: ZF equalization, MMSE equalization, and MLSE equalization. [Section 12.4](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0015) provides the details of the NN models to be used for channel equalization, and presents the structure as well as the training process of NN‐based equalization. Then, in [Section 12.5](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0025), we investigate the performance of orthogonal frequency‐division multiplexing (OFDM) systems involving NN‐based channel equalization. Finally, [Section 12.6](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0030) concludes this chapter.

 

## 12.2 Overview of Neural Network‐Based Channel Equalization

By exploiting the nonlinear characteristics of neural networks (NNs), NN‐based channel equalizers are capable of extracting the key features of communication channels and combating inter‐symbol interference (ISI) intelligently with the aid of high‐efficiency NN algorithms, including MLP (Gibson et al., [1989a](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0020), [b](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0021)), functional link artificial NN (FLANN) (Patra and Pal, [1995](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0037); Patra et al., [1999](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0038)), radial basis function NN (RBFNN) (Chen et al., [1992](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0009), [1993b](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0011)), self‐constructing recurrent fuzzy NN (SCRFNN) (Lin et al., [2005](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0031); Chang et al., [2010](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0007)), recurrent neural networks (RNNs) (Kechriotis et al., [1994](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0028); Zhang et al., [2004](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0068)), deep learning (DL) (Ye and Li, [2017](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0065); Ye et al., [2018](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0066)), extreme learning machines (ELMs) (Tang et al., [2016](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0054); Yang et al., [2018](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0062)), etc. In the following, we provide a detailed overview of research on NN‐based channel equalization.

 

### 12.2.1 Multilayer Perceptron‐Based Equalizers

Channel equalization can be regarded as a classification problem, where the equalizer is constructed as a decision‐making device with the motivation to classify the transmitted signals as accurately as possible. In this way, (Gibson et al., [1989a](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0020), [b](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0021)) proposed an adaptive equalizer using a NN architecture based on the MLP, to combat ISI over linear channels with white Gaussian noise. Following this work, (Chen et al., [1990](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0008); Gibson et al., [1991](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0022)) applied the MLP‐based equalizer for nonlinear channels with colored Gaussian noise, which demonstrated that the MLP‐based equalizer is able to achieve bit error rate (BER) performance close to that of the optimal equalizer. However, MLP‐based equalizers in these references considered mainly real‐valued and bipolar signals.

In the MLP‐based equalizers considered previously, the sigmoid function used by the output layer nodes confines network output to the range ![images](images/c12-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>. Therefore, by relaxing or replacing it with other functions, MLP‐based equalizers can be designed to support multiple amplitude signals, such as pulse amplitude modulation (PAM) signals. Furthermore, in order to support complex quadratic‐amplitude modulation (QAM) signals, (Peng et al., [1991](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0042), [1992](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0043)) proposed to separately process the real and imaginary parts of the threshold relied weighted sum in the neural unit. They demonstrated that the MLP‐based equalizer outperforms the least mean square (LMS) based linear equalizer, when nonlinear channel distortions exist. Similarly, (Chang and Wang, [1995](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0005)) proposed a MLP‐based equalizer to equalize complex‐valued phase shift keying (PSK) signals received from nonlinear satellite channels.

In these works, all the MLP equalizers are supported by supervised learning. Similar to the ML algorithms considered in the previous chapters, a large amount of channel input/output data are usually needed to train the equalizer – using, for example, the backward propagation (BP) algorithm or its variants – before the equalizers are used for data detection. In contrast, in blind equalization where training data is unavailable, channel equalizers can also be designed on the basis of the MLP by exploiting the higher‐order statistics of the source sequences, as done, for example, in (You and Hong, [1998](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0067); Gao et al., [2009](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0019)). Moreover, (Gao et al., [2009](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0019)) showed that their proposed blind equalizer is capable of achieving a faster convergence rate and a smaller mean square error (MSE) in comparison with the original MLP‐based equalizer requiring training data, when communicating in an underwater acoustic digital communication scenario.

 

### 12.2.2 Functional Link Artificial Neutral Network‐Based Equalizers

Because a FLANN is typically a single‐ or flat‐layer perceptron, it has low computational complexity and can be readily implemented using hardware (Patra et al., [2008](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0040)). In a FLANN, functional expansion can not only be applied to enhance the original input pattern but also be exploited to increase the pattern dimension. Specifically, the functional expansion of the input pattern can be implemented with the aid of basis functions such as trigonometric, Gaussian, Chebyshev, and Legendre polynomials (Burse et al., [2010](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0003)).

In comparison with the MLP, the FLANN has no hidden layers, but nonlinear mappings. Owing to its simplicity, FLANNs have attracted wide research interest and have also applied for channel equalization (Patra and Pal, [1995](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0037); Patra et al., [1999](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0038)). In these FLANN‐based equalizers, functional expansions are achieved with the aid of orthogonal trigonometric functions. In (Weng and Yen, [2004](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0058)), a reduced decision feedback FLANN (RDF‐FLANN) based channel equalizer was introduced. Instead of taking the channel output as the input signals to the network, the RDF‐FLANN‐based equalizer also feeds back its own output signals to the input layer of the network. Moreover, the Chebyshev NN (ChNN) designed according to the FLANN was proposed for channel equalizations where four types of QAM signals were considered (Patra and Kot, [2002](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0036); Patra et al., [2005](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0039)). Studies show that by expanding the input space, ChNNs can provide more efficient computation for the static function approximation than trigonometric polynomials.

FLANN‐based equalizers may provide better performance than MLP‐based equalizers. However, FLANN‐based equalizers have the weakness of a higher‐order complexity increase, especially in cases when the input space dimensionality is expanded at lower BER (Burse et al., [2010](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0003)).

 

### 12.2.3 Radial Basis Function‐Based Equalizers

RBFs were initially regarded as good alternatives for sigmoidal transfer function networks (Burse et al., [2010](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0003)). Then, the RBF NN was proposed for data interpolation in the multidimensional space (Mulgrew, [1996](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0032)). Furthermore, the cyclostationary characteristics of received signals are not required to be known in RBF NNs; hence, RBF NNs can also mitigate distortion caused by co‐channel and adjacent channel interference.

In RBF‐aided equalizers, received signals are classified according to their center vectors. As the network structure of RBF NNs is designed on the basis of Bayesian principles, the output in RBF‐based equalizers is different from that in MLP and FLANN‐based equalizers. According to (Chen et al., [1992](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0009),[1993b](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0011),[a](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0010)), in comparison with adaptive MLSE, RBF‐based equalizers achieve superior performance over time‐varying Rayleigh fading channels and also have lower computational complexity.

Moreover, in (Chen et al., [1994](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0012)) and (Cha and Kassam, [1995](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0004)), the real‐valued RBF was generalized to the complex‐valued RBF (CRBF). Correspondingly, a stochastic‐gradient training algorithm was developed to train the CRBF network (Cha and Kassam, [1995](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0004)). To implement blind equalization with the aid of RBF, many techniques were proposed and studied (Tan et al., [2001](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0053); Uncini and Piazza, [2003](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0056); Xie and Leung, [2005](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0060)).

In order to solve practical problems more effectively and to further improve the performance of RBF NN‐based equalization, neuron fuzzy systems were developed according to the fuzzy logic methodology (Soria‐Olivas et al., [2003](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0051); Rong et al., [2006](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0048)). For example, the sequential fuzzy extreme learning algorithm was proposed in (Rong et al., [2009](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0049)), which has been regarded as a good alternative to the batch‐processing algorithm. This is because the sequential fuzzy extreme learning algorithm does not require a complete dataset for training, and the data can be utilized either in the form of small blocks or one by one during the training process. Therefore, in comparison with batch learning algorithm, retraining new datasets is not necessary in the sequential fuzzy learning algorithm.

 

### 12.2.4 Recurrent Neural Networks‐Based Equalizers

In principle, a RNN can ideally implement the inverse of a finite memory system, with the result that it can substantially model a nonlinear infinite memory filter. Therefore, RNNs have the capability to effectively mitigate all the interference introduced by channels.

RNNs have been applied to channel equalization in various scenarios. The authors of (Kechriotis et al., [1994](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0028)) proposed an adaptive RNN‐based equalizer that can be operated either in trained mode, aided by a sequence of training data, or in blind equalization mode without training data. This adaptive RNN‐based equalizer is suitable for both linear and nonlinear communication channels. Studies and simulation results show that RNN‐based equalizers may outperform traditional linear filter‐based equalizers in some specific application scenarios.

Subsequently, (Zhang et al., [2004](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0068)) proposed a blind equalization algorithm on the basis of the bilinear RNN (BLRNN) and demonstrated that it is able to achieve better convergence performance and lower BER than the traditional constant modulus algorithm (CMA) (Zhang et al., [2004](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0068)). The complex version of BLRNN (Park, [2008](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0035)) supported by genetic algorithms was applied to channel equalization in wireless asynchronous transfer mode (ATM), and it was shown that better MSE or symbol error rate (SER) performance than conventional equalizers can be achieved. Furthermore, RNNs were applied to implement blind equalization in underwater acoustic communications, showing that a significant performance improvement can be achieved in comparison with traditional feedforward neural networks (FNNs) (Xiao et al., [2008](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0059)).

In addition to RNNs, in (Li et al., [2017](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0030)), convolutional neural networks (CNNs) were employed for channel equalization in order to combat nonlinear channel distortions and temporal changes of radio signals. In this joint CNN‐RNN network, received radio signals are passed first through a CNN‐based subnetwork and then through a RNN‐based subnetwork. With the aid of CNN, the previous internal state can be exploited by the current state at each step. Therefore, a RNN with long short‐term memory (LSTM) is capable of learning the temporal dependency. Consequently, the RNN has the potential to solve the problem of temporal variation of radio signals.

 

### 12.2.5 Self‐Constructing Recurrent Fuzzy Neural Network‐Based Equalizers

Fuzzy NN employs both the favorable interpretation of fuzzy logic and a high capability of learning (Chang and Ho, [2009](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0006)). Owing to this, an adaptive network‐based fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) was presented in (Jang et al., [1997](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0027)). Furthermore, as the fuzzy NN is able to construct nonlinear decision boundaries, fuzzy NN‐based channel equalizers can achieve high efficiency for ISI mitigation.

As fuzzy NN‐based equalizers are capable of directly forming decision boundaries according to received signals, no information about channel characteristics, including channel coefficients and channel order, has to be known. SCRFNN is the combination of a RNN and a self‐constructing fuzzy NN. In online learning processes, parameter learning is based on the supervised gradient descent approach with the aid of a delta adaptation law, and structure learning is based on the partition of the input space (Lin et al., [2005](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0031)). Hence, the parameters and structure of SCRFNNs can be self‐adjusted simultaneously. Note that SCRFNNs can restrict the generation of new fuzzy rules by setting constraints and therefore are more compact compared with ANFIS.

In terms of channel equalization, a SCRFNN‐based nonlinear equalizer was proposed in (Lin et al., [2005](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0031)). In contrast, (Chang et al., [2010](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0007)) focused on time‐varying and time‐invariant wireless channels, and proposed a fast self‐constructing fuzzy NN‐based decision feedback equalizer (FSCFNN‐DFE). In comparison with the SCRFNN, the FSCFNN‐DFE can achieve improvement in terms of BER performance, hardware cost, and computational complexity, while enjoying the merit that channel characteristics are not required to be known to the receiver.

 

### 12.2.6 Deep‐Learning‐Based Equalizers

DL neural networks employing a number of hidden layers have great representation capability (Ye and Li, [2017](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0065)). With the aid of DL, (Ye and Li, [2017](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0065)) applied the MLP to joint channel equalization and decoding, and demonstrated robust performance under various channel conditions, including a time‐varying frequency selective channel that generates severe ISI. Following this work, in (Ye et al., [2018](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0066)), the DL neural network (DNN) structure was utilized to recover data symbols conveyed in OFDM principles. Furthermore, studies show that although DNNs are trained using data generated by the statistics of known channel models, the considered DNN‐aided equalizer is robust, even when the maximum delay spread and number of paths assumed in training are different from those used at the test stage.

 

### 12.2.7 Extreme Learning Machine–Based Equalizers

Extreme learning machines (ELMs) have the capability to provide high learning accuracy by minimizing training error at the training stage as well as the norm of output weights. Since, in general, smaller training error results in a smaller norm of weights, this type of feedforward neural network allows the achievement of a desirable generalization performance with fixed hidden‐layer parameters. For this reason, it has attracted increasing research interest in computer version applications (Tang et al., [2016](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0054)).

Likewise, researchers in wireless communications have applied ELM to design channel equalizers for ISI mitigation and performance enhancement. Thanks to its merits of learning accuracy and efficiency, an ELM‐based channel equalizer was demonstrated (Yang et al., [2018](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0062)) to have the capability to converge fast in short data‐packet transmissions where quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) is used.

In general, when properly trained with the aid of training data, NN‐based equalizers can effectively suppress ISI intelligently and significantly improve the reliability of communication. However, we should note that NN‐based equalizers are required to extract the key features of wireless channels via training, which may induce concern about convergence, computation complexity, and spectrum efficiency of communication. In order to address these concerns, in recent years, the support vector machine (SVM) and Gaussian processes for regression (GPR) techniques have been introduced in channel equalization in wireless communications, and will be briefly reviewed in the next subsection.

 

### 12.2.8 SVM‐ and GPR‐Based Equalizers

According to (Cover, [1965](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0015)), Cover's theorem states that it's highly possible to create linearly separable clouds of data by projecting the pattern space ![images](images/c12-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> P</mi></mrow></math> to the higher‐dimensional feature space ![images](images/c12-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> F</mi></mrow></math> via nonlinear mapping. Based on this theorem, the SVM nonlinearly maps the inner products of data in the pattern space, instead of the data themselves, via a kernel, so as to use an optimal hyperplane to separate clouds of data in the feature space (Sebald and Bucklew, [2000](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0050)).

In the context of applications of SVM for channel equalization, in (Perez‐Cruz et al., [2001](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0044)), the authors presented a SVM‐based equalizer for equalizing burst time division multiple access (TDMA) channels. In order to obtain SVM‐based equalization, an iterative re‐weighted least squares (IRWLS) procedure is used to reduce the computational complexity of the conventional SVM, in which the training procedure is implemented according to quadratic programming (QP). Then, a blind equalization algorithm based on the least squares support vector regressor (LSSVR) was proposed by (Yao et al., [2011](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0064)), which exploits only characteristics of the transmitted signal and does not have to use training sequences to achieve spectrum efficiency of communications.

However, SVM‐based blind equalization does not work well if the actual channel does not fit the channel model (Perez‐Cruz et al., [2001](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0044)). In order to improve the performance of SVM‐based blind equalization algorithms, (Wang et al., [2016](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0057)) proposed to combine the conventional cost function of the support vector regressor (SVR) with the probability density function (PDF) of the error function. Thus the PDF of the equalizer's output signals is formulated so that it can match the PDF of the constellations known to the receiver. Simulation results demonstrated that this equalization method outperforms legacy algorithms, such as the PDF algorithm and the SVR algorithm, when considering communications over ISI channels. However, in SVM‐based equalizers, the hyperparameters have to be either prespecified or estimated by cross‐validations. Moreover, SVM‐based equalizers need a long training sequence and hence have high complexity. Thus, in practice, SVM‐based equalizers can usually only tune one or two hyperparameters by cross‐validation.

In order to address these issues, a nonlinear channel equalizer designed according to GPR was proposed in (Perez‐Cruz et al., [2008](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0045)). In comparison with SVM‐based methods, GPR algorithms have the advantage of optimizing kernel hyperparameters based on maximum likelihood. This allows significant performance improvement in the case of short training sequences, making GPR‐based equalizers outperform SVM‐aided equalizers. In contrast, in the case of using long training datasets, hyperparameters only slightly affect the solution, with the result that SVM and GPR‐based equalizers achieve similar performance. In order to further improve the performance of GPR‐based equalizers, (Olmos et al., [2010](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0033)) combined nonlinear channel equalization with low‐density parity checking (LDPC) codes (Yang et al., [2015](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0063)). This design motivates the use of short training sequences to obtain an accurate posterior probability estimation for the LDPC code, rather than directly working on the error rate of the LDPC decoding, which was considered in the previous research.

Having outlined all the NN‐ and ML‐based channel equalization solutions, next we will address these techniques in more detail by considering the algorithm design, complexity analysis, and performance comparison. First, let us present the principles and problem formulations of channel equalization and related signal detection.

[(12.3)](#c12.xhtml#c12-R_disp-0003)![equation](images/c12-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>g</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8855;</mo> <msub> <mi>h</mi> <mrow> <mi>e</mi> <mi>q</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#948;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </math> 

When Eq. ([12.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0003)) is satisfied, the ISI induced by the channel can be fully eliminated. Considering the frequency domain, from Eq. ([12.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0003)) we have

[(12.4)](#c12.xhtml#c12-R_disp-0004)![equation](images/c12-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>F</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mrow> <mi>e</mi> <mi>q</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> are, respectively, the Fourier transformations of ![images](images/c12-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Equation ([12.4](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0004)) means the ideal equalizer is an inverse filter of the combined channel ![images](images/c12-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. From Eq. ([12.4](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0004)), we know that when communicating over frequency‐selective fading channels, frequency components with low response gains are enhanced, while frequency components with high response gains are reduced after the equalization, so that the spectrum after equalization becomes flat. Consequently, the channel‐fading effect can be efficiently mitigated.

Channel equalization is a classic, well‐known technique in telecommunication engineering, and considerable research has been done. Typical equalization algorithms include the ZF algorithm, MMSE algorithm, optimum MLSE algorithm, etc. Before introducing the ML‐based equalization algorithms, let us first briefly review the principles of these three equalizers.

   Zero‐Forcing Equalization 

In ZF equalization, according to Eq. ([12.4](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0004)), the frequency response of the equalizer is designed to be

[(12.5)](#c12.xhtml#c12-R_disp-0005)![equation](images/c12-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mrow> <mi>e</mi> <mi>q</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>F</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mi>F</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </math> 

The ZF‐equalizer in Eq. ([12.5](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0005)) can ideally eliminate the ISI introduced by a channel. However, the noise embedded in the received signal varies with the frequency response of the equalizer. To demonstrate this effect, we can analyze the noise power spectral density (PSD) function after the ZF equalization, which can be expressed as

[(12.6)](#c12.xhtml#c12-R_disp-0006)![equation](images/c12-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mrow> <mi>e</mi> <mi>q</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>Z</mi> <mi>F</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>F</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> is the noise power before ZF equalization. As shown in Eq. ([12.6](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0006)), if the combined channel response ![images](images/c12-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> has a frequency component with a very small amplitude, the corresponding noise power will be amplified significantly with an amplification factor of ![images](images/c12-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math>. In order to achieve a better trade‐off between ISI elimination and noise‐power amplification, a MMSE algorithm has been introduced (Haykin, [1986](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0026)), which has the following principles.

 

##### *Minimum Mean Square Error Equalization*

The aim of the MMSE‐equalizer is to minimize the MSE between the desired equalizer's output and the actual equalizer's output. Referring to [Figure 12.1](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0001), the detection error is

Then the frequency response of the equalizer is

where ![images](images/c12-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mi>L</mi><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></math> represent, respectively, the weighted vector of the equalizer and the channel output vector input to the equalizer for detecting ![images](images/c12-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>k</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

Note that, in the case where the length of the equalizer is infinite, i.e. ![images](images/c12-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>&#8734;</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, it can be shown that the frequency response of the MMSE‐equalizer can be expressed as (Stuber, [1999](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0052))

[(12.15)](#c12.xhtml#c12-R_disp-0015)![equation](images/c12-math-0015.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>H</mi> <mrow> <mi>e</mi> <mi>q</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>M</mi> <mi>M</mi> <mi>S</mi> <mi>E</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mi>F</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </math> 

Comparing Eq. ([12.5](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0005)) with Eq. ([12.15](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0015)), it can be seen that when the noise power is zero, meaning the signal‐to‐noise ratio (SNR) is infinite, the MMSE‐equalizer is equivalent to the ZF‐equalizer. By contrast, when noise exists, the MMSE‐equalizer is capable of achieving a better balance between ISI mitigation and noise‐power reduction, yielding more reliable detection than the ZF‐equalizer.

 

##### *Maximum Likelihood Sequence Estimation–Assisted Equalizers*

To attain near‐optimum error performance, researchers have proposed various nonlinear equalizers for application in mobile communication systems. Among them, there are a range of nonlinear equalizers that are designed according to the classical maximum likelihood detection algorithm. One of them is the MLSE‐equalizer. In the principle of MLSE equalization, the posteriori detection probabilities of all the possible data sequences are first calculated. Then the data sequence with the maximum posteriori probability is selected as the desired output. While the MLSE‐equalizer is capable of minimizing the probability of the sequence error, it has a main defect of high computational complexity, which is extreme when the delay spread of the channel is large.

Let us consider the detection of ![images](images/c12-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> most recent input data symbols. Then, there are ![images](images/c12-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mi>L</mi></msup></mrow></math> states, when the size of the symbol alphabet of the modulation is ![images](images/c12-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>. As shown in [Figure 12.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0002), with the aid of the Gram‐Schmidt orthogonal operation, the received signals corresponding to the ![images](images/c12-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> symbols can be expressed as

[(12.16)](#c12.xhtml#c12-R_disp-0016)![equation](images/c12-math-0016.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> is a set of ![images](images/c12-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> orthogonal basis, ![images](images/c12-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c12-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the sampling time. Furthermore, in Eq. ([12.16](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0016)), the coefficients ![images](images/c12-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math> are computed by the formulas of

where ![images](images/c12-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8747;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></msubsup><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>k</mi><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8747;</mo></mrow><mrow><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></msubsup><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>d</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>.

It can be shown that the coefficient vector ![images](images/c12-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>N</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></math> follows the multidimensional Gaussian distribution with the PDF given by

(12.18)![equation](images/c12-math-0018.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">d</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8719;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mi>&#960;</mi> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mi mathvariant="normal">exp</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>d</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mi>k</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </math>

Here we have reviewed the principles of three types of classic equalization schemes. It can be seen that all these equalizers assume that the channel impulse response is a priori known to the equalizer. However, in practice, especially in wideband wireless communication systems, the exact channel response can hardly be retrieved due to the time‐varying nature of wireless channels. This results in a significant challenge to the design of traditional equalizers. In order to adapt to channel variation intelligently, NN‐ and ML‐based equalization algorithms have been developed, which will be the focus of the next section.

 

## 12.4 NN‐Based Equalization and Detection

In this section, we first briefly introduce a quintessential model for the feedback neural network, i.e. the MLP, in order to provide some insight into the construction and training of NNs. Then, based on the MLP and DL, a DNN solution is proposed for the implementation of channel equalizers. Finally, equalizers based on different types of NNs are briefly described.

 

### 12.4.1 Multilayer Perceptron Model

Generally, NNs need to be trained with a large set of data in order to extract the key feature parameters. The training process is usually implemented by the gradient descent algorithm, which uses forward and backward propagation in each iteration. This subsection briefly introduces the principles of the MLP as well as its training method.

 

#### 12.4.1.1 Generalized Multilayer Perceptron Structure

A general neural node, as shown in [Figure 12.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0003), is the basic unit of a MLP. Given the inputs ![images](images/c12-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub></mrow></math>, the output of the neural node is denoted by ![images](images/c12-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c12-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the weighting of ![images](images/c12-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is the bias, and ![images](images/c12-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the nonlinear function, which is called the *activation function*. There are various choices for the activation function (Goodfellow et al., [2016](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0024)), including the sigmoid function, hyperbolic tangent function, and ReLu function, among which the ReLu function is defined as:

(12.23)![equation](images/c12-math-0023.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mtext>ReLu</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>max</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

A MLP has the typical structure as shown in [Figure 12.4](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0004), where multiple neural nodes are arranged to form multiple layers, including an input layer, possibly multiple hidden layers, and an output layer. The neural nodes of two adjacent layers are fully connected, with the inputs to a neural node of the current layer consisting of all the outputs of the neural nodes in the last layer. The input layer is used to feed data into the network, while the output layer is used to output the computation results. The other layers between the input and output layers are called hidden layers because the training data of NNs do not generate the desired output for each of these layers (Goodfellow et al., [2016](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0024)). The MLP in [Figure 12.4](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0004) has four hidden layers.

Denote the number of layers of a MLP as ![images](images/c12-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>.
