stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>b</mi><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">T</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Therefore, the input to the ![images](images/c12-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math>th neural node of layer ![images](images/c12-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> is ![images](images/c12-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></munderover><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>j</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msubsup><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>.

![Figure 12.3 Neural node.](images/c12f003.jpg)

[Figure 12.3](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0003) Neural node.

![Figure 12.4 An example of the MLP model.](images/c12f004.jpg)

[Figure 12.4](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0004) An example of the MLP model.

In principle, a MLP implements a nonlinear mapping expressed as ![images](images/c12-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><msup><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, where the mapping function is constructed in an iterative way expressed as:

(12.24)![equation](images/c12-math-0024.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>f</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>L</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>f</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>L</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <msup> <mi>f</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the activation function at the ![images](images/c12-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math>th layer. The goal of MLP is to approximate some function ![images](images/c12-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></math> in order to generate the desired output denoted by ![images](images/c12-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>f</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. To achieve a close approximation, the MLP should be trained by tuning the weighting factors and the bias of each layer in a supervised way. For this purpose, the loss function can be defined to measure the difference between the actual output and the desired output, which should be minimized by the training process.

Considering a training set with ![images](images/c12-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> examples, the loss function in the ![images](images/c12-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> norm is defined as

(12.25)![equation](images/c12-math-0025.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <msub> <mi>L</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>M</mi> </mfrac> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>M</mi> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> are, respectively, the actual output and the desired output of the MLP corresponding to the ![images](images/c12-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>th example; ![images](images/c12-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> are defined as ![images](images/c12-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, respectively.

In MLP, the training process is usually completed with the aid of the gradient descent algorithm or its variants, some of which are introduced as follows.

 

#### 12.4.1.2 Gradient Descent Algorithm

The basic principle behind the gradient descent algorithm is to use the derivative of the objective function to update the decision variables, so that the value of the objective function (or the cost) can be reduced.

Consider a function ![images](images/c12-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> in the real domain, and denote its derivative as ![images](images/c12-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Then, at the point ![images](images/c12-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> for small ![images](images/c12-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> can be approximated as ![images](images/c12-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Furthermore, we can see that, provided ![images](images/c12-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mtext>sign</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is smaller than ![images](images/c12-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. In other words, the derivative gives the information to reduce the function value by introducing a small change in the variable ![images](images/c12-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>. In this way, we may repeatedly update the variable using ![images](images/c12-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#949;</mi><mtext>sign</mtext><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>r</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> to derive the minimal value of the function as well as the point achieving this minimum value.

Return to the MLP training, the objective function is the loss function, and the variables include the weighing factors and the bias in each layer, i.e. ![images](images/c12-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c12-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>. According to the principles of the gradient descent algorithm, these variables are updated as

<mrow> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msub> <mi>L</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>L</mi> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> (12.27)![equation](images/c12-math-0027.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi> <mrow> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msub> <mi>L</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>L</mi> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> is called the *learning rate*. The value of ![images](images/c12-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> can be set to a small constant; or, alternatively, it can be adaptively changed with the aid of the line‐search strategy (Goodfellow et al., [2016](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0024)), which evaluates the objective function for several ![images](images/c12-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow></math> values and chooses the one resulting in the smallest function value.

In the gradient descent algorithm, the cost of calculating the partial derivatives is ![images](images/c12-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, with the result that the loss function is related to all the training examples. This may be expensive when the training set is large, which is necessary for good generalization. To reduce the complexity, the stochastic gradient descent algorithm (Goodfellow et al., [2016](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0024)) has been developed as a variant of the gradient descent algorithm. In the stochastic gradient descent algorithm, ![images](images/c12-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> uniformly chosen examples are used to estimate the whole data set, where ![images](images/c12-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> is called the *minibatch size* and is usually much smaller than ![images](images/c12-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>. In this way, we may fit a training set with millions of examples using updates computed from a smaller number of examples, while the cost of calculating the partial derivative is reduced to ![images](images/c12-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> instead of ![images](images/c12-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

Another drawback of the gradient descent algorithm is that it may be trapped at a local minimum. However, (Goodfellow et al., [2016](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0024)) argued that many ML models can work well when they are trained with the gradient descent algorithm. Furthermore, the authors pointed out that even though it's not guaranteed to find the global minimum within a reasonable time, the algorithm can usually quickly find the value of the loss function, which is low enough for practical purposes. Hence, this property makes the gradient descent algorithm practically useful.

 

#### 12.4.1.3 Forward and Backward Propagation

In each iteration of the gradient descent algorithm, forward propagation is utilized to evaluate the loss function value, while backward propagation is utilized to compute the partial derivatives. Considering a stochastic gradient descent algorithm with minibatch size ![images](images/c12-i0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math>, the loss function is written as:

(12.28)![equation](images/c12-math-0028.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <msub> <mi>L</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Y</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <msup> <mi>M</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>M</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </munderover> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

Starting from the input layer, the forward propagation processes carry out the linear and activation operations layer by layer until the output layer. Specifically, at the ![images](images/c12-i0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math>th layer, when denoting, respectively, the results of the linear and activation operations as ![images](images/c12-i0123.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0124.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, whose dimensions are both ![images](images/c12-i0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup><mo>&#215;</mo><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math>, the operations can be formulated as:

(12.29)![equation](images/c12-math-0029.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> (12.30)![equation](images/c12-math-0030.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>f</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

Hence, when given ![images](images/c12-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, the computational chain of forward propagation is as follows:

![equation](images/c12-math-0031.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtable columnalign="left"><mtr><mtd><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mtd><mtd><mo>&#8594;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd><mo>&#8594;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd><mo>&#8594;</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo></mtd></mtr><mtr><mtd/><mtd><mo>&#8594;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Z</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup><mo>,</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">A</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mtd></mtr></mtable></mrow></math> 

where ![images](images/c12-i0128.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is the initialization operation.

Finally, the output of the MLP is given by the loss functions after the operations at the ![images](images/c12-i0129.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>th layer.

In contrast, backward propagation starts from the output layer and processes in a layer‐by‐layer manner until the input layer. The chain rule is used for computing the partial derivatives in terms of each of the ![images](images/c12-i0130.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> layers. Specifically, for the ![images](images/c12-i0131.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math>th layer, the corresponding partial derivatives are calculated as follows:

### 12.4.2 Deep‐Learning Neural Network‐Based Equalizers

As the MLP becomes deeper, i.e. as it has more hidden layers, it becomes more powerful for the representation of complicated functions, e.g. time‐varying channel impulse responses. Therefore, with the aid of DL, this subsection extends the MLP to construct a DL NN, based on which a channel equalizer is further presented.

 

#### 12.4.2.1 System Model and Network Structure

By introducing more fully connected hidden layers, a MLP is extended to a DNN, which has the structure as shown in [Figure 12.5](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0005). Like other neural networks, DNNs may be trained using different tasks so as to perform different functions. Specifically, when it is trained with the task of recovering signals undergoing channel distortions, a DNN is capable of learning channel features and hence approximating the equalization function, so as to bring the received signals close to the desired signals. In this way, a DNN‐based channel equalizer can be constructed.

The architecture of a generalized communication system with a DNN‐based channel equalizer is illustrated in [Figure 12.6](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0006). At the transmitter side, the information message is first encoded and the codeword is digital modulated according to certain baseband modulation scheme. The modulated symbols are then sent to the wireless channel, where different distortions may be experienced. At the receiver side, the DNN‐based channel equalizer is utilized to combat channel distortion before data demodulation and decoding. In [Figure 12.6](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0006), the DNN is usually trained offline before online deployment, i.e. actual real‐time application. Details of the network training are provided in the following subsection. Note that, at the online development stage, DNN‐based equalizers can recover the desired signals without explicit channel estimations.

As shown in [Figure 12.6](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0006), channel distortions may consist of ISI, nonlinear distortion, and additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN). Here, nonlinear distortion, denoted as a ![images](images/c12-i0137.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi></mrow></math>‐function, is mainly introduced by amplifiers and mixers, at both the transmitter and receiver, which can be viewed as part of the channel effects. #### 12.4.2.2 Network Training

In order to perform channel equalization, the DNN is first required to be trained in a supervised way using a training set with a great amount of channel input/output data. Conventionally, online training is adopted to train small‐size MLP‐based channel equalizers, which utilize, for example, transmitted pilot data to adjust network parameters. However, this online training method is not suitable for DNNs, because many parameters in a DNN need to be determined. Therefore, a large training set is required, and a long training period needs to take place in the DNN‐based scheme, which can actually degrade overall equalization performance.

In order to circumvent the disadvantages of online training, DNNs are usually trained offline (Ye and Li, [2017](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0065); Ye et al., [2018](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0066)) using various information sequences obtained under diverse channel conditions. After being properly trained, DNNs can efficiently recover the received data online without relying on time‐consuming online training.

One merit of offline training of DNNs is that, unlike many other ML tasks where a large size training set is difficult to obtain, the training data for DNN‐based equalizers can be directly generated with the aid of simulation approaches, once the channel model and other parameters are known or correctly estimated. In detail, for each simulation, a random message ![images](images/c12-i0143.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">m</mi></mrow></math> is generated, based on which the encoder chooses a corresponding codeword ![images](images/c12-i0144.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">c</mi></mrow></math> from the codebook. Then, data modulation is executed to yield the symbol sequence ![images](images/c12-i0145.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi></mrow></math>; it is transmitted over the wireless channel, which can be modeled as a black box. At the receiver, the channel output ![images](images/c12-i0146.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi></mrow></math> is collected together with the corresponding symbol sequence transmitted, which are assigned a supervising label to form a training example. From this one can see that training examples are generated based on modeling and simulation. Thus, an arbitrarily large training set can be obtained to train a DNN‐based equalizer.

As shown in [Figure 12.6](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0006), at the offline training stage, DNNs are required to be trained to minimize the difference between transmitted symbols ![images](images/c12-i0147.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi></mrow></math> and estimated ones ![images](images/c12-i0148.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#349;</mi></mrow></math>. More explicitly, the input to a DNN is the received signal ![images](images/c12-i0149.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi></mrow></math>, while ![images](images/c12-i0150.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0151.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#349;</mi></mrow></math>, respectively, denote the targeted output and the actual output of the DNN, and ![images](images/c12-i0152.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#349;</mi></mrow></math> is the estimate of ![images](images/c12-i0153.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi></mrow></math>. Therefore, the loss function of the DNN is

[(12.37)](#c12.xhtml#c12-R_disp-0039)![equation](images/c12-math-0039.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <msub> <mi>L</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#349;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <msup> <mi>M</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>M</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#349;</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#8214;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

where the superscript ![images](images/c12-i0154.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> denotes the index of the training example, and ![images](images/c12-i0155.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> is the minibatch size. Naturally, the vectors ![images](images/c12-i0156.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c12-i0157.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#349;</mi></mrow></math> have size ![images](images/c12-i0158.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>M</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math>. To elaborate a bit further, with the aid of the known input ![images](images/c12-i0159.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi></mrow></math> to the DNN, the actual output can be expressed as ![images](images/c12-i0160.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#349;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c12-i0161.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> represents the nonlinear mapping of the DNN determined by the weights that are unknown but obtained via the known “![images](images/c12-i0162.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi></mrow></math>” and “![images](images/c12-i0163.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi></mrow></math>”.

Through the minimization of the loss function ![images](images/c12-i0164.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#349;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> of Eq. ([12.37](#c12.xhtml#c12-disp-0039)), by using the gradient descent algorithm with forward/backward propagation, as shown in [Section 12.4.1.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0018) and [Section 12.4.1.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0019), offline training can be implemented with the aid of known transmitted and received signals. Since the received signals potentially experience various channel variations, after the training stage, the resultant DNN can be used to effectively detect the received signals experiencing various channel variations.

The main concern of offline training of DNNs is that the channels used for generating training data might be mismatched with the actual channels. However, the simulation results in (Ye et al., [2018](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0066)) show that variations of channel statistics usually do not significantly degrade the achievable performance of signal detection. A possible reason for this may be the generalization capability of DNNs, which can extend a DNN trained according to a specific model to the application scenarios where constant channel changes may occur.

 

### 12.4.3 Convolutional Neural Network‐Based Equalizers

A convolutional neural network (CNN) is a kind of neural network for processing data with known grid‐like topologies. Rather than using fully connected layers, as in MLP, CNN is constituted by convolutional layers, as shown in [Figures 12.7](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0007) and [12.8](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0008): a convolution stage, a detection stage, and a pooling stage are utilized to implement the convolution operations, activation operations, and down‐samplings.

[Figure 12.9](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0009) shows a CNN‐based equalizer, which is similar to [Figure 12.6](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0006) for a DNN‐based equalizer from a data‐flow point of view. Similar to the discussion in [Section 12.4.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0020) for DNN‐based equalizers, the training set can be generated on the basis of the channel model and parameters that are derived from practice. Furthermore, with the similar system model and the same optimization objective, a CNN‐based equalizer can be trained in the same way as a DNN‐based equalizer. Specifically, the ![images](images/c12-i0165.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> loss function and the stochastic gradient descent algorithm with forward/backward propagations can be adopted to obtain the appropriate network parameters.

![Figure 12.7 A typical convolutional layer.](images/c12f007.jpg)

[Figure 12.7](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0007) A typical convolutional layer.

![Figure 12.8 Structure of a CNN.](images/c12f008.jpg)

[Figure 12.8](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0008) Structure of a CNN.

![Figure 12.9 System model for CNN‐based equalizer.](images/c12f009.jpg)

[Figure 12.9](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0009) System model for CNN‐based equalizer.

It is worth pointing out that the convolutional layer introduced by CNN‐based equalizers has the following merits, which are beneficial to channel equalization:

1.  1\. Convolutional neural nodes only process data from a restricted subarea of the previous layer. This property agrees with the channel characteristic that ISI only exists between bits transmitted consecutively, while the nonlinear effect usually influences different bits independently (Xu et al., [2018](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0061)).
2.  2\. CNNs have shift‐invariant properties, which can be used to learn for matched filters and reduce temporal variations during signal detection (O'Shea et al., [2016](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0034); Li et al., [2017](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0030)). This is because the information recovery process in wireless communication systems is usually invariant to time shifting, scaling, rotation, linear mixing, and convolution through random filters.

 

### 12.4.4 Recurrent Neural Network‐Based Equalizers

Recurrent neural networks (RNN)are another widely used neural network framework, and are powerful for one‐dimensional data processing (Goodfellow et al., [2016](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0024)). In RNNs, the current output of a hidden node depends not only on its current input but also on its past output. In other words, RNNs have memory, which enables them to model an infinite impulse response (IIR) filter. This property is important for the application of RNNs in channel equalization.

The RNN with three hidden recurrent units shown in [Figure 12.10](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0010), where the neural nodes are represented by circles, was proposed in (Kechriotis et al., [1994](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0028)) for channel equalization. In [Figure 12.10](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0010), the left part is a folded computational graph for the RNN, while the right part is an unfolded version corresponding to the time series that guide the computation (Goodfellow et al., [2016](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0024)).

RNNs can also be trained using the method for DNN‐ and CNN‐based equalizers, described in [Sections 12.4.2](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0020) and [12.4.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0023), respectively. Furthermore, the ![images](images/c12-i0166.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> loss function and the stochastic gradient descent algorithm with forward/backward propagation can be adopted to obtain the appropriate network parameters.

In summary, with the aid of these neural networks, equalizers are able to extract the key features of wireless channels and reduce ISI adaptively and intelligently. Based on MLP, we can design DNN‐based equalizers having the capability to mitigate ISI, thanks to embedded multiple‐layered neural networks. Moreover, as shown in [Figure 12.11](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0011), the channel‐favorite properties of RNN and CNN facilitate equalizer design; owing to this, RNNs and CNNs have been widely used to combat ISI and achieve reliable communications. In the next section, we will present a range of simulation results to demonstrate the achievable performance of NN‐based equalizers in OFDM systems.

## 12.5 Performance of OFDM Systems With Neural Network‐Based Equalization

In this section, we investigate the performance of OFDM systems, which adopt DL techniques, including CNN and DNN, for channel equalization. Before providing the simulation performance, let us first describe the system model and network structure used for this performance investigation.

 

### 12.5.1 System Model and Network Structure

[Figure 12.12](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0012) illustrates the structure of an OFDM system with a NN‐based equalizer. The baseband OFDM system is identical to traditional ones (E. Dahiman and Skold, [2014](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0016)). At the transmitter side, the transmitted QAM modulated symbols associated with the pilots for channel estimation are first converted to a parallel data representation. After that, the inverse fast Fourier transform (IFFT) module converts the data from the frequency domain to the time domain. Then, a cyclic prefix (CP) is inserted in order to avoid inter‐block interference. Finally, after a parallel‐to serial conversion, the signals are transmitted over the channel, which is usually dispersive.

Let the discrete sample‐spaced multiple‐path channel be expressed as ![images](images/c12-i0167.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, where the complex random variable ![images](images/c12-i0168.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the channel gain at instant ![images](images/c12-i0169.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. Then the discrete received signal can be expressed as

(12.38)![equation](images/c12-math-0040.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8855;</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> ![Figure 12.12 System model for OFDM with a DNN‐ or CNN‐based equalizer.](images/c12f012.jpg)

where ![images](images/c12-i0170.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8855;</mo></mrow></math> denotes the circular convolution, ![images](images/c12-i0171.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the transmitted time‐domain signal, and ![images](images/c12-i0172.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the AWGN.

As shown in [Figure 12.12](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0012), at the receiver side, after the serial‐to‐parallel conversion and removing the cyclic prefix, the fast Fourier transform (FFT) converts the received signal from the time domain to the frequency domain. Hence, in the OFDM system considered, the DNN‐ or CNN‐based equalizer operates in the frequency domain. Finally, received information is recovered by demodulation based on the output of the equalizer, as seen in [Figure 12.12](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0012).

 

### 12.5.2 DNN and CNN Network Structure

For OFDM systems, [Figure 12.13](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0013) depicts the specific structure of the DNN, which consists of six layers, four of them being hidden layers marked as ELU. In our study, the numbers of neurons in each layer are set to 256, 600, 400, 300, 200, and 128, respectively. The number of the input to the network is the number of real parts and that of imaginary parts of an OFDM frame containing both a pilot block and a data block. In contrast, the number of outputs equals the number of real parts plus the number of the imaginary parts of the data symbols derived from the data block.

In our performance study, the exponential linear unit (ELU) function (Goodfellow et al., [2016](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0024)) is used as the activation function in all the layers other than the last layer. The ELU function is

![Figure 12.14 The CNN network structure for OFDM systems.](images/c12f014.jpg)

[Figure 12.14](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0014) The CNN network structure for OFDM systems.

In the context of an OFDM system with a CNN‐based equalizer, [Figure 12.14](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0014) illustrates the structure of a nine‐layer CNN. Thanks to the CNN's properties of facilitation of channel equalization, as mentioned in [Section 12.4.3](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0023), a one‐dimension (1D) convolution layer is introduced in the first hidden layer to extract the useful features of the received OFDM frames.

The inputs are OFDM frames, where every frame is constructed by the in‐phase and quadrature‐phase (IQ) parts. In order to improve the performance and stability of the CNN, batch normalization is always used by hidden layers to normalize the output. Then, a flattened layer is concatenated to flatten the input without affecting the batch size. After that, two identical sub‐blocks are connected in tandem. Each sub‐block consists of a fully connected layer (FCL) with ELU activation function and batch normalization. Finally, we use the tanh activation function to output data at the last layer.

To be more specific, the parameter settings of the CNN shown in [Figure 12.14](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0014), which consists of one input layer, one output layer, and seven hidden layers, are given as follows. Note that the layer index has been labeled above each module. At the first layer, the inputs to the CNN are None ![images](images/c12-i0175.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#215;</mo><mspace width="0.2em"/><mn>2</mn><mspace width="0.2em"/><mo>&#215;</mo></mrow></math> 128 3‐dimension (3D) vectors, where “None” is the batch size, 2 is the width of the input, and 128 is the number of input channels. Subsequently, a 1D convolution operation with an ELU activation function is carried out in TensorFlow, where the number of kernels is set to 256. After the batch normalization and flattening operations, at the FCL layer, the number of neurons is set to 1024. Similarly, except for the batch normalization layers which do not require parameters, the neuron numbers of the following FCL and output tanh layers are 512 and 128, respectively.

 

### 12.5.3 Offline Training and Online Deployment

To obtain an effective NN for equalization, two stages are required: offline training and online deployment. In the offline training stage, we obtain training data by simulations based on a system with channel modeling. Specifically, for each simulation, a random data sequence is generated and modulated to form the transmitted symbols ![images](images/c12-i0176.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi></mrow></math>, which are then grouped into OFDM frames in combination with a sequence of pilot symbols. The pilot symbols are arranged in the first block of the OFDM frame, followed by the block of data symbols. We assume that the pilot symbols remain the same during both the training stage and the deployment stage. The channel used for training is obtained according to the channel models derived from practice measurements. We assume block channel fading, meaning the channel remains constant in spanning the pilot block and the data blocks of a frame, but changes from one frame to another independently. After undergoing channel distortions, the received signal ![images](images/c12-i0177.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi></mrow></math> from the pilot block and data blocks of a frame as well as the transmitted symbols ![images](images/c12-i0178.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi></mrow></math> are used, respectively, as the input and the expected output of the NN for its training.

As mentioned previously in [Section 12.4](#c12.xhtml#c12-sec-0015), the NN is trained with the objective to minimize the difference between the actual output of the NN ![images](images/c12-i0179.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#349;</mi></mrow></math> and the targeted output ![images](images/c12-i0180.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi></mrow></math>. Hence, in our experimental setting, the loss function to achieve this objective is

### 12.5.4 Simulation Results and Analyses

In this subsection, we provide a range of BER performance results for the OFDM system with a DNN‐ or CNN‐based equalizer. The BER performance of a DNN‐ or CNN‐based equalizer is compared with that of the conventional least square (LS) method (Farzamnia et al., [2017](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0018)) and that of the MMSE method (Edfors et al., [1998](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0017)).

In our experiments, we assume an OFDM system with 64 subcarriers, 64 pilot symbols, and a CP length of 16. We assume 4‐QAM for data modulation and a Rayleigh fading channel with a single path, whose real and imaginary parts are Gaussian distributed with zero mean and variance 0.5. We also consider the extended pedestrian A model (EPA) (3GPP, [2017](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0001)) in which the number of paths is set to 7 and the maximum delay spread is 9 sampling periods. In addition, the extended typical urban model (ETU) (3GPP, [2017](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0001)) with 9 paths and a maximum delay spread of 16 sampling periods is taken into account.

In [Figure 12.15](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0015), we compare the BER performance of OFDM systems employing, respectively, our proposed DNN‐ and CNN‐based equalizers with that of the OFDM systems with the traditional LS‐ and MMSE‐based equalizers, when assuming communication over a single‐path Rayleigh fading channel. [Figure 12.15](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0015) shows that the LS method performs the worst among the four equalizers, with the result that it does not exploit the prior knowledge of the channel statistics, which is useful for channel equalization. In contrast, the MMSE method outperforms the LS method owing to utilizing the second‐order statistics of the channel. It can be observed that both DNN‐ and CNN‐based equalizers are capable of attaining better BER performance than the LS and MMSE methods from low to moderate SNRs. However, in the high SNR region, DNN‐ and CNN‐based equalizers may be outperformed by the MMSE‐based equalizer. Furthermore, the CNN‐based equalizer achieves a lower BER than the DNN‐based equalizer, thanks to the CNN's properties, which contribute more time‐domain information of the signal and channel.

![Figure 12.15 BER performance comparison of OFDM systems with DNN, CNN, LS, and MMSE‐based equalizers, when communicating over single‐path Rayleigh fading channels.](images/c12f015.jpg)

[Figure 12.15](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0015) BER performance comparison of OFDM systems with DNN, CNN, LS, and MMSE‐based equalizers, when communicating over single‐path Rayleigh fading channels.

![Figure 12.16 BER performance comparison of OFDM systems employing, respectively, DNN‐, CNN‐, LS‐, and MMSE‐based equalizers, when communicating over wireless channels following the EPA model (3GPP, 2017).](images/c12f016.jpg)

[Figure 12.16](#c12.xhtml#R_c12-fig-0016) BER performance comparison of OFDM systems employing, respectively, DNN‐, CNN‐, LS‐, and MMSE‐based equalizers, when communicating over wireless channels following the EPA model (3GPP, [2017](#c12.xhtml#c12-bib-0001)).

In [Figure 12.15](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0015), the frequency non‐selective fading channels were considered. In contrast, in [Figures 12.16](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0016) and [12.17](#c12.xhtml#c12-fig-0017), we compare the BER performance of OFDM systems employing, respectively, the previously mentioned four equalizers, assuming communications over the frequency‐selective fading channels modeled by the EPA model and the ETU model, respectively. As seen from the results, DNN‐ and CNN‐based equalizers achieve better BER performance than the LS and MMSE methods over the main SNR regions considered in both the EPA and ETU channels. In the low SNR region, the BER of the DNN‐based equalizer is either similar to or slightly lower than that of the CNN‐based equalizer. In contrast, when the SNR is sufficiently high, the BER performance of the CNN‐based equalizer is better than that of the DNN‐based equalizer, when communicating over both the EPA and ETU channels. The observation implies that DNN‐based equalizers are efficient for combating frequency‐selective fading, but not as efficient as CNN‐based equalizers for handling background noise. Furthermore, we should point out that CNN‐based equalizers usually take much less time to converge than DNN‐based equalizers.

 

## 12.6 Conclusions and Discussion

In this chapter, we first discussed various NN structures and learning methods in order to address the issues of channel equalization. Then, several representative NN algorithms were considered. Furthermore, two ML‐based equalizers, DNN‐ and CNN‐based equalizers, were presented, and their performance was investigated and compared with two conventional equalizers developed based on the LS and MMSE principles. Our study and performance results show that unlike traditional channel equalization and detection methods, no channel statistics are required to be separately computed in ML‐based equalization methods. More importantly, the BER performance of OFDM systems employing ML‐based equalizers is typically better than that of OFDM systems employing conventional LS‐ and MMSE‐based equalizers. This implies that ML‐based equalizers have a higher capability to learn and analyze complicated properties of wireless channels, and are also more effective to combat ISI. Meanwhile, ML‐based equalization approaches exhibit better BER performance than LS‐ and MMSE‐based equalization approaches, when communicating over channels with or without frequency‐selective fading. Owing to their properties that no prior knowledge about the structure and characteristics of wireless channels are required, NN‐based equalizers constitute promising candidates for channel equalization in future ultra‐high‐data‐rate wireless communication systems.

![Figure 12.17 BER performance comparison of OFDM systems employing, respectively, DNN‐, CNN‐, LS‐, and MMSE‐based equalizers, when communicating over frequency‐selective fading channels described by the ETU model (3GPP, 2017).](images/c12f017.jpg)

67.  C. You and D. Hong. Nonlinear blind equalization schemes using complex‐valued multilayer feedforward neural networks. IEEE Transactions on Neural Networks, 9(6): 1442–1455, 1998.

# Chapter 13  
Neural Networks for Signal Intelligence: Theory and Practice

*Jithin Jagannath¹, Nicholas Polosky¹, Anu Jagannath¹, Francesco Restuccia², and Tommaso Melodia²*

¹*Marconi‐Rosenblatt AI/ML Innovation Laboratory, ANDRO Computational Solutions LLC, New York, USA*

²*Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Northeastern University, Boston, USA*

 

The significance of robust wireless communication in both commercial and military applications is indisputable. The commercial sector struggles to balance limited spectral resources with the ever‐growing bandwidth demand that includes multimedia support with specific quality of service (QoS) requirements. In tactical scenarios, it has always been challenging to operate in a hostile congested and contested environment. Both these scenarios can benefit from efficient spectrum‐sensing and signal‐classification capabilities. While this problem has been studied for decades, the recent rejuvenation of machine learning has made a significant footprint in this domain. Accordingly, this chapter aims to provide readers with a comprehensive account of how machine learning techniques, specifically artificial neural networks, have been applied to solve some of the key problems related to gathering signal intelligence. To accomplish this, we begin by presenting an overview of artificial neural networks. Next, we discuss the influence of machine learning on the physical layer in the context of signal intelligence. Thereafter, we discuss directions taken by the community towards hardware implementation. Finally, we identify the key hurdles associated with the applications of machine learning at the physical layer.

 

## 13.1 Introduction

According to the latest *Ericsson Mobility Report*, there are now 5.2 billion mobile broadband subscriptions worldwide, generating more than 130 exabytes per month of wireless traffic (Ericsson Incorporated, [2018](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0014)). Moreover, it is expected that by 2020, over 50 billion devices will be absorbed into the Internet, generating a global network of “things” of dimensions never seen before (Cisco Systems, [2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0010)). Given that only a few RF spectrum bands are available to wireless carriers (Federal Communications Commission \[2016\]), technologies such as radio frequency (RF) spectrum sharing through beamforming (Shokri‐Ghadikolaei et al., [2016](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0058); Vázquez et al., [2018](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0061); Lv et al., [2018](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0041)), dynamic spectrum access (DSA) (Jin et al., [2018](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0032); Chiwewe and Hancke, [2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0009); Jagannath et al., [2018a](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0029); Federated Wireless, [2018](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0016); Agarwal and De, [2016](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0002)), and anti‐jamming technologies (Zhang et al., [2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0070); Huang et al., [2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0026); Chang et al., [2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0007)) will become essential in the near future.

Software‐defined radios were introduced as a solution to the limitations associated with a rigid radio hardware design that prevents reconfigurability and operational flexibility. Equipping radios with the ability to learn and observe operational scenarios to make cognitive decisions can improve spectrum sharing and spectral situation awareness. Spectrum sharing will allow radios to sense and utilize unused/underutilized spectrums to avoid spectrum congestion caused by unintentional/intentional interference. Further, signal sensing and classification can bolster the spectral knowledge of the radios to reinforce and foster situational awareness. Commercial and tactical military operators can exploit this cognitive ability to maximize spectrum utility and provide more robust communications links.

The recent introduction of machine learning (ML) to wireless communications has in part to do with the newfound pervasiveness of ML throughout the scientific community and in part to do with the nature of the problems that arise in wireless communications. With the advent of advances in computing power and the ability to collect and store massive amounts of data, ML techniques have found their way into many different scientific domains in an attempt to put both of the aforementioned to good use. This concept is equally true in wireless communications. Additionally, problems that arise in wireless communication systems are frequently formulated as classification, detection, estimation, and optimization problems, all of which ML techniques can provide elegant and practical solutions to. In this context, the application of ML to wireless communications seems almost natural and presents a clear motivation (Bkassiny et al., [2013](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0005); Jiang et al., [2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0031); Chen et al., ).

The objective of this chapter is to provide detailed insight into the influence artificial neural networks (ANNs) have had on the physical layer. To begin, we provide an overview of ANNs in [Section 13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-0003). In [Section 13.3](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-0006), we discuss the applications of ANNs to the physical layer specifically to acquire signal intelligence. Next, in [Section 13.4](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-0009), we discuss the implications of hardware implementations in the context of ML. Finally, in [Section 13.5](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-0015), we discuss the open problems that may be currently debilitating the application of ML in wireless systems.
