### 13.2.1 Feedforward Neural Networks

The original formulation of feedforward neural networks was proposed by Rosenblatt ([1962](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0052)). It can be seen as an extension to the perceptron algorithm, originally developed by Rosenblatt ([1957](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0051)), with an element‐wise nonlinear transition function applied to the linear classifier. This nonlinear transition function allows the hyperplane decision boundary to take a nonlinear form, allowing the model to separate training data that is not linearly separable. The formulation for a single layer is as follows,

(13.1)![equation](images/c13-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#963;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> is the training example input, ![images](images/c13-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> is the layer output, ![images](images/c13-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi></mrow></math> are the layer weights, ![images](images/c13-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is the bias. One common approach to handling the bias is to add an additional parameter to the weight vector and append a 1 to the input vector. When a bias term is omitted, this formulation can be assumed unless otherwise stated throughout the section.

The nonlinear transition function, ![images](images/c13-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow></math>, is also referred to the *activation function* throughout literature. This is often chosen from a handful of commonly used nonlinear functions for different applications. The most widely used activation functions are the following:

(13.2)![equation](images/c13-math-0002.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>z</mi> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> (13.3)![equation](images/c13-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtext mathvariant="italic">ReLU</mtext> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="2.77695pt"/> <mtext>and</mtext> </mrow> </math> (13.4)![equation](images/c13-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">tanh</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mi>z</mi> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>z</mi> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mi>z</mi> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>z</mi> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </math> 

Additionally, the radial basis function (RBF) kernel function can be used as an activation function, and doing so gives rise to the radial basis function neural network (RBFNN), as introduced by Broomhead and Lowe ([1988](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0006)). To increase the complexity of the model, and thus its ability to learn more complex relationships between the input features, network layers can be subsequently added to the model that accept the previous layer's output as input. Doing so results in a deep neural network (DNN). The function of the network as a whole, ![images](images/c13-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, becomes,

(13.5)![equation](images/c13-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where the weight matrices ![images](images/c13-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> are indexed according to the layer they belong to. Intuitively, this allows the first layer to learn linear functions between the input features, the second layer to learn nonlinear combinations of these functions, and the third layer to learn increasingly more complex nonlinear combinations of these functions. This formulation additionally gives rise to a nice graphical interpretation of the model, which is widely used in literature and given in [Figure 13.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0001).

![Figure 13.1 Standard framework of a feedforward neural network.](images/c13f001.jpg)

[Figure 13.1](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0001) Standard framework of a feedforward neural network.

This graphical interpretation is also where the feedforward neural network gets its loose biological interpretation. Each solid line in [Figure 13.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0001) denotes a weighted connection in the graph. The input, output, and hidden layers are denoted as such in the graph, and a close‐up of one node in the graph is provided. This close‐up calls the single node a neuron but it can equivalently be referred to simply as a *unit* in this text and throughout literature. The close‐up also shows the inputs to the neuron, the weighted connections from the previous layer, the weighted sum of inputs, and the activation value, denoted as ![images](images/c13-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>i</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>k</mi></mrow><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>z</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c13-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>k</mi><mi>l</mi></msubsup></mrow></math>, respectively. Occasionally, a neuron employing a given activation function may be referred to as that type of unit in this text and throughout literature, i.e. a unit with a *ReLU* activation function may be called a *ReLU unit*.

The most common way to train most types of neural networks is the optimization method called stochastic gradient descent (SGD). SGD is similar to well‐known gradient descent methods with the exception that the true gradient of the loss function with respect to the model parameters is not used to update the parameters. Usually, the gradient is computed using the loss with respect to a single training example or some subset of the entire training set, which is typically referred to as a *mini‐batch*, resulting in mini‐batch SGD. This results in the updates of the network following a noisy gradient, which in fact often helps the learning process of the network by being able to avoid convergence on local minima that are prevalent in the non‐convex loss landscapes of neural networks. The standard approach to applying SGD to the model parameters is through the repeated application of the chain rule of derivation using the famous back‐propagation algorithm developed by Rumelhart et al. ([1986](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0053)).

The last layer in a given neural network is called the output layer. The output layer differs from the inner layers in that the choice of the activation function used in the output layer is tightly coupled with the selection of the loss function and the desired structure of the output of the network. Generally, the following discussion of output layers and loss functions applies to all neural networks, including the ones introduced later in this section.

Perhaps the simplest of output unit activation functions is that of the linear output function. It takes the following form,

(13.6)![equation](images/c13-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mtext mathvariant="italic">y</mtext> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi></mrow></math> is the output layer weight matrix, ![images](images/c13-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">h</mi></mrow></math> are the latent features output from the previous layer, and ![images](images/c13-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mtext mathvariant="italic">y</mtext><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> are the estimated output targets. Coupling a linear output activation function with a mean squared error loss function results in the maximizing the log‐likelihood of the following conditional distribution,

(13.7)![equation](images/c13-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>N</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>;</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi>y</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mo>,</mo> <mi>I</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Another task prominent among ML problems is that of binary classification. In a binary classification task, the output target assumes one of two values and thus can be characterized by a Bernoulli distribution, ![images](images/c13-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Since the output of a purely linear layer has a range over the entire real line, we motivate the use of a function that “squashes” the output to lie in the interval ![images](images/c13-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, thus obtaining a proper probability. The logistic *sigmoid* does exactly this and is, in fact, the preferred method to obtain a Bernoulli output distribution. Accordingly, the output layer becomes,

(13.8)![equation](images/c13-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>y</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The negative log‐likelihood loss function, used for maximum likelihood estimation, of this output layer is given as,

[(13.9)](#c13.xhtml#c13-R_disp-0009)![equation](images/c13-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#952;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>g</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>l</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>x</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is called the *softplus* function and ![images](images/c13-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is called the *activation value*. The derivation of Eq. ([13.9](#c13.xhtml#c13-disp-0009)) is not provided here but can be found in (Goodfellow et al., 2016) for the interested reader.

In the case when the task calls for a multi‐class classification, we want a Multinoulli output distribution rather than a Bernoulli output distribution. The Multinoulli distribution assigns a probability that a particular example belongs to a particular class. Obviously, the sum over class probabilities for a single example should be equal to 1. The Multinoulli distribution is given as the conditional distribution: ![images](images/c13-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mover accent="true"><mi>y</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. It is important to note that the output, ![images](images/c13-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mtext mathvariant="bold">y</mtext><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>, is now an ![images](images/c13-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>‐dimensional vector containing the probability that ![images](images/c13-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> belongs to class ![images](images/c13-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> at each index ![images](images/c13-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> in the output vector. The targets for such a classification task are often encoded as an ![images](images/c13-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>‐dimensional vector containing ![images](images/c13-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> zeros and a single one, located at an index ![images](images/c13-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> denoting that the associated training example belongs to the class ![images](images/c13-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>. This type of target vector is commonly referred to as a *one‐hot vector*. The output function that achieves the Multinoulli distribution in the maximum likelihood setting is called the *softmax* function and is given as,

(13.10)![equation](images/c13-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>s</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>f</mi> <mi>t</mi> <mi>m</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>x</mi> <msub> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold">z</mi> </msup> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>z</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>z</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the linear activation at an output unit ![images](images/c13-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>. Softmax output units are almost exclusively coupled with a negative log‐likelihood loss function. Not only does this give rise to the maximum likelihood estimate for the Multinoulli output distribution, but the log in the loss function is able to undo the exponential in the softmax, which keeps the output units from saturating and allows the gradient to be well‐behaved, allowing the learning to proceed (Goodfellow et al., [2016](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0020)).

 

### 13.2.2 Convolutional Neural Networks

The convolutional neural network (CNN) was originally introduced by LeCun et al. ([1989](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0040)) as a means to handle grid‐like input data more efficiently. Input of this type could be in the form of a time‐series but is more typically found as image‐based input. The formulation of CNNs additionally has biological underpinnings related to the human visual cortex.

CNNs are very similar to the feedforward networks introduced previously, with the exception that they use a convolution operation in place of a matrix multiplication in the computation of a unit's activation value. In this section, we assume that the reader is familiar with the concept of the convolution operation on two continuous functions, where one function, the input function, is convolved with the convolution kernel. The primary differences from the aforementioned notion of convolution and convolution in the CNN setting are that the convolution operation is discretized (for practical implementation purposes) and that it is often truly the cross‐correlation operation that is performed in CNNs rather than true convolution. This means the kernel is not typically flipped before convolving it with the input function. This is primarily done for practical implementation purposes and does not typically affect the efficacy of the CNN in practice.

Convolution in the context of CNNs is thus defined as the following, for an input image ![images](images/c13-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow></math>,

(13.11)![equation](images/c13-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>K</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> <mi>I</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mi>m</mi> </munder> <munder> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mi>n</mi> </munder> <mi>I</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>K</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> is the convolution kernel, and the output, ![images](images/c13-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi></mrow></math>, is often referred to as the *feature map* throughout literature. It is important to note that this formulation is for two‐dimensional convolution but can be extended to input data of different dimensions. The entries of ![images](images/c13-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> can be seen as analogous to the weight parameters described previously ([Section 13.2.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-0004)) and can be learned in a similar manner using SGD and the back‐propagation (BP) algorithm Rumelhart et al. ([1986](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0053)). Intuitively, one can imagine having multiple ![images](images/c13-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> kernels in a single CNN layer being analogous to having multiple neurons in a single feedforward neural network layer. The output feature maps will be grid‐like and subsequent convolutional layers can be applied to these feature maps after the element‐wise application of one of the aforementioned nonlinear activation functions.

In addition to convolutional layers, CNNs often employ a separate kind of layer called *pooling layers*. The primary purpose of a pooling layer is to replace the output of the network at a certain location with a type of summarization of the outputs within a local neighborhood. Examples of pooling layers include max pooling (Zhou and Chellappa, [1988](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0071)), average pooling, ![images](images/c13-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> norm pooling, and distance weighted average pooling. A max pooling layer would summarize some rectangular region of the input image by selecting only the maximum activation value present in the region as output from the pooling layer. Pooling layers improve the efficacy of CNNs in a few different ways. First, they help make the learned representation of the input invariant to small translations, which is useful when aiming to determine the presence of a feature in the input rather than its location. Second, pooling layers help condense the size of the network since convolutional layers do not inherently do so. A binary classification task taking image data with size ![images](images/c13-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>256</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>256</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> will need to reduce the size of the net to a single output neuron to make use of the output layer and cost function pairs described previously in [Section 13.2.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-0004). Lastly, pooling layers lead to infinitely strong prior distributions, making the CNN more statistically efficient (Goodfellow et al., 2016).

Some common adaptations applied to CNNs come in the form of allowing information flow to skip certain layers within the network. While the following adaptions were demonstrated on CNNs and LSTM (a type of RNN), the concepts can be applied to any of the networks presented in this chapter. A RN, or ResNet (He et al., [2015](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0022)), is a neural network that contains a connection from the output of a layer, say ![images](images/c13-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, to the input of the layer ![images](images/c13-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. This connection allows the activation of the ![images](images/c13-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> layer to skip over the layer ![images](images/c13-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> such that a “residual function” is learned from layer ![images](images/c13-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to layer ![images](images/c13-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. The RN uses an identity operation on the activation of the ![images](images/c13-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math> layer, meaning the values are unchanged, prior to adding them to the values input to layer ![images](images/c13-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Conversely, a highway neural network (Srivastava et al., [2015](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0059)), allows a similar skip connection over layers but additionally applies weights and activation functions to these connections so a nonlinear relationship can be learned. Lastly, a dense neural network (Huang et al., [2016](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0025)) is a network that employs such weighted connections between each layer and all of its subsequent layers. The motivation behind each of these techniques is similar in that they attempt to mitigate learning problems associated with vanishing gradients (Hochreiter et al., [2001](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0024)). For each of these networks, the BP algorithm that Rumelhart et al. ([1986](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0053)) used must be augmented to incorporate the flow of error over these connections.

 

## 13.3 Neural Networks for Signal Intelligence

ML techniques for signal intelligence typically manifest themselves as solutions to discriminative tasks. That is, many applications focus on multi‐class or binary classification tasks. Perhaps the most prevalent signal intelligence task solved using ML techniques is that of automatic modulation classification (AMC). In short, this task involves determining what scheme was used to modulate the transmitted signal, given the raw signal observed at the receiver. Other signal intelligence tasks that employ ML solutions include wireless interference classification. In this section, different state‐of‐the‐art ML solutions to these signal intelligence tasks are discussed in further detail.

 

### 13.3.1 Modulation Classification

Deep learning (DL) solutions to modulation classification tasks have received significant attention in the last two years (O'Shea et al., [2018](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0046); O'Shea and Hoydis, [2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0045); Wang et al., [2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0062); West and O'Shea, [2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0063); Kulin et al., [2018](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0038); Karra et al., [2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0034)). O'Shea et al. ([2018](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0046)) present several DL models to address the modulation recognition problem, while Karra et al. ([2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0034)) train hierarchical deep neural networks to identify data type, modulation class, and modulation order. Kulin et al. ([2018](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0038)) present a conceptual framework for end‐to‐end wireless DL, followed by a comprehensive overview of the methodology for collecting spectrum data, designing wireless signal representations, forming training data, and training deep neural networks for wireless signal classification tasks.

The task of AMC is pertinent in signal intelligence applications as the modulation scheme of the received signal can provide insight into what type of communication frameworks and emitters are present in the local RF environment. The problem at large can be formulated as estimating the conditional distribution, ![images](images/c13-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c13-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> represents the modulation structure of the signal and ![images](images/c13-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow></math> is the received signal.

Traditionally, AMC techniques are broadly classified as maximum likelihood–based approaches (Ozdemir et al., [2013](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0047), [2015](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0048); Wimalajeewa et al., [2015](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0064); Foulke et al., [2014](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0017); Jagannath et al., [2015](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0027)), feature‐based approaches (Azzouz and Nandi, [1996](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0004); Hazza et al., [2012](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0021); Kubankova et al., [2010](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0037)), and hybrid techniques (Jagannath et al., [2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0028)). Prior to the introduction of ML, AMC tasks were often solved using complex hand‐engineered features computed from the raw signal. While these features alone can provide insight about the modulation structure of the received signal, ML algorithms can often provide a better generalization to new unseen datasets, making their employment preferable over solely feature‐based approaches. The logical remedy to the use of complex hand‐engineered feature‐based classifiers are models that aim to learn directly from received data. Recent work done by O'Shea and Corgan ([2016](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0044)) shows that deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) trained directly on complex time‐domain signal data outperform traditional models using cyclic moment feature‐based classifiers. In the work done by Shengliang Peng and Yao ([2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0056)), the authors propose a DCNN model trained on two‐dimensional constellation plots generated from received signal data and show that their approach outperforms other approaches using cumulant based classifiers and SVMs (support vector machines).

While strictly feature‐based approaches may become antiquated with the advent of the application of ML to signal intelligence, expert feature analysis can provide some useful inputs to ML algorithms. In (Jagannath et al., [2018b](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0030)), we compute hand‐engineered features directly from the raw received signal and apply a feedforward neural network classifier to the features to provide an AMC. The discrete time complex valued received signal can be represented as

(13.12)![equation](images/c13-math-0012.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width="2.77695pt"/> <mspace width="2.77695pt"/> <mspace width="2.77695pt"/> <mspace width="2.77695pt"/> <mspace width="2.77695pt"/> <mspace width="2.77695pt"/> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>.</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>N</mi> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the discrete‐time transmitted signal, ![images](images/c13-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the complex valued channel gain that follows a Gaussian distribution, and ![images](images/c13-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>w</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the additive complex zero‐mean white Gaussian noise process at the receiver with two‐sided power spectral density (PSD) ![images](images/c13-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>. The received signal is passed through an automatic gain control prior to the computation of feature values.

The first feature value computed from the received signal is the variance of the amplitude of the signal and is given by

(13.13)![equation](images/c13-math-0013.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>V</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>s</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>s</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></math> is the absolute value of the over‐sampled signal and ![images](images/c13-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> represents the mean computed from ![images](images/c13-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> samples. This feature provides information that helps distinguish frequency shift keying (FSK) modulations from the phase shift keying (PSK) and quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) modulation structures also considered in the classification task. The second and third features considered are the mean and variance of the maximum value of the power spectral density of the normalized centered‐instantaneous amplitude, which is given as

(13.14)![equation](images/c13-math-0014.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>x</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>x</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>F</mi> <mi>F</mi> <mi>T</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mrow> <mi>c</mi> <mi>n</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>s</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>.</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> represents the fast Fourier transform (FFT) function, ![images](images/c13-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8796;</mo><mfrac><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></mfrac><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></msubsup><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c13-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the absolute value of the complex‐valued received signal. This feature provides a measure of the deviation of the PSD from its average value. The mean and variance of this feature computed over subsets of a given training example are used as two separate entries in the feature vector input into the classification algorithm, corresponding to the second and third features, respectively.

The fourth feature used in our work was computed using higher‐order statistics of the received signal: cumulants, which are known to be invariant to the various distortions commonly seen in random signals and are computed as follows,

(13.15)![equation](images/c13-math-0015.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mi>k</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mtext>No. of partitions in</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi>l</mi> </mrow> </munderover> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>!</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8719;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>j</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </munderover> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>l</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>k</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msup> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mrow> <mo>&#42;</mo> <msub> <mi>k</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> denotes the order and ![images](images/c13-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> denotes the number of conjugations involved in the computation of the statistic. We use the ratio ![images](images/c13-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>40</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>C</mi><mn>42</mn></msub></mrow></math> as the fourth feature, which is computed using

(13.16)![equation](images/c13-math-0016.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mn>42</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>y</mi> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mn>4</mn> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>y</mi> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> (13.17)![equation](images/c13-math-0017.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mn>40</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mn>4</mn> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The fifth feature used in our work is called the in‐band spectral variation as it allows discrimination between the FSK modulations considered in the task. We define ![images](images/c13-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> as

(13.18)![equation](images/c13-math-0018.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>V</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>V</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>r</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> F</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>F</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> is the step size, ![images](images/c13-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>F</mi><mi>F</mi><mi>T</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c13-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is the frequency band of interest.

The final feature used in the classifier is the variance of the deviation of the normalized signal from the unit circle, which is denoted as ![images](images/c13-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. It is given as

(13.19)![equation](images/c13-math-0019.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#916;</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

This feature helps the classifier discriminate between PSK and QAM modulation schemes.

The modulations considered in the work are the following: binary phase shift keying (BPSK), quadrature phase shift keying (QPSK), 8‐PSK, 16‐QAM, continuous phase frequency shift keying (CPFSK), Gaussian frequency shift keying (GFSK), and Gaussian minimum shift keying (GMSK). This characterizes a seven‐class classification task using the aforementioned six features computed from each training example. To generate the dataset, a total of 35,000 examples were collected: 1,000 examples for each modulation at each of the five SNR scenarios considered in the work. Three different feedforward neural network structures were trained at each SNR scenario using a training set consisting of ![images](images/c13-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>80</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of the data collected at the given SNR and a test set consisting of the remaining ![images](images/c13-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>. The three feedforward nets differed in the number of hidden layers, ranging from one to three. Qualitatively, the feedforward network with one hidden layer outperformed the other models in all but the least favorable SNR scenario, achieving the highest classification accuracy of ![images](images/c13-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>98</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> in the most favorable SNR scenario. The seemingly paradoxical behavior is attributed to the over‐fitting of the training data when using the higher‐complexity models, leading to poorer generalization in the test set.

This work has been further extended to evaluate other ML techniques using the same features. Accordingly, we found that training a random forest classifier for the same AMC task yielded similar results to the feedforward network classifier. Additionally, the random forest classifier was found to outperform the DNN approach in scenarios when the exact center frequency of the transmitter was not known, which was assumed to be given in Jagannath et al. ([2018b](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0030)). The random forest classifier comprised 20 classification and regression trees (CARTs) constructed using the gini impurity function. At each split, a subset of the feature vectors with cardinality equal to 3 was considered.

An alternative approach to the previously described method is to learn the modulation of the received signal from different representations of the raw signal. Kulin et al. ([2018](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0038)) train DCNNs to learn the modulation of various signals using three separate representations of the raw received signal. In the work, the raw complex valued received signal training examples are denoted as ![images](images/c13-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>C</mi><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c13-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> indexes the procured training dataset and ![images](images/c13-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> is the number of complex valued samples in each training example. We inherit this notation for presentation of their findings. The dataset in the work was collected by sampling a continuous transmission for a period of time and subsequently segmenting the received samples into ![images](images/c13-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> dimensional data vectors.

Kulin et al. ([2018](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0038)) train separate DCNNs on three different representations of the raw received signal and compare their results to evaluate which representation provides the best classification accuracy. The first of the three signal representations are given as a ![images](images/c13-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> dimensional in‐phase/quadrature (I/Q) matrix containing real‐valued data vectors carrying the I/Q information of the raw signal, denoted ![images](images/c13-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>q</mi></msub></mrow></math>, respectively. Mathematically,

(13.20)![equation](images/c13-math-0020.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mrow> <mi>I</mi> <mi>Q</mi> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msubsup> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mi>q</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msubsup> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>I</mi><mi>Q</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. The second representation used is a mapping from the complex values of the raw received signal into two real‐valued vectors representing the phase, ![images](images/c13-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi></mrow></math> and the magnitude, ![images](images/c13-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi></mrow></math>,

(13.21)![equation](images/c13-math-0021.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mrow> <mi>A</mi> <mo stretchy="false">/</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mi>A</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msubsup> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msubsup> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c13-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> and the phase vector ![images](images/c13-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi></mrow><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow></math> and magnitude vector ![images](images/c13-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>x</mi><mi>A</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow></math> have elements

(13.22)![equation](images/c13-math-0022.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">arctan</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mi>r</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>r</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>i</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>A</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msubsup> <mi>r</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>r</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>i</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </math> 

respectively. The third representation is a frequency domain representation of the raw time‐domain complex signal. It is characterized by two real‐valued data vectors, one containing the real components of the complex FFT, ![images](images/c13-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8476;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and the other containing the imaginary components of the complex FFT, ![images](images/c13-i0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8465;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>X</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, giving

(13.23)![equation](images/c13-math-0023.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mi>k</mi> <mi>F</mi> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8476;</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </msup> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8465;</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>X</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </msup> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> 

Using these three representations of the raw signal, three DCNNs with identical structure are trained on each representation, and the accuracy of the resultant models is compared to determine which representation allows for learning the best mapping from raw signal to modulation structure.

Each training example comprised ![images](images/c13-i0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow></math> samples of the raw signal sampled at ![images](images/c13-i0123.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn mathvariant="normal">1</mn><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">MS</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow></math> (mega‐samples per seconds), and the following 11 modulation formats were considered in the classification task: BPSK, QPSK, 8‐PSK, 16‐QAM, 64‐QAM, CPFSK, GFSK, 4‐PAM, wideband frequency modulation (WBFM), amplitude modulation–double‐sideband modulation (AM‐DSB), and amplitude modulation–single‐sideband modulation (AM‐SSB). Thus, the training targets ![images](images/c13-i0124.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mn>11</mn></msup></mrow></math> are encoded as one‐hot vectors where the index holding an ![images](images/c13-i0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> corresponds to the modulation of the signal. A total of 220,000 training examples ![images](images/c13-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>k</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>R</mi><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>128</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> were acquired uniformly over different SNR scenarios ranging from ![images](images/c13-i0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>20</mn><mi>d</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math> to ![images](images/c13-i0128.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>20</mn><mi>d</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>.

The DCNN structure used for each signal representation is the same and consists of two convolutional layers, a fully connected layer, and a softmax output layer trained using the negative log‐likelihood loss function. The activation function used in each of the convolutional layers and the fully connected layer is the ReLU function. The DCNNs were trained using a training set comprising ![images](images/c13-i0129.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>67</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of the total dataset, with the rest of the dataset being used as test and validation sets. An Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba, [2014](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0035)) was used to optimize the training processes for a total of 70 epochs. The metrics used to evaluate each of the models include the precision, recall, and F1 score of each model. In the work, a range of values is provided for the three aforementioned metrics for the CNN models trained on different data representations for three different SNR scenarios: high, medium, and low, corresponding to ![images](images/c13-i0130.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>18</mn><mi>d</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c13-i0131.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>0</mn><mi>d</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c13-i0132.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>8</mn><mi>d</mi><mi>B</mi></mrow></math>, respectively. In the high SNR scenario, it is reported that the precision, recall, and F1 score of each of the three CNN models fall in the range of 0.67–0.86. For the medium and low SNR scenarios, the same metrics are reported in the ranges of 0.59–0.75 and 0.22–0.36, respectively. This relatively low performance can be attributed to the choice of the channel model used when generating the data, namely, a time‐varying multipath fading channel.

Furthermore, the evaluation criteria also includes the classification accuracy of each of the three models trained using different data representations under similar SNR conditions. Qualitatively, each of the three DCNN models performs similarly at low SNR, while the DCNN trained on the I/Q representation of data yields a better accuracy at medium SNR, and the DCNN trained on the amplitude and phase representation yields a better accuracy at high SNR. Interestingly, the DCNN trained on the frequency domain representation of the data performs significantly worse than the ![images](images/c13-i0133.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>I</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0134.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>A</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow></math> DCNNs at high SNR. This could potentially be due to similar characteristics exhibited in the frequency domain representation of the PSK and QAM modulations used in the classification problem. The primary takeaways from this work are that learning to classify modulation directly from different representations of the raw signal can be an effective means of developing a solution to the AMC task; however, the efficacy of the classifier is dependent on how the raw signal is represented to the learning algorithm.

 

### 13.3.2 Wireless Interference Classification

Wireless interference classification (WIC) is a classification task that is concerned with identifying what type of wireless emitter exists in the environment. The motivation behind such a task is that it can often be helpful to know what type of emitters are present (WiFi, Zigbee, Bluetooth, etc.) so that you can effectively attempt to avoid interference and coexist with other emitters sharing the resources. Recent work done by Selim et al. ([2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0054)) shows the use of DCNNs to classify radar signals using both spectrogram and amplitude‐phase representations of the received signal. In the work presented by Akeret et al. ([2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0003)), DCNN models are proposed to accomplish interference classification on two‐dimensional time‐frequency representations of the received signal to mitigate the effects of radio interference in cosmological data. Additionally, the authors of Czech et al. ([2018](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0011)) employ DCNN and LSTM models to achieve a similar end.

Kulin et al. ([2018](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0038)) propose to employ DCNNs for the purpose of the wireless interference classification of three different wireless communication systems based on the WiFi, Zigbee, and Bluetooth standards. They look at 5 different channels for each of the 3 standards and construct a 15‐class classification task for which they obtain ![images](images/c13-i0135.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>225</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>225</mn></mrow></math> training vectors consisting of 128 samples each, where samples were collected at ![images](images/c13-i0136.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn mathvariant="normal">10</mn><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">MS</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow></math>. A flat fading channel with additive white Gaussian noise is assumed for this classification task.

Three DCNNs were trained and evaluated using the wireless interference classification dataset described. Each of the three DCNNs was trained on one of the representations of the data that were presented in the previous section that discussed AMC. The DCNN architectures were also the same as presented previously in [Section 13.3.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-0007).

Each of the three DCNNs trained using different data representations were evaluated in a similar fashion to the evaluation method described in [Section 13.3.1](#c13.xhtml#c13-sec-0007), namely, using precision, recall, and F1 score under different SNR scenarios. For the wireless interference classification task, the precision, recall, and F1 score of each of the three DCNNs all fell in the interval from 0.98–0.99 under the high SNR scenario. For the medium and low SNR scenarios, the analogous intervals were from 0.94–0.99 and 0.81–0.90, respectively.

Additionally, Kulin et al. ([2018](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0038)) provide an analysis of classification accuracy for each of the three DCNN models at varying SNRs. For the task of wireless interference classification, the DCNN model trained on the frequency‐domain representation of the data outperforms the other models at all SNRs and especially so in lower SNR scenarios. These findings are due to the fact that the wireless signals that were considered have more expressive features in the frequency domain as they have different bandwidth, modulation, and spreading characteristics.

Youssef et al. ([2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0069)) take a different approach to the wireless interference classification task and primarily compare different types of learning models rather than different types of data representation. The proposed models include deep feedforward networks, deep convolutional networks, support vector machines using two different kernels, and a MST (minimum‐spanning‐tree) algorithm using two different learning algorithms. In the work, 12 different transmitters are considered, and 1,000 packets from each transmitter are collected for a total of 12,000 packets forming the entire dataset. Each transmitter transmitted the same exact 1,000 packets, which were generated using pseudo‐random values injected into the modem. All of the transmitters used a proprietary orthogonal frequency‐division multiplexing (OFDM) protocol with a QPSK modulation scheme and a baseband transmitter sample rate of ![images](images/c13-i0137.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn mathvariant="normal">1.92</mn><mspace width="0.3em"/><mi mathvariant="normal">MS</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">s</mi></mrow></math>. At the receiver, each packet is represented by 10,000 time‐domain I/Q samples. Each of the models was trained on datasets consisting of training examples made up of 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, and 1024 samples from each packet, and their performance is compared across datasets. Given the complex‐valued received signal,

![Figure 13.2 Adaptation of MST MLP used by Youssef et al. (2017).](images/c13f002.jpg)

[Figure 13.2](#c13.xhtml#R_c13-fig-0002) Adaptation of MST MLP used by Youssef et al. ([2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0069)).

The DNN architecture considered in the work consisted of two fully connected hidden layers, consisting of 128 ReLU units each and an output layer consisting of logistic sigmoid units. The network was trained using the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba, [2014](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0035)) and a mini‐batch size of 32.

The DCNN model used by the authors was composed of two convolutional layers using 64 (![images](images/c13-i0145.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>8</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math>) and 32 (![images](images/c13-i0146.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>16</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>) filters, respectively. Each convolutional layer was input into a max‐pool layer with a pool size of ![images](images/c13-i0147.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0148.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, respectively. The output of the second max‐pool layer was fed into a fully connected layer consisting of 128 ReLU units. An output layer employing logistic sigmoid units was used on top of the fully connected layer.

The two SVM architectures analyzed in the work differ only in the kernel function used. The first architecture employed the polynomial kernel and the second employed the Pearson VII universal kernel (Üstün et al., [2005](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0060)). Both architectures used Platt's minimization optimization algorithm to compute the maximum‐margin hyperplanes.

Furthermore, an analysis of the performance of MST multi‐layer perceptrons (MLPs) trained using first‐order and second‐order methods is provided. A high‐level description of MST MLPs is presented here, and we refer the interested reader to Youssef et al. ([2015](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0068)) for a more rigorous derivation. The MST method to training neural networks, as presented in the work, is essentially a hierarchical way to solve an optimization problem by solving smaller constituent optimization problems. To this end, in what is called the first stage, a number of separate MLPs would be trained on different subsets of the training dataset. This can be seen in the lowest layer of the hierarchical representation adapted from Youssef et al. ([2017](#c13.xhtml#c13-bib-0069)) and provided in [Figure 13.2](#c13.xhtml#c13-fig-0002).

Once the first stage is trained, a second stage is trained by taking the concatenation of the network outputs from the first stage as input. Training can continue in this fashion for subsequent stages. One of the advantages of training networks in this way is that the many smaller MLPs that form the larger classifier can be efficiently trained using second‐order optimization methods. Second‐order optimization methods such as Newton, Gauss‐Newton, and Levenberg‐Marquardt methods are usually intractable due to the size of typical networks but can provide better convergence when applicable. Two three‐stage MST systems were trained in the work, one using the first‐order method of SGD, and the other using the second‐order accelerated Levenberg‐Marquardt method (K. Youssef). Each MST system had an identical structure where stage 1 consisted of 60 MLPs with 2 hidden layers and 10 units in each layer. Stages 2 and 3 had the same architecture and consisted of 30 MLPs, with each MLP consisting of 2 hidden layers made up of 15 units each. All hidden units employed the tanh activation function, and all output layers contained linear units.

All of the models described were trained on 10 different iterations of the collected dataset, and their performance was compared. Five datasets were constructed using training examples made up of 32, 64, 128, 256, and 512 samples, and then each model was trained twice, using a training set consisting of ![images](images/c13-i0149.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c13-i0150.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of the total dataset, for a total of 10 different datasets for each model. In general, the MST system trained using second‐order methods on ![images](images/c13-i0151.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of the training data performed best across all sizes of training examples, yielding a classification accuracy of ![images](images/c13-i0152.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>100</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> for each dataset. All of the models performed better when trained using ![images](images/c13-i0153.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>90</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of the dataset as opposed to ![images](images/c13-i0154.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of the training dataset. Generally, each model performed better when provided with training examples that contained more samples, with the exception of the deep feedforward network model, which could be attributed to the fact that longer sequences of samples may contain an increasing number of artifacts to which the DNN may not be robust.
