# 15  
Deep Learning Techniques for Decoding Polar Codes

*Warren J. Gross Nghia Doan Elie Ngomseu Mambou and Seyyed Ali Hashemi*

*Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, McGill University, Montreal, Quebec, Canada*

 

In recent decades, the challenge of designing capacity‐approaching codes has been one of the main focuses in digital communications. In this regard, polar codes were introduced as the first class of error‐correcting codes that provably achieve the capacity for any channel at infinite code length. Recently, deep learning (DL) has shown great potential in a wide range of applications in digital communications including channel coding for forward error correction (FEC) codes. Therefore, we believe that a literature review on the intersection between DL and FEC codes, especially polar codes, can contribute to the coding community. Organized into four sections, this chapter first provides background and motivation for the use of DL in various FEC schemes used for wireless communication systems. [Section 15.2](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-0003) introduces polar codes and their traditional decoding algorithms. In [Section 15.3](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-0008), three major DL‐based approaches for decoding polar codes are presented in terms of decoding performance, algorithm complexity, and decoding latency. The last section of this chapter, [Section 15.4](#c15.xhtml#c15-sec-0015), offers further discussion and conclusions.

 

## 15.1 Motivation and Background

Deep learning (DL) (LeCun et al., [2015](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0024)) has been widely used in digital communications through applications such as channel decoding, prediction, equalization, modulation/demodulation, detection, quantization, compression, and spectrum sensing (Ibnkahla, [2000](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0021)). In (O'Shea and Hoydis, [2017](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0029)), a new approach in communication systems based on DL was introduced, where the entire channel transmission was abstracted as an autoencoder: that is, an end‐to‐end pipeline designed by joint concatenation of transmitters and receivers in a single process. It has been established that the block error rate (BLER) of traditional communication systems can be improved through this scheme. Furthermore, this idea of end‐to‐end channel modeling was extended to multiple‐input and multiple‐output (MIMO) systems. MIMO suffers from interference between channels in a way that obtaining the optimal signal is very difficult. It has been shown that such systems can be represented as multiple‐input and ‐output generative adversarial nets (Goodfellow et al., [2014](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0015)), which can be optimized using a customized loss function for the joint model. The challenges and opportunities related to DL for the wireless physical layer were presented in (Wang et al., [2017](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0038)).

In (Farsad et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0014)), a DL‐based approach for joint source‐channel coding of a text was proposed. This approach is quite similar to the idea presented in (O'Shea and Hoydis, [2017](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0029)), where the source is jointly trained with the channel to reduce transmission distortion. This architecture makes use of a long short‐term memory (LSTM)‐based model, as proposed in (Graves and Schmidhuber, [2005](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0016), Hasim et al., [2014](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0019)), over a binary erasure channel (BEC) to ensure a gain in word error rate (WER) when compared to separate source‐channel word processing. However, the fixed‐length word‐processing scheme does not allow flexibility at the incoming source. Similarly, an end‐to‐end neural network (NN) system was proposed for communication over the air between two software‐defined radios (SDRs) in (Dörner et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0013)).

The concept of an end‐to‐end NN was also extended for MIMO relays in (Sun and Jing, [2012](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0034)). In this work, channel training and coherent decoding under estimated channel error were studied for relay networks, and the setup of a single‐antenna as transmitter, ![images](images/c15-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> distinct antenna relays, and a single ![images](images/c15-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> antenna receiver is considered. Note that many coherent cooperative decoding methods assume perfect and global channel state information (CSI), which is in reality imperfect, especially in cooperative relay networks. Two types of approaches were considered: decoding where CSI is assumed noise‐free, and matched decoding where the noise estimation is evaluated. Simulations demonstrate that at least ![images](images/c15-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> symbol intervals of training are needed for mismatched decoding versus ![images](images/c15-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> for matched decoding to achieve full diversity. In addition, adaptive decoding was presented to compensate for the complexity in the matched decoding. Several works concerning NNs applied to MIMO systems can be found in (Wen et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0039), O'Shea and Hoydis, [2017](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0029), Samuel et al., [2017](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0033)).

It was established that DL decoding for linear block codes is equivalent to deriving the maximum energy function of a NN (Bruck and Blaum, [1989](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0008)). In order to maximize the energy function of a NN, (Bruck and Blaum, [1989](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0008)) suggested that decoding of FEC codes can be done through maximizing polynomials over the ![images](images/c15-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>‐cube for a ![images](images/c15-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> block code, where ![images](images/c15-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> is the length and ![images](images/c15-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> is the dimension of the code. With similar logic, (Tallini and Cull, [1995](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0036)) predicted that the NP‐complete problem of receiving an error‐free message through a channel can be solved through NN. In (Wu et al., [2002](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0040)), a neural structure was described as a perceptron with a higher‐order polynomial as a discriminant function. A ![images](images/c15-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mi>m</mi></msup><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> Hamming code was decoded through only ![images](images/c15-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> assigned weights on each perceptron, ![images](images/c15-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> being a positive integer. This architecture combines two layers: the first is made of a set of parity bits, and the second is a linear classifier. This proves that high‐order codes such as Bose Chaudhuri Hocquenghem (BCH) codes can be learned successfully through a multilayer perceptron (MLP).

In channel coding, DL‐based decoders can provide improvements in error probabilities over conventional decoders. In (Nachmani et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0028)), the conventional belief propagation (BP) decoding algorithm is formalized as a partially connected NN. In addition, by assigning trainable weights to the BP‐based NN, neural BP decoders can achieve the same performance as the conventional sum‐product BP decoding algorithm with a significantly smaller number of iterations. In (Kim et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0022)), the sequential decoding of turbo and convolutional codes (Berrou et al., [1993](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0007), Viterbi, [1971](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0037)) was performed through recurrent neural network (RNN)‐based models. It has been demonstrated that a trained RNN architecture can decode these codes over additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channels with performance near that of the maximum a posteriori (MAP) decoding given by the Bahl‐Cocke‐Jelinek‐Raviv (BCJR) algorithm and the maximum likelihood (ML) decoding given by Viterbi algorithm for sequential codes. This result was confirmed in (Kim et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0022)) through the same architecture and extended to codes with larger block lengths. In (Bennatan et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0006)), a syndrome‐based DL technique was proposed to decode linear block codes. For a BCH code of length 127, an 11‐layer vanilla MLP and a RNN of 4 stacks were considered separately to estimate the channel noise rather than the transmitted codeword. The syndrome decoding and soft channel reliabilities were helpful to eliminate the problem of overfitting of the training codeword set. BCH decoding performance was compared under traditional BP decoding, syndrome‐based vanilla MLP, and syndrome‐based stacked RNN. Results showed that syndrome‐based stacked RNN performance approached that of the ordered statistics decoding (OSD) of order 2 while outperforming that of the syndrome‐based vanilla MLP at the cost of high complexity and latency.

In the following section, we will focus on DL techniques used for polar codes as a case study of DL for FEC codes.

 

## 15.2 Decoding of Polar Codes: An Overview

Polar codes are a recent breakthrough in the field of channel coding, as they were proven to achieve channel capacity with efficient encoding and decoding algorithms (Arıkan, [2009](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0003)). Successive cancellation (SC) and BP decoding algorithms are first introduced to decode polar codes (Arıkan, [2009](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0003)). Although SC decoding can provide a low‐complexity implementation, its serial nature prevents the decoder from reaching a high decoding throughput. In addition, the error‐correction performance of SC decoding for short to moderate polar codes does not satisfy the requirements of the fifth generation of cellular mobile communications (5G). SC list (SCL) decoding was introduced in (Tal and Vardy, [2015](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0035)) to improve the performance of SC decoding. SCL can provide a significant improvement in terms of error probability if the decoder is aided by a cyclic redundancy check (CRC). With these appealing properties, polar codes have been selected to be used in the enhanced mobile broadband (eMBB) control channel of 5G, together with a CRC (3GPP, [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0001)).

Recently, it has been shown that polar codes can also be decoded using off‐the‐shelf DL decoders, which may lead to high decoding throughput thanks to their one‐shot‐decoding property (Cammerer et al., [2017](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0009)). In addition, it was observed that by assigning trainable weights to the unrolled factor graph of polar codes, neural BP decoders can provide a significant error‐correction performance gain over conventional BP decoding (Nachmani et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0028)). Other approaches such as using DL models for channel noise estimation have also demonstrated great potential for DL techniques when applied to well‐established problems in channel coding (Bennatan et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0006), Liang et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0025)).

In this section, we first provide some basic knowledge about polar codes and conventional polar decoders. In the next section, several DL‐based decoding algorithms and their variants for polar codes are discussed, followed by a detailed evaluation concerning error‐correction performance and decoding latency of state‐of‐the‐art DL‐aided decoders for a 5G polar code.

 

### 15.2.1 Problem Formulation of Polar Codes

The locations of the frozen bits are known to both the encoder and the decoder, and their values are set to 0. The soft vector of the transmitted codeword received by the decoder in this setting can be written as

### 15.2.2 Successive‐Cancellation Decoding

The SC decoding algorithm can be illustrated on a polar‐code factor graph as shown in [Figure 15.1](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0001)a, where ![images](images/c15-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>8</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c15-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>. The messages are propagated through the SC processing elements (SCPEs) as shown in [Figure 15.1](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0001)b, where ![images](images/c15-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> denotes a left‐to‐right message and ![images](images/c15-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> denotes a right‐to‐left message of the ![images](images/c15-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>‐th bit index at stage ![images](images/c15-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> of the factor graph.

In SC decoding, the right‐to‐left messages ![images](images/c15-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are soft LLR values, and the left‐to‐right messages ![images](images/c15-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> are hard decision bits. ### 15.2.3 Successive‐Cancellation List Decoding

SCL decoding improves the error‐correction performance of SC decoding by running multiple SC decoders in parallel. Instead of using Eq. ([15.9](#c15.xhtml#c15-disp-0009)) to estimate ![images](images/c15-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi></mrow></math> as in SC decoding, each bit is estimated considering both its possible values 0 and 1. Therefore, at each bit estimation, the number of candidates doubles. In order to constrain the high complexity of SCL decoding, at each bit estimation, a set of only ![images](images/c15-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> candidates are allowed to survive, based on a path metric that is calculated as (Balatsoukas‐Stimming et al., [2015](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0005), Hashemi et al., [2016](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0018))

### 15.2.4 Belief Propagation Decoding

[Figure 15.2](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0002)a demonstrates BP decoding on the factor graph representation of ![images](images/c15-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. The messages are iteratively propagated through the BP processing elements (BPPEs) (Arıkan, [2010](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0004)) located in each stage. Each update iteration starts with a right‐to‐left message pass that propagates the LLR values from the channel (rightmost) stage to the information bit (leftmost) stage, and ends with the left‐to‐right message pass, which occurs in the opposite order. [Figure 15.2](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0002)b illustrates a BPPE with its corresponding soft messages, where ![images](images/c15-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>r</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> denotes a left‐to‐right message and ![images](images/c15-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>l</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>s</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> denotes a right‐to‐left message of the ![images](images/c15-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>‐th bit index at stage ![images](images/c15-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>. One can also apply BP decoding on the unrolled polar‐code factor graph (Doan et al., [2018b](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0012)); thus the BP iterations in this setup are performed sequentially. Figures [15.2](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0002)c and [15.2](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0002)d illustrate the input and output messages of a BPPE for the right‐to‐left and left‐to‐right message updates on an unrolled factor graph, where the superscript ![images](images/c15-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow></math> denotes the iteration number. The update rule (Arıkan, [2010](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0004)) for the right‐to‐left messages of a BPPE is

## 15.3 DL‐Based Decoding for Polar Codes

As mentioned earlier, this section is devoted to the use of DL in decoding polar codes with emphasis on off‐the‐shelf DL decoders and DL‐aided decoders by addressing their working principles, algorithm details, and performance evaluations.

 

### 15.3.1 Off‐the‐Shelf DL Decoders for Polar Codes

In (Gruber et al., [2017](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0017)), it was shown that a MLP decoder can generalize structured codes, e.g. polar codes, more effectively than random codes, where the MAP performance was obtained for structured codes but not for random codes. However, the considered code length in (Gruber et al., [2017](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0017)) is limited to 16. A more detailed investigation was carried out in (Lyu et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0027)), where a comparison was performed between different off‐the‐shelf network models including MLP, a convolutional neural network (CNN), and a RNN for polar codes. The RNN model outperforms the MLP and CNN models in terms of error‐correction performance, at the cost of the highest decoding complexity. On the other hand, the CNN model provided a performance gain over the MLP model, with higher computational time. It was also observed in (Lyu et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0027)) that the code length impacts the fitting (underfitting versus overfitting) of the deep NN, and each type of NN has a saturation code length, which is related to the learning capabilities of the model.

For all the aforementioned off‐the‐shelf decoders, the networks are formalized to solve a multi‐category classification problem where the correct codewords are used as the training labels and the corresponding values of ![images](images/c15-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">LLR</mi><mi>x</mi></msub></mrow></math> are used as the network's input. Normally, the size of the DL decoder scales with the size of the codeword and the natural architecture of the DL models in use. Finding the network parameters or weights is done by backpropagation (LeCun et al., [2015](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0024)) with various optimization methods such as ADAM (Kingma and Ba, [2014](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0023)) or RMSPROP (Hinton et al.). Polar decoding under off‐the‐shelf DL decoders is carried out by performing the inference phase of the trained DL models, given the channel LLR values.

The main problem associated with off‐the‐shelf DL decoders when applied to polar codes or other linear block codes is *the curse of dimensionality* (Gruber et al., [2017](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0017)), which states that the number of required training samples scales exponentially with code length. To overcome this issue, a scaling approach was introduced in (Cammerer et al., [2017](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0009)) constraining DL decoders to only work with sub‐codes with small code sizes. Specifically, a partitioned NN (PNN) decoder for a polar code of size 128 was proposed. The considered polar code was divided into smaller sub‐blocks, and the partitioned DL decoders are trained individually so that the performance obtained for each sub‐block was close to that of MAP decoding. However, the bit‐error‐rate (BER) performance of the integrated system is only similar to that of SC decoding. It is worth mentioning that the latency of the proposed decoder can be reduced as parallel computations can be exploited for the DL decoders thanks to their one‐shot‐decoding property.

In (Doan et al., [2018a](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0011)), a neural decoder was introduced on the basis of the partitioning idea of (Cammerer et al., [2017](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0009)). The proposed neural SC (NSC) in (Doan et al., [2018a](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0011)) preserves the same decoding performance in terms of BER and frame error rate (FER) as that of PNN, with a decoding latency improved by ![images](images/c15-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>42.5</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> for a polar code of length 128 and rate 0.5.

 

### 15.3.2 DL‐Aided Decoders for Polar Codes

 

#### 15.3.2.1 Neural Belief Propagation Decoders

In contrast to off‐the‐shelf DL decoders, another approach is to exploit *domain knowledge* to design DL‐aided decoders. In (Nachmani et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0028)), a deep neural BP decoder is proposed to improve conventional BP decoding where trainable weights are assigned to the edges of the unrolled factor graph. The deep network in this case is constrained to be a partially connected NN, and its inference functions resemble the operations of conventional BP decoding. This idea was first evaluated on high‐density parity check (HDPC) codes in (Nachmani et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0028)) and then on polar codes in (Doan et al., [2018b](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0012)). It was observed that the trainable weights help the conventional BP decoding to mitigate the detrimental effects of the code's short cycles, which are often found in practical linear codes.

Another problem associated with BP decoding is the costly sum‐product (SP) algorithm (Ryan and Lin, [2009](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0032)). Instead, a low complexity min‐sum (MS) algorithm is used in practical applications (Ryan and Lin, [2009](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0032)). However, the MS algorithm also introduces decoding errors due to its poor estimation compared to the SP algorithm. With the objective of tackling this challenge, neural offset min‐sum (NOMS) decoding was proposed in (Lugosch and Gross, [2017](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0026)). The NOMS algorithm trains offset parameters and uses them to correct the MS approximation. It should be noted that NOMS decoding only requires additions, which makes this decoder particularly attractive for hardware implementation.

![Figure 15.3 A neural BP decoder architecture with two iterations for images.](images/c15f003.jpg)

[Figure 15.3](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0003) A neural BP decoder architecture with two iterations for ![images](images/c15-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>8</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

In (Nachmani et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0028)), the architectures from (Nachmani et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0028)) and (Lugosch and Gross, [2017](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0026)) were changed to resemble an RNN by reusing the weights at each iteration; this reduces their complexity, as fewer parameters are needed. Furthermore, an RNN architecture based on a successive relaxation technique was constructed, which further improved the proposed RNN‐like neural BP decoders.

In (Xu et al., [2017](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0041)), a neural normalized min‐sum (NNMS) decoder was developed, which adapts the idea in (Nachmani et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0028)) for the case of polar codes. NNMS also uses a multiplicative weight to correct the min‐sum approximation. This setup can be scaled to large size polar codes while still maintaining low decoding latency and complexity.

It was shown in (Ren et al., [2015](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0030)) that the CRC capability is only used as an early stopping criterion with incremental error‐correction performance improvement for BP decoding of polar codes. In (Doan et al., [2018b](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0012)), by assigning trainable weights to the CRC‐Polar concatenated graph, the proposed decoder has shown a performance gain of 0.5 dB over the conventional CRC‐aided BP at the FER of ![images](images/c15-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, for a 5G polar code of length 128. The authors in (Doan et al., [2018b](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0012)) also derived a general neural BP decoder architecture specified for polar codes. [Figure 15.3](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0003) illustrates an example of this architecture where the weights are shared between each neural BP decoding iteration. The weight‐assignment schemes of state‐of‐the‐art neural BP decoders when applied to the BPPE update functions in Eqs. ([15.12](#c15.xhtml#c15-disp-0012)) and ([15.13](#c15.xhtml#c15-disp-0013)) are summarized as follows:

Optimizing the weights of the neural BP decoders, as depicted in [Figure 15.3](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0003), can be done through backpropagation in order to minimize the following objective function

where ![images](images/c15-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>H</mi><mtext>CE</mtext></msub></mrow></math> is the cross‐entropy function, and ![images](images/c15-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">h</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">s</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the correct hard value vector at stage ![images](images/c15-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> of the polar code factor graph that is obtained from the training samples. In the decoding phase, only the hard estimated values at stage 0 of the polar code factor graph, i.e. ![images](images/c15-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#293;</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn><mi>i</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> ![images](images/c15-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, is required to obtain the decoded message bits.

 

#### 15.3.2.2 Joint Decoder and Noise Estimator

In (Liang et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0025)) a CNN‐based noise estimator is used to remove interference noise between channels. The noise estimator is then coupled with a conventional BP decoder. Although the proposed iterative denoising‐decoding approach in (Liang et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0025)) showed a significant performance gain in the case of strong correlations between channels, when there is no correlation, this approach only achieved a negligible error probability gain over the conventional BP decoder.

A multiplicative noise model was introduced in (Bennatan et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0006)) based on the decoding syndrome. This noise model has two advantages compared to that of the additive noise‐estimation model used in (Liang et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0025)). First, it reduces the regression problem of the noise model in (Liang et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0025)) to a classification problem, i.e. only learn to estimate the sign of the noise instead of the actual noise value, which is more feasible given the high dimensional state of the model inputs. Second, the multiplicative noise‐estimation model also preserves the code symmetry conditions (Richardson and Urbanke, [2008](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0031)), allowing for the use of all‐zero codewords during training.

[Figure 15.4](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0004) depicts a joint decoder‐noise estimator approach derived from (Liang et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0025), Bennatan et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0006)), where the noise estimator is a DL model such as NN, CNN, or RNN. Unlike off‐the‐shelf DL decoders, which try to directly predict the message words given the channel LLRs, the joint decoder and noise estimator approach only utilizes off‐the‐shelf DL models to denoise the channel LLR values, while the main decoding algorithm is still carried out by conventional BP decoding.

![Figure 15.4 A joint BP decoder‐DL noise estimator as proposed in (Liang et al., 2018). The input of the noise estimator is the syndrome of the estimated codeword and the magnitude of the estimated channel LLRs (Bennatan et al., 2018).](images/c15f004.jpg)

[Figure 15.4](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0004) A joint BP decoder‐DL noise estimator as proposed in (Liang et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0025)). The input of the noise estimator is the syndrome of the estimated codeword and the magnitude of the estimated channel LLRs (Bennatan et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0006)).

The iterative decoding algorithm in [Figure 15.4](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0004) starts with the first decoding attempt by running the conventional BP decoding given the channel input ![images](images/c15-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">LLR</mi><mi>x</mi></msub></mrow></math>. If the estimated codeword ![images](images/c15-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo mathvariant="bold-italic">&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> and the estimated message word ![images](images/c15-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#251;</mi></mrow></math> do not satisfy the ![images](images/c15-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math>‐matrix‐based termination condition (Yuan and Parhi, [2013](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0042)), the channel LLR values will be denoised and followed by another BP decoding attempt. Given the syndrome of the conventional BP decoding algorithm, ![images](images/c15-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo mathvariant="bold">&#770;</mo></mover><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold">T</mi></msup></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c15-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi></mrow></math> is the parity‐check matrix of polar codes, and the absolute values of the channel LLR values, ![images](images/c15-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">LLR</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></math>, the DL‐based noise estimator predicts the channel noise by estimating its sign values, ![images](images/c15-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mi><mo mathvariant="bold-italic">&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>. The channel LLR values are then updated by flipping the signs at certain positions predicted by the noise estimator, which results in the denoised channel LLR values, ![images](images/c15-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">LL</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">R</mi><mo mathvariant="bold">&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow><mi>x</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Another BP decoding attempt is then carried out given the denoised LLR values. Finally, the decoding is terminated if the mentioned termination condition is satisfied or a predetermined maximum number of decoding attempts is reached.

It is worth noticing that the training samples of the noise estimator depicted in [Figure 15.4](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0004) only include the erroneous syndromes after the first BP decoding, i.e. when ![images](images/c15-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo mathvariant="bold">&#770;</mo></mover><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">H</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi></msup></mrow></math> is a nonzero vector, and the corresponding absolute values of the channel LLRs. The label ![images](images/c15-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c15-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">q</mi><mo>&#8834;</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mi>N</mi></msup></mrow></math>, is used as the correct output label, where ![images](images/c15-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> indicates a flip at the ![images](images/c15-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>‐th element of the channel LLRs, while ![images](images/c15-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>q</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> indicates there is no change required for the ![images](images/c15-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math>‐th element.

 

### 15.3.3 Evaluation

In this section, we provide a performance comparison in terms of FER for various state‐of‐the‐art DL‐aided BP decoders when applied to a polar code. In addition, the FER performance of conventional decoders including BP (Arıkan, [2010](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0004)) and SCL (Balatsoukas‐Stimming et al., [2015](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0005), Hashemi et al., [2016](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0018)) decoding is also plotted. The examined polar code has a code length of 64, with 32 information bits, and is selected for the eMBB control channel of 5G (3GPP, [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0001)). We denote BP![images](images/c15-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c15-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>30</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>, as the conventional min‐sum BP decoder with ![images](images/c15-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>I</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub></mrow></math> iterations, and SCL32 (Tal and Vardy, [2015](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0035)) as the SCL decoder with a list size of 32. All the neural BP decoders considered in this section contain five unrolled BP iterations.

We also examine a joint decoder and channel equalizer decoding system by exploiting the idea proposed in (Liang et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0025), Bennatan et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0006)). We denote the joint decoding systems as BP5‐MLP‐BP5 and BP5‐LSTM‐BP5, where MLP and LSTM refer to the noise‐estimator models using fully connected NNs and stacked LSTM networks, respectively. Note that the network architectures and parameters of the DL‐based noise estimators are adopted from (Bennatan et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0006)).

As all the DL‐aided decoders considered in this section satisfy the code symmetry conditions (Richardson and Urbanke, [2008](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0031)), only all‐zero codewords are required for training. The training data is obtained for various ![images](images/c15-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> values where ![images](images/c15-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>7</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>8</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>. At each ![images](images/c15-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> value, ![images](images/c15-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>5</mn></msup></mrow></math> all‐zero codewords are obtained using BPSK modulation and the AWGN channel model. All neural BP‐based decoders are trained for 100 epochs, while BP5‐MLP‐BP5 and BP5‐LSTM‐BP5 are trained for 1000 epochs. The mini‐batch size is set to 320, and RMSPROP (Hinton et al.) is used as the optimization algorithm for training. Keras (Chollet et al., [2015](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0010)) and TensorFlow (Abadi et al., [2016](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0002)) are used as our DL frameworks. During testing, each decoder decodes at least ![images](images/c15-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow></math> random codewords to obtain at least 50 frames in errors at each ![images](images/c15-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> value.

![Figure 15.5 FER performance of various decoders for images selected for 5G.](images/c15f005.jpg)

[Figure 15.5](#c15.xhtml#R_c15-fig-0005) FER performance of various decoders for ![images](images/c15-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>64</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>32</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> selected for 5G.

[Figure 15.5](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0005) illustrates the FER performance of the mentioned decoders. [Table 15.1](#c15.xhtml#c15-tbl-0001) summarizes the error‐correction performance gains of all the decoders in [Figure 15.5](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0005) with respect to the baseline BP5 decoder at a target FER of ![images](images/c15-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. As observed from [Table 15.1](#c15.xhtml#c15-tbl-0001), NOMS provides a gain of 0.5 dB compared to the baseline BP5 decoder, while NNMS and BP5‐MLP‐BP5 both have a gain of 0.7 dB. On the other hand, NNMS‐RNN and BP30 have the same error‐correction performance, which is around 1.0 dB better than that of the baseline BP5, while BP5‐LSTM‐BP5 is slightly worse than NNMS‐RNN. It is worth mentioning that the best neural BP decoder, NNMS‐RNN, is still 0.5 dB away from SCL32.

[(15.23)](#c15.xhtml#c15-R_disp-0023)![equation](images/c15-math-0023.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script">T</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mtext>BP</mtext> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>2</mn> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>N</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

As the unrolled factor graphs of the NOMS, NNMS, and NNMS‐RNN decoders are equivalent to that of a traditional BP decoder with five iterations, their decoding latency can also be calculated by Eq. ([15.23](#c15.xhtml#c15-disp-0023)). For BP5‐MLP‐BP5 and BP5‐LSTM‐BP5 decoders, their decoding latency in time steps is the sum of the time steps consumed by two successive BP decoders with five iterations, and a deep NN with a depth of 5. Therefore, their decoding latency can be calculated as (Liang et al., [2018](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0025)):

(15.24)![equation](images/c15-math-0024.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script">T</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mtext>BP</mtext> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> </msub> <mtext>&#8208;MLP/LSTM&#8208;</mtext> <mtext>BP</mtext> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>4</mn> <msub> <mi>I</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>N</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>D</mi> <mi>e</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mi>t</mi> <msub> <mi>h</mi> <mtext>MLP/LSTM</mtext> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

On the other hand, the SCL32 decoder of (Balatsoukas‐Stimming et al., [2015](#c15.xhtml#c15-bib-0005)) requires ![images](images/c15-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> time steps.

[Figure 15.6](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0006) illustrates the decoding latency in time steps for all the neural decoders considered in [Figure 15.5](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0005). It should be noted that by assigning trainable weights to the factor graph of polar codes, NNMS‐RNN with 5 iterations is able to achieve the same error‐correction performance of BP30, which also results in a saving of 300 time steps. In addition, the decoding latency of BP5‐MLP‐BP5 and BP5‐LSTM‐BP5 is 65 time steps greater than that of NNMS‐RNN.

[Table 15.2](#c15.xhtml#c15-tbl-0002) gives a detailed comparison in the number of weights required by different DL‐aided BP decoders in [Figure 15.5](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0005). Although it is demonstrated in [Figure 15.5](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0005) that off‐the‐shelf deep networks are able to estimate channel noise, this approach shows inefficiency since relatively large DL models are required for the task. On the contrary, by incorporating the conventional BP decoding algorithm to define a constrained network model, NNMS‐RNN can provide a reasonable error probability while only requiring a small number of weights compared to those of BP5‐MLP‐BP5 and BP5‐LSTM‐BP5. Furthermore, although NOMS and NNMS only require ![images](images/c15-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>33.33</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of the number of weights consumed by NNMS‐RNN, the smaller number of weights results in a considerable error‐correction performance loss, as observed in [Figure 15.5](#c15.xhtml#c15-fig-0005).

## 15.4 Conclusions

In this chapter, we have discussed a wide range of fruitful applications of digital communications where deep learning can play a vital role. We provided an overview of DL techniques with a focus on FEC codes and examined state‐of‐the‐art DL‐aided decoders for polar codes as our case study. It was demonstrated that off‐the‐shelf DL decoders can reach MAP decoding performance for short code lengths and that they enable parallel execution thanks to their one‐shot‐decoding property. However, for longer code lengths, off‐the‐shelf DL decoders require a training dataset that scales exponentially with the code length. This issue becomes the main challenge for those decoders in practical applications. On the other hand, domain knowledge can be exploited to design DL‐aided decoders, as demonstrated by various neural BP decoders. It was shown that neural BP decoders can obtain significant decoding performance gains over their conventional counterpart, while maintaining the same decoding latency.

Future research on applying DL techniques to FEC can be carried out in various directions, such as designing jointly trained systems of customized DL‐aided decoders and neural channel‐noise estimators for various nonlinear communication channels. In addition, the sequential decoding of linear block codes such as polar codes can be suitably formalized as a RL problem, thus greatly enabling the applications of state‐of‐the‐art RL algorithms to FEC. Other approaches may include the use of DL techniques as optimization methods for well‐defined problems of conventional decoding algorithms, whose solutions are obtained based on an approximation or a massive Monte Carlo simulation.

# 16  
Neural Network–Based Wireless Channel Prediction

*Wei Jiang¹, Hans Dieter Schotten², and Ji‐ying Xiang³*

¹*Intelligent Networking Group, German Research Center for Artificial Intelligence, Kaiserslautern, Germany*

²*Institute for Wireless Communication and Navigation, University of Kaiserslautern, Kaiserslautern, Germany*

³*ZTE Ltd., Shenzhen, China*

 

## 16.1 Introduction

The advantages of wireless communication over wired are its flexibility, scalability, mobility, convenience, and economical efficiency, thanks to the free propagation of electromagnetic waves through a wireless channel from the transmitter to the receiver. Due to the reflection, diffraction, and scattering of electromagnetic waves traveling along different paths, as well as the mobility of surrounding objects or mobile stations, a wireless channel exhibits an extremely challenging condition for the design and implementation of wireless systems. By adapting transmission parameters such as the constellation size, coding rate, transmit power, time or frequency resources, transmit or receive antennas, and relaying nodes to instantaneous channel conditions, adaptive transmission systems can potentially aid the achievement of great performance. To fully realize this potential, the transmitter needs to know accurate channel state information (CSI). In a frequency‐division duplex (FDD) system, the CSI is estimated at the receiver and fed back to the transmitter through a limited feedback channel. Owing to time delays in the process of channel estimation, signal processing, and feedback, the available CSI at the transmitter may become outdated before its actual usage. In a time‐division duplex (TDD) system, although the feedback delay can be avoided by taking advantage of channel reciprocity, it is still possible that the CSI is outdated, especially in high‐mobility environments.

It has been extensively recognized that outdated CSI severely deteriorates the performance of a wide variety of adaptive transmission systems, including precoded multiple‐input and multiple‐output (MIMO) (Zheng and Rao, [2008](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0046)), multi‐user MIMO (Wang et al., [2014a](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0040)), massive MIMO (Truong and Heath, [2013](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0037)), beamforming (Kim et al., [2014](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0022)), interference alignment (Aquilina and Ratnarajah, [2015](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0004)), closed‐loop transmit diversity (Onggosanusi et al., [2001](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0028)), transmit antenna selection (Yu et al., [2017](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0044)), orthogonal frequency‐division multiple access (Wang et al., [2014b](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0041)), opportunistic relaying (Vicario et al., [2009](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0039)), coordinated multi‐point (CoMP) transmission (Ramirez et al., [2014](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0032)), physical layer security (Hyadi et al., [2016](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0013)), mobility management (Teng et al., [2017](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0036)), etc. In the fifth generation (5G) system, new applications and services such as Industry 4.0, the Internet of Things, the Tactile Internet, virtual and augmented reality, and autonomous driving impose a great demand for high‐data‐rate, ultra‐reliable, low‐latency, ubiquitous, high‐mobility, secure wireless connections, where adaptive transmission systems are required to play more important roles. However, the fluctuation of time‐varying channels speeds up if the velocity of moving objects increases or the wavelength of radio signals decreases according to the Doppler effect of electromagnetic radiation. Some 5G deployment scenarios, e.g. millimeter wave‐enabled networks (having shorter wavelength), unmanned aerial vehicles, and high‐speed trains (with higher velocity), experience wireless channels changing more rapidly, leading to difficult or impossible availability of accurate CSI.

To cope with outdated CSI, a large number of mitigation algorithms and protocols have been proposed in the literature. These methods compensate for the performance loss passively at the cost of scarce wireless resources (Jiang et al., [2016](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0019)) or aim to achieve only a portion of the full performance potential by recognizing the assumption of imperfect CSI (Love et al., [2008](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0026)). In contrast, an alternative technique referred to as *channel prediction* provides an efficient and effective approach to improve the accuracy of CSI directly without spending extra wireless resources, and therefore has attracted much attention from researchers. Through statistical modeling of wireless channels, two classical model‐based prediction schemes – parametric models (Adeogun et al., [2014](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003)) and autoregressive (AR) models (Baddour and Beaulieu, [2005](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0005)) – were developed. The former assumes that a fading channel is a superposition of a finite number of complex sinusoids, and its parameters, e.g. amplitude, angles of arrival and departure, Doppler shift, and number of scattering sources, vary slowly relative to the channels' fluctuation rate and can be estimated accurately. But the estimation process is tedious, and the estimated parameters will quickly expire with the fluctuation of the fading channel and therefore need to be re‐estimated iteratively, leading to high computational complexity. In contrast, the AR model approximates the fading channel as an AR process and extrapolates future CSI using a weighted linear combination of past and current CSI. Although the AR model is simple, it is sensitive to noise, and the problem of error propagation makes it unattractive in multi‐step predictions.

In March 2016, when AlphaGo, a computer program developed by Google DeepMind (Silver et al., [2016](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0035)), achieved an overwhelming victory versus a human champion in the game of Go, the passion for exploring artificial intelligence (AI) technology was sparked in almost all scientific and engineering branches (Jiang et al., [2017](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0020)). Actually, the wireless research community started to apply AI techniques to solve communication problems long ago. Making use of its capability of time‐series prediction (Connor et al., [1994](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0007)), a recurrent neural network (RNN) was first proposed in (Liu et al., [2006](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0025)) to build a narrow‐band single‐antenna predictor and was further extended to MIMO channels in (Potter et al., [2008](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0031), Ding and Hirose, [2014](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0008)). The feasibility of applying a deep neural network to predict fading channels was also studied in (Liao et al., [2018](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0024)). In (Jiang and Schotten, [2018a](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0015)), the authors proposed to employ a real‐valued RNN to implement a multi‐step predictor and further verified its effectiveness in a MIMO system (Jiang and Schotten, [2018b](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0016)). In (Jiang and Schotten, [2019b](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0018)), a frequency‐domain predictor was designed and validated for frequency‐selective multi‐antenna channels in wideband communications.

This chapter provides a comprehensive introduction to channel prediction methods with an emphasis on neural network (NN)‐based prediction. The rest of this chapter is organized as follows: [Section 16.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0002) briefly describes adaptive transmission systems using transmit antenna selection and opportunistic relaying as examples, followed by the impact of outdated CSI on the performance of adaptive transmission systems in [Section 16.3](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0005). Then, [Section 16.4](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0008) reviews two kinds of classical prediction methods: parametric and AR models. [Section 16.5](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0011) details the principles of RNN‐based predictors applied from flat‐fading single‐antenna channels to frequency‐selective multi‐antenna channels, as well as their achievable performance and computational complexity. Finally, conclusive remarks are made in [Section 16.6](#c16.xhtml#c16-sec-0026).

 

## 16.2 Adaptive Transmission Systems

The temporal fluctuation and frequency selectivity of channels impose a fundamental barrier on wireless communications to achieve large capacity and high reliability. By adapting transmission parameters such as scheduled users, modulation and coding schemes, transmit power, relaying nodes, time slots, sub‐carriers, and transmit or receive antennas to the instantaneous channel condition, adaptive transmission systems can remarkably boost system performance. In this section, we briefly review two representative examples, i.e. transmit antenna selection (TAS) in a MIMO system and opportunistic relaying in a cooperative network, in order to make clear their working mechanisms.

 

### 16.2.1 Transmit Antenna Selection

Time and frequency resources in a wireless system are extremely constrained, so a particularly appealing approach is to exploit the spatial domain by the application of antenna arrays, achieving attractive multiplexing and diversity gains by simply installing additional antennas. With the capability of remarkably improving the capacity and reliability of wireless communications, multiple‐antenna systems, also known as MIMO, have been widely adopted in prevalent commercial systems such as 4G and WiFi. However, the design and implementation of the radio frequency (RF) part of a transceiver become challenging because the complexity, size, and cost scale with the number of antennas. As a low‐cost, low‐complexity alternative, a technique known as *antenna selection* that is able to alleviate this limitation and at the same time capture many of the benefits from MIMO systems has been exploited (Yu et al., [2017](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0044)).

### 16.2.2 Opportunistic Relaying

Because of the constraints on power supply, cost, and hardware size of antenna arrays at sub‐![images](images/c16-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>6</mn><mtext>GHz</mtext></mrow></math> frequency bands, it is difficult for a mobile terminal to obtain the benefits of MIMO technology. Alternatively, taking advantage of the broadcast nature of radio signals, a technique called *cooperative relaying* (Sendonaris et al., [2003](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0034)), which can alleviate these constraints by forming a virtual antenna array using multiple single‐antenna terminals, draws much attention from researchers.

[Figure 16.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0002) illustrates a typical dual‐hop cooperative network consisting of a single source ![images](images/c16-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math>, a single destination ![images](images/c16-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c16-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> decode‐and‐forward relays. To avoid harmful self‐interference between the transmitter and receiver, the relays operate in a half‐duplex mode. Without loss of generality, signal transmission can be divided into two phases, i.e. broadcasting and forwarding. In the broadcasting phase, as shown in [Figure 16.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0002), the source sends out a transmit signal ![images](images/c16-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Those relays that can correctly decode this signal constitute a *decoding subset*, which is mathematically defined as

where ![images](images/c16-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> denotes the instantaneous received signal‐to‐noise ratio (SNR) at relay ![images](images/c16-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c16-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>k</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the channel gain experienced in the channel between the source and relay ![images](images/c16-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c16-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> stands for the transmit power, ![images](images/c16-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> is the variance of additive white noise, and ![images](images/c16-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> is an end‐to‐end target data rate. Note that a relay can be regarded as correctly decoding the transmit signal only if the instantaneous capacity for the corresponding source‐relay channel is higher than ![images](images/c16-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>, recalling that the relay works in a half‐duplex mode.

![Figure 16.2 Block diagram of an opportunistic relay system.](images/c16f002.jpg)

[Figure 16.2](#c16.xhtml#R_c16-fig-0002) Block diagram of an opportunistic relay system.

In the forwarding phase, several *multi‐relay* selection methods have been studied in the literature. Choosing a number of ![images](images/c16-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> relays to orthogonally forward the original signal, a scheme called *generalized selection combining* (Xiao and Dong, [2006](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0043)) suffers from substantially degraded spectral efficiency to ![images](images/c16-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> compared to the full potential. To avoid this loss, a simultaneous transmission method referred to as *distributed beamforming* has been proposed in (Jing and Jafarkhani, [2009](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0021)). However, beamforming is very sensitive to phase noise, and *a priori* knowledge of forward channels is mandatory. The authors of (Laneman and Wornell, [2003](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0023)) presented an approach called *distributed space‐time coding* (DSTC) to achieve full diversity. But designing such a code is infeasible since the number of distributed antennas is unknown and randomly varies. In addition, the problem of synchronization among simultaneously transmitting relays for multi‐relay methods is difficult to solve, especially when the number of relays is large. In contrast, a *single‐relay* approach referred to as *opportunistic relaying* or *opportunistic relay selection* (ORS) (Bletsas et al., [2006](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0006)) has been recognized as a simple but efficient solution to achieve a full cooperative diversity. Despite using only a single node with the best channel condition serving as the relay, it can achieve full diversity the same as that of DSTC. From the viewpoint of a multiplexing‐diversity trade‐off, it is optimal, while avoiding the implementation complexity of multi‐relay methods.

As shown in [Figure 16.2](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0002), a relay with the largest SNR in relay‐destination channels is selected from ![images](images/c16-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">D</mi><mi mathvariant="script">S</mi></mrow></math> to serve as the best relay ![images](images/c16-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>, i.e.

[(16.3)](#c16.xhtml#c16-R_disp-0003)![equation](images/c16-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>k</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mi> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script">D</mi> <mi mathvariant="script">S</mi> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>d</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c16-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub><msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> denotes instantaneous received SNR at the destination, ![images](images/c16-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the channel gain experienced in the channel between relay ![images](images/c16-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>k</mi></mrow></math> and the destination, and the transmit power of the best relay is assumed to be identical to that of the source.

 

## 16.3 The Impact of Outdated CSI

From a practical point of view, the CSI at the time of selecting transmission parameters may substantially differ from the CSI at the instant of using the selected parameters to transmit. Utilizing an outdated version of the CSI rather than the actual CSI may severely deteriorate system performance. This section first provides a mathematical model to quantify the inaccuracy of outdated CSI and then uses the ORS system as an example to illustrate the impact of outdated CSI on the performance of adaptive transmission systems.

 

### 16.3.1 Modeling Outdated CSI

For simplicity, let us ignore time indices and denote the actual CSI by ![images](images/c16-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and the outdated CSI ![images](images/c16-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. To quantify the inaccuracy of the outdated CSI, the correlation coefficient between ![images](images/c16-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> in the condition of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) channels is introduced, as follows:

[(16.4)](#c16.xhtml#c16-R_disp-0004)![equation](images/c16-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>c</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>v</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>h</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>r</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi>h</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>r</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>n</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mrow> <msup> <mi>h</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c16-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>v</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> stands for the covariance of two random variables, ![images](images/c16-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow></math> is the standard deviation, and ![images](images/c16-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the gain of the channel between transmit antenna ![images](images/c16-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> and receive antenna ![images](images/c16-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Due to i.i.d. elements in ![images](images/c16-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c16-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi></mrow></math> is independent of ![images](images/c16-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Thus, Eq. ([16.4](#c16.xhtml#c16-disp-0004)) can be simplified into

Since the elements of ![images](images/c16-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> are both zero mean circularly symmetric Gaussian distributed, according to (Ramya and Bhashyam, [2009](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0033)), their relationship can be given by
