where ![images](images/c16-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">E</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is a matrix consisting of normalized Gaussian random variables, i.e. ![images](images/c16-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Assuming the Jakes' scattering model, ![images](images/c16-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> follow joint complex Gaussian distribution with correlation coefficient ![images](images/c16-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>J</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>&#960;</mi><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mi>&#964;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c16-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow></math> denotes the maximal Doppler frequency, ![images](images/c16-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> is the delay, and ![images](images/c16-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>J</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> represents the zeroth order Bessel function of the first kind. Thus, ![images](images/c16-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi></mrow></math> conditioned on ![images](images/c16-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup></mrow></math> is also Gaussian distributed:

![equation](images/c16-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msup><mi>&#961;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> 

Due to the assumption of a normalized channel gain ![images](images/c16-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>h</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, the long‐term average SNR ![images](images/c16-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>h</mi><msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math> is simplified to ![images](images/c16-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><msub><mrow/><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math>. Thus, an instantaneous SNR ![images](images/c16-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></mfrac></mrow></math> can be rewritten as ![images](images/c16-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math>. Conditioned on its outdated version ![images](images/c16-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#8242;</mo></msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c16-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi></mrow></math> follows a noncentral chi‐square distribution with two degrees of freedom. As given in Eq. (3) of (Jiang et al., [2016](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0019)), its probability density function (PDF) is expressed as

(16.7)![equation](images/c16-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </msup> <msub> <mi>J</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mfrac> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <msqrt> <mrow> <msup> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi> <msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> </mrow> </msqrt> </mrow> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>&#961;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math>  

### 16.3.2 Performance Impact

Outdated CSI causes an inaccurate or even wrong selection of transmission parameters, leading to severe performance degradation of adaptive transmission systems. As an example, let us use the ORS system in this section to illustrate the severity of this impact. In contrast to Eq. ([16.3](#c16.xhtml#c16-disp-0003)), the best relay in the presence of outdated CSI is decided as follows

(16.8)![equation](images/c16-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>k</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mi> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script">D</mi> <mi mathvariant="script">S</mi> </mrow> </munder> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>d</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c16-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8242;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> is the outdated version of the instantaneous received SNR for the relay‐destination channel. The instantaneous channel capacity below a target rate of ![images](images/c16-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>, i.e. ![images](images/c16-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mi>R</mi></mrow></math>, denotes an *outage* event, in which reliable communication cannot be realized no matter what coding is used. The probability measuring such an outage event is defined as the outage probability, notated by ![images](images/c16-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>R</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and expressed as the following definition (Tse and Viswanath, [2005](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0038)):

From Eq. ([16.10](#c16.xhtml#c16-disp-0011)), it is still difficult to offer insightful thoughts about the impact of outdated CSI. It is worth providing an asymptotic analysis in a high SNR regime to clarify their achievable diversity, like the definition of ![images](images/c16-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>u</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> in (Vicario et al., [2009](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0039)). The ORS system can achieve a full diversity of ![images](images/c16-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math> with the prefect CSI. However, its diversity degrades to 1 in the presence of outdated CSI no matter how close the outdated CSI is to its actual value, even if the former arbitrarily tends to the latter (![images](images/c16-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>). As proved in (Vicario et al., [2009](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0039)), the achievable diversity order of the ORS system is

[Figure 16.3](#c16.xhtml#R_c16-fig-0003) Performance impact of outdated CSI on the ORS system.

[Figure 16.3](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0003) illustrates the impact of outdated CSI on a cooperative network with ![images](images/c16-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> decode‐and‐forward relays, among which the best relay is selected. As a benchmark, the performance curve of another cooperative network having only ![images](images/c16-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> relay in between is also given, representing no diversity gain, namely ![images](images/c16-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. As indicated by the curve of ![images](images/c16-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> in [Figure 16.3](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0003), the outage probability of the ORS system decays at a rate of ![images](images/c16-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="normal">&#947;</mi><mo>&#175;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>5</mn></msup></mrow></math> in high SNR, and a full diversity gain of ![images](images/c16-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> is achieved. The curves marked by ![images](images/c16-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.5</mn></mrow></math>, 0.9, and 0.99 are all parallel with that of ![images](images/c16-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> in high SNR. It is implied that the diversity order achieved by the ORS system in the presence of outdated CSI is only ![images](images/c16-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. The performance degradation is substantial, e.g. a performance loss of nearly 15 dB is observed in the case of ![images](images/c16-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.9</mn></mrow></math> in comparison with that of the perfect CSI at a given outage probability of ![images](images/c16-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. In other words, the performance gain originated from adaptive transmission systems might be thoroughly overwhelmed by the loss brought about by outdated CSI, highlighting the importance of channel prediction.

 

## 16.4 Classical Channel Prediction

Relying on traditional statistical methodology, a prediction model with a number of parameters can be formed to approximate the dynamics of a fading channel. Given the knowledge of current and past CSI, these parameters can be estimated, and then future CSI is extrapolated through this model. Existing model‐based channel prediction is mainly differentiated into two categories, i.e. AR and parametric. Their principles, modelings, parameter estimation methods, and constraints are briefly discussed in this section.

 

### 16.4.1 Autoregressive Models

By exploiting temporal correlation, this scheme models the impulse response of a time‐varying channel as an autoregressive process and employs a Kalman filter (KF) to estimate AR coefficients so as to build a linear predictor, which extrapolates future CSI by combining weighted current and past CSI (Eyceoz et al., [1998](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0010), Duel‐Hallen et al., [2000](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0009), Peng et al., [2017](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0030), Wu and Lee, [2013](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0042)). According to (Baddour and Beaulieu, [2005](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0005)), a complex AR process of order ![images](images/c16-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi></mrow></math> denoted by ![images](images/c16-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">AR</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">p</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> can be generated via a time domain recursion

stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mtd> <mtd> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd> <mi>R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> (16.18)![equation](images/c16-math-0019.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> [(16.19)](#c16.xhtml#c16-R_disp-0020)![equation](images/c16-math-0020.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold">v</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mtd> <mtd> <mi>R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mtd> <mtd> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd> <mi>R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

and

(16.20)![equation](images/c16-math-0021.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>&#963;</mi> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mi>R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#931;</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </msubsup> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mi>R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>k</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Substituting Eqs. ([16.17](#c16.xhtml#c16-disp-0018))–([16.19](#c16.xhtml#c16-disp-0020)) into Eq. ([16.16](#c16.xhtml#c16-disp-0017)), ![images](images/c16-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> are determined. Thus, we can get a KF predictor for a single‐input and single‐output (SISO) system in a frequency‐flat channel:

(16.21)![equation](images/c16-math-0022.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#293;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>k</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

By processing a MIMO channel as a set of parallel, independent SISO channels, a KF predictor for a multi‐antenna system can also be derived:

[(16.22)](#c16.xhtml#c16-R_disp-0023)![equation](images/c16-math-0023.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>k</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>k</mi> </msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>k</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

This scheme is not optimal since it only takes advantage of temporal correlation of individual SISO channels, while ignoring spatial correlation among multiple antennas in a MIMO channel. Due to the fact that the KF predictor can only provide one‐step prediction, multi‐step prediction is achieved by reusing the extrapolated CSI at previous time instants, which causes the problem of error propagation. Moreover, this scheme is vulnerable to noise (Jiang and Schotten, [2019a](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0017), Fung and Chan, [2002](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0012)), making it unattractive in practice.

 

### 16.4.2 Parametric Models

This scheme models a fading channel as a superposition of a finite number of complex sinusoids, each of which has its respective amplitude, Doppler shift, and phase (Adeogun et al., [2014](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0003)). The rationale is based on an observation that multi‐path parameters change slowly in comparison with the fading rate of channels, and future CSI within a certain range can be extrapolated if these parameters are known.

Following a commonly used sum of sinusoids model, a MIMO channel is expressed as the superposition of ![images](images/c16-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> scattering sources

[(16.23)](#c16.xhtml#c16-R_disp-0024)![equation](images/c16-math-0024.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>P</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi> <mi>r</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>&#952;</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi> </mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mi>j</mi> <msub> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mi>t</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c16-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the amplitude of the ![images](images/c16-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> scattering source; ![images](images/c16-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#969;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> denotes its Doppler shift; ![images](images/c16-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> stand for the angles of arrival and departure, respectively; ![images](images/c16-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> represents the response vector of the receive antenna array; and ![images](images/c16-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> represents the response vecor for the transmit antenna array. Using a uniform linear array (ULA) with ![images](images/c16-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> equally spaced elements as an example, its steering vector can be formulated as

(16.24)![equation](images/c16-math-0025.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#968;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>j</mi> <mfrac> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mi>&#960;</mi> </mrow> <mi>&#955;</mi> </mfrac> <mi>d</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#968;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>j</mi> <mfrac> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mi>&#960;</mi> </mrow> <mi>&#955;</mi> </mfrac> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>M</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">sin</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#968;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c16-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#968;</mi></mrow></math> stands for the angle of arrival or departure, ![images](images/c16-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> is the antenna spacing, and ![images](images/c16-i0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#955;</mi></mrow></math> denotes the wavelength of the carrier frequency. Prediction of a MIMO channel in terms of the model of Eq. ([16.23](#c16.xhtml#c16-disp-0024)) is essentially a problem of parameter estimation, in which the number of scattering sources, the amplitude and Doppler shift for each path, as well as its angles of arrival and departure need to be estimated. In other words, the main work of building a parametric model is to figure out ![images](images/c16-i0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0123.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#966;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> with the knowledge of a number of discrete‐time channel gain samples ![images](images/c16-i0124.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>k</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>k</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>.

![Figure 16.4 The procedure of parameter estimation in the parametric model. Source: Figure 4.1 in (Adeogun, 2014).](images/c16f004.jpg)

[Figure 16.4](#c16.xhtml#R_c16-fig-0004) The procedure of parameter estimation in the parametric model. Source: [Figure 4.1](#c04.xhtml#c04-fig-0001) in (Adeogun, [2014](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0001)).

As shown in [Figure 16.4](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0004), the procedure of parameter estimation for the parametric model is divided into the following stages:

1.  i. Use the K available channel matrices to form a sufficiently large matrix exhibiting the required translational invariance structure in all dimensions. According to (Adeogun et al., [2013](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0002)), therefore, form an ![images](images/c16-i0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> block‐Hankel matrix, which can be written as (16.25)![equation](images/c16-math-0026.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mtd> <mtd> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mtd> <mtd> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mtd> <mtd> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mtd> <mtd> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>S</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> <mtd> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> <mtd> <mi>&#8945;</mi> </mtd> <mtd> <mi>&#8942;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>Q</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mtd> <mtd> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>Q</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mtd> <mtd> <mi>&#8943;</mi> </mtd> <mtd> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>K</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> where ![images](images/c16-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> is the size of Hankel matrix and ![images](images/c16-i0127.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>S</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>K</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>Q</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.
2.  ii. From the transformed data, calculate a covariance matrix containing the temporal and spatial correlation. The spatio‐temporal covariance matrix ![images](images/c16-i0128.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> is then derived as ![images](images/c16-i0129.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><msup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">D</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>H</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mi>S</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c16-i0130.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>H</mi></msup></mrow></math> denotes the Hermitian conjugate transpose.
3.  iii. Then, the number of dominant scattering sources can be estimated using the minimum description length (MDL) criterion as (16.26)![equation](images/c16-math-0027.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>P</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">arg</mi> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">min</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>r</mi> </msub> <mi>Q</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munder> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>S</mi> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi>p</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mi>p</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mi>S</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> where ![images](images/c16-i0131.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the ![images](images/c16-i0132.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> eigenvalue of ![images](images/c16-i0133.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math>.
4.  iv. The invariance structure in ![images](images/c16-i0134.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">C</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> is exploited to jointly estimate the structural parameters. Making full use of classical estimation algorithms, such as multiple signal classification (MUSIC) and estimation of signal parameters by rotational invariance techniques (ESPRIT), the angles of arrival and departure, as well as the Doppler shifts, i.e. ![images](images/c16-i0135.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#966;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, can be computed. For simplicity, the details of the calculation process and algorithms are omitted in this chapter.
5.  v. By obtaining the estimated structural parameters ![images](images/c16-i0136.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#952;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#966;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#969;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, together with ![images](images/c16-i0137.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow></math>, the complex amplitudes ![images](images/c16-i0138.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>P</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> then can be calculated.
6.  vi. Once all parameters have been determined, the channel prediction is conducted as follows (16.27)![equation](images/c16-math-0028.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#964;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>P</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi> <mi>r</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#952;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi> </mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mi>j</mi> <msub> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#969;</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mi>&#964;</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> where ![images](images/c16-i0139.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> denotes a time range for which the CSI is to be predicted.

As we can see, the process of estimating parameters is tedious, leading to high computational complexity. More importantly, the estimated parameters become invalid quickly with the change of mobile propagation environments, especially in a fast‐fading channel. That means these parameters need to be periodically estimated, which is unattractive from a practical viewpoint.

 

## 16.5 NN‐Based Prediction Schemes

This section highlights novel channel prediction approaches making full use of the capability of time‐series prediction enabled by NNs. First, the internal structure of a recurrent NN is provided, followed by an application of a RNN to implement a multi‐step predictor for frequency‐flat single‐antenna channels, which is further extended to multi‐antenna channels. Then, a frequency‐domain predictor suited to frequency‐selective multi‐antenna channels is described, as well as its integration into a MIMO‐OFDM system. Finally, the performance and computational complexity of the RNN predictor are analyzed and compared with those of the KF predictor.

 

### 16.5.1 The RNN Architecture

RNNs are an effective AI technique that has shown great potential in the field of time‐series prediction (Connor et al., [1994](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0007)). The internal structure of a RNN used for constructing a multi‐step multi‐antenna channel predictor is provided in [Figure 16.5](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0005). Basically, it consists of three layers: an input layer with ![images](images/c16-i0140.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> neurons consisting of ![images](images/c16-i0141.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></math> external input and ![images](images/c16-i0142.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></mrow></math> feedback input, where ![images](images/c16-i0143.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></mrow></math>; a hidden layer with ![images](images/c16-i0144.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> neurons; and an output layer with ![images](images/c16-i0145.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></mrow></math> neurons. Using a feedback function ![images](images/c16-i0146.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> to represent the transformation from an output vector denoted by ![images](images/c16-i0147.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> to a desired feedback ![images](images/c16-i0148.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">f</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mspace width="0.1em"/><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, we have ![images](images/c16-i0149.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">f</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>F</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">y</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Denoting the external input by ![images](images/c16-i0150.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mi>e</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, together with the feedback, the whole input can thus be written as an ![images](images/c16-i0151.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>‐dimensional input vector ![images](images/c16-i0152.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>e</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math>.

The behavior of a RNN is decided by connection weights and transfer functions. Each connection between the output of a neuron in the predecessor layer and the input of a neuron in the successor layer is assigned a weight. As shown in [Figure 16.5](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0005), ![images](images/c16-i0153.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> denotes the weight connecting the ![images](images/c16-i0154.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> input and the ![images](images/c16-i0155.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>l</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> hidden neuron, while ![images](images/c16-i0156.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>l</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the weight for connecting hidden neuron ![images](images/c16-i0157.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi></mrow></math> and output ![images](images/c16-i0158.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>o</mi></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c16-i0159.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>n</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c16-i0160.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>l</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c16-i0161.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>o</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Transfer functions typically fall into one of three categories: linear, threshold, and sigmoid. For example, a sigmoid function generally used in a hidden neuron is defined as

where ![images](images/c16-i0163.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>l</mi></msub></mrow></math> denotes the bias, and ![images](images/c16-i0164.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>&#183;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> stands for the dot product of the input vector ![images](images/c16-i0165.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi></mrow></math> and the ![images](images/c16-i0166.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>l</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> weight vector that is defined as the collection of all weights upon connections pointing to the ![images](images/c16-i0167.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>l</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> hidden neuron, i.e. ![images](images/c16-i0168.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">w</mi><mi>l</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msub><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>. [Figure 16.5](#c16.xhtml#R_c16-fig-0005) The internal structure of a recurrent neural network.

[(16.30)](#c16.xhtml#c16-R_disp-0031)![equation](images/c16-math-0031.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>c</mi> <mrow> <mi>o</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>l</mi> </mrow> </msub> <msub> <mi>z</mi> <mi>l</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Like other data‐driven AI techniques, the operation of a RNN predictor has two phases: training and prediction. Once the parameters of a network have been determined, it is ready to be trained. Provided with a training dataset, the RNN processes each input data and compares its resulting output against the desired value. Errors are then propagated back through the network, causing the network to adjust its weights iteratively. Once the training process completed, the trained RNN can be used to predict upcoming samples based on the current state. The training of a NN has already been well studied and can be found in the literature such as (Nerrand et al., [1994](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0027), Fu et al., [2015](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0011)).

 

### 16.5.2 Flat‐Fading SISO Prediction

To begin with, consider a frequency‐flat fading channel with one transmit antenna and one receive antenna:

(16.31)![equation](images/c16-math-0032.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>r</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi>s</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c16-i0170.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>r</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> represents the received signal at time ![images](images/c16-i0171.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c16-i0172.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is the transmitted symbol, ![images](images/c16-i0173.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> stands for additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN), and ![images](images/c16-i0174.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> denotes the channel gain. Due to feedback and processing delays, the channel condition at the time of selecting adaptive transmission parameters may be outdated before its actual usage, namely ![images](images/c16-i0175.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8800;</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#964;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c16-i0176.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> denotes the delay. Outdated CSI imposes a severely negative impact on a wide variety of adaptive transmission systems. The aim of channel prediction is to get a predicted gain ![images](images/c16-i0177.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#293;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#964;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> that is as close as possible to its actual value ![images](images/c16-i0178.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#964;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> at the instant ![images](images/c16-i0179.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>&#964;</mi></mrow></math> when the actual transmission using the selected parameters happens.

 

#### 16.5.2.1 Channel Gain Prediction with a Complex‐Valued RNN

Since channel gains are complex‐valued, a RNN with complex‐valued weights (called a complex‐valued RNN hereinafter) needs to be applied (Liu et al., [2006](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0025), Potter et al., [2008](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0031), Ding and Hirose, [2014](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0008)). At time ![images](images/c16-i0181.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c16-i0182.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is obtained through channel estimation, for example, while a number of ![images](images/c16-i0183.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> past values ![images](images/c16-i0184.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> can be stored through a tapped delay line, as illustrated in [Figure 16.6](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0006). These ![images](images/c16-i0185.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> channel gains are fed into the RNN as the external input, i.e.

![Figure 16.6 (a) Schematics of applying a complex‐valued recurrent neural network to predict one‐step‐ahead channel state information images; (b) applying a real‐valued RNN to predict a channel gain by means of processing the real and imaginary parts separately.](images/c16f006.jpg)

[Figure 16.6](#c16.xhtml#R_c16-fig-0006) (a) Schematics of applying a complex‐valued recurrent neural network to predict one‐step‐ahead channel state information ![images](images/c16-i0180.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#293;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>; (b) applying a real‐valued RNN to predict a channel gain by means of processing the real and imaginary parts separately.

(16.32)![equation](images/c16-math-0033.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mi>e</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

With the aid of the delayed feedback, the prediction of a future channel gain ![images](images/c16-i0186.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#293;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> at the next time instant ![images](images/c16-i0187.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> is obtained, as shown in [Figure 16.6](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0006).

 

#### 16.5.2.2 Channel Gain Prediction with a Real‐Valued RNN

In comparison with a complex‐valued RNN, a RNN with real‐valued weights (called a real‐valued RNN) has the advantages of lower computational complexity and higher prediction accuracy, but it can only deal with real‐valued input. Fortunately, a complex‐valued channel gain can be decomposed into two real values, namely the real and imaginary parts, i.e. ![images](images/c16-i0188.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>h</mi><mi>r</mi></msup><mo>+</mo><mi>j</mi><msup><mi>h</mi><mi>i</mi></msup></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c16-i0189.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>j</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> is the imaginary unit. Therefore, a real‐valued RNN was proposed in (Jiang and Schotten, [2018a](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0015)) to build a simpler predictor with higher accuracy by means of separately predicting the real and imaginary parts and then combining them together. As shown in [Figure 16.6](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0006), the external input of the RNN is then

(16.33)![equation](images/c16-math-0034.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mi>e</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mi>h</mi> <mi>r</mi> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>h</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>h</mi> <mi>r</mi> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>h</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

In this case, the output of the RNN is ![images](images/c16-i0190.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#293;</mi><mi>r</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0191.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#293;</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>. By combining the predicted real and imaginary parts, the prediction of the channel gain at the next time instant can be obtained, i.e. ![images](images/c16-i0192.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#293;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#293;</mi><mi>r</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>j</mi><msup><mi>&#293;</mi><mi>i</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>.

 

#### 16.5.2.3 Channel Envelope Prediction

Many adaptive transmission systems only need to know the envelope of the channel response, ![images](images/c16-i0193.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></math>, rather than a complex‐valued coefficient ![images](images/c16-i0194.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math> itself. Therefore, a real‐valued RNN was proposed in (Jiang and Schotten, [2018a](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0015)) to predict ![images](images/c16-i0195.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></math> directly, which in turn can lower computational complexity, speed up the training process, and improve prediction accuracy, in comparison with predicting channel gains. The channel envelope at time ![images](images/c16-i0196.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> denoted by ![images](images/c16-i0197.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></math> is known, while a number of ![images](images/c16-i0198.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi></mrow></math> past values ![images](images/c16-i0199.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></math> can be kept through a tapped delay line. The CSI for the next time instant ![images](images/c16-i0200.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>&#293;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></math> can be predicted by feeding these ![images](images/c16-i0201.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> channel values into the RNN as the external input, which in this case is written as

(16.34)![equation](images/c16-math-0035.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">x</mi> <mi>e</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8230;</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> ![Figure 16.7 The architecture of a multi‐step predictor.](images/c16f007.jpg)

[Figure 16.7](#c16.xhtml#R_c16-fig-0007) The architecture of a multi‐step predictor.

 

#### 16.5.2.4 Multi‐Step Prediction

So far, the predictor is only set to forecast one step ahead, extrapolating ![images](images/c16-i0202.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#293;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> from the current and past CSI ![images](images/c16-i0203.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>. In practice, an adaptive transmission system probably needs to know a long‐range prediction of the CSI, which is enabled only by a multi‐step predictor. Luckily, the structure of a RNN is quite flexible, as shown in [Figure 16.7](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0007), where a multi‐step predictor is constructed by tuning the tapped delay lines for input and feedback. Using the response of a single‐antenna channel as an example for simplicity, the external input contains the current CSI ![images](images/c16-i0204.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> and its delays ![images](images/c16-i0205.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>. Meanwhile, a number of ![images](images/c16-i0206.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> channel gains ![images](images/c16-i0207.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#293;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#293;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>d</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> are input as the feedback. The output is ![images](images/c16-i0208.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#293;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c16-i0209.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> stands for the number of steps being predicted ahead. The parameter ![images](images/c16-i0210.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is an positive integer ![images](images/c16-i0211.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> and the predictor returns back to the previous one‐step‐ahead prediction if ![images](images/c16-i0212.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. From the perspective of training, there is no intrinsic distinction between one‐step and multi‐step prediction. The only difference is that the desired value for calculating the prediction error in the training process is shifted from ![images](images/c16-i0213.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> to ![images](images/c16-i0214.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, resulting in different weights. With the increase of ![images](images/c16-i0215.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>, the prediction accuracy will degrade due to the intrinsic characteristics of the predicted channel itself.

A multi‐antenna wireless system with ![images](images/c16-i0216.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> transmit and ![images](images/c16-i0217.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math> receive antennas in a flat fading channel is modeled as

where ![images](images/c16-i0218.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">r</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo ![images](images/c16-i0223.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">n</mi></mrow></math> stands for the vector of additive mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> represents the gain of the channel between transmit antenna ![images](images/c16-i0226.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> and receive antenna ![images](images/c16-i0227.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>n</mi><mi>r</mi></msub></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c16-i0228.png)<math
