### 16.5.6 Performance and Complexity

The computational complexity of RNNs is a concern for their application in practical systems. This section analyzes the complexity in terms of the number of complex multiplications required in the process of channel prediction. Meanwhile, the achievable performance of the RNN predictor, in comparison with the KF predictor, is illustrated through numerical results in terms of outage probability in a MIMO‐OFDM system.

 

#### 16.5.6.1 Computational Complexity

In general, the number of complex multiplications is used as a measure for computational complexity. As can be derived from Eqs. ([16.29](#c16.xhtml#c16-disp-0030)) and ([16.30](#c16.xhtml#c16-disp-0031)), the hidden and output layer need ![images](images/c16-i0359.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0360.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> times multiplication operations to conduct one time prediction, respectively, amounting to a total of ![images](images/c16-i0361.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. The number of required input neurons is proportional to the number of MIMO subchannels ![images](images/c16-i0362.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>: we have ![images](images/c16-i0363.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> if the feedback contains only one channel matrix, as illustrated in [Figure 16.8](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0008), and similarly the number of output neurons is ![images](images/c16-i0364.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Then, the complexity of the RNN predictor can be computed by ![images](images/c16-i0365.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>. In contrast, derived from Eq. ([16.22](#c16.xhtml#c16-disp-0023)), the KF predictor requires ![images](images/c16-i0366.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>p</mi><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> times multiplication operations per prediction. Since a small filter order such as ![images](images/c16-i0367.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> is generally optimal and thus ![images](images/c16-i0368.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></math>, it is concluded that the KF predictor is simpler than the RNN predictor.

Further, it is meaningful to make clear how many computing resources are required. The number of pilot sub‐carriers per OFDM symbol is around ![images](images/c16-i0369.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>P</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and there are ![images](images/c16-i0370.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> OFDM symbols per second, from which the number of predictions per second can be figured out, i.e. ![images](images/c16-i0371.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#968;</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>P</mi></msub></mrow></math>. The required multiplications per second by the KF predictor are exactly the product of ![images](images/c16-i0372.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#968;</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0373.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, i.e. ![images](images/c16-i0374.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>P</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c16-i0375.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>P</mi></msub></mrow></math> in the case of the RNN predictor. Assuming a RNN with ![images](images/c16-i0376.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0377.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> is applied for a ![images](images/c16-i0378.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>4</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> MIMO system with a signal sampling rate of ![images](images/c16-i0379.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>6</mn></msup><mspace width="0.3em"/><mtext>Hz</mtext></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0380.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>, we have ![images](images/c16-i0381.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0382.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#937;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>r</mi><mi>n</mi><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>s</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>6</mn></msup></mrow></math>. Compared with off‐the‐shelf digital signal processors (DSPs), e.g. TI 66AK2x, which provides a capability of nearly ![images](images/c16-i0383.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow></math> million instructions executed per second (MIPS), the required resource of the RNN predictor is ![images](images/c16-i0384.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>0.3</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math>. Even in a massive MIMO system with a dimension of ![images](images/c16-i0385.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>32</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>, it consumes only ![images](images/c16-i0386.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>10</mn><mo>%</mo></mrow></math> of the computing power of a single DSP. In summary, the computing resources required by a channel predictor are affordable, which is promising from a practical perspective.

 

#### 16.5.6.2 Performance

The numerical results of the performance achieved by prediction‐assisted TAS in a MIMO‐OFDM system in a frequency‐selective channel are illustrated. The signal bandwidth is 1 ![images](images/c16-i0387.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mi>H</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow></math>, which is converted into ![images](images/c16-i0388.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>64</mn></mrow></math> parallel sub‐carriers by the OFDM modulation, resulting in a sub‐carrier spacing around ![images](images/c16-i0389.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#9651;</mo><mi>f</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>15</mn></mrow></math> ![images](images/c16-i0390.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mi>H</mi><mi>z</mi></mrow></math>. The number of hidden neurons is ![images](images/c16-i0391.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math>, and the length of the tapped delay line is ![images](images/c16-i0392.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>. The details of setting up the Monte Carlo simulation can be found in (Jiang and Schotten, [2019b](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0018)).

To train a RNN, a training dataset containing a series of consecutive CSI ![images](images/c16-i0393.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mfenced open="|" close="}" separators=""><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math> extracted from an arbitrary sub‐carrier during 10 periods of fluctuation (i.e. channel's coherence time) is built. A training process starts from an initial state where all weights can be randomly selected. At iteration ![images](images/c16-i0394.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>, feeding ![images](images/c16-i0395.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> into the RNN, the resultant output is compared with the desired value, and the prediction error ![images](images/c16-i0396.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>r</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is propagated back through the network so as to update the weights by means of training algorithms such as Levenberg‐Marquardt (Fu et al., [2015](#c16.xhtml#c16-bib-0011)). This process is iteratively carried out until the RNN reaches a certain convergence condition. In contrast, the KF predictor does not need training. Its filter coefficients required in Eq. ([16.22](#c16.xhtml#c16-disp-0023)) can be figured out if ![images](images/c16-i0397.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>d</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c16-i0398.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math> are known. Once the training process of a RNN is completed and the coefficients of a Kalman filter are determined, channel prediction can be conducted. [Figure 16.10](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0010) provides a direct view of prediction accuracy, where the amplitudes and phases of a series of predicted channel gains are compared with their actual values.

Suppose a multi‐antenna system with a uniform linear array has ![images](images/c16-i0399.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> transmit and ![images](images/c16-i0400.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>r</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> receive antennas, and a single transmit antenna with the largest instantaneous channel gain is selected. Outage probability is investigated: it is an important performance metric over fading channels, defined as ![images](images/c16-i0401.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>Pr</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mtext>SNR</mtext><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#60;</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c16-i0402.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Pr</mi></mrow></math> is the notation of mathematical probability and ![images](images/c16-i0403.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> means a target end‐to‐end data rate that is set to ![images](images/c16-i0404.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi mathvariant="normal">bps</mi><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">Hz</mi></mrow></math> in general. Three different CSI modes are compared:

*   The perfect mode where a transmit antenna for subcarrier ![images](images/c16-i0405.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> at OFDM symbol ![images](images/c16-i0406.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> is chosen in terms of the actual CSI ![images](images/c16-i0407.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, despite it never existing in practice owing to delay and noise.
*   As in a traditional TAS system, only outdated CSI ![images](images/c16-i0408.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is available.
*   With the aid of channel prediction, the predicted CSI ![images](images/c16-i0409.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>D</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> that is possible to closely approximate the actual CSI is used.

![Figure 16.10 Predicted amplitudes and phases (dotted lines) versus actual values (solid lines).](images/c16f010.jpg)

[Figure 16.10](#c16.xhtml#R_c16-fig-0010) Predicted amplitudes and phases (dotted lines) versus actual values (solid lines).

![Figure 16.11 Performance comparison of outdated, predicted, and perfect channel state information in a multiple‐input and multiple‐output orthogonal frequency‐division multiplexing system.](images/c16f011.jpg)

[Figure 16.11](#c16.xhtml#R_c16-fig-0011) Performance comparison of outdated, predicted, and perfect channel state information in a multiple‐input and multiple‐output orthogonal frequency‐division multiplexing system.

[Figure 16.11](#c16.xhtml#c16-fig-0011) illustrates the performance achieved by a MIMO‐OFDM system in a frequency‐selective channel specified by the 3GPP extended typical urban (ETU) model with a maximal Doppler shift of ![images](images/c16-i0410.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>300</mn></mrow></math> Hz. First, the RNN predictor is tuned to one‐step prediction mode (![images](images/c16-i0411.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>) in order to make a direct comparison with the KF predictor. The prediction step ![images](images/c16-i0412.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> is equivalent to a time range of 64 us in contrast with a coherence time of ![images](images/c16-i0413.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>&#8776;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>d</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3.3</mn></mrow></math> ms. Using the curve of the perfect mode as a benchmark, the KF predictor achieves optimal performance. Although the RNN predictor is slightly inferior to the KF predictor, it is still quite close to optimal performance and clearly outperforms the outdated mode. Channel interpolation error, which is defined as the difference between the perfect CSI and the interpolated CSI, is also a concern in the process of channel estimation, so the impact of interpolation errors on performance is evaluated. For the purpose of a better illustration, the results for a pilot interval of ![images](images/c16-i0414.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>P</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math> are selected to show in the figure. Even in the mode of one‐step prediction ![images](images/c16-i0415.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, outdated CSI has a remarkable loss of 3.6 dB in comparison with the perfect mode at the outage probability of ![images](images/c16-i0416.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. The KF predictor is vulnerable to interpolation errors, corresponding to a worse result that is very comparable to the outdated mode. In contrast, the RNN predictor is robust and outperforms the KF predictor with an SNR gain of 3.1 dB. To look at the effect of channel correlation, correlated channels generated by the correlation matrix recommended by 3GPP LTE standard for ETU channels are applied. Under the medium correlation indicated by ![images](images/c16-i0417.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.3</mn></mrow></math> and a multi‐step mode of ![images](images/c16-i0418.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math>, outdated CSI has a performance loss of approximately 5 dB given ![images](images/c16-i0419.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> in comparison with the perfect mode, while the channel prediction can take back nearly 4 dB. As mentioned previously, the KF predictor can merely conduct one‐step prediction and therefore is not applicable to this case.

 

## 16.6 Summary

This chapter provided a comprehensive view of channel prediction techniques with an emphasis on NN‐based prediction. At the beginning, the principles of two representative adaptive transmission systems –: transmit antenna selection and opportunistic relaying – were briefly introduced, followed by the performance impact of outdated CSI. Then, classical channel prediction methods based on statistical modeling, i.e. parametric models and autoregressive models, were reviewed. After an explanation of the internal structure of a recurrent NN, the RNN‐based multi‐step prediction were detailed, which can be applied for either SISO or MIMO systems in both flat‐fading and frequency‐selective channels. To further shed light on the mechanism of RNN predictors, the integration of a predictor into a MIMO‐OFDM system to improve the correctness of selecting antennas at the transmitter was illustrated. Performance results in multi‐path fading environment specified by the 3GPP ETU channel model, taking into account a number of influential factors including the spatial correlation, Doppler shift, as well as interpolation error, were shown. It is verified that applying the RNN predictors to combat the problem of outdated CSI is effective and efficient. Although its computational complexity is higher than the Kalman filter, the required computing resources are still affordable relative to off‐the‐shelf hardware. In summary, the RNN exhibits great flexibility, generality, scalability, and applicability in the application of wireless fading‐channel prediction, and can therefore be regarded as a very promising machine learning technique for future wireless communications.

#  Part III  
Network Intelligence and Adaptive System Optimization

# 17  
Machine Learning for Digital Front‐End: a Comprehensive Overview

*Pere L. Gilabert¹, David López‐Bueno², Thi Quynh Anh Pham¹, and Gabriel Montoro¹*

¹*Dept. of Signal Theory and Communications, UPC‐Barcelona Tech., Castelldefels, Barcelona, Spain*

²*CTTC/CERCA & Dept. of Signal Theory and Communications, UPC‐Barcelona Tech., Castelldefels, Barcelona, Spain*

 

## 17.1 Motivation and Background

In wireless and wired communications, the power amplifier (PA) is a critical subsystem in the transmitter chain – not only because it is one of the most power‐hungry devices and accounts for most of the direct current (DC) power consumed in macro base stations, but also because it is the main source of nonlinear distortion in the transmitter. Amplitude‐ and phase‐modulated communication signals presenting a high peak‐to‐average power ratio (PAPR) have a negative impact on the transmitter's power efficiency, because the PA has to be operated at high power back‐off levels to avoid introducing nonlinear distortion. As shown in [Figure 17.1](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0001), to prevent the peaks of the signal from going into compression, it is necessary to operate far from saturation, where the PA is more efficient. Consequently, the mean power added efficiency (PAE) is low, mainly in linear but inefficient class‐A or class‐AB PAs.

Power amplifier system level linearizers, such as digital predistortion (DPD), as shown in [Figure 17.2](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0002), extend the linear range of PAs. Properly combined with crest factor reduction (CFR) techniques, DPD allows PAs to be driven harder into compression while meeting linearity requirements (López et al. ([2014](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0067))). DPD linearization can overcome or at least mitigate the efficiency versus linearity trade‐off in PAs. However, the resulting power efficiency achieved with linearization techniques applied to PAs operating as controlled current sources (e.g. class A, B, AB) is limited. To avoid wasting excessive power resources when handling high PAPR signals, either the operating conditions of a current source mode PA can be forced to follow its envelope, or switched‐mode amplifying classes can be properly introduced. Among the set of techniques aimed at dynamic bias or load adaptation, envelope tracking (ET) PAs (Wang ([2015](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0122)), Popovic ([2017](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0092)), Watkins and Mimis ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0123))), Doherty PAs (Pengelly et al. ([2016](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0086)), Darraji et al. ([2016](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0021))), and LINC or outphasing PAs (Barton ([2016](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0003)), Popovic and García ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0093))) are the most widely proposed in literature. In either case, these highly efficient topologies demand linearization techniques to guarantee the linearity levels specified in the communications standards.

In 5G‐NR (Shafi et al. ([2017](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0102))), the same network infrastructure will be able to efficiently serve different types of traffic with a very wide range of requirements, such as a huge number of users for the Internet of Things, ultra‐low latency and high reliability for mission‐critical systems, and enhanced transmission rates for broadband mobile communications. 5G‐NR intends to provide very high data rates everywhere. To achieve this goal, bandwidths up to GHz will be allocated at mmWave bands, while at sub‐6 GHz, bandwidths of hundreds of MHz will be required.

Achieving these new capabilities requires coping with multiple demanding challenges that, particularizing for the design of radio transceivers, are related to: (i) ensuring the linearity of signals having bandwidths of several hundreds of MHz and peak factors exceeding 10 dB in order to ensure high transmission rates; (ii) improving energy and computational efficiency, as more dense deployments of base stations is expected to scale down the need for transmitted power; (iii) transmitting architectures with multiple antennas (massive multiple‐input and multiple‐output \[MIMO\] in millimeter bands) and multiple power amplifiers to apply beamforming techniques that allow increasing capacity and focusing energy where needed to minimize interference; and (iv) simultaneous transmission and reception (full‐duplex FDD in sub‐6 GHz bands).

![Figure 17.1 Linearity versus power efficiency trade‐off.](images/c17f001.jpg)

[Figure 17.1](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0001) Linearity versus power efficiency trade‐off.

![Figure 17.2 Block diagram of DPD linearization.](images/c17f002.jpg)

[Figure 17.2](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0002) Block diagram of DPD linearization.

The use of 5G spectrally efficient waveforms featuring high PAPR and occupying wider bandwidths in multiple‐antenna transmitters (Suryasarman and Springer ([2015](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0108))) only aggravates the inherent PA linearity versus efficiency trade‐off. When considering wide bandwidth signals, carrier aggregation, or multi‐band configurations (Jaraut et al. ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0048))) in highly efficient transmitter architectures, such as Doherty PAs, envelope tracking PAs, or outphasing transmitters, the number of parameters required in the DPD model to compensate for both static nonlinearities and dynamic memory effects can be unacceptably high. This has a negative impact on the DPD model extraction/adaptation process, because it increases the computational complexity, which may provoke overfitting and uncertainty in the DPD estimation stages (Chani‐Cahuana et al. ([2017](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0013))). However, by applying regularization or dimensionality reduction techniques (Braithwaite ([2017](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0008))), we can both avoid the numerical ill‐conditioning of the estimation and reduce the number of coefficients of the DPD function in the forward path, which ultimately impacts the baseband processing computational complexity and power consumption.

This chapter is devoted to the use of machine learning (ML) algorithms in digital front‐end with the emphasis on CFR techniques, DPD linearization, and in‐phase/quadrature (I/Q) imbalance mitigation. Due to their powerful nonlinear mapping and distributed processing capability, neural network (NN)‐based ML technology can offer a more powerful digital front‐end (DFE) solution than conventional approaches in many aspects including system performance, computational complexity, power consumption, and processing latency. The rest of this chapter is organized into the following five sections. [Section 17.2](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0002) focuses on the problem formulations and fundamental principles of the use of ML and artificial NNs (ANNs) in the DFE, by providing an overview of the need for CFR and DPD techniques and the importance of regularization. [Section 17.3](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0011) addresses feature‐selection and feature‐extraction techniques used to reduce the number of parameters of the DPD linearization system as well as to ensure proper, well‐conditioned estimation for related variables. [Sections 17.4](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0018) and [17.5](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0031) discuss some advanced solutions for ANNs and support vector regression (SVR) approaches to model and compensate for unwanted nonlinear effects in the transmitter chain as well as to reduce the PAPR of the signals. Finally, [Section 17.6](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0032) will further discuss the use of ML techniques in DFE linearization and provides some conclusions.

 

## 17.2 Overview of CFR and DPD

 

### 17.2.1 Crest Factor Reduction Techniques

When dealing with signals presenting high PAPR, the digital‐to‐analog converter (DAC) and PA of the transmitter require large dynamic ranges to avoid amplitude clipping (and thus avoid introducing nonlinear distortion), which implies increasing both the power consumption and cost of the transceiver. In addition, signals with large dynamic range lead to increased power dissipation in DACs, as well as to a shrinking of both the signal‐to‐noise ratio (SNR) and spurious‐free dynamic range. Therefore, high PAPR makes the converter behave as if it were of a lower number of bits than it actually is (Giannopoulos and Paliouras). In addition, as discussed in the previous subsection, operating the PA with significant back‐off levels to prevent the signal peaks from going into compression degrades the power efficiency of the overall amplification system. Combining CFR with linearization techniques can enhance overall PA power efficiency while preserving required linearity levels at the output of the PA.

In OFDM‐based multi‐carrier systems (e.g. LTE, LTE‐A, WiMax), when some of the subcarriers are added with the same phase, what is produced is a peak power that increases the PAPR. In the literature, it is possible to find several published CFR techniques aimed at reducing the PAPR, mainly for OFDM‐based signals (Han and Lee ([2005](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0038)), Jiang and Wu ([2008](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0050)), Kaur and Saini ([2017](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0057))), such as the following examples:

*   *Coding*: The idea of the coding schemes is to reduce the occurrence probability of the same phase of the signals by selecting codewords that minimize the PAPR (avoiding in‐phase addition of signals) in the transmission. Several coding techniques have been published in literature, such as simple block coding, (Fragiacomo et al. ([1998](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0026))), complement block coding (Jiang and Zhu ([2005](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0052))), and modified complement block coding (Jiang and Zhu ([2004](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0051))), among others.
*   *Partial transmit sequence (PTS)*: In the PTS technique presented in Müller and Huber ([1997](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0079)), an input data block of ![images](images/c17-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> frequency‐domain symbols is partitioned into disjoint sub‐blocks. Then, the sub‐carriers in each sub‐block are IFFT transformed into time‐domain partial transmit sequences and independently rotated (weighted) by phase factors. These phase factors are selected in such a manner as to minimize the PAPR of the output signal that results from the combination of each of the sub‐blocks. The phase information vector needs to be transmitted to the receiver for the correct decoding of the transmitted bit sequence.
*   *Selected mapping technique (SLM)*: Similarly to PTS, in the SLM technique the input data (consisting of ![images](images/c17-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> frequency‐domain symbols) are multiplied by a vector of phase‐shifts to generate an alternative (rotated) input. This operation is done in parallel ![images](images/c17-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> times. Each of these ![images](images/c17-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> alternative input data sequences is IFFT processed and then the PAPR is evaluated for each of these possible candidates. Finally, the data sequence with the lowest PAPR is selected for transmission (Bäuml et al. ([1996](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0005))).
*   *Interleaving technique*; Similarly to the SLM technique, a set of interleavers (instead of phase sequences) is used to generate new data blocks targeting the PAPR reduction of the OFDM‐based signals. The interleaver takes a block of ![images](images/c17-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> symbols and reorders or permutes them (Hill et al. ([2000](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0041)), Han and Lee ([2005](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0038))). From the original data block, ![images](images/c17-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> new data blocks can be obtained by permuting the original data using interleavers. After the ![images](images/c17-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> IFFT operations, the data block with the lowest PAPR is chosen for transmission.
*   *Tone reservation (TR) and tone injection (TI)*: Both TR and TI are the methods based on adding a time‐domain signal to the original multi‐carrier signal in such a way that its contribution reduces the overall PAPR (Tellado ([1999](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0109))). The time‐domain signal is computed at the transmitter side and simply removed at the receiver side. In the case of TR, the additional subcarriers (or time‐domain signal) used to reduce the PAPR are reserved for this purpose (i.e. not used for data transmission) and known by the transmitter and receiver. In TI, instead of using reserved tones, the subcarriers carrying data information are used to reduce the PAPR by extending the original constellation size (Tellado ([1999](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0109))). Consequently, each of the points in the original constellation can be mapped into several equivalent points in the expanded constellation, providing several extra degrees of freedom to be used for minimizing the PAPR.
*   *Active constellation extension (ACE)*: Similarly to TI, in ACE (Krongold and Jones ([2003](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0064))) some of the outer signal constellation points in the data block are dynamically extended toward the outside of the original constellation to reduce the PAPR of the signal. The constellation symbols (in M‐QAM modulations) allocated in corners may be allocated within the quarter‐plane outside of the nominal constellation point. By properly changing the modulus and phase of these symbols, the signal PAPR can be reduced at the expense of increasing the mean power of the transmit signal.
    
    ![Figure 17.3 Block diagram of the clipping and filtering CFR technique.](images/c17f003.jpg)
    
    [Figure 17.3](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0003) Block diagram of the clipping and filtering CFR technique.
    
*   *Clipping and filtering*: Clipping techniques may be classified as hard‐clipping, soft‐clipping, and companding. In hard‐clipping, the output signal is strictly limited at the established threshold; while in soft‐clipping, the output signal follows a piecewise law where several threshold levels are defined. In the companding technique, the dynamic range of the signal is compressed at the transmitter side by means of a memoryless transformation (i.e. companding function). As observed in [Figure 17.3](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0003), these clipping techniques require some kind of spectral shaping procedure to mitigate the clipping noise that appears as spectral regrowth in the adjacent channels. To cope with the spectral shaping of the clipping noise, several techniques have been proposed, such as *clipping pulses* (Kim et al. ([2007](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0061))), *pulse windowing* (Vaananen et al. ([2005](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0115))), or *noise shaping* (Saul ([2004](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0099))).

The amount of PAPR reduction that can be achieved depends on the chosen CFR technique and always comes at a price. The harmful effects that appear when reducing the signal's PAPR depend on the specific CFR technique; and, in general, the more PAPR reduction, the more critical are these side effects. Some of the collateral factors that need to be taken into account are (Han and Lee ([2005](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0038))): (i) power increase in the transmit signal (e.g. TR, TI, or ACE); (ii) BER increase at the receiver (e.g. clipping and filtering techniques: TR, TI, and ACE if the transmit signal power is fixed; SLM, PTS, and interleaving if the side information is not properly received); (iii) loss in data rate (e.g. block coding technique, SLM, PTS, and interleaving due to the side information sent to inform the receiver of what has been done in the transmitter); and (iv) computational complexity increase (e.g. SLM, PTS, interleaving, TI, and ACE, have to run search for the best configurations).

As will be addressed in sub[section 17.4.3](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0026), several of the aforementioned CFR techniques make use of ML strategies. For example, ANNs are employed to reduce the computational complexity of CFR techniques such as SLM, PTS, TI, and ACE that require running intensive search (that may take several iterations) to find the best configuration of their parameters; or, in the case of iterative clipping and filtering algorithms, to avoid several FFT/IFFT complex operations.

![Figure 17.4 Identification of the power amplifier behavior.](images/c17f004.jpg)

[Figure 17.4](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0004) Identification of the power amplifier behavior.

 

### 17.2.2 Power Amplifier Behavioral Modeling

Power amplifier behavioral models, or black‐box models, are mathematical descriptors of the non‐ideal behavior of a power amplifier, mainly describing its nonlinear behavior and memory effects (i.e. PA dynamic behavior). Unlike physical models, where it is necessary to know the electronic elements that form the PA, their constitutive relations, and the theoretical rules describing their interactions, the extraction of PA behavioral models relies only on a set of input‐output observations. Consequently, their accuracy is highly sensitive to the adopted model structure and the parameter extraction procedure. In general, the same model used for approximating the response of the PA is also used to estimate its inverse response. For this reason, the behavioral models listed in this subsection are valid approximations of the inverse behavior of the PA and will be used in the following subsection when describing the digital predistortion linearizer.

It is possible to find in literature an enormous number of publications on PA behavioral modeling to address not only single‐input and single‐output (SISO) systems but also multiple‐input and single‐output (MISO) systems, for example when having to characterize concurrent multi‐band transmissions or dynamic supply modulation strategies for the PA. Some of the most commonly used polynomial‐based behavioral models can be seen as a simplified approximations of the general Volterra series. Volterra series are aimed at describing time‐invariant nonlinear systems with fading memory. The discrete‐time low‐pass equivalent Volterra series formulation is described in the following. Considering the general input‐output notation in [Figure 17.4](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0004), the estimated output ![images](images/c17-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#375;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> of the Volterra series is

(17.1)![equation](images/c17-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>P</mi> </munderover> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>Q</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>Q</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>h</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8719;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </munderover> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>q</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The series is composed by ![images](images/c17-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> kernels of increasing dimensional order. The main drawback of using the full Volterra series is that the number of parameters grows exponentially when considering higher‐order kernels, and typical communication signals do not present enough richness to fully excite these kernels, which ultimately may lead to an ill‐conditioned problem.

One of the most widely used models in literature due to its simplicity is the memory polynomial (MP), presented in Kim and Konstantinou ([2001](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0060)). Another widely used model for SISO systems is the generalized memory polynomial (GMP) behavioral model, proposed in D.R. Morgan, Z. Ma et al. ([2006](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0023)). Unlike the MP, the GMP has bi‐dimensional kernels (considering cross‐term products between the complex signal and the lagging and leading envelope terms), which increases the accuracy of the modeling at the price of increasing the number of parameters. There are plenty of other behavioral models in literature used for DPD purposes in SISO systems: just to mention a couple of examples, the NARMA model proposed in Montoro et al. ([2007](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0077)) and the dynamic deviation reduction Volterra series in Zhu et al. ([2006](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0129)). Further information on PA behavioral models for SISO systems can be found in Scheurs et al. ([2009](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0100)). In addition, when considering concurrent multi‐band transmissions such as in Roblin et al. ([2013](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0096)), or combined with PA dynamic supply modulation strategies as in Gilabert and Montoro ([2015](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0030)), or also in multi‐antenna systems where each transmit path has its own PA and antenna element as in Hausmair et al. ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0039)), MISO behavioral models are required to characterize the different sources of nonlinear behavior. In addition, as an alternative to polynomial‐based behavioral models, ANN and SVR approaches have been used in literature for PA behavioral modeling and DPD linearization purposes. As will be presented in [Sections 17.4](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0018) and [17.5](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0031), ANNs and SVR can outperform the modeling capabilities of classical polynomial‐based solutions (inherently local approximations) by providing global approximation and better extrapolation capabilities.

In general, the estimated PA behavioral model output ![images](images/c17-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#375;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> (for ![images](images/c17-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>) can be defined following a matrix notation as

[(17.2)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0002)![equation](images/c17-math-0002.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#375;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c17-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>M</mi></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></math> is the ![images](images/c17-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> vector of parameters and ![images](images/c17-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> is the ![images](images/c17-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> data matrix (with ![images](images/c17-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8811;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>) containing the basis functions or components. The data matrix can be defined as

(17.3)![equation](images/c17-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi> <mi>x</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </msup> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c17-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi><mi>x</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>x</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>x</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></math> is the ![images](images/c17-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> vector of basis functions ![images](images/c17-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>x</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> (with ![images](images/c17-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>) at time ![images](images/c17-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. This general equation can be particularized for any behavioral model.

Generally, the problem in Eq. ([17.2](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0002)) has no exact solution since it is *over‐determined* (i.e. more equations than unknowns). To identify the vector of coefficients ![images](images/c17-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow></math>, we define a cost function that takes into account the identification error ![images](images/c17-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi></mrow></math>, expressed, as depicted in [Figure 17.4](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0004), as

(17.4)![equation](images/c17-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#375;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Taking the ![images](images/c17-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8467;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>‐norm squared of the identification error, the least squares (LS) minimization problem can be defined as follows:

[(17.5)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0005)![equation](images/c17-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <munder> <mi>min</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> </munder> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mo>&#8214;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi> <msubsup> <mrow> <mo>&#8214;</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mi>min</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> </munder> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mo>&#8214;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <msubsup> <mrow> <mo>&#8214;</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Taking the derivative of the cost function ![images](images/c17-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>J</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8214;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8214;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> and setting it to zero, it can be proved that the solution to the LS minimization problem in Eq. ([17.5](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0005)) is given by

[(17.6)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0006)![equation](images/c17-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi>H</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi>H</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The most common numerical methods (Trefethen and Bau ([1997](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0114))) used to solve the LS problem are Cholesky factorization, QR factorization, and singular value decomposition (SVD).

 

### 17.2.3 Closed‐Loop Digital Predistortion Linearization

In the forward path, the input‐output relationship at the DPD block can be described as

(17.7)![equation](images/c17-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>u</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c17-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is the signal at the output of the DPD block, ![images](images/c17-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is the input signal, and ![images](images/c17-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is the distortion signal that can be described using the aforementioned PA behavioral models that can be found in the literature. Therefore, in general,

[(17.8)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0008)![equation](images/c17-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>u</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi> <mi>u</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c17-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>M</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></math> is a vector of coefficients at time ![images](images/c17-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> with dimensions ![images](images/c17-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c17-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> being the order of the behavioral model; ![images](images/c17-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi></msub></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mn>1</mn><mi>u</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>u</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>&#966;</mi><mi>M</mi><mi>u</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math> is the vector containing the basis functions ![images](images/c17-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi><mi>u</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> (with ![images](images/c17-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>) at time ![images](images/c17-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. As explained in the previous section, the same behavioral model or basis functions used for approximating the response of the PA can be also used for DPD purposes to estimate the inverse response of the PA. Now, considering a matrix notation, Eq. ([17.8](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0008)) can be rewritten as

[(17.9)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0009)![equation](images/c17-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c17-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c17-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mi>u</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c17-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, are the predistorted and input ![images](images/c17-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> vectors, respectively. The ![images](images/c17-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> data matrix is defined as

[(17.10)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0010)![equation](images/c17-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8943;</mi> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The DPD function in the forward path described in Eq. ([17.8](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0008)) can be implemented to operate in real time in a programmable logic (PL) device following different approaches, such as look‐up tables (LUTs) (e.g. in Molina et al. ([2017](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0076)), Gilabert et al. ([2007](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0033))), complex multipliers following a polynomial approach using the Horner's rule as in Mrabet et al. ([2012](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0078)), or some combination of complex multipliers and memory blocks as in Cao et al. ([2017](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0012)).

Unlike the DPD in the forward path, the identification/adaptation of the parameters does not need to be carried out in real time, and thus it can be implemented in a processing system (PS). Therefore, the DPD coefficients can be extracted and adapted iteratively in a slower time scale than real time. The extraction of the DPD coefficients can be carried out following either a direct learning or an indirect learning approach.

The block diagram of a closed‐loop adaptive DPD architecture following an indirect learning approach is shown in [Figure 17.5](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0005). The DPD function in the forward path is described in Eq. ([17.8](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0008)) or, considering a matrix notation, in Eq. ([17.9](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0009)). However, with the indirect learning approach, the inverse PA model is estimated as a postdistortion. That is, the assumption made is that the coefficients of the postdistortion are equal to the coefficients of the predistortion; as mentioned in Braithwaite ([2015](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0007)), the approximation can be considered a valid approximation as long as there is no saturation in either the transmit path or observation path.

The block diagram of a closed‐loop adaptive DPD architecture following a direct learning approach is shown in [Figure 17.6](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0006). As explained in Braithwaite ([2015](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0007)), in comparison to the indirect learning approach, with the direct learning estimation we gain robustness against noisy PA output observations and avoid the offset of the coefficient vector from its optimal value.

In both direct and indirect learning approaches, the coefficients can be extracted iteratively:

[(17.11)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0011)![equation](images/c17-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mrow> <mi>j</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#916;</mi> <mi>w</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> ![Figure 17.5 Closed‐loop digital predistortion linearization: indirect learning approach.](images/c17f005.jpg)

[Figure 17.5](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0005) Closed‐loop digital predistortion linearization: indirect learning approach.

![Figure 17.6 Closed‐loop digital predistortion linearization: direct learning approach.](images/c17f006.jpg)

[Figure 17.6](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0006) Closed‐loop digital predistortion linearization: direct learning approach.

However, considering a direct learning approach, ![images](images/c17-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#916;</mi><mi>w</mi></mrow></math> is obtained by finding the following LS solution,

[(17.12)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0012)![equation](images/c17-math-0012.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#916;</mi> <mi>w</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold">H</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c17-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi></mrow></math> is the ![images](images/c17-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> vector of the identification error defined as

(17.13)![equation](images/c17-math-0013.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>G</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c17-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>G</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> determines the desired linear gain of the PA, and where ![images](images/c17-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c17-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi></mrow></math> are the ![images](images/c17-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> vectors of the PA output and the transmitted input, respectively.

 

### 17.2.4 Regularization

The method of LS performs well to approximate the solution of overdetermined systems when considering big datasets. However, it may face the risk of *underfitting* or *overfitting* (see [Figure 17.7](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0007)). An underfitted model lacks essential coefficients in the model description. On the contrary, an overfitted model contains more parameters than the model really needs. Both underfitted and overfitted models tend to misrepresent the training data and will therefore have poor predictive performance.

Coefficient estimates for the PA models described in Eq. ([17.6](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0006)) assume the independence of the model basis functions. When the basis functions are correlated and the columns of the data matrix ![images](images/c17-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow></math> have an approximate linear dependence, the inverse of the covariance matrix ![images](images/c17-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> becomes close to singular. Consequently, the LS estimate becomes highly sensitive to random errors in the observed response ![images](images/c17-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi></mrow></math> (e.g. random noise, quantization noise of the measurement setup, etc.).

![Figure 17.7 Underfitting and overfitting in the least square identification of the power amplifier behavior.](images/c17f007.jpg)

[Figure 17.7](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0007) Underfitting and overfitting in the least square identification of the power amplifier behavior.

Regularization is a process of introducing additional information in order to prevent overfitting. In general, the main idea of the regularization techniques is to add a regularization term ![images](images/c17-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> to the cost function:

(17.14)![equation](images/c17-math-0014.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>J</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mo>&#8214;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <msubsup> <mrow> <mo>&#8214;</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </math> 

In the following, the regularization term will be particularized. Therefore, the cost functions for the Ridge regression, the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO), and the elastic net will be presented as constrained versions of the ordinary least squares (OLS) regression cost function. In the case of Ridge regression or Tikhonov regularization (Tikhonov and Arsensin ([1977](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0113))), it will be subject to a constraint on the squared ![images](images/c17-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8467;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>‐norm (Euclidean norm) of the vector of coefficients, while in the case of LASSO (Tibshirani ([1994](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0111))), it will be subject to a constraint on the ![images](images/c17-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8467;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math>‐norm of the vector of coefficients. Finally, the elastic net (Zou and Hastie ([2005](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0130))) combines both the Ridge regression and the Lasso constraints.

 

#### 17.2.4.1 Ridge Regression or Tikhonov ![images](images/c17-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8467;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> Regularization

In ![images](images/c17-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8467;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> regularization, the goal is to minimize the residual sum of squares subject to a constraint on the sum of squares of the coefficients:

(17.15)![equation](images/c17-math-0015.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="right left left"> <mtr> <mtd class="eqnarray-1"/> <mtd/> <mtd class="eqnarray-3"> <munder> <mi>min</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> </munder> <mspace width="1em"/> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi> <mi>x</mi> <mi>H</mi> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="eqnarray-1"/> <mtd/> <mtd class="eqnarray-3"> <mtext>subject to</mtext> <mspace width="1em"/> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>M</mi> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <msub> <mi>w</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

This constraint forces the coefficients to stay within a sphere of radius ![images](images/c17-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>. As depicted in [Figure 17.8](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0008), the contours represent the values of coefficients estimated by the least squares regression. The solution to the Ridge regression or Tikhonov regularization is the coefficients on the contours that meet the constraint. The constrained cost function can also be written as a penalized residual sum of squares

![Figure 17.8 Ridge, LASSO, and elastic net regularization.](images/c17f008.jpg)

[Figure 17.8](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0008) Ridge, LASSO, and elastic net regularization.
