<mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <msubsup> <mo>&#8214;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c17-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> (![images](images/c17-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>) is the shrinkage parameter. Taking the derivative of the cost function and setting it to zero, we obtain the following solution,

[(17.17)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0017)![equation](images/c17-math-0017.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mrow> <mi>R</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mi>d</mi> <mi>g</mi> <mi>e</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi>H</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi>H</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

with ![images](images/c17-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi></mrow></math> being the identity matrix. This approach also avoids the problem of rank deficiency because ![images](images/c17-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">I</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is invertible even if ![images](images/c17-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is not (Hoerl and Kennard ([1970](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0042))). As shown in Eq. ([17.17](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0017)), the coefficients' solution ![images](images/c17-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> depends on the shrinkage parameter ![images](images/c17-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>. It controls the size of the coefficients and thus the amount of regularization (i.e. as ![images](images/c17-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8594;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c17-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> tends to the OLS solution; while as ![images](images/c17-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>&#8594;</mo><mi>&#8734;</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c17-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mrow><mi>R</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>d</mi><mi>g</mi><mi>e</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> tends to 0). A common approach to properly tune the ![images](images/c17-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> parameter is to use K‐fold cross validation.

As an example, [Figure 17.9](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0009)‐left shows the normalized mean square error (NMSE) of a PA nonlinear behavior identification when considering a memory polynomial model and different configurations of nonlinear order and memory. It can be observed that adding more terms does not guarantee better NMSE: on the contrary, the NMSE starts degrading when the parameter identification is ill‐conditioned due to overparametrization, and consequently the estimated parameters take high power values, as depicted [Figure 17.10](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0010)‐left. After Ridge or Tikhonov regularization, the possible LS solutions are the ones that meet the constraint on the power of the coefficients (bounded coefficients values in [Figure 17.10](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0010)‐right), and acceptable NMSE values are maintained even when the system is clearly overfitted, as depicted in [Figure 17.9](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0009)‐right.

 

#### 17.2.4.2 LASSO or ![images](images/c17-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8467;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> Regularization

The least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression analysis method was introduced in Tibshirani ([1994](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0111)). Similarly to Ridge regression, LASSO can be used for both regularization and to generate a sparse model (i.e. reducing the number of parameters or components of the model). Whereas the constraint of the Ridge regression is the sum of square of the coefficients, the LASSO constraint consists of the sum of the absolute value of the coefficients. Thus, the solution of LASSO regression satisfies the following ![images](images/c17-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8467;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> optimization problem:

![Figure 17.9 NMSE for different values of nonlinear order and memory taps when considering a memory polynomial model, without (left) and with (right) Tikhonov regularization.](images/c17f009.jpg)

[Figure 17.9](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0009) NMSE for different values of nonlinear order and memory taps when considering a memory polynomial model, without (left) and with (right) Tikhonov regularization.

![Figure 17.10 Squared norm of the vector of coefficients of the PA behavior identification for different values of nonlinear order and memory taps using a memory polynomial model, without (left) and with (right) Tikhonov regularization.](images/c17f010.jpg)

[Figure 17.10](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0010) Squared norm of the vector of coefficients of the PA behavior identification for different values of nonlinear order and memory taps using a memory polynomial model, without (left) and with (right) Tikhonov regularization.

Unlike Ridge regression, LASSO has no closed form. The regression coefficients are estimated as

where the elements ![images](images/c17-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> of ![images](images/c17-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi></mrow></math> are either ![images](images/c17-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> or ![images](images/c17-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, depending on the sign of the corresponding regression coefficient ![images](images/c17-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>. Despite the fact that the original implementation involves quadratic programming techniques from convex optimization, Efron et al. in Tibshirani et al. ([2004](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0112)) proposed the least angle regression (LARS) algorithm that can be used for computing the LASSO path efficiently.

 

#### 17.2.4.3 Elastic Net

The elastic net was proposed in Zou and Hastie ([2005](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0130)) to overcome the LASSO limitations of selecting at most ![images](images/c17-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> components (or basis functions) when the number of components ![images](images/c17-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> is bigger than the number of observations ![images](images/c17-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> (i.e. ![images](images/c17-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>), and of selecting only one component from a group of highly correlated components.

The elastic net combines both the Ridge regression and the LASSO constraints (see [Figure 17.8](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0008)),

The minimization of the elastic net cost function in Eq. ([17.22](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0022)) is similar to minimizing the LASSO cost function, and all the elastic net regularization paths can be estimated almost as efficiently as the LASSO paths with the LARS‐EN algorithm proposed in Zou and Hastie ([2005](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0130)).

 

## 17.3 Dimensionality Reduction and ML

 

### 17.3.1 Introduction

The objective of dimensionality‐reduction techniques is to reduce the number of features (dimensions, variables, basis functions, components) under consideration in a given dataset by obtaining a set of the principal features (i.e. eliminating redundant or irrelevant variables), which can allow keeping or even improving the model's performance. These techniques can be sorted as follows:

*   *Feature selection*, selecting the most relevant variables from a random set of original variables.
*   *Feature extraction*, creating a reduced set of new variables that are linear or nonlinear combinations of the original variables.

[Figure 17.11](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0011) illustrates the hierarchical structure of dimensionality‐reduction techniques.

***Feature‐selection techniques*** are typically presented in three categories: filter methods, wrapper methods, and embedded methods.

*Filter methods* are relatively fast pre-processing (as in [Figure 17.12](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0012)) algorithms that do not assume the use of a specific model (which makes them less accurate than, for example, wrapper methods). These methods suppress the least‐interesting variables based only on general features. Filter approaches select features according to their scores evaluated via statistical measures. First, a feature‐ranking technique is used to evaluate the features and rank them. Then, low‐score features are suppressed, leaving only the features with higher scores. Cross‐validation (Kohavi ([1995](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0062))) can be used to decide the cut‐off point in the ranked list of features. The score of the features can be considered by: the distance from them to their class and the class nearby (as in Relief), the correlation between the features and their class (as in correlation‐based feature selection \[CFS\] (Li et al. ([2011](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0065))), and fast correlated based filter \[FCBF\] (Yu and Liu ([2003](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0126)))), mutual information (as presented in Guyon and Elisseeff ([2003](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0036))), pointwise mutual information (as in Yang and Pedersen ([1997](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0125))), etc. Obviously, different ranking techniques can lead to different rankings and thus to different selected subsets.

![Figure 17.11 Hierarchical structure of dimensionality‐reduction techniques.](images/c17f011.jpg)

[Figure 17.11](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0011) Hierarchical structure of dimensionality‐reduction techniques.

*Wrapper methods*, unlike filter methods, employ specific learning algorithms to score the candidate feature subsets. The learning algorithm is chosen depending on the target of the problem Jovic et al. ([2015](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0054)): for example, for regression problems, the wrapper approach evaluates subsets based on the performance of a regression algorithm (e.g. support vector machines \[SVMs\] Li et al. ([2011](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0065)), LASSO regression Tibshirani ([1994](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0111)), or Ridge regression Hoerl and Kennard ([1970](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0042))); for clustering, the wrapper approach rates subsets based on the performance of a clustering algorithm (e.g. K‐means Khan and Ahmad ([2004](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0058)) or mean‐shift clustering Comaniciu and Meer ([2002](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0019))); for classification tasks, the wrapper technique evaluates subsets based on the performance of a classification algorithm (e.g. naive Bayes Buzic and Dobsa ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0009)) or decision trees Quinlan ([1986](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0094))). The evaluation is repeated for each subset; therefore, with wrapper methods, it is possible to obtain better results than with filter methods at the price of being less general and more computationally expensive.

*Embedded methods* try to combine the advantages of both previous methods. As schematically depicted in [Figure 17.12](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0012), embedded methods differ from other feature‐selection methods in the way feature selection and learning interact. Filter methods do not incorporate learning. Wrapper methods use a learning machine to measure the quality of subsets of features without incorporating knowledge about the specific structure of the classification or regression function, and can therefore be combined with any learning machine. In contrast to filter and wrapper approaches, in embedded methods the learning part and the feature selection part cannot be separated – the structure of the class of functions under consideration plays a crucial role. The embedded methods can be divided into three groups: (i) forward‐backward methods, (ii) optimization of scaling factors, and (iii) sparsity term. For example, one of the greedy‐search algorithms used for dimensionality reduction in DPD linearization applications is orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP), which belongs to the family of forward‐backward methods – in particular, to the family of sequential forward‐selection algorithms (Marcano‐Cedeno et al. ([2010](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0072))).

![Figure 17.12 Feature selection embedded approach.](images/c17f012.jpg)

[Figure 17.12](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0012) Feature selection embedded approach.

***Feature‐extraction*** techniques are aimed at finding a reduced set of features that are a combination of the original ones. Feature extraction can be classed in two subgroups: linear dimension reduction and nonlinear dimension reduction. As will be presented in the following subsections, in the field of DPD linearization, some popular linear dimensionality reduction methods such as principal component analysis (PCA) Gilabert et al. ([2013b](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0032)) and partial least squares (PLS) P. L. Gilabert, G. Montoro, et al. ([2016](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0084)) have been used. Linear dimensionality reduction methods perform the reduction by first generating the new components, which are the linear combinations of the original basis, and then retaining the most significant components and suppressing the irrelevant ones. These methods consider many data features of interest, such as covariance, correlation between datasets, and input‐output relationships.

 

### 17.3.2 Dimensionality Reduction Applied to DPD Linearization

As depicted in the block diagram in [Figure 17.13](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0013), the DPD linearization system can be divided into two subsystems: a forward‐path subsystem operating in real time, where the input signal is conveniently predistorted; and a feedback or observation path subsystem, where the coefficients characterizing the nonlinear DPD function in the forward path are estimated and updated in a more relaxed time scale. When targeting an implementation in a signal‐processing platform – for example, in a system on chip (SoC) FPGA device – the DPD function in the forward path can be implemented in a programmable logic (PL) unit: for example, by following a LUT approach, as in Gilabert et al. ([2007](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0033)), Molina et al. ([2017](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0076)); or by considering a polynomial approach using Horner's rule, as in Mrabet et al. ([2012](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0078)); or by combining both complex multipliers/adders and memory, as in Cao et al. ([2017](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0012)). Therefore, the DPD function in the forward path should be designed as simply as possible (i.e. including the minimum and most relevant basis functions) to save as many hardware logic resources and memory as possible. On the other hand, the adaptation of the DPD coefficients can be carried out in a processing system (PS) in a much slower time scale than in the forward path (i.e. not in real time).

![Figure 17.13 Block diagram of the digital predistortion linearization forward and feedback/observation paths.](images/c17f013.jpg)

[Figure 17.13](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0013) Block diagram of the digital predistortion linearization forward and feedback/observation paths.

In the field of DPD linearization, dimensionality‐reduction techniques are used with a double objective: on the one hand, to ensure proper, well‐conditioned parameter identification; and on the other hand, to reduce the number of coefficients to be estimated and thus relax the computational complexity and memory requirements of a hardware implementation.

Some of the proposed solutions for dimensionality reduction of DPD linearizers are based on feature‐selection techniques. The objective of these techniques is to enforce the sparsity constraint on the vector of parameters by minimizing the number of active components (i.e. ![images](images/c17-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8467;</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>‐norm) subject to a constraint on the ![images](images/c17-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8467;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>‐norm squared of the identification error. For example, particularizing for the identification of the PA behavioral model coefficients described in Eqs. ([17.2](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0002))‐([17.6](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0006)), the optimization problem can be described as

[(17.24)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0024)![equation](images/c17-math-0024.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="right left left"> <mtr> <mtd class="eqnarray-1"/> <mtd class="eqnarray-2"> <munder> <mi>min</mi> <mi>w</mi> </munder> <mo>&#8214;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <msub> <mo>&#8214;</mo> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd class="eqnarray-3"/> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="eqnarray-1"> <mtext>subject to</mtext> <mspace width="0.4em"/> </mtd> <mtd class="eqnarray-2"> <mo>&#8214;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <msubsup> <mo>&#8214;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mn>2</mn> </msubsup> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> <mtd/> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

Unfortunately, this is a non‐deterministic polynomial‐time hard (NP‐hard) combinatorial search problem. Therefore, in the field of DPD linearization, several sub‐optimal approaches have been proposed, targeting both robust identification and model order reduction, such as LASSO, used for example by Wisell et al. in (Wisell et al. ([2008](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0124))) and consisting of a ![images](images/c17-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8467;</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math>‐norm regularization; the Ridge regression, used for example by Guan et al. in (Guan and Zhu ([2012](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0034))) and consisting of a ![images](images/c17-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8467;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>‐norm regularization; the sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) algorithm, used by Peng et al. in (Peng et al. ([2016](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0085))); and the orthogonal matching pursuit (OMP), a greedy algorithm for sparse approximation used in (J. Reina‐Tosina, M. Allegue et al. ([2015](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0046))) by Reina et al. to select the most relevant basis functions of the DPD function.

Another approach to address the dimensionality reduction in DPD linearization consists of applying feature‐extraction techniques. In commercial products and in publications addressing DPD implementation, one of the most common solutions used to solve the least squares regression problem consists of extracting the parameters through QR factorization combined with recursive least squares (QR‐RLS) (Muruganathan and Sesay ([2006](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0080))). However, by considering feature‐extraction techniques such as PCA (Gilabert et al. ([2013a](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0031))) and PLS (Pham et al. ([2018b](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0088))), it is possible to ensure both a proper, well‐conditioned estimation and a reduction in the number of parameters in the identification process. The DPD dimensionality reduction is carried out by calculating a new, reduced set of orthogonal components that are linear combinations of the original basis functions. However, unlike feature‐selection techniques, with feature‐extraction techniques the number of coefficients of the DPD function in the forward path are not reduced.

Alternatively, both feature‐selection and feature‐extraction techniques can be properly combined as in Pham et al. ([2018c](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0089)), by:

*   Doing an a priori offline search (e.g. OMP, LASSO) to reduce the number of basis functions of the DPD function in the forward path.
*   Using PCA or PLS techniques for the parameter extraction in the adaptation path.

In the following, examples of feature‐selection and feature‐extraction techniques that have been used for DPD dimensionality reduction will be further described. In particular, further details of the OMP greedy algorithm and the PCA and PLS techniques applied to DPD linearization will be given.

 

### 17.3.3 Greedy Feature‐Selection Algorithm: OMP

The OMP is a greedy algorithm, also referred to as forward greedy selection in the ML literature (Mallat and Zhang ([1993](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0069))). The OMP algorithm can be used to perform an a priori offline study, to properly select the best basis functions that will contribute to linearize the PA. Therefore, this study is carried out once and then applied to both reduce the number of coefficients of the forward path behavioral model and improve the conditioning and robustness of the adaptation subsystem.

In order to minimize the number of coefficients being required by the DPD function in the forward path, we assume that the optimal subset of selected basis functions of the DPD function will be the same as that used for PA behavioral modeling. Therefore, the OMP algorithm is the sub‐optimal approach considered to solve Eq. ([17.24](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0024)).

The support set containing the indices of the basis functions describing the PA behavioral model is defined as ![images](images/c17-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Considering that ![images](images/c17-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the number of basis functions under study (i.e. ![images](images/c17-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>), the OMP algorithm is defined in Algorithm 1. At every iteration of the OMP search, the basis function that better contributes to minimize the residual error is selected and added to the support set ![images](images/c17-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. The elements of ![images](images/c17-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> have been normalized in power to simplify the index ![images](images/c17-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>i</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> calculation in line 6 of the algorithm, which can be obtained by maximizing the absolute value of the correlation between the basis function ![images](images/c17-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and the residual error ![images](images/c17-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>m</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> of the previous iteration. After a complete OMP search, we obtain a vector ![images](images/c17-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> with the indices of all the original basis functions (active components) sorted according to their relevance. Then, by using some information criterion, such as the Akaike (AIC) or Bayesian (BIC) (J. Reina‐Tosina, M. Allegue et al. ([2015](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0046))), it is possible to determine the optimum number of coefficients (![images](images/c17-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c17-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>m</mi><mi>a</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Finally, the subset of selected basis functions, ![images](images/c17-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">X</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, is used in Eqs. ([17.8](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0008))–([17.9](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0009)) as ![images](images/c17-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi></mrow><mrow><msup><mi>S</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>m</mi><mrow><mi>o</mi><mi>p</mi><mi>t</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></msub></mrow></math> to carry out the DPD.

### 17.3.4 Principal Component Analysis

PCA is a statistical learning technique suitable for converting an original basis of eventually correlated features or components into a new, uncorrelated orthogonal basis set called *principal components*. The principal components are linear combinations of the original variables oriented to capture the maximum variance in the data.

![Figure 17.14 Principal component analysis transformation considering two‐dimensional data.](images/c17f014.jpg)

[Figure 17.14](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0014) Principal component analysis transformation considering two‐dimensional data.

[Figure 17.14](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0014) presents an example of PCA transformation considering two‐dimensional data. The original coordinate axes are ![images](images/c17-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c17-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></msub></mrow></math>. The new coordinate axes are ![images](images/c17-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c17-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></msub></mrow></math>, corresponding to the two eigenvectors of the original data. The first eigenvector (corresponding to axis ![images](images/c17-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></msub></mrow></math>) has much larger variance than the second eigenvector (corresponding to axis ![images](images/c17-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></msub></mrow></math>) (i.e. ![images](images/c17-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>&#62;</mo><msub><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#963;</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>). In the original coordinate axes, the difference of the variances of the data on the two axes is not significantly different. In this example, ![images](images/c17-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></msub></mrow></math> is the principal component of the considered data. Therefore, if we discard the unimportant component ![images](images/c17-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">2</mn></msub></mrow></math> and project the data on the dimension ![images](images/c17-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi><mn mathvariant="bold">1</mn></msub></mrow></math>, the information loss will not be very significant, whereas, in the original coordinate axes, if we simply remove one dimension and retain the other, we will encounter relevant information loss.

An independent DPD parameter estimation based on the adaptive PCA (APCA) algorithm for dimensionality reduction was proposed in López‐Bueno et al. ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0068)). The proposed solution addresses the DPD model parameter extraction in order to enable implementation in an FPGA containing a programmable logic device and a processing system.

Taking into account the transformation matrix ![images](images/c17-i0137.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> in Eq. ([17.28](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0028)) with orthogonal basis functions, the direct learning coefficients extraction in Eqs. ([17.11](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0011)) and ([17.12](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0012)) can be rewritten as

where

with ![images](images/c17-i0139.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> being the eigenvalues of ![images](images/c17-i0140.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi>H</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c17-i0141.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mi>H</mi></msup></mrow></math> (with ![images](images/c17-i0142.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>). By exploiting the orthogonality of the resulting transformed basis functions, the coefficient adaptation can therefore be carried out independently as follows,

(17.33)![equation](images/c17-math-0033.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#373;</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>&#373;</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#956;</mi> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>&#955;</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>&#977;</mi> </mrow> <mi>j</mi> <mi>u</mi> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi>e</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </math> 

with ![images](images/c17-i0144.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> and where ![images](images/c17-i0145.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#977;</mi></mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>u</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is the ![images](images/c17-i0146.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>j</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> transformed basis function at time ![images](images/c17-i0147.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. A schematic flowchart describing the independent DPD extraction is depicted in [Figure 17.15](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0015). The goal is to estimate the minimum necessary number of transformed coefficients ![images](images/c17-i0148.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#373;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> to meet the target linearity levels, specified in terms of adjacent channel power ratio (ACPR) and NMSE. As explained in Pham et al. ([2018a](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0087)), with the proposed block deflated adaptive principal component (BD‐APCA) algorithm, the columns ![images](images/c17-i0149.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> (![images](images/c17-i0150.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>) of the transformation matrix ![images](images/c17-i0151.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi></mrow></math> are iteratively found one by one. Therefore, the next column is estimated by using the values of the previously extracted components. Eventually, the ![images](images/c17-i0152.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> transformation matrix ![images](images/c17-i0153.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mi>L</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> will converge to ![images](images/c17-i0154.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">V</mi></mrow></math>. Therefore, as shown in [Figure 17.15](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0015), until the desired linearity levels are met, the algorithm increases the number of transformed coefficients to be estimated. More specifically, after several APCA iterations, a new transformation vector ![images](images/c17-i0155.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> is obtained. This vector, together with the other ![images](images/c17-i0156.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> previously calculated vectors (i.e. ![images](images/c17-i0157.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>j</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, defines the ![images](images/c17-i0158.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> components of the transformation matrix ![images](images/c17-i0159.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>j</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Then, each one of the ![images](images/c17-i0160.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> transformed coefficients ![images](images/c17-i0161.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#373;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> can be estimated/updated independently (e.g. in parallel) by following an LMS approach,

(17.34)![equation](images/c17-math-0034.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#373;</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>&#373;</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#956;</mi> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>&#955;</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>j</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <msup> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">r</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi>e</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> ![Figure 17.15 Flowchart of the independent digital predistortion identification process using adaptive principal components analysis.](images/c17f015.jpg)

[Figure 17.15](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0015) Flowchart of the independent digital predistortion identification process using adaptive principal components analysis.

Consequently, the input‐output relationship of the DPD function in the forward path described in Eq. ([17.8](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0008))‐ Eq. ([17.9](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0009)) can be rewritten as

or, alternatively, be expressed in terms of the original basis functions ![images](images/c17-i0162.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#981;</mi><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> and the transformation matrix ![images](images/c17-i0163.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">R</mi></mrow></math>

Experimental results showing the viability and robustness of the independent DPD algorithm described in [Figure 17.15](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0015) can be found in López‐Bueno et al. ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0068)).

 

### 17.3.5 Partial Least Squares

Similarly to PCA, PLS is a statistical technique used to construct a new basis of components that are linear combinations of the original basis functions. However, while PCA obtains new components that maximize their own variance, PLS finds linear combinations of the original basis functions that maximize the covariance between the new components and the reference signal. This enables PLS to outperform PCA in applications such as dimensionality reduction for PA behavioral modeling and DPD linearization P. L. Gilabert, G. Montoro, et al. ([2016](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0084)), Pham et al. ([2018c](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0089)).

In Pham et al. ([2018c](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0089)), for example, with the PLS technique, a set of new components is generated from the original basis functions. By properly selecting the most relevant components from the set, it is possible to guarantee a well‐conditioned identification while reducing the number of estimated parameters without loss of accuracy. In addition, thanks to the orthonormality among the components of the new basis, the matrix inversion operation of the LS Moore‐Penrose inverse is significantly simplified.

To obtain with PLS a basis of orthonormal components, the iterative SIMPLS algorithm was proposed in de Jong ([1993](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0022)). In a similar manner as it was done for PCA in Eq. ([17.28](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0028)), the new basis ![images](images/c17-i0164.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> is defined by means of the ![images](images/c17-i0165.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> (with ![images](images/c17-i0166.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>) transformation matrix ![images](images/c17-i0167.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math>,

[(17.37)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0037)![equation](images/c17-math-0037.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi> </mrow> </math> 

with ![images](images/c17-i0168.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi></mrow></math> being the ![images](images/c17-i0169.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#215;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> matrix of basis functions defining the DPD linearizer in Eq. ([17.9](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0009)). The new orthonormal components of the transformed matrix ![images](images/c17-i0170.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> are sorted according to their contribution to maximize the covariance between the new components and the error signal ![images](images/c17-i0171.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">e</mi></mrow></math>. Taking into account the transformation matrix ![images](images/c17-i0172.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> in Eq. ([17.37](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0037)) with orthonormal basis functions, the direct learning coefficients extraction in Eqs. ([17.11](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0011)) and ([17.12](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0012)) can be rewritten as

(17.38)![equation](images/c17-math-0038.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#373;</mi> <mrow> <mi>j</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#373;</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#956;</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>H</mi> </msup> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <msup> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>H</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Now, considering the orthonormal property of the transformed matrix ![images](images/c17-i0173.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> (i.e. ![images](images/c17-i0174.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="bold">I</mi></mrow></math>), the update of the transformed coefficients is significantly simplified:

[(17.39)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0039)![equation](images/c17-math-0039.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#373;</mi> <mrow> <mi>j</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#373;</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mi>&#956;</mi> <msup> <mover accent="true"> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mi>H</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Finally, the original coefficients are obtained through the following anti‐transformation:

(17.40)![equation](images/c17-math-0040.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#373;</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

When comparing the accuracy versus coefficient reduction between the PLS and PCA techniques, such as in P. L. Gilabert, G. Montoro, et al. ([2016](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0084)), Pham et al. ([2018c](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0089)), we observe that the PLS technique is more robust than PCA in terms of performance degradation (e.g. in linearization or modeling accuracy) when reducing the number of parameters of the estimation (i.e. coefficients of the transformed basis). This is because PLS, unlike PCA, also considers the information of the PA output signal for creating the transformation matrix.

Another approach presented in Pham et al. ([2019](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0090)) consists of using the PLS technique for estimating and adapting the DPD coefficients with a dynamic basis matrix. Therefore, PLS is employed inside the DPD adaptation loop to actively adjust the basis matrix in the DPD identification subsystem. The dynamic basis reduction is carried out at every iteration according to the *residual linearization error*, defined as the difference between the actual and the desired linear PA output signals. In comparison to the QR decomposition (commonly used in conventional DPD estimation/adaptation to avoid the costly mathematical computation of the LS Moore‐Penrose inverse of the covariance matrix), the proposed technique allows dynamic adjustment of the number of coefficients to meet the targeted linearity level.

[Figure 17.16](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0016) depicts the DPD estimation/adaptation employing the dynamic basis matrix approach presented in Pham et al. ([2019](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0090)). The proposed dynamic orthonormal transformation matrix (DOTM) algorithm, which is a modification of the iterative SIMPLS algorithm in de Jong ([1993](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0022)), calculates the linear combinations of the original basis with maximum covariance between the new basis and the signal to be estimated. Whereas the size of the transformation matrix ![images](images/c17-i0175.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math> is predetermined and given as an input information in SIMPLS, in DOTM, the number of columns of ![images](images/c17-i0176.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math> are iteratively added and calculated until the power of the estimated error is close enough to a desired threshold ![images](images/c17-i0177.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, defined as a percentage ![images](images/c17-i0178.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi></mrow></math> of the power of the error signal ![images](images/c17-i0179.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi></mrow></math>. Therefore, thanks to the DOTM algorithm, at each iteration ![images](images/c17-i0180.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>j</mi></mrow></math> of the DPD adaptation, the number of columns ![images](images/c17-i0181.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> (with ![images](images/c17-i0182.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>) of the transformation matrix ![images](images/c17-i0183.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">P</mi></mrow></math> varies, and only the minimum necessary number of columns that meet the ![images](images/c17-i0184.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> threshold requirements are selected. By taking into account the orthonormality among the components, the transformed coefficients increment ![images](images/c17-i0185.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#916;</mi><mi>&#373;</mi></mrow></math> is calculated as described in Eq. ([17.39](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0039)), i.e. ![images](images/c17-i0186.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#916;</mi><mi>&#373;</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>&#956;</mi><msup><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">U</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mi>H</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">e</mi></mrow></math>. Then, as shown in [Figure 17.16](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0016), after the antitransformation, the estimated DPD coefficients are used in the forward path to predistort the input signal, and the DPD adaptation will continue until it achieves the desired ACPR level.

![Figure 17.16 Flowchart of digital predistortion estimation/adaptation using a dynamic basis matrix.](images/c17f016.jpg)

## 17.4 Nonlinear Neural Network Approaches

 

### 17.4.1 Introduction to ANN Topologies

An artificial NN (ANN) is a modeling technique, originally inspired by some partial knowledge on the behavior of the neurons in the human brain, that can be trained to learn the structure of the data and model complex nonlinear functions. Essentially, the neurons are distributed between different layers and communicate with each other through neuron output‐to‐input weighted interconnections (or synapses). Based on the interconnection pattern or architecture, we can distinguish between feedforward networks (FNNs) and recurrent (or feedback) networks (RNNs).

FNNs, which are among the most used ANN, have unidirectional interconnections between the neurons of every layer since the flow of data is from input to outputs, without feedback (one input pattern produces one output). The most common FNN is called a multilayer perceptron (MLP), which is composed of fully connected layers where all the output activations are composed of a weighted sum of input activations (the neurons of a specific layer are fed by the outputs of all the neurons of the preceding layer). The larger the weight, the more influential the corresponding input will be. Enabling full connection in a densely populated NN may require significant hardware resources, but in many applications the weight of some interconnections can be set to zero without loss of accuracy, which results in sparsely connected layers. In a RNN, the inputs of the neurons of a specific layer may be fed by the output of the neurons either in the same layer or at any of the following layers, which senses time and memory of previous states. These concepts are shown in [Figure 17.17](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0017)a, where a modified MLP‐based FNN is displayed (a classic MLP would have full connection between at all layers).

In more detail, [Figure 17.17](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0017)b shows a single‐layer perceptron model and the operation of this fundamental building block of an MLP NN. The ![images](images/c17-i0187.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>j</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> neuron of the ![images](images/c17-i0188.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> layer receives as input each ![images](images/c17-i0189.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> from the previous layer. Each ![images](images/c17-i0190.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c17-i0191.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>, is then multiplied by a weight ![images](images/c17-i0192.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>w</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>i</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> and the resulting values are all summed together. A single bias or offset value ![images](images/c17-i0193.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#952;</mi><mi>j</mi></msub></mrow></math> is added to the summation and, finally, an activation or transfer function ![images](images/c17-i0194.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#981;</mi><mi>k</mi></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> (different activation functions can be applied to different layers) is applied to provide the output of the ![images](images/c17-i0195.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>j</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> neuron found in the ![images](images/c17-i0196.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>k</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math> layer, as shown in Eq. A brief historical review follows. When the SLP was defined in the late 1950s by Rosenblatt ([1958](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0097)), the activation function being used was the step or threshold function, and the concept of hidden layers was not yet exploited. This model was a first practical implementation that could be used for simple linearly separable binary classification problems but was not valid for more complicated modeling requiring nonlinear outputs. The solution to this limitation came in the mid and late 1980s thanks to a few works, such as Rumelhart and McClelland ([1986](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0098)), that considered a MLP with hidden layers to enable the NN to learn more complicated features, proposed backpropagation algorithms to adjust the weights and minimize the difference between the actual output and the desired output, and employed nonlinear activation functions such as the sigmoid function that could enable gradually changing the weights of the NN and introduce nonlinearity. The universal approximation theorem in Cybenko ([1989](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0020)) proved that a feedforward ANN with a single hidden layer (a three‐layer network considering the input and output layers) and non‐constant, bounded, and monotone‐increasing continuous activation function can approximate any nonlinear function with any desired error. [Figure 17.18](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0018) shows a summary of the main activation functions.

In the past, and generally speaking, FNNs were considered static and memoryless in the sense that the response of an input was independent of the previous network state, while RNNs were considered dynamic systems because of the feedback connections. Nowadays, and given the highest complexity of RNNs versus FNNs, RNN architectures are frequently unrolled in a way that they are redrawn and reformulated similarly to a FNN to simplify the processing complexity. In addition, the need for modeling nonlinear system dynamics considering memory effects has grown over the last decades in multiple applications. For instance, the ever‐increasing signal bandwidth at each wireless communication standard generation makes the modeling of PA memory effects, which are more evident when this component is excited by higher bandwidth signals, a relevant topic for enhancing the performance of the physical layer.

In order to solve time‐series prediction and thus enable dynamic nonlinear system identification, focused time‐delayed NNs (FTDNNs), which include tapped delay lines to generate delayed samples of the input variables, have been proposed. The FTDNN can be seen as combining a linear time invariant (LTI) system such as a finite impulse response (FIR) filter, which enables performing dynamic mappings depending on past input values, and a nonlinear memoryless MLP network that can be trained using static backpropagation algorithms. The memory depth of the system being modeled will be reflected in the length of the taps imposed by the required bandwidth accuracy. A FTDNN structure could be seen as a special case of the Wiener model (i.e. a linear time‐invariant system followed by a memoryless nonlinear system). [Figure 17.19](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0019) shows a four‐layer architecture (with two hidden layers) of a fully connected FTDNN whose input‐output relation is defined in Eq. ([17.42](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0042)) according to the notation of the aforementioned SLP concept.

![Figure 17.18 Activation or transfer functions.](images/c17f018.jpg)

[Figure 17.18](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0018) Activation or transfer functions.

In this example, the input layer contains ![images](images/c17-i0197.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> neurons (including the input signal and all the delayed versions, ![images](images/c17-i0198.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>z</mi><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is the unit delay operator), the first hidden layer has ![images](images/c17-i0199.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> neurons, the second hidden layer has ![images](images/c17-i0200.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> neurons, and there is a final output layer with a single neuron. For the sake of simplicity, the output layer in this example is considered a unitary weighted summation (![images](images/c17-i0201.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>w</mi><mrow><mn>1</mn><mi>l</mi></mrow><mn>3</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> for ![images](images/c17-i0202.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>l</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>) of the signals coming from the previous layer, just followed by a pure linear activation function. The total number of coefficients to be tuned in backpropagation would be the sum of the number of weights (![images](images/c17-i0203.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>) and biases (![images](images/c17-i0204.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>). For example, if we considered four memory taps (5 neurons in the input layer), 8 neurons in the first hidden layer, and 6 neurons in the second hidden layer, we would need to tune 88 weights and 14 biases totaling 102 parameters:

Generally speaking, and when comparing the ANN approach with the polynomial one (discussed in previous sections), the polynomials have inherent local approximating properties in contrast to the global approximation capability of ANNs, when modeling strongly nonlinear systems. In addition, when compared to classical models, the ANN may adapt better to extrapolating beyond the zone exploited for parameter extraction (Gilabert ([2007](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0029))).

![Figure 17.19 Four‐layer focused time‐delayed neural network architecture.](images/c17f019.jpg)

[Figure 17.19](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0019) Four‐layer focused time‐delayed neural network architecture.

Based on this introduction and illustration, we now present more details of the use of ANN in digital front‐end with the emphasis on addressing undesired effects such as PA nonlinearity, in‐phase/quadrature (I/Q) modulator imbalances, DC offsets, and multi‐antenna cross‐couplings that have a negative impact on today's complex 5G communication systems. There is not a universal recipe to set up the best ANN architecture, learning algorithm, or activation function given a specific problem. Trial and error is frequently employed, but some physical knowledge of the phenomena to be modeled can be important when optimizing the resources and aiming to reach the best modeling performance. However, some design considerations (architectures, activation functions, backpropagation detail and learning algorithms, metrics, etc.) found in literature and being experimentally validated and benchmarked will be given to assist in the modeling and compensation of the previously mentioned RF transceiver impairments.

 

### 17.4.2 Design Considerations for Digital Linearization and RF Impairment Correction

ANNs are considered an alternative to complex Volterra‐based nonlinear models that require an unaffordable complexity to characterize the RF impairments in highly demanding transceiver architectures such as massive MIMO. The FTDNN architecture, combined with a back propagation learning algorithm (BPLA), over the last 10 years has been one of the most attractive approaches for dynamic nonlinear modeling. Another frequent type of FNN being widely exploited to predict the behavior of the PA is the radial basis function NN (RBFNN), which can progressively keep increasing the number of neurons in the hidden layer until the desired performance is met, as shown in Isaksson et al. ([2005](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0045)). RNNs, which have been preferred to model dynamic nonlinear systems with feedback paths or frequency‐dependent phenomena, allow for better characterization of the interaction between input and output samples and the cross terms. However, these networks have traditionally employed lengthy training algorithms, making real‐time implementation difficult. While MLPNN variations are predominantly employed for PA modeling and DPD, RNNs are found in works dealing with I/Q modulator gain and phase imbalances or to apply CFR. When all the impairments, including strong PA nonlinearities, have to be solved with a common architecture, the RNN may be hardly implementable or outperformed by the MLPNN‐based approaches, as will be shown in the next subsections. The better the dynamic nonlinearities are modeled, the better the linearization performance will be.

 

#### 17.4.2.1 ANN Architectures for Single‐Antenna DPD

In order to extract amplitude and phase information from modulated complex waveforms, ANNs need to consider operating with either complex‐valued (CV) input signals, weights and activation outputs, or real‐valued (RV) double‐inputs double‐outputs (and real weights and activation outputs), i.e. in the form of multiple I and Q components. Complex‐valued operation leads to heavy calculations and a longer training phase. In addition, the architectures that employ independent NNs to separately model the AM/AM and AM/PM behavior may fail in the synchronous convergence of the two NNs and thus tend to overtrain the fastest‐converging one (Rawat et al. ([2010](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0095))). RV FTDNNs, which combine I/Q RV processing with input time‐delay lines (TDLs) to handle memory effects (but not output‐to‐input TDLs, as would happen in a RNN), can offer superior performance and easy baseband implementation when used for inverse modeling of PAs with strong nonlinearities and memory effects. As seen in Rawat et al. ([2010](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0095)), these ANNs utilize a similar structure to that shown in [Figure 17.19](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0019); but instead of a single‐input, single output NN, now we have double‐input, double‐output (I/Q inputs and outputs). In this case, the weighted summation at each first hidden layer neuron will include a sequence of input samples both for the I and Q components (this information will propagate throughout the NN according to the activation functions), and the output layer may have a non‐unitary weighted summation at each I and Q output accounting for the contributions of each neuron output in the second hidden layer. This ANN has therefore a maximum of ![images](images/c17-i0205.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>M</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>L</mi><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> weights and ![images](images/c17-i0206.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> biases (considering the notation in [Figure 17.19](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0019)) that will be adjusted using feedforward backpropagation.

As previously introduced, RNNs can be modified or unrolled in most cases in such a way as to emulate a FNN scheme where consolidated BPLAs are applied. A relevant design consideration is that choosing an ANN architecture without taking into account which sources generate the nonlinearities may impact negatively on performance or be highly resource inefficient. For instance, when modeling PA nonlinear dynamic effects, it can be worth paying attention to the PA physical model to reflect output‐to‐input interactions or account for memory effects given a signal bandwidth. One example of the previous design considerations is found in Mkadem and Boumaiza ([2011](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0075)) and is displayed in [Figure 17.20](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0020).

In this example, nonlinear activation functions are used to model static PA nonlinearities (typically, the stronger the nonlinearities, the more neurons are required) while linear activation functions will be used to model the feedback mechanism FIR filter (with memory depth ![images](images/c17-i0207.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi></mrow></math>). The input FIR (input signal) models the memory effects that result from combining a wideband modulated signal with a non‐flat response input matching network (![images](images/c17-i0208.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> is the memory depth of the input signal). For FNN deployment, the connection between the initial input samples and the neurons is 1 (at the first hidden layer). To train this NN, only measured past data from the PA output will be used at the input (not during validation, since the delayed output data will be fed back once the necessary outputs are produced).

![Figure 17.20 Power amplifier physics‐aware complex‐valued recurrent neural network, reformulated as a modified real‐valued focused time‐delayed neural network.](images/c17f020.jpg)

[Figure 17.20](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0020) Power amplifier physics‐aware complex‐valued recurrent neural network, reformulated as a modified real‐valued focused time‐delayed neural network.

Moreover, some recent works have shown the benefits brought by adding envelope‐dependent terms as inputs to the ANN. Jueschke and Fischer ([2017](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0055)) propose a two‐hidden layer RV FTDNN that includes one additional input based on the calculation of the modulus of the I and Q samples. This input is fed not only to the first hidden layer but also directly to the output layer, all of which helps to improve numerical stability and training convergence. Wang et al. ([2019](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0119)) inject additional envelope‐dependent term combinations (i.e. between the modulus raised to the power of two, three, four, and five) as inputs of a single‐hidden‐layer NN (no direct connection between envelope‐related inputs and the output layer is enabled in this case). This obtains better modeling performance since these new terms are able to generate some desired even‐order intermodulation terms throughout the NN that cannot be obtained if only I and Q components are used as inputs.

 

#### 17.4.2.2 ANN Architectures for MIMO DPD, I/Q Imbalances, and DC Offset Correction

Over the last 10 years, the need for wireless communication technologies fulfilling user mobile broadband capacity requirements has been coupled with the need to reduce costs and ![images](images/c17-i0209.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mtext>CO</mtext><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> emissions. This has boosted the research, development, and industrial release of MIMO transceiver solutions with a high number of elements both for macro base stations and for the next generation of small cells to be used in ultra‐dense deployments. The high number of RF transceiver chains in these solutions makes integration, power consumption, and cost‐effectiveness prominent design constraints that may play against employing the best‐performing solution. High‐channel density radio frequency integrated circuits (RFICs) integrating the data‐conversion stages, I/Q modulators and demodulators, and LO signal synthesis and distribution are employed together with typically moderate‐cost PAs from high‐volume markets to benefit from economies of scale. [Figure 17.21](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0021)a shows a generic architecture of a base station highly integrated MIMO transmitter (the Rx blocks have been omitted). At the Tx side, crosstalk may occur in the multi‐channel I/Q modulation stages sharing a common LO in the same integrated circuit or at the PA output (for instance, due to the antenna cross‐couplings). These effects invalidate the classical single‐antenna DPD approaches since they cannot fulfill the desired performance under strong or medium‐level couplings (i.e. typically −15—30 dB). The use of direct‐conversion Tx/Rx chains and thus I/Q modulators/demodulators is clearly advantageous with respect to the use of superheterodyne architectures in terms of integration and cost; however, this architecture suffers from I/Q gain and phase imbalances due to mismatches between the I and Q branches, DC offsets, and in‐band LO couplings. The image rejection ratio (IRR) characterizes the I/Q imbalances through measuring the ratio between the image signal generated by the imperfections and the signal of interest at the output of the modulator (i.e. typical values are −20—40 dB). The joint effect of all these impairments is depicted in [Figure 17.21](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0021)b.

![Figure 17.21 (a) Multi‐antenna transmitter architecture; (b) spectra of the complex baseband signal and the radio frequency signal at power amplifier output (with RF impairments).](images/c17f021.jpg)

[Figure 17.21](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0021) (a) Multi‐antenna transmitter architecture; (b) spectra of the complex baseband signal and the radio frequency signal at power amplifier output (with RF impairments).

Many of the existing MIMO DPD models that account for cross‐couplings and that consider nonlinear crosstalk at the PA input and linear crosstalk at the PA output are mainly based on the crossover memory polynomial model (COMPM) found in Bassam et al. ([2009](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0004)). The parallel Hammerstein (PH) model in Amin et al. ([2014](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0001)) shows better linearization performance and includes terms compensating for nonlinear crosstalk at the PA output, but requires more coefficients. These models are insufficient to mitigate the I/Q modulator imbalances and DC offsets. By adding a complex conjugate function and a DC term, the PH model will be able to handle not only crosstalk but the modulator imbalances, as found in Khan et al. ([2017](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0059)). However, this model requires extraction of a high number of coefficients and inverse modeling for each Tx path, which is unaffordable for systems employing a large number of antennas. Hausmair et al. ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0039)) present a model to deal with the PA nonlinearities, any crosstalk between Tx channels, and the PA mismatch effects due to antenna couplings (i.e. seeking to enable circulator‐less MIMO transceiver operation). The authors in the previous reference propose employing dual‐input DPD blocks at each PA branch and a single common linear crosstalk and mismatch model that feeds them all to reduce the complexity of previous developments. Regarding the use of ANNs in MIMO DPD applications, the authors in Zayani et al. ([2010](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0127)) presented one of the first works aiming at using a MLP‐based NN to compensate both for cross‐couplings and PA nonlinearities for a STBC OFDM MIMO system. However, the reach of this work is limited since only system‐level simulation is conducted with a Saleh PA model. In Jaraut et al. ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0049)), the authors propose and experimentally validate an ANN for inverse nonlinear modeling of a number of transmitters with a single DPD block and thus overcome some previous implementation burdens. This modified RV FTDNN architecture, shown in [Figure 17.22](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0022), is able to deal with all the mentioned RF impairments more efficiently than some previous works. In this ANN, we have four fully connected layers with ![images](images/c17-i0210.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> inputs and ![images](images/c17-i0211.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>R</mi></mrow></math> outputs, where
