#### 17.4.3.4 Clipping and Filtering

As described before, these techniques feature a trade‐off between PAPR reduction and the amount of in‐band and out‐of‐band distortion induced by the clipping process. Since the filtering process to suppress out‐of‐band distortion may provoke some spectral regrowth, this technique requires a certain amount of iterations. The iterative clipping and filtering (ICF) algorithm in Armstrong ([2002](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0002)) is a well‐known approach but requires a large number of repetitions involving complex FFT operations. The simplified CF (SCF) in Wang and Tellambura ([2005](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0121)) can obtain the same PAPR reduction as ICF in a single iteration but also requires several FFT/IFFT complex operations (increasing with the number of subcarriers being employed). In this context, the authors in Sohn and Kim ([2015](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0105)) propose a RV MLPNN mapper that emulates the SCF featuring similar CM performance but at much lower complexity, as can be seen in [Figure 17.25](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0025). Two independent NN modules do the processing of the ![images](images/c17-i0287.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow></math> and the ![images](images/c17-i0288.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> signal components separately. These modules have again two neurons in the hidden layer and a triangular activation function, and use the backpropagation LM learning algorithm to tune the parameters, minimizing the error between the ANN output and the expected signals. The ![images](images/c17-i0289.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c17-i0290.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> components of the original OFDM signals are used as training data, while the ![images](images/c17-i0291.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>I</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c17-i0292.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> components of the time‐domain SCF signal are used as the desired output data. The computational complexity analysis shows that the proposed ANN remarkably reduces the computational complexity in terms of complex operations by one order of magnitude when compared with SLM, one‐seventh when compared with ICF, and one‐third when compared with SCF. In terms of the CM, the ANN performs in simulation similarly to the ICF and the SCF schemes and about 0.8 dB better than the SLM at ![images](images/c17-i0293.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mi>r</mi><mi>o</mi><mi>b</mi><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><mi>C</mi><mi>M</mi><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>C</mi><msub><mi>M</mi><mrow><mi>t</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></msup></mrow></math>. Regarding the BER versus ![images](images/c17-i0294.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>E</mi><mi>b</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></mrow></math> characteristic (considering AWGN channel), and as expected, all the clipping and filtering techniques do worse than the SLM. Considering QPSK subcarrier modulation (considering 256 subcarriers), the ICF, SCF, and proposed ANN perform similarly. For 16‐QAM, the proposed ANN has a performance loss of about 1.5 dB when compared with SCF, about 2.4 dB when compared with ICF, and 2.8 dB when compared with SLM. Increasing the constellation size makes it harder for the ANN to emulate the SCF mapping, which results in partial frequency‐domain information loss.

All of this shows that much more investigation is needed on the use of ANNs in digital front‐end, as will be further discussed in [Section 17.6](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0032).

 

## 17.5 Support Vector Regression Approaches

Support vector machine (SVM) is a well‐established supervised learning algorithm in the field of ML that can be used either for classification or for predicting and modeling. In the later case, when the SVM is used for regression, it is known as support vector regressor (SVR). Both use very similar algorithms but predict different types of variables. SVR has been successfully extended to nonlinear regression problems (Vapnik ([1998](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0117))) by converting it into a linear regression one. In particular, SVR is oriented at optimizing the generalization bounds of a nonlinear function through a linear method in a high‐dimensional feature space, by emphasizing the data on the margins of the search space, known as *support vectors* (Chen and Brazil ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0016))). In order to reduce the computational cost, SVR uses kernel functions to perform a nonlinear mapping to a high‐dimensional feature space. In comparison with ANN techniques, the SVR method can obtain the optimal model in a short time with performance quality similar to that obtained with ANN. Due to these good properties, SVR has been employed in different applications in the DFE: for example, for the modeling and design of filters, antennas, and PAs, and even for nonlinear equalization and DPD linearization.

![Figure 17.26 The soft margin loss setting for a linear support vector regressor (Smola and Schölkopf (2004)).](images/c17f026.jpg)

[Figure 17.26](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0026) The soft margin loss setting for a linear support vector regressor (Smola and Schölkopf ([2004](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0103))).

The basic idea of support vector regression theory is presented in Smola and Schölkopf ([2004](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0103)). Given training data with ![images](images/c17-i0295.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> dimensional variables and 1 target‐variable ![images](images/c17-i0296.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>n</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c17-i0297.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi>&#8476;</mi><mi>m</mi></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c17-i0298.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi>&#8476;</mi></mrow></math>, the objective is to find a function ![images](images/c17-i0299.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> that returns the best fit, taking into account certain margin ![images](images/c17-i0300.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>, and that at the same time is as flat as possible. As shown in [Figure 17.26](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0026), certain deviation (at most ![images](images/c17-i0301.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math>) from the actually obtained targets ![images](images/c17-i0302.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> is tolerated for all the training data.

Assuming that the relationship between ![images](images/c17-i0303.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c17-i0304.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi></mrow></math> is approximately linear, ![images](images/c17-i0305.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> takes the form

[(17.47)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0047)![equation](images/c17-math-0047.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c17-i0306.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow></math> is the vector of coefficients and ![images](images/c17-i0307.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is an intercept or bias term. In the case of Eq. ([17.47](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0047)), flatness means that the solution has to consider a small ![images](images/c17-i0308.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow></math>, i.e. a regularization condition (as in Ridge regression) consisting of minimizing the Euclidean norm ![images](images/c17-i0309.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8214;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><msup><mo>&#8214;</mo><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> (also know as ![images](images/c17-i0310.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#8467;</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>‐norm ![images](images/c17-i0311.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8214;</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><msubsup><mrow><mo>&#8214;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math>). Formally, we can write this problem as a convex optimization problem such as

[(17.48)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0048)![equation](images/c17-math-0048.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd> <munder> <mtext>minimize</mtext> <mrow/> </munder> </mtd> <mtd> <mspace width="1em"/> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <msup> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mtext>subject to:</mtext> </mtd> <mtd> <mspace width="1em"/> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>&#949;</mi> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd> <mspace width="1em"/> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

In Eq. ([17.48](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0048)), it is assumed that the convex optimization problem is feasible. When this is not the case, one can introduce slack variables ![images](images/c17-i0312.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c17-i0313.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#958;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> (i.e. that allow for some errors) to cope with otherwise infeasible constraints of the optimization problem in Eq. ([17.48](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0048)). This leads to the formulation stated in Vapnik ([1995](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0116)),

(17.49)![equation](images/c17-math-0049.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd> <munder> <mtext>minimize</mtext> <mrow/> </munder> </mtd> <mtd> <mspace width="1em"/> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <msup> <mo>&#8741;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mi>C</mi> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mtext>subject to:</mtext> </mtd> <mtd> <mspace width="1em"/> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd> <mspace width="1em"/> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd> <mspace width="1em"/> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

where C is a regularization term that determines the trade‐off between the flatness of the model and the constraint violation error. As shown in [Figure 17.26](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0026), only the points outside the shaded region contribute to the cost, as the deviations are penalized in a linear fashion (Smola and Schölkopf ([2004](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0103))).

This constrained optimization problem is more easily solved in its dual formulation, since it allows extending SVR to nonlinear functions. Therefore, using the method of Lagrange multipliers (Fletcher ([1987](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0025))), follows

[(17.50)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0050)![equation](images/c17-math-0050.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>L</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mo>&#8214;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <msup> <mo>&#8214;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mi>C</mi> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <msubsup> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#949;</mi> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c17-i0314.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> is the Lagrangian and ![images](images/c17-i0315.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#951;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c17-i0316.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#951;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c17-i0317.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c17-i0318.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> are Lagrange multipliers. The partial derivatives of ![images](images/c17-i0319.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> with respect to the primal variables (![images](images/c17-i0320.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#958;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>) have to vanish for optimality,

[(17.51)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0051)![equation](images/c17-math-0051.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> </mtd> <mtd> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>b</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msub> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mi>C</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <mi>L</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8706;</mi> <msubsup> <mi>&#958;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>=</mo> <mi>C</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#951;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

Substituting Eq. ([17.51](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0051)) into Eq. ([17.50](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0050)) yields the dual optimization problem

(17.52)![equation](images/c17-math-0052.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd> <munder> <mtext>maximize</mtext> <mrow/> </munder> <mspace width="1em"/> </mtd> <mtd> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mn>2</mn> </mfrac> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>j</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>j</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#60;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>j</mi> </msub> <mo>&#62;</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#949;</mi> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mtext>subject to:</mtext> <mspace width="1em"/> </mtd> <mtd> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd/> <mtd> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mn>0</mn> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msubsup> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>C</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </math> 

From Eq. ([17.51](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0051)), ![images](images/c17-i0321.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow></math> can be defined as ![images](images/c17-i0322.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>n</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#945;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and thus the SVR fitting equation can be described as

[(17.53)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0053)![equation](images/c17-math-0053.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>&#945;</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#60;</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#62;</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

This is the so‐called support vector expansion, where ![images](images/c17-i0323.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow></math> can be described as a linear combination of the training patterns ![images](images/c17-i0324.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. As explained in Smola and Schölkopf ([2004](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0103)), note that the complexity of a function's representation by support is independent of the dimensionality of the input space and depends only on the number of support vectors. In addition, the complete algorithm can be described in terms of dot products between the data and, even for evaluating ![images](images/c17-i0325.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, it is not necessary to explicitly compute ![images](images/c17-i0326.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow></math>.

For applications such as PA modeling, nonlinear equalization, and DPD linearization, the next step is to make the SV algorithm nonlinear. For a nonlinear regression problem, SVR converts it into a linear regression one. At first, we convert training sets to a high‐dimension feature space by utilizing a nonlinear function ![images](images/c17-i0327.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and then get the linear regression function in this space:

(17.54)![equation](images/c17-math-0054.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Instead of computing a mapping function, ![images](images/c17-i0328.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, explicitly, the inner product in the feature space can be expressed by a kernel function, ![images](images/c17-i0329.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>K</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, which has to satisfy the Mercer theorem (Mercer ([1909](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0073))). Thus, the support vector expansion in Eq. ([17.53](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0053)) can be written as

[(17.55)](#c17.xhtml#c17-R_disp-0055)![equation](images/c17-math-0055.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">T</mi> </msup> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#934;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>n</mi> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mi>&#945;</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>i</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mi>K</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>x</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Some examples of kernel functions (Smola and Schölkopf ([2004](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0103)), Cai et al. ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0010))) are:

*   Homogeneous polynomial kernels (17.56)![equation](images/c17-math-0056.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>K</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mo>&#60;</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <msup> <mo>&#62;</mo> <mi>p</mi> </msup> </mrow> </math> 
*   Inhomogeneous polynomial kernels (17.57)![equation](images/c17-math-0057.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>K</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mo>&#60;</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>&#62;</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </msup> </mrow> </math> 
*   Radial basis function (RBF) kernel (17.58)![equation](images/c17-math-0058.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>K</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <mo>&#8214;</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <msup> <mo>&#8214;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <msup> <mi>&#963;</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </math> 
*   Hyperbolic tangent (or sigmoidal) kernel (17.59)![equation](images/c17-math-0059.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>K</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mi>a</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mi>h</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#947;</mi> <mo>&#60;</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#8242;</mo> </msup> <mo>&#62;</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </math> 

As discussed in [Section 17.2](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0002), for PA behavioral modeling and DPD linearization we use input‐output baseband signals, i.e. datasets of complex data (![images](images/c17-i0330.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></mrow></math>). However, the nonlinear function in Eq. ([17.55](#c17.xhtml#c17-disp-0055)) is defined as a real‐valued function of one real variable. Thus, in order to use SVR for PA modeling and linearization, both the input and the output values are separated into real part and imaginary part, ![images](images/c17-i0331.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mi>R</mi><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>j</mi><mi>I</mi><mi>m</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>, as in Cai et al. ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0010)); or magnitude and phase components, ![images](images/c17-i0332.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><mi>&#8736;</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow></math>, as in Chen et al. ([2005](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0014)). For example, [Figure 17.27](#c17.xhtml#c17-fig-0027) shows the block diagram of a PA behavioral model that includes two different SVR machines giving the real and imaginary parts of the output signal as distinct outputs. The real part and the imaginary part of the input signal are separated and taken as the inputs of the two SVR machines. In Cai et al. ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0010)), the authors provide a comparison of the modeling capabilities among different PA behavioral models, including their proposed SVR solution. In particular, they compared the modeling performance in terms of NMSE between the actual PA output and the modeled one, number of parameters used by the model, and simulation time. The PA behavioral models under comparison were: generalized memory polynomial (GMP) model (D.R. Morgan, Z. Ma et al. ([2006](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0023))), decomposed vector rotation (DVR) model (Cao and Zhu ([2017](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0011))), a two‐layer real‐valued time‐delay NN (RVTDNN) model (Liu et al. ([2004](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0066))), a RBF NN model (Isaksson et al.) and the SVR model proposed by the authors. In terms of NMSE (or modeling accuracy), the SVR model outperformed the models based on analytic functions and ANNs, but at the price of using more coefficients and simulation time. The ANN prediction accuracy could have been improved through careful modification of the optimization algorithm and NN complexity. This process, however, would be time‐consuming.

![Figure 17.27 Block diagram of a power amplifier behavioral model based on time‐delay support vector regression (Cai et al. (2018)).](images/c17f027.jpg)

[Figure 17.27](#c17.xhtml#R_c17-fig-0027) Block diagram of a power amplifier behavioral model based on time‐delay support vector regression (Cai et al. ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0010))).

SVRs have been used not only for PA behavioral modeling, but also (or mainly) for circuit‐level modeling and PA design. For example, in Chen and Brazil ([2018](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0016)), the authors use SVR to design an optimization‐oriented method to design a broadband Doherty power amplifier (DPA); in Chen and Brazil ([2017](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0015)), a method to classify load‐pull contours for the design of a broadband high‐efficiency; and in Chen et al. ([2015](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0017)), to design an automatic optimization method to control the harmonic impedances of continuous Class‐F PAs. In addition, in Guo et al. ([2007](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0035)), a SVR method is presented for electrothermal modeling of power FETs; and in Maoliu and Xiaojie ([2008](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0071)), SVRs are used to obtain large signal behavior models for RF PAs. In Zhou and Huang ([2013](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0128)), instead of modeling PAs, the authors present an intelligent alignment method for an automatic tuning device of microwave filters based on SVR that is particularly suited to computer‐aided tuning devices or an automatic tuning robot of volume‐producing filters. Similarly, in Koziel and Bandler ([2008](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0063)), the authors propose an SVR method for microwave device modeling. Another field of application for SVR is nonlinear equalization (Nguyen et al. ([2016](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0081)), Mallouki et al. ([2016](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0070))). For example, in Sebald and Bucklew ([2000](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0101)), SVRs are reported to perform as well as conventional decision feedback equalizers, with the advantage that a smaller number of parameters for the model can be identified in a manner that does not require the extent of prior information or heuristic assumptions being required by some previous techniques. Regarding DPD linearization, some works have been published (e.g. Eda et al. ([2001](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0024)) and Chen et al. ([2005](#c17.xhtml#c17-bib-0014))) providing simulation results while lacking the detailed performance comparison of their solution with that achieved by ANNs. In the field of DPD linearization, ANN is the most used ML approach reported in literature, as discussed in [Section 17.4](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0018).

In summary, for the aforementioned fields of device design or modeling, SVR methods generally require fewer samples in statistical learning and are free of local minima in optimization in comparison with ANN‐based methods.

 

## 17.6 Further Discussion and Conclusions

In this chapter, we have discussed some ML algorithms and strategies to be applied in the DFE. These techniques are mainly aimed at coping with the unwanted nonlinear distortion effects that appear when dealing with current high PAPR and wide‐bandwidth communications signals, while targeting high power‐efficient operation to save energy consumption.

The principles of CFR techniques and DPD for nonlinear distortion mitigation were discussed in [Section 17.2](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0002). In order to deal with current highly efficient power amplifier architectures, MIMO, or concurrent multi‐band systems, the number of parameters required for DPD or PA behavioral modeling based on parametric approaches grows exponentially, which increases the computational complexity and may provoke overfitting and uncertainty in estimation. Feature‐selection and feature‐extraction dimensionality‐reduction techniques oriented at reducing the number of required parameters and guaranteeing a well‐conditioned extraction were discussed and particularized for DPD linearization in [Section 17.3](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0011).

As an alternative to polynomial‐based models, in [Sections 17.4](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0018) and [17.5](#c17.xhtml#c17-sec-0031), we presented some design guidelines for ANNs and SVR approaches to model and compensate for the nonlinear distortion introduced by the PA or other unwanted distortion effects such as I/Q imbalances and DC offset. In addition, CFR strategies based on ANNs were also discussed, pointing out their advantages in terms of performance and computational complexity reduction.

Some pros and cons that need to be taken into account in order to decide whether to use the solutions based on ANNs or SVRs are discussed in the following. While ANN‐based models permit a compact representation of a multidimensional function, they suffer from two main weaknesses: (i) ANNs often converge on local minima rather than global minima, and (ii) they can suffer from the overfitting problem due to the traditional empirical risk‐minimization principle employed by ANNs. SVR techniques instead use the structural risk‐minimization principle that avoids the model becoming too strongly tailored to the particularities of the training set, thus preventing it from overfitting. Additionally, the solution to SVR is global and unique. Regarding the dimensions, ANNs are parametric models whose size is fixed and depends on their specific architecture, while SVRs (based on kernels) consist of a set of support vectors, selected from the training set, with a weight for each. In the worst case, the number of support vectors is exactly the number of training samples, and in general its model size scales linearly. Thus, if the number of training samples is high, so is the computational complexity of the SVR. Finally, while ANNs may have any number of outputs, SVRs have only one. The most direct way to create a MIMO system with SVR is to create multiple support vector machines and train each of them one by one.

Under the current practical circumstances, ANNs have been successfully employed in several applications in the DFE for their capability to approximate any continuous function. ANNs have been reported in the literature to be used for modeling at the transistor, circuit, and system level. The SVR technique has been successfully applied to circuit modeling for characterizing and designing antennas, filters, and power amplifiers. At the system level, however, solutions based on SVR methods to model or linearize PAs through DPD are not as extended as those based on ANNs. It is strongly believed that ANN‐ or SVR‐based solutions will play a very important role in future DFE implementation and deployment, including intelligent vector processors and functional IP blocks.

# 18  
Neural Networks for Full‐Duplex Radios: Self‐Interference Cancellation

*Alexios Balatsoukas‐Stimming*

*Department of Electrical Engineering, Eindhoven University of Technology, Eindhoven, The Netherlands*

 

Bi‐directional wireless communications are usually achieved by separating the uplink and downlink signals using either time‐division duplexing (TDD) or frequency‐division duplexing (FDD). In‐band full‐duplex (FD) is a promising method to increase the spectral efficiency of current communications systems by transmitting and receiving data simultaneously in the same frequency band Jain et al. ([2011](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0011)), Duarte et al. ([2012](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007)), Bharadia et al. ([2013](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0006)). A fundamental challenge in FD communications is that the transmitter of a node induces a self‐interference (SI) signal at the receiver of the same node. This SI signal is several orders of magnitude stronger than the signal that the node is trying to receive. Thus, in order for an FD node to operate correctly, the SI signal needs to be canceled, ideally to the level of the receiver noise floor.

A combination of SI cancellation in both the radio frequency (RF) domain and the digital domain is usually required in order to cancel the SI signal to the level of the receiver noise floor. RF cancellation can be achieved either through physical isolation between the transmitter and the receiver (*passive RF cancellation*) or through the injection of a cancellation signal (*active RF cancellation*), and it is necessary in order to avoid saturating the analog front‐end of the receiver. Passive RF cancellation can be obtained through several passive devices and techniques, such as circulators, directional antennas, beamforming, polarization, or shielding. Active RF cancellation is commonly implemented by coupling into the transmitted RF signal; adding an appropriate time delay, phase rotation, and attenuation; and adding the resulting SI cancellation signal to the received SI signal Jain et al. ([2011](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0011)), Bharadia et al. ([2013](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0006)). Alternatively, a second transmitter chain can be used to generate the SI cancellation signal Duarte et al. ([2012](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0007)).

Perfect RF cancellation is challenging and costly to achieve, meaning that a residual SI signal is usually still present at the receiver after the RF cancellation stage. In principle, this residual SI signal can be easily canceled in the digital domain, since it is caused by a known transmitted baseband signal. Unfortunately, in practice this is not the case, as several transceiver nonlinearities distort the SI signal. Some examples of nonlinearities include baseband nonlinearities (e.g. digital‐to‐analog converter \[DAC\] and analog‐to‐digital converter \[ADC\]) Balatsoukas‐Stimming et al. ([2015](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0004)), in‐phase/quadrature (I/Q) imbalance Balatsoukas‐Stimming et al. ([2015](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0004)), Korpi et al. ([2014](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0013)), phase‐noise Sahai et al. ([2013](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0020)), Syrjala et al. ([2014](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0021)), and power amplifier (PA) nonlinearities Balatsoukas‐Stimming et al. ([2015](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0004)), Korpi et al. ([2014](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0013)), Anttila et al. ([2014](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0001)), Korpi et al. ([2017](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0014)). Complicated nonlinear cancellation methods, which are usually based on polynomial expansions, are required in order to fully cancel the SI to the level of the receiver noise floor. A commonly used nonlinear SI cancellation method employs a parallel Hammerstein model that incorporates both PA nonlinearities and IQ imbalance Korpi et al. ([2017](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0014)).

Polynomial models have been shown to work well in practice, but they generally have a high implementation complexity as the number of estimated parameters grows rapidly with the maximum considered nonlinearity order and because a large number of nonlinear basis functions have to be computed. Principal component analysis (PCA) is an effective complexity‐reduction technique that can identify the most significant nonlinearity terms in a parallel Hammerstein model Korpi et al. ([2017](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0014)). However, with PCA‐based methods, the transmitted digital baseband samples need to be multiplied with a transformation matrix to generate the SI cancellation signal, thus introducing additional complexity. Moreover, whenever the SI channel changes significantly, the high‐complexity PCA operation needs to be re‐run. Neural networks (NNs) have been widely used in the literature to model and compensate for nonlinear effects in communications systems (see e.g. Ibnkahla ([2000](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0010)), Naskas and Papananos ([2004](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0017)), Rawat et al. ([2010](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0018)), Mkadem and Boumaiza ([2011](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0016)) and references therein) and, recently, they have also been used for SI cancellation in FD radios Balatsoukas‐Stimming ([2018](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0002)), Guo et al. ([2018](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0008)). Due to their powerful nonlinear modeling capabilities, NN‐based solutions for digital SI cancellation have been shown to provide a good trade‐off between computational complexity and SI cancellation performance in FD radios. This chapter covers technical aspects of digital SI cancellation in FD radios in a self‐contained manner, using both conventional polynomial models and NNs.

The rest of this chapter is organized as follows. [Section 18.1](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0002) describes how the nonlinear effects of various transceiver components can be modeled and derives a comprehensive nonlinear SI model. [Section 18.2](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0004) describes various linear and nonlinear cancellation methods, with emphasis on a NN canceler. In this section, the computational complexity of each approach is also analyzed and compared. For further illustration and comparison, [Section 18.3](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0012) provides experimental results using measured samples from a hardware testbed, which demonstrate that a simple NN‐based nonlinear canceler can match the performance of a state‐of‐the‐art polynomial model for nonlinear cancellation with a significantly lower computational complexity. Finally, [Section 18.4](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0016) concludes this chapter by discussing a number of interesting future research directions.

 

## 18.1 Nonlinear Self‐Interference Models

Each active component in the transceiver chain shown in [Figure 18.1](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0001) is essentially a dynamic nonlinear system, which can be modeled in a variety of ways. The Volterra series is one of the most accurate models, but it has a very large number of parameters and is thus rarely used in practice. Instead, a simplification of the Volterra series, called a *parallel Hammerstein model*, is often used. In the parallel Hammerstein model, the input‐output relation of a dynamic nonlinear system with input ![images](images/c18-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></mrow></math> and output ![images](images/c18-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></mrow></math> is modeled as:

(18.1)![equation](images/c18-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>P</mi> </munderover> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>L</mi> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>L</mi> <mn>2</mn> </msub> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>h</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi>x</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c18-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math> is the maximum considered nonlinearity order, ![images](images/c18-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c18-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> are the numbers of considered pre‐cursor and post‐cursor memory taps, respectively, and ![images](images/c18-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>h</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></mrow></math> are the model parameters. To simplify the notation, in this section it is assumed that ![images](images/c18-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is already pre‐shifted by ![images](images/c18-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>L</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> samples, so that Eq. ([18.1](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0001)) can be equivalently rewritten using a single parameter ![images](images/c18-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> as:

(18.2)![equation](images/c18-math-0002.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>P</mi> </munderover> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>h</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi>x</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> ![Figure 18.1 Model of a full‐duplex transceiver with active radio frequency cancellation and active digital cancellation. A few components have been omitted for simplicity; a more detailed diagram can be found in Korpi et al. (2017).](images/c18f001.jpg)

[Figure 18.1](#c18.xhtml#R_c18-fig-0001) Model of a full‐duplex transceiver with active radio frequency cancellation and active digital cancellation. A few components have been omitted for simplicity; a more detailed diagram can be found in Korpi et al. ([2017](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0014)).

 

### 18.1.1 Nonlinear Self‐Interference Model

Let the complex‐valued digital signal that enters the digital‐to‐analog converter (DAC) in [Figure 18.1](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0001) at time instant ![images](images/c18-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> be denoted by ![images](images/c18-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>. The transmitter uses two distinct DACs for the real and the imaginary parts of ![images](images/c18-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, respectively. As these are distinct components, they generally have different nonlinear characteristics. As such, each DAC has to be modeled separately using a parallel Hammerstein model, and the complex‐valued output of the two DACs is given by:

[(18.3)](#c18.xhtml#c18-R_disp-0003)![equation](images/c18-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mtext>DAC</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>P</mi> <mtext>DAC</mtext> </msup> </mrow> </munderover> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>L</mi> <mtext>DAC</mtext> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>h</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8476;</mi> </mrow> <mtext>DAC</mtext> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi>&#8476;</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mi>j</mi> <msubsup> <mi>h</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8465;</mi> </mrow> <mtext>DAC</mtext> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi>&#8465;</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </msup> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c18-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8476;</mi></mrow><mtext>DAC</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c18-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8465;</mi></mrow><mtext>DAC</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math> are the model parameters for the real and imaginary parts of ![images](images/c18-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, respectively. The IQ mixer introduces IQ imbalance and phase noise, which can be modeled as:

(18.4)![equation](images/c18-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mtext>IQ,TX</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>K</mi> <mn>1</mn> <mtext>TX</mtext> </msubsup> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mtext>DAC</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>K</mi> <mn>2</mn> <mtext>TX</mtext> </msubsup> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mtext>DAC</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </mfenced> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mi>j</mi> <msup> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mtext>TX</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c18-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn><mtext>TX</mtext></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c18-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn><mtext>TX</mtext></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></mrow></math> are parameters, and ![images](images/c18-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#966;</mi><mtext>TX</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is the baseband equivalent of the transmitter phase noise process at discrete time‐instant ![images](images/c18-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. The upconverted signal ![images](images/c18-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>x</mi><mtext>IQ,TX</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is amplified by a power amplifier (PA), which introduces further nonlinearities. The even‐powered nonlinearity terms are filtered out by the transmitter bandpass filter, so the PA nonlinearities can be modeled as:

[(18.5)](#c18.xhtml#c18-R_disp-0005)![equation](images/c18-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mtext>PA</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>p</mi> <mspace width="0.15em"/> <mtext>odd</mtext> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>P</mi> <mtext>PA</mtext> </msup> </mrow> </munderover> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>L</mi> <mtext>PA</mtext> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msubsup> <mi>h</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mtext>PA</mtext> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mtext>IQ,TX</mtext> </msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> <msup> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mtext>IQ,TX</mtext> </msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The output signal of the PA is transmitted over the air and received at the receiving antenna through a linear SI channel, which can be modeled as:

(18.6)![equation](images/c18-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>RX</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>L</mi> <mtext>SI</mtext> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msup> <mi>h</mi> <mtext>SI</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mtext>PA</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Note that the effect of active RF cancellation is captured by the linear SI channel, in the sense that if active RF cancellation is present, the average power of ![images](images/c18-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>h</mi><mtext>SI</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is significantly lower. The received signal is amplified using a low‐noise amplifier (LNA), whose nonlinear effects can be modeled as:

[(18.7)](#c18.xhtml#c18-R_disp-0007)![equation](images/c18-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>LNA</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>p</mi> <mspace width="0.15em"/> <mtext>odd</mtext> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>P</mi> <mtext>LNA</mtext> </msup> </mrow> </munderover> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>L</mi> <mtext>LNA</mtext> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msubsup> <mi>h</mi> <mi>p</mi> <mtext>LNA</mtext> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>RX</mtext> </msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> <msup> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>RX</mtext> </msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

After the LNA, the signal ![images](images/c18-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mtext>LNA</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is downconverted using an I/Q mixer, which introduces I/Q imbalance and phase noise:

(18.8)![equation](images/c18-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>IQ,RX</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>K</mi> <mn>1</mn> <mtext>RX</mtext> </msubsup> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>LNA</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>K</mi> <mn>2</mn> <mtext>RX</mtext> </msubsup> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>LNA</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#42;</mo> </mrow> </msup> </mrow> </mfenced> <msup> <mi>e</mi> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>j</mi> <msup> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mtext>RX</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c18-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn><mtext>RX</mtext></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c18-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn><mtext>RX</mtext></msubsup><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></mrow></math> are parameters, and ![images](images/c18-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#966;</mi><mtext>RX</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is the baseband equivalent of the receiver phase noise process at discrete time‐instant ![images](images/c18-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. Finally, ![images](images/c18-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mtext>IQ,RX</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> passes through a potentially nonlinear analog‐to‐digital converter (ADC), which introduces a nonlinearity of the form:

[(18.9)](#c18.xhtml#c18-R_disp-0009)![equation](images/c18-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>SI</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>P</mi> <mtext>ADC</mtext> </msup> </mrow> </munderover> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>L</mi> <mtext>ADC</mtext> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>h</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8476;</mi> </mrow> <mtext>ADC</mtext> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi>&#8476;</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>IQ,RX</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <mi>j</mi> <msubsup> <mi>h</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>&#8465;</mi> </mrow> <mtext>ADC</mtext> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi>&#8465;</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <msup> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>IQ,RX</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </msup> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c18-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8476;</mi></mrow><mtext>ADC</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c18-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>h</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8465;</mi></mrow><mtext>ADC</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi></mrow></math> are the model parameters for the real and imaginary parts of ![images](images/c18-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>y</mi><mtext>IQ,RX</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, respectively.

In these derivations, the thermal noise and the desired signal received from a remote node were omitted for simplicity. The actual received signal ![images](images/c18-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> at time‐instant ![images](images/c18-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is given by:

(18.10)![equation](images/c18-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi>d</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>SI</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>z</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c18-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is the desired signal, ![images](images/c18-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mtext>SI</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is given in Eq. ([18.9](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0009)), and ![images](images/c18-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>z</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8764;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">C</mi><mi mathvariant="script">N</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><msup><mi>&#963;</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is complex‐valued additive white Gaussian noise.

 

## 18.2 Digital Self‐Interference Cancellation

The goal of digital SI cancellation is to produce an approximation of ![images](images/c18-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mtext>SI</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, denoted by ![images](images/c18-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mtext>SI</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, based on ![images](images/c18-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> as accurately as possible using digital signal processing (DSP) techniques and to subtract ![images](images/c18-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mtext>SI</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> from ![images](images/c18-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> in order to cancel the SI. The achieved SI cancellation over a sample window of length ![images](images/c18-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>, measured in dB, is commonly calculated as:

(18.11)![equation](images/c18-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>C</mi> <mtext>dB</mtext> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>10</mn> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mn>10</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>N</mi> </mfrac> <munderover> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <mfrac> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi>y</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mtext>SI</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The SI cancellation is usually calculated when no desired signal ![images](images/c18-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is present. If all transceiver nonlinearities described in [Section 18.1](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0002) are taken into account, then the overall system model is the composition of the seven functions given in Eqs. ([18.3](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0003))–([18.9](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0009)). Such a model, while potentially very accurate, has a prohibitively large number of parameters to be practically useful. As such, significantly simpler models that attempt to focus on the dominant nonlinearities are used in practice.

 

### 18.2.1 Linear Cancellation

The simplest form of digital cancellation ignores all nonlinear effects described in Eqs. ([18.3](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0003))–([18.5](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0005)) and Eqs. ([18.7](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0007))–([18.9](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0009)) and only considers the effect of the (linear) SI channel of length ![images](images/c18-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>L</mi><mtext>SI</mtext></msup></mrow></math> given in Eq. ([18.6](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0006)). Let ![images](images/c18-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>L</mi><mtext>SI</mtext></msup></mrow></math> for simplicity. Then, the SI cancellation signal ![images](images/c18-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mtext>SI</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is constructed as:

(18.12)![equation](images/c18-math-0012.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mtext>SI</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msup> <mi>&#293;</mi> <mtext>SI</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where the SI channel ![images](images/c18-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#293;</mi><mtext>SI</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> can be estimated on the basis of training samples using e.g. least‐squares (LS) estimation.

 

### 18.2.2 Polynomial Nonlinear Cancellation

Linear cancellation alone is, in most scenarios, not powerful enough to cancel a sufficient portion of the SI signal. As such, polynomial models that consider a subset of the nonlinearities described in Eqs. ([18.3](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0003))–([18.9](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0009)) are often used in order to achieve better SI cancellation. It has been shown that, in most cases, the transmitter IQ imbalance and the PA nonlinearities, given in Eq. ([18.4](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0004)) and Eq. ([18.5](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0005)), respectively, dominate all remaining nonlinearities. This is true in particular when the transmitter and receiver chains use the same local oscillator signal for upconversion, as shown in [Figure 18.1](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0001), so that ![images](images/c18-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#966;</mi><mtext>TX</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>&#966;</mi><mtext>RX</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> and the effect of phase noise becomes negligible. As such, the SI cancellation signal ![images](images/c18-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#375;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> can be constructed as Anttila et al. ([2014](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0001)), Korpi et al. ([2017](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0014)):
