(18.13)![equation](images/c18-math-0013.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mtext>SI</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>p</mi> <mspace width="0.15em"/> <mtext>odd</mtext> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>P</mi> <mtext>PA</mtext> </msup> </mrow> </munderover> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>L</mi> <mtext>PA</mtext> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msup> <mi>L</mi> <mtext>SI</mtext> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>&#293;</mi> <mi>p</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>K</mi> <mn>1</mn> <mtext>TX</mtext> </msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>K</mi> <mn>2</mn> <mtext>TX</mtext> </msubsup> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <msup> <mfenced open="|" close="|" separators=""> <mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>K</mi> <mn>1</mn> <mtext>TX</mtext> </msubsup> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>K</mi> <mn>2</mn> <mtext>TX</mtext> </msubsup> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c18-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#293;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></mrow></math> is the convolution of ![images](images/c18-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#293;</mi></mrow><mi>p</mi><mtext>PA</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c18-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#293;</mi><mtext>SI</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>. Let ![images](images/c18-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>L</mi><mtext>PA</mtext></msup><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>L</mi><mtext>SI</mtext></msup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c18-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>P</mi><mtext>PA</mtext></msup></mrow></math> for simplicity. Then, with some arithmetic manipulations ![images](images/c18-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mtext>SI</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> can be rewritten as  Anttila et al. ([2014](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0001)), Korpi et al. ([2017](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0014)):

(18.14)![equation](images/c18-math-0014.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mtext>SI</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>p</mi> <mspace width="0.15em"/> <mtext>odd</mtext> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> <mi>P</mi> </munderover> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </munderover> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>&#293;</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>q</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi>x</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> <mi>q</mi> </msup> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>q</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c18-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#293;</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></mrow></math> captures the joint effect of ![images](images/c18-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#293;</mi><mi>p</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> and IQ imbalance parameters ![images](images/c18-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>1</mn><mtext>TX</mtext></msubsup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c18-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>K</mi><mn>2</mn><mtext>TX</mtext></msubsup></mrow></math>. The parameters ![images](images/c18-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#293;</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> can be estimated based on training samples using e.g. LS estimation. The *basis functions* of the polynomial model in Eq. ([18.14](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0014)) are defined as:

(18.15)![equation](images/c18-math-0015.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>B</mi> <msub> <mi>F</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>q</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>=</mo> <mi>x</mi> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> <mi>q</mi> </msup> <msup> <mi>x</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <msup> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>q</mi> </mrow> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Using Eq. ([18.15](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0015)), the expression for ![images](images/c18-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mtext>SI</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> in Eq. ([18.14](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0014)) can be rewritten in a more compact form:

(18.16)![equation](images/c18-math-0016.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mtable> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>p</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd> <mi>p</mi> <mspace width="0.15em"/> <mtext>odd</mtext> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> <mi>P</mi> </munderover> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>q</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mi>p</mi> </munderover> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>m</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msub> <mi>&#293;</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>q</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi>B</mi> <msub> <mi>F</mi> <mrow> <mi>p</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>q</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Linear cancellation is actually a special case of the previous model for ![images](images/c18-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c18-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.

 

### 18.2.3 Neural Network Nonlinear Cancellation

NN SI cancelers are an attractive alternative to polynomial‐based SI cancelers, as they can extract the essential structure of the SI signal from training data, thus significantly reducing the complexity of the SI model Balatsoukas‐Stimming ([2018](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0002)), Guo et al. ([2018](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0008)). The main challenge with NN cancelers is that the training process is inherently noisy due to the use of mini‐batches for gradient estimation. Thus, it is difficult to achieve very accurate reconstruction of the SI signal, which is essential to achieve high levels of SI cancellation. One way to overcome this challenge is to use a NN to reconstruct only a particular part of the SI signal, while using conventional (e.g. linear) cancellation for the remaining part Balatsoukas‐Stimming ([2018](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0002)). More specifically, the SI signal can be conceptually decomposed into a linear component and a nonlinear component:

(18.17)![equation](images/c18-math-0017.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>SI</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>linear</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>nonlinear</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Then, the SI cancellation can be carried out in two steps. First, standard linear cancellation is used in order to reconstruct ![images](images/c18-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mtext>linear</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> as:

(18.18)![equation](images/c18-math-0018.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mtext>linear</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>l</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msup> <mi>L</mi> <mtext>SI</mtext> </msup> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msup> <mi>&#293;</mi> <mtext>SI</mtext> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>l</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The parameters ![images](images/c18-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#293;</mi><mtext>SI</mtext></msup><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> are obtained using LS estimation while considering the (significantly weaker) signal ![images](images/c18-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mtext>nonlinear</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> as noise. The linear SI cancellation signal is subtracted from the SI signal in order to obtain:

(18.19)![equation](images/c18-math-0019.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>nonlinear</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>&#8776;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mtext>SI</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mtext>linear</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The goal of the NN is to reconstruct each ![images](images/c18-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mtext>nonlinear</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> sample based on the subset of ![images](images/c18-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> that this ![images](images/c18-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mtext>nonlinear</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> sample depends on (see Eq. ([18.9](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0009))). Since NNs generally operate on real numbers, all complex‐valued baseband signals are split into their real and imaginary parts.

Due to the universal approximation theorem Hornik ([1991](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0009)), a feedforward NN with one hidden layer, as depicted in [Figure 18.2](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0002), can be used in order to reconstruct the nonlinear SI signal Balatsoukas‐Stimming ([2018](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0002)). The NN has ![images](images/c18-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> input nodes, which correspond to the real and imaginary parts of the ![images](images/c18-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> delayed versions of ![images](images/c18-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> in Eq. ([18.9](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0009)), and two output nodes, which correspond to the real and imaginary parts of the target ![images](images/c18-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mtext>nonlinear</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> sample. The number of hidden nodes is denoted by ![images](images/c18-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> and is a parameter that can be chosen freely.

More specifically, let the vector ![images](images/c18-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">l</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> contain the ![images](images/c18-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> inputs to the NN:

(18.20)![equation](images/c18-math-0020.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">l</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8476;</mi> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8465;</mi> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8230;</mi> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8476;</mi> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>L</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8465;</mi> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>x</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>L</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Then, the outputs of the hidden layer neurons are given by:

(18.21)![equation](images/c18-math-0021.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">l</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">l</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> ![Figure 18.2 Example of a neural network with one hidden layer used for the reconstruction of the nonlinear self‐interference cancellation signal images.](images/c18f002.jpg)

[Figure 18.2](#c18.xhtml#R_c18-fig-0002) Example of a neural network with one hidden layer used for the reconstruction of the nonlinear self‐interference cancellation signal ![images](images/c18-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mtext>nonlinear</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>.

where ![images](images/c18-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> is a ![images](images/c18-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> matrix containing the hidden layer weights, ![images](images/c18-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> is an ![images](images/c18-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> vector containing the hidden layer biases, and ![images](images/c18-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the (vectorized) activation function used in the hidden layer. The outputs of the output layer neurons are in turn given by:

(18.22)![equation](images/c18-math-0022.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">l</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">l</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> (18.23)![equation](images/c18-math-0023.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mspace width="0.95em"/> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">l</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c18-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></mrow></math> is a ![images](images/c18-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> matrix containing the output layer weights, ![images](images/c18-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></mrow></math> is a ![images](images/c18-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> vector containing the output layer biases, and ![images](images/c18-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the activation function used in the output layer. As can be seen in [Figure 18.2](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0002), for ![images](images/c18-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">l</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></mrow></math> we have:

(18.24)![equation](images/c18-math-0024.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold">l</mi> <mi>o</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8476;</mi> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mtext>nonlinear</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mtd> <mtd columnalign="center"> <mi>&#8465;</mi> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mtext>nonlinear</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The goal of the NN is to minimize the following mean squared error between the expected NN output and the actual NN output:

![equation](images/c18-math-0025.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mtext>MSE</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>N</mi></mrow></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></munderover><msup><mrow><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>&#8476;</mi><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mtext>non&#8208;linear</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>&#8476;</mi><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>&#375;</mi><mtext>non&#8208;linear</mtext></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mn>2</mn></msup></mrow></math> (18.25)![equation](images/c18-math-0026.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mspace width="3.5em"/> <mo>+</mo> <mspace width="0.2em"/> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mrow> <mn>2</mn> <mi>N</mi> </mrow> </mfrac> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>N</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msup> <mrow> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>&#8465;</mi> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>y</mi> <mtext>non&#8208;linear</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>&#8465;</mi> <mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#375;</mi> <mtext>non&#8208;linear</mtext> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c18-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> is the total number of training samples. In practice, the expected NN output can be easily obtained by transmitting a frame of known ![images](images/c18-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> samples using an experimental testbed and recording the corresponding SI at the receiver.

The MSE can be minimized by choosing appropriate values for ![images](images/c18-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c18-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c18-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">W</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c18-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold">b</mi><mi>o</mi></msub></mrow></math>. These values can be computed iteratively by starting from randomly initialized values, calculating the derivative of MSE with respect to each weight and each bias through backpropagation Rumelhart et al. ([1986](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0019)), and using a weight‐adaptation algorithm (e.g. Adam Kingma and Ba ([2015](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0012))).

 

### 18.2.4 Computational Complexity

In this section, the computational complexity of the polynomial canceler and the NN canceler is examined. The polynomial canceler operates on complex numbers, while the NN canceler operates on real numbers. Thus, in order to perform a fair comparison, the number of real additions and real multiplications that are required to perform the computations of each method are counted. Let ![images](images/c18-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">C</mi></mrow></math> and let ![images](images/c18-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>R</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#8476;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c18-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>a</mi><mi>I</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mi>&#8465;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>a</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> for simplicity. Then, complex addition can be written as:

(18.26)![equation](images/c18-math-0027.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>a</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>R</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>R</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mi>j</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>I</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>I</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

and complex multiplication can be written as:

(18.27)![equation](images/c18-math-0028.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>a</mi> <mi>b</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>R</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>j</mi> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>I</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>R</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mi>j</mi> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>I</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </math> (18.28)![equation](images/c18-math-0029.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mspace width="1.3em"/> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>R</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>R</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>I</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>I</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mi>j</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>R</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>I</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>R</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>I</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>R</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>R</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mi>I</mi> </msub> <msub> <mi>b</mi> <mi>I</mi> </msub> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Thus, one complex addition is equivalent to two real additions, while one complex multiplication is equivalent to three real multiplications and five real additions.

 

#### 18.2.4.1 Linear Cancellation

The evaluation of the linear cancellation expression in Eq. ([18.18](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0018)) requires ![images](images/c18-i0097.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> complex multiplications and ![images](images/c18-i0098.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> complex additions. Equivalently, it requires ![images](images/c18-i0099.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>MUL,linear</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> real multiplications and ![images](images/c18-i0100.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>MUL,linear</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></math> real additions.

 

#### 18.2.4.2 Polynomial Nonlinear Cancellation

The total number of complex‐valued parameters ![images](images/c18-i0101.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#293;</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> in Eq. ([18.14](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0014)) can be calculated as Korpi et al. ([2017](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0014)):

(18.29)![equation](images/c18-math-0030.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mtext>poly</mtext> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mi>L</mi> <mn>4</mn> </mfrac> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>P</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfenced> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>P</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>3</mn> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

which grows quadratically with the PA nonlinearity order ![images](images/c18-i0102.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>. In order to perform a best‐case complexity analysis for the polynomial canceler, it is assumed that the calculation of the basis functions ![images](images/c18-i0103.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi><msub><mi>F</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow></math> in Eq. ([18.14](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0014)) comes at no computational cost Balatsoukas‐Stimming ([2018](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0002)). One complex multiplication is performed for each of the ![images](images/c18-i0104.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>poly</mtext></msub></mrow></math> complex‐valued parameters ![images](images/c18-i0105.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#293;</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> in Eq. ([18.14](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0014)), requiring a total of ![images](images/c18-i0106.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>3</mn><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>poly</mtext></msub></mrow></math> real multiplications and ![images](images/c18-i0107.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>5</mn><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>poly</mtext></msub></mrow></math> real additions. Moreover, the results of the ![images](images/c18-i0108.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>poly</mtext></msub></mrow></math> complex multiplications need to be summed up in order to calculate ![images](images/c18-i0109.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#375;</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, which requires a total of ![images](images/c18-i0110.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>poly</mtext></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> real additions. Thus, the polynomial canceler requires a total of:

(18.30)![equation](images/c18-math-0031.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mtext>MUL,poly</mtext> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>3</mn> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mtext>poly</mtext> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>3</mn> <mn>4</mn> </mfrac> <mi>L</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>P</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfenced> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>P</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>3</mn> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> (18.31)![equation](images/c18-math-0032.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mtext>ADD,poly</mtext> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mn>5</mn> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mtext>poly</mtext> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mtext>poly</mtext> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mn>7</mn> <mn>4</mn> </mfrac> <mi>L</mi> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>P</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </mfenced> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mi>P</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>3</mn> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

real multiplications and real additions, respectively.

 

#### 18.2.4.3 Neural Network Nonlinear Cancellation

Apart from the connections that are visible in [Figure 18.2](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0002), each node also has a *bias* input, which is omitted from the figure for simplicity. Thus, the total number of real‐valued weights in the NN is:

(18.32)![equation](images/c18-math-0033.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>w</mi> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>L</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Excluding the biases that are not involved in multiplications, there are ![images](images/c18-i0111.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> real weights in the hidden layer that are multiplied with the real input values, and ![images](images/c18-i0112.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> real weights in the output layer that are multiplied with the real output values from the hidden nodes. Moreover, the linear cancellation stage that precedes the NN requires ![images](images/c18-i0113.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> complex multiplications, which correspond to ![images](images/c18-i0114.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>3</mn><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> real multiplications and ![images](images/c18-i0115.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> real additions. Thus, the total number of real multiplications required by the NN canceler is:

(18.33)![equation](images/c18-math-0034.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mtext>MUL,NN</mtext> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>L</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mi>L</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

For each of the ![images](images/c18-i0116.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> hidden neurons, ![images](images/c18-i0117.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> incoming real values need to be summed, which requires a total of ![images](images/c18-i0118.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> real additions. Moreover, at each of the 2 output neurons, ![images](images/c18-i0119.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>+</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> real values need to be summed, which requires a total of ![images](images/c18-i0120.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> real additions. The computation of each of the ![images](images/c18-i0121.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> ReLU activation functions requires one multiplexer (and one comparator with zero, which can be trivially implemented by looking at the most significant bit of the input). Moreover, the linear cancellation stage that precedes the NN requires summing up ![images](images/c18-i0122.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> complex values, which requires ![images](images/c18-i0123.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> real additions. Thus, assuming a worst case where a multiplexer has the same complexity as an addition, the total number of real additions required by the NN canceler is:

(18.34)![equation](images/c18-math-0035.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mtext>ADD,NN</mtext> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mi>L</mi> <mo>+</mo> <mn>3</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <msub> <mi>N</mi> <mi>h</mi> </msub> <mo>+</mo> <mn>7</mn> <mi>L</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>2</mn> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

The complexity expressions for the polynomial and the NN‐based canceler are summarized in [Table 18.1](#c18.xhtml#c18-tbl-0001). It is important to note that the complexity expressions for the two methods cannot be compared directly because they contain different sets of parameters. Thus, in order to perform a fair comparison, appropriate values for ![images](images/c18-i0124.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c18-i0125.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c18-i0126.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub></mrow></math> are selected in [Section 18.3](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0012) so that the two methods have the same SI cancellation performance.

![ Table 18.1  Computational complexity of polynomial and neural network cancelers.](images/c18-i0127.png)

 [Table 18.1](#c18.xhtml#R_c18-tbl-0001)  Computational complexity of polynomial and neural network cancelers.

 

## 18.3 Experimental Results

In this section, the performance and complexity of the standard polynomial nonlinear canceler described in [Section 18.2.2](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0006) is compared with the NN canceler described in [Section 18.2.3](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0007) using experimental results from a FD testbed.

 

### 18.3.1 Experimental Setup

The FD hardware testbed that is used to obtain the results in this section uses a National Instruments FlexRIO device and two FlexRIO 5791R RF transceiver modules as described in more detail in Balatsoukas‐Stimming et al. ([2013](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0003)), Belanovic et al. ([2013](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0005)), Balatsoukas‐Stimming et al. ([2015](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0004)). The transmitted signal is a QPSK‐modulated OFDM signal with a passband bandwidth of 10 MHz and ![images](images/c18-i0131.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1024</mn></mrow></math> carriers. At the receiver, the signal is sampled with a sampling frequency of 20 MHz so that the signal side‐lobes can be observed. Each transmitted OFDM frame consists of ![images](images/c18-i0132.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>20</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>480</mn></mrow></math> baseband samples, out of which 90% are used for training and the remaining 10% are used to calculate the achieved SI cancellation, both for the polynomial canceler and for the NN canceler. The average transmit power is 10 dBm and the two‐antenna FD testbed setup provides a passive analog cancellation of 53 dB. No active RF cancellation is performed as the achieved passive cancellation is sufficient for the results presented in this section.

For both cancelers, it was found through trial and error that ![images](images/c18-i0133.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math> memory taps are sufficient to model the equivalent SI channel. Moreover, for the polynomial canceler, a maximum nonlinearity order of ![images](images/c18-i0134.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math> is used, since further increasing this parameter results in very limited gains in the achieved SI suppression, and after some point even decreased performance due to overfitting. The NN was implemented using the Keras framework with a TensorFlow back‐end. Moreover, the Adam optimization algorithm is used for training with a mean squared error cost function, a learning rate of ![images](images/c18-i0135.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.004</mn></mrow></math>, and a mini‐batch size of ![images](images/c18-i0136.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>B</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></math>. All remaining parameters have their default values. The NN has ![images](images/c18-i0137.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>26</mn></mrow></math> input units and ![images](images/c18-i0138.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn></mrow></math> hidden units. The neurons in the hidden layer use a rectified linear unit (ReLU) activation function, defined as ![images](images/c18-i0139.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, while the output neurons use the identity activation function, defined as ![images](images/c18-i0140.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>o</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></math>.

 

### 18.3.2 Self‐Interference Cancellation Results

[Figure 18.3](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0003) shows SI cancellation results using the polynomial canceler of [Section 18.2.2](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0006) and the NN canceler of Section  [18.2.2](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0006). It can be observed that digital linear cancellation provides approximately 37.9 dB of cancellation, reducing the residual SI power to ![images](images/c18-i0141.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>80.6</mn></mrow></math> dBm. Both the polynomial canceler and the NN canceler reduce the SI by an additional 6.9 dB, leading to a residual SI power of ![images](images/c18-i0142.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>87.5</mn></mrow></math> dBm, which is only 3.3 dB away from the receiver noise floor. In [Figure 18.5](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0005) it can be observed that after only four training epochs, the NN can already achieve a nonlinear SI cancellation of over 6 dB on both the training and the test frames. After 20 training epochs, the nonlinear SI cancellation reaches approximately 7 dB and there is no obvious indication of overfitting since the SI cancellation on the training and on the test data is very similar.

![Figure 18.3 Power spectral densities of the self‐interference signal, the SI signal after linear cancellation, as well as the SI signal after nonlinear cancellation using both a polynomial canceler and a neural network canceler.](images/c18f003.jpg)

[Figure 18.3](#c18.xhtml#R_c18-fig-0003) Power spectral densities of the self‐interference signal, the SI signal after linear cancellation, as well as the SI signal after nonlinear cancellation using both a polynomial canceler and a neural network canceler.

In [Figure 18.4](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0004), it can be seen that, if no linear cancellation is performed before the NN canceler, then the achieved SI cancellation is significantly worse. Specifically, in this case even a large NN canceler with ![images](images/c18-i0143.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow></math> hidden neurons trained for a total of 1000 epochs achieves only 37.1 dB of cancellation (care was taken to ensure that no overfitting occurred). This amount of SI cancellation is similar to the cancellation achieved by simply using the (much lower complexity) linear canceler. In principle the NN should be able to learn to jointly cancel both the linear and the nonlinear part of the signal. However, because the nonlinear part of the SI signal is significantly weaker than the linear part, it seems that the noise in the gradient computation due to the use of mini‐batches essentially completely hides the nonlinear structure of the SI signal from the learning algorithm.

 

### 18.3.3 Computational Complexity

Having found the set of parameters ![images](images/c18-i0144.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>P</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>7</mn></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c18-i0145.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>13</mn></mrow></math>, and ![images](images/c18-i0146.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>18</mn></mrow></math> that lead to the same SI cancellation performance, it is possible to fairly compare the complexity of the polynomial canceler with the complexity of the NN canceler by evaluating the complexity expressions derived in [Section 18.2.4](#c18.xhtml#c18-sec-0008). More specifically, the polynomial canceler requires ![images](images/c18-i0147.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>ADD,poly</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1818</mn></mrow></math> real additions and ![images](images/c18-i0148.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>MUL,poly</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>780</mn></mrow></math> real multiplications, while the NN canceler requires ![images](images/c18-i0149.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>ADD,NN</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>611</mn></mrow></math> real additions and ![images](images/c18-i0150.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>MUL,NN</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>543</mn></mrow></math> real multiplications. In other words, the NN canceler requires 66% fewer real additions and 30% fewer real multiplications than the polynomial canceler. This complexity reduction is also reflected well in hardware implementations of the two types of cancelers. Specifically, a NN canceler was shown to be 11% smaller and 60% faster than a polynomial canceler when implemented as an ASIC using a 28 nm FD‐SOI technology Kurzo et al. ([2018](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0015)). All implementation results are summarized in [Table 18.2](#c18.xhtml#c18-tbl-0002).

![Figure 18.4 Power spectral densities of the self‐interference signal, the SI signal after linear cancellation, and the SI signal after neural network–based nonlinear cancellation with and without a linear cancellation stage.](images/c18f004.jpg)

## 18.4 Conclusions

This chapter provided a self‐contained and comprehensive overview of FD communications and digital SI cancellation methods. In particular, a detailed FD transceiver model was presented and the main transceiver non‐idealities that make digital SI cancellation challenging were described and modeled. Based on the aforementioned models, a polynomial SI cancellation method was presented, which is commonly used in the literature for SI cancellation. Then, an alternative NN‐based SI cancellation method was presented and the computational complexity of the two methods was examined and compared. Finally, experimental results showed that the NN‐based SI canceller achieves identical digital SI cancellation performance to the polynomial SI canceller, but with significantly lower computational and hardware implementation complexity.

![ Table 18.2  Comparison of polynomial and neural network canceler implementations.](images/c18-i0151.png)

 [Table 18.2](#c18.xhtml#R_c18-tbl-0002)  Comparison of polynomial and neural network canceler implementations.

 

### 18.4.1 Open Problems

The NN‐based cancellation method described in this chapter uses a simple single‐layer feedforward NN. Even though the method works well, significant improvements in performance and/or complexity could be achieved by considering other NN architectures. For example, deep feedforward NNs have been shown to generally outperform single‐layer feedforward NNs for a wide variety of applications. As such, a deep and narrow (i.e. with few neurons per layer) NN may outperform a shallow and wide NN for the same number of trainable parameters, or it may provide similar performance with fewer trainable parameters. Moreover, since the SI signal has memory, a natural choice would be to use a recurrent NN (RNN) that can reproduce the SI memory with only two inputs (i.e. the real and imaginary parts of ![images](images/c18-i0152.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>), instead of the ![images](images/c18-i0153.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>2</mn><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> inputs that are required by the feedforward NN.

The SI channel changes over time and needs to be tracked. For the polynomial canceler, the SI channel can be tracked by re‐estimating the parameters ![images](images/c18-i0154.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#293;</mi><mrow><mi>p</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>q</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>l</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> in Eq. ([18.16](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0016)), using either standard least‐squares estimation or an adaptive version of the least‐squares estimation algorithm, such as least mean squares or recursive least squares. For the NN‐based canceler, the SI channel can be tracked by re‐running the backpropagation training algorithm. It is essential to examine and compare the SI channel‐tracking methods for the polynomial and the NN‐based canceler. It particular, it would be interesting to compare the computational complexity, the convergence speed, and the required number of training samples for each tracking method.

Finally, existing NN‐based methods for SI cancellation do not take any expert knowledge about the problem into account. Both the SI transceiver system diagram in [Figure 18.1](#c18.xhtml#c18-fig-0001) and Eq. ([18.16](#c18.xhtml#c18-disp-0016)) provide valuable information that could be used in order to derive physically inspired NN architectures for digital SI cancellation, similarly to the physically inspired RF power amplifier modeling of Mkadem and Boumaiza ([2011](#c18.xhtml#c18-bib-0016)).

# 19  
Machine Learning for Context‐Aware Cross‐Layer Optimization

*Yang Yang¹, Zening Liu¹, Shuang Zhao², Ziyu Shao¹, and Kunlun Wang¹*

¹*SHIFT, School of Information Science and Technology, ShanghaiTech University, Shanghai, China*

²*Interactive Entertainment Group, Tencent Inc., Shanghai, China*

 

## 19.1 Introduction

In recent years, global mobile data traffic has experienced an explosive growth. It is expected to grow to 49 exabytes per month by 2021, a sevenfold increase over 2016 Cisco ([2016](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0013)). Current wireless technologies, such as 4G and WiFi, do not have localized data analysis and processing capabilities so that they cannot handle such a bursty traffic increase Chen et al. ([2014](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0006)), Yang et al. ([2018b](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0049)). As machine‐type communications (MTC) have been adopted in 5G networks Ge et al. ([2016](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0013)), Shi et al. ([2014](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0040)), Wang et al. ([2016](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0044)), Chen et al. ([2016a](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0007)), new flexible network architectures and service strategies are desperately needed to support more and more data‐centric and delay‐sensitive Internet‐of‐Things (IoT) applications Yang ([2019](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0048)), Chen et al. ([2018a](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0005)), such as smart city, environment surveillance, intelligent manufacturing, and autonomous driving. If only centralized cloud computing architecture is applied to those various IoT applications, it is envisaged that the underlayer communication networks, especially backhaul connections, will face heavy bursty traffic burdens and experience dramatic performance degradation. On the other hand, Moore's Law has significantly driven down the prices of computing and storage devices, and more and more smart network nodes and user terminals are deployed and connected into modern communication networks. They provide a rich collection of ubiquitous local computing, communication, and storage resources. In view of this technological trend, the concept of fog computing is proposed to enable computing anywhere along the cloud‐to‐thing continuum Bonomi et al. ([2012](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0004)), Vaquero and Rodero‐Merino ([2014](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0042)), Ouyang et al. ([2018](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0036)), Chen et al. ([2018](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0010)). In other words, fog‐enabled network architecture and services can effectively leverage those local resources to support fast‐growing data‐centric and delay‐sensitive IoT‐applications in regional environments, thus reducing backhual traffic transmissions and centralized computing needs, and at the same time improving the overall network throughput performance and users' quality of experience (QoE) Chiang and Zhang ([2016](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0011)), Yang et al. ([2017b](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0046)), Chen et al. ([2017](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0009)).

Without loss of generality, let us consider a multi‐tier content delivery wireless network consisting of user terminals (UTs), access tier, and control tier, as shown in [Figure 19.1](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0001), where (i) a node in access tier is typically located close to the UTs and is called a *fog access node*(FAN); (ii) a node in the control tier, which is usually far away from UTs, manages a group of FANs through reliable but expensive backhaul connections and is called a *fog control node*(FCN). As UTs are moving around and can make requests of any contents at anytime anywhere, it is obvious that popular contents should be placed in multiple FANs in advance, according to their resources and capabilities. In doing so, most content delivery requests are handled in the network edge, and thus service delay and backhaul traffic transmission can be greatly reduced.

![Figure 19.1 A sample fog‐enabled multi‐tier network with three fog access nodes and five user terminals.](images/c19f001.jpg)

[Figure 19.1](#c19.xhtml#R_c19-fig-0001) A sample fog‐enabled multi‐tier network with three fog access nodes and five user terminals.

In such a complex multi‐tier network with heterogeneous node capabilities and dynamic network resources, in terms of computing power, storage capacity, transmission power, and communication bandwidth, how to conduct effective multi‐tier operations scheduling is a key challenge to be resolved Zhang et al. ([2018b,a](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0055)), Yang et al. ([2018e](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0052)). To deal with the node capacity and dynamic network resources management in fog computing networks, many techniques have been explored. Recently, applying AI to solve the resource management in such complex networks has gained considerable attention Yang et al. ([2019](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0053)), Huang et al. ([2018](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0016)), Yang et al. ([2018c](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0050)). Luong et al. ([2018](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0031)) proposed a deep learning (DL)‐based algorithm for edge resource management. Li et al. ([2018](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0024)) introduced DL for IoT into the edge computing environment to improve learning performance as well as to reduce network traffic. He et al. ([2017](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0015)) presented a novel big data deep reinforcement learning (RL) approach. Chen et al. ([2018](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0010)) proposed an efficient RL‐based resource management algorithm, which learned on‐the‐fly the optimal policy of dynamic workload offloading. However, the shortcomings of these existing machine learning techniques cannot be overlooked:

1.  (1) The training data for both DL and deep RL is essential for training the models, while it is difficult to collect, especially in large‐scale fog networks.
2.  (2) The number of optimized parameters is typically very large for such a large‐scale fog network, and thus the computing resources and time required for training the models are usually rather high.
3.  (3) The network is dynamic, and learning from the models is time‐consuming, as well as resource‐consuming, so it is hard for DL or deep RL to effectively realize online or real‐time resource management.
4.  (4) The performance of DL and deep RL cannot be guaranteed in theory.

Different from these machine learning techniques for resource management, in this chapter, we employ Lyapunov optimization‐based learning techniques and propose an online (real‐time) low‐complexity fog‐enabled multi‐tier operations scheduling (FEMOS) algorithm, which is data‐free and performance‐guaranteed. The FEMOS algorithm simultaneously addresses the following challenging problems:

1.  (1) When popular contents are randomly cached at different FANs, how to identify the most feasible FAN for every UT's request in order to maximize network throughput and global fairness.
2.  (2) Under dynamic wireless network conditions and fading channel characteristics, how to effectively allocate communication bandwidth for associated FAN‐UT pairs in order to minimize service delay.

It is worth noting that, since the file placement has been widely investigated in the design of content delivery networks Baştug et al. ([2015](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0002)), Li et al. ([2015](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0025)), Liu et al. ([2017](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0026)), the dynamic association between UTs and FANs is the focus of this chapter, which has rarely been investigated.

Although the most commonly used AI techniques, such as DL and deep RL, may be not best suited to be immediately applied to conduct all the resource management in fog networks, is it possible to deploy AI techniques to realize partial functions, and as a result all resource management can benefit from it? Motivated by this question and the recent advancement in data mining for learning user behaviors Kumar and Tomkins ([2010](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0021)), Huang et al. ([2016b](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0019)), Yang et al. ([2017a](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0045)), Zhang et al. ([2014](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0054)), Wang et al. ([2015](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0043)), this chapter presents a predictive scheduling model and develops the predictive multi‐tier operations scheduling (PMOS) algorithm, where the FCN is assumed to be aware of users' future request information within a limited future time window.

In addition, this chapter further addresses a cost model and the resulting cost‐minimization user‐scheduling problem in multi‐tier fog computing networks. Generally, the FCN is operated by a telecom operator that signs a service contract with UTs, while the FANs belong to different individuals. To better motivate the FANs to share resources, the cost model, especially for FANs, should be taken into consideration. For this purpose, this chapter presents a unified multi‐tier cost model, including the service delay and a linear inverse demand dynamic payment scheme. Correspondingly, a cost‐oriented user scheduling (COUS) algorithm, based on a potential game, is reported in this chapter.

The rest of this chapter is organized as follows. The system model is presented in [Section 19.2](#c19.xhtml#c19-sec-0002). Under the fog‐enabled network architecture, the problem is formulated in [Section 19.3](#c19.xhtml#c19-sec-0007). The online FEMOS algorithm is proposed in [Section 19.3.1](#c19.xhtml#c19-sec-0012) and corresponding performance analysis is conducted in [Section 19.3.2](#c19.xhtml#c19-sec-0017). [Section 19.4](#c19.xhtml#c19-sec-0021) further develops the PMOS algorithm based on the proposed FEMOS algorithm and predicted users' information. Furthermore, [Section 19.5](#c19.xhtml#c19-sec-0025) proposes a unified multi‐tier cost model to motivate the FANs for resources sharing, and develops the COUS algorithm to effectively solve the resulted cost‐minimization user scheduling problem. [Section 19.6](#c19.xhtml#c19-sec-0046) concludes this chapter.

 

## 19.2 System Model

We consider a fog‐enabled multi‐tier network with heterogeneous nodes as shown in [Figure 19.1](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0001), which involves a FCN tier, a FAN tier, and a set of multiple stationary or low‐mobility UTs in the region under consideration. Each UT possesses a small storage capacity, minor communication ability, and little or no computation ability. UTs request files to be downloaded from the FAN tier through wireless links. Due to the restricted transmission power and dynamic wireless environment, the communication channels between a FAN and its neighboring UTs are unreliable and time‐varying. Each FAN in the FAN tier is equipped with limited storage capacity, medium computation ability, but strong communication ability. All of them cached a subset of popular files. Through reliable backhaul links, FANs are connected with a FCN, which is next to the cloud and core network, has the global information about the network, and is the server of the file library. The FCN has both sufficient storage capacity and powerful computation ability. We emphasize here that in our model, the backhaul links transmit control information from the FCN to FANs, and files cached at each FANs are only refreshed at off‐peak times. To be clear, if the UT requested file is not cached on the FANs, the FAN will not fetch the file from the operation center through the backhaul link. Under these conditions, we can see more clearly the benefit of dynamic assignment of FAN and resource scheduling.

Denote the set of FANs as ![images](images/c19-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">H</mi></mrow></math>, the set of UTs as ![images](images/c19-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">U</mi></mrow></math>, and the file library as ![images](images/c19-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi></mrow></math>. The large‐scale fading and small‐scale fading coefficients seen by each FAN are assumed to be mutually independent. We assume that the network operates in a slotted system, indexed by ![images](images/c19-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>, and the time slot length is ![images](images/c19-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi></mrow></math>. The FCN determines the dynamic FAN assignment for UTs at the beginning of each slot, to optimize the network throughput in a memoryless pattern, based on the network states, request queue length and disregarding all such previous decisions. Each UT requested file will be then transmitted by its associated FAN through the wireless link. The queue length of current unserved request buffers will in turn influence the FCN's decision about FAN assignment in the next slot. Each FAN then independently implements its per‐slot scheduling policy including the bandwidth and service rate allocation over the UTs associated with it. Consistent with this setting, the requested file ![images](images/c19-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> can only be downloaded from the FAN that has cached it. The service rate would be zero if the requested file is not cached on the FAN that the UT is associated with.

stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Here ![images](images/c19-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>h</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> if ![images](images/c19-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>h</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="script">E</mi><mo>&#818;</mo></munder></mrow></math>, and 0 otherwise.

Define the file placement (FAN‐File association) as a bipartite graph ![images](images/c19-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="script">H</mi><mo>,</mo><mi mathvariant="script">F</mi><mo>,</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="script">E</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, where edges ![images](images/c19-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="script">E</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow></math> indicates that files with type ![images](images/c19-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow></math> are cached in FAN ![images](images/c19-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>h</mi></mrow></math>. The file set cached at each FAN is ![images](images/c19-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> N</mi></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c19-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> N</mi><mo>&#8838;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> F</mi></mrow></math>, with ![images](images/c19-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> N</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></math> different file types.

Let us first focus on dynamic FAN assignment and the resource scheduling problem. As said before, the backhaul updates the storages at a time scale much larger than the time scale of UTs placing file requests. Therefore, assuming fixed file placement (FAN‐File Association) is justified. Let ![images](images/c19-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi></mrow></math> denote a ![images](images/c19-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mo>&#215;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> F</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></math> file placement matrix of ![images](images/c19-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="script">G</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c19-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">Y</mi><mo>&#8796;</mo><msub><mrow><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><mspace width="0.1em"/><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mfenced></mrow><mrow><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>. Here, ![images](images/c19-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> if ![images](images/c19-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>h</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8712;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="script">E</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow></math>, and 0 otherwise.

We assume that each UT can be associated with at most one FAN and each FAN can associate with at most ![images](images/c19-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> UTs in one time slot. Thus ![images](images/c19-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">X</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> should be chosen from the feasible set ![images](images/c19-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> A</mi></mrow></math>,

##### *UT Traffic Model*

All UTs are assumed to generate file‐request traffic randomly in each time slot, and this traffic generation is independent of the FCN's operation.

Let ![images](images/c19-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo
