In this subsection, we evaluate the performance of the proposed FEMOS algorithm and compare its greedy FAN assignment with the other two dynamic schemes: *select best channel* (SBC) and *selecq longest queue* (SLQ). In the SBC scheme, each FAN associates with the UT with the best channel condition between them in each time slot. In the SLQ scheme, in each time slot, the UTs with top‐![images](images/c19-i0204.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></math> queue length access the network, and each of them associates with the FAN with the best transmission condition.

[Figure 19.2](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0002) first validates the theoretical results for the proposed FEMOS algorithm derived in Theorem 1. The average network throughput performance is shown in [Figure 19.2](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0002)a, while the average service delay per UT is shown in [Figure 19.2](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0002)b. It can be observed from [Figure 19.2](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0002)a that the average network throughput obtained by the greedy FAN assignment in FEMOS increases as ![images](images/c19-i0205.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> increases and converges to the maximum value when ![images](images/c19-i0206.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> is sufficiently large. Meanwhile, as shown in [Figure 19.2](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0002)b, the average service delay experienced by per UT of FEMOS increases linearly with the control parameter ![images](images/c19-i0207.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math>. This is in accordance with the analysis that with ![images](images/c19-i0208.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> increasing, the importance of request queue backlogs decreases, which makes the dynamic assignment bias toward good channel conditions. Those observations verify the ![images](images/c19-i0209.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> trade‐off between average network throughput and average queue backlog as demonstrated in Theorem 1.

[Figure 19.2](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0002) also compares the greedy FAN assignment in FEMOS with SBC and SLQ assignment schemes. We observe that the average network throughput performance of SBC stabilizes around ![images](images/c19-i0210.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1.7</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow></math> kbits/slot, which approaches the maximum value of FEMOS. However, the average network throughput performance deteriorates severely under SLQ assignment scheme for any ![images](images/c19-i0211.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math>. The average service delay in both SBC and SLQ assignment schemes is much larger than that of greedy assignment in FEMOS when ![images](images/c19-i0212.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>&#60;</mo><mn>2000</mn></mrow></math>. Specifically, when ![images](images/c19-i0213.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, the average delay in FEMOS approaches zero, but it is ![images](images/c19-i0214.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>5</mn><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c19-i0215.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>45</mn><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> for the SLQ and SBC schemes, respectively. These comparisons demonstrate the advantages of the greedy assignment in FEMOS.

In [Figure 19.3](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0003), we further explore the relationship between network throughput and average service delay of the FEMOS algorithm regarding different workloads (![images](images/c19-i0216.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub></mrow></math>) and different UT amounts (![images](images/c19-i0217.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math>). Specifically, in [Figure 19.3](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0003)a we explore the average network throughput versus average service delay in terms of different numbers of workloads (![images](images/c19-i0218.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></math> kbits, 80 kbits, 100 kbits, and 120 kbits, respectively). The random caching strategy is adopted here. It can be observed that for a given control parameter ![images](images/c19-i0219.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math>, the proposed FEMOS algorithm with a lower workload obtains better network throughput performance and experiences shorter service delay. For example, when ![images](images/c19-i0220.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2000</mn></mrow></math>, the average delay per UT experienced in FEMOS with ![images](images/c19-i0221.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>120</mn></mrow></math> kbits is 3.2 s, which is about twice as large a that with ![images](images/c19-i0222.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></math> kbits. The average network throughput obtained by FEMOS with ![images](images/c19-i0223.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>60</mn></mrow></math> kbits is ![images](images/c19-i0224.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1.512</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow></math> kbits/slot when ![images](images/c19-i0225.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2000</mn></mrow></math>, while it is ![images](images/c19-i0226.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mn>1.317</mn><mo>&#215;</mo><mn>1</mn><msup><mn>0</mn><mn>4</mn></msup></mrow></math> kbits/slot obtained by FEMOS with ![images](images/c19-i0227.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>120</mn></mrow></math> kbits. The reason behind these observations is, according to Eqs. ([19.18](#c19.xhtml#c19-disp-0018)) and ([19.19](#c19.xhtml#c19-disp-0019)) in *Theorem 1*, both the lower bound of the average network throughput ![images](images/c19-i0228.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow><mtext>FEMOS</mtext></msubsup></mrow></math> and the upper bound of average service delay ![images](images/c19-i0229.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#923;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow><mtext>FEMOS</mtext></msubsup></mrow></math> are determined by parameters ![images](images/c19-i0230.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c19-i0231.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c19-i0232.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#956;</mi></mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>+</mo><msubsup><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Larger workload leads to larger ![images](images/c19-i0233.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">K</mi></mrow></math>, and thus a smaller average network throughput and a longer average service delay are obtained.

![Figure 19.2 Comparison of fog‐enabled multi‐tier operations scheduling and other fog access node assignment schemes, images, images = 100.](images/c19f002.jpg)

[Figure 19.2](#c19.xhtml#R_c19-fig-0002) Comparison of fog‐enabled multi‐tier operations scheduling and other fog access node assignment schemes, ![images](images/c19-i0202.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn><mspace width="1em"/><mtext>kbits</mtext></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c19-i0203.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> = 100.

![Figure 19.3 Network throughput‐delay trade‐off for FEMOS under different parameters.](images/c19f003.jpg)

[Figure 19.3](#c19.xhtml#R_c19-fig-0003) Network throughput‐delay trade‐off for FEMOS under different parameters.

In [Figure 19.3](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0003)b, we show the impacts of UT amount ![images](images/c19-i0234.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> on the network throughput‐delay trade‐off performance of the FEMOS algorithm. A similar phenomenon exists for the curves with different workloads. A network throughput‐delay trade‐off also exists under different UT amounts. In addition, it can be observed that by increasing ![images](images/c19-i0235.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math>, the average service delay increases and the average network throughput decreases for a given ![images](images/c19-i0236.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math>. This is also consistent with Theorem 1 that the UT amount ![images](images/c19-i0237.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>U</mi></mrow></math> influences the value of parameter ![images](images/c19-i0238.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> K</mi></mrow></math>, and thus impacts both throughput and service‐delay performance. Intuitively, in this case along with different workload scenarios, the FCN has to fully utilize the network resources to serve UTs' traffic demands, and either high workload or large UT amount certainly will deteriorate both network throughput and delay performance.

 

## 19.4 Predictive Multi‐tier Operations Scheduling (PMOS) Algorithm

Motivated by recent advancements in data mining for learning user behaviors Kumar and Tomkins ([2010](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0021)), the FCN is assumed to be aware of users' future request information within a limited future time window. With this predictive information, the FCN can control the FANs serving the upcoming requests and pre‐push files to UTs beforehand when the link condition is good, instead of waiting for them to submit their requests, which may lead to a large service latency.

 

### 19.4.1 System Model

Similar to the system model in Zhao et al. ([2018](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0057)), a general fog‐enabled multi‐tier network architecture is shown in [Figure 19.4](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0004). The network involves a powerful FCN tier with both strong computation and sufficient storage capacities, a FAN tier with limited storage capacity and computation capacities but strong communication capacity, and a set of multiple stationary or low‐mobility UTs in the region under consideration. Each UT possesses small storage capacity, minor communication ability, and little or no computation ability. Each FAN in the FAN tier caches a subset of popular files. FANs are connected to a FCN through backhaul links, which is next to the cloud and core network and acts as the server of the file library. UTs request files to be downloaded from the FAN tier through wireless links. Due to the restricted transmit power and dynamic wireless environment, the communication channels between a FAN and its neighboring UTs are unreliable and time varying.

![Figure 19.4 A sample fog‐enabled multi‐tier network with three FANs and five UTs, operating predictive scheduling in slot images.](images/c19f004.jpg)

[Figure 19.4](#c19.xhtml#R_c19-fig-0004) A sample fog‐enabled multi‐tier network with three FANs and five UTs, operating predictive scheduling in slot ![images](images/c19-i0239.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>.

Different from the model in Zhao et al. ([2018](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0057)), the FCN here is powerful enough to predict the UTs' request information within a limited future time window. With the global information about the network and the limited future information, the FCN performs the centralized assignment of access node for UTs and controls the FANs to preserve the future requests in advance when link condition is good. Then each FAN in the FAN tier executes a predictive online bandwidth allocation (POBA) scheme and proactive online service rate‐scheduling scheme locally, to guarantee the transmission delay and ensure the QoE for UTs.

We introduce a *prediction window* in our predictive scheduling model that was developed by Huang et al. ([2016a](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0018)). Specifically, the FCN is assumed to have access to future arrival information ![images](images/c19-i0240.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c19-i0241.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo>,</mo><mo>&#8704;</mo><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi></mrow></math> within the prediction window. Here ![images](images/c19-i0242.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>u</mi></msub></mrow></math> is the prediction window size of UT ![images](images/c19-i0243.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>u</mi></mrow></math> with ![images](images/c19-i0244.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>. Without loss of generality, the imperfect prediction is considered in such a predictive scheduling model.

The expression ![images](images/c19-i0245.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> is introduced to denote the service rate scheduled by the FCN in time slot ![images](images/c19-i0246.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math> serving for arrival requests in time slot ![images](images/c19-i0247.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>. Here, ![images](images/c19-i0248.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> is the predictive phase. Let ![images](images/c19-i0249.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> denote the service rate allocated for the file requests already in the system queues in time slot ![images](images/c19-i0250.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>.

In each time slot, the arrived but not yet served requests will be queued in the request buffers at the FCN with sufficiently large capacity. Next, we introduce prediction queues, which record the residual requests for different type of files in the prediction window ![images](images/c19-i0251.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>. Specifically, ![images](images/c19-i0252.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> denotes the number of file request queues already in the system at the beginning of time slot ![images](images/c19-i0253.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi></mrow></math>. The expression ![images](images/c19-i0254.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> denotes the number of file request queues in future slot ![images](images/c19-i0255.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi></mrow></math>. Note that ![images](images/c19-i0256.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the only actual backlog in the network and the network is stable if and only if ![images](images/c19-i0257.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is stable. The expression ![images](images/c19-i0258.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> represents virtual queues that simply record the residual arrivals in the prediction window.

Under the scenario of imperfect prediction, the false predicted arrivals will appear in prediction queues ![images](images/c19-i0259.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mspace width="0.2em"/><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>&#8804;</mo><mi>d</mi><mo>&#8804;</mo><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, and the fraction of false predicted arrivals is ![images](images/c19-i0260.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>e</mi></mrow></math> on average. Thus, the effective queue length of ![images](images/c19-i0261.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is ![images](images/c19-i0262.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi>e</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>. Define ![images](images/c19-i0263.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">Q</mi><mo mathvariant="bold-italic">&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8796;</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mn>1</mn><mtext>sum</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow><mtext>sum</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> as the vector of total effective queue length of request buffers, specifically,

(19.21)![equation](images/c19-math-0021.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>Q</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mtext>sum</mtext> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script">F</mi> </mrow> </munder> <msubsup> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>Q</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mi>f</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi>e</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <munder> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script">F</mi> </mrow> </munder> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>D</mi> <mi>u</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msubsup> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>Q</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mi>f</mi> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math>

where ![images](images/c19-i0268.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow><mo>+</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c19-i0269.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c19-i0270.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>A</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><msub><mi>I</mi><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>d</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

The queuing process ![images](images/c19-i0271.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mi>u</mi><mtext>sum</mtext></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is stable if the following condition holds Neely ([2010](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0034)):

(19.25)![equation](images/c19-math-0025.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>Q</mi> <mo>&#175;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mtext>sum</mtext> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">lim</mi> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8594;</mo> <mi>&#8734;</mi> </mrow> </munder> <mfrac> <mn>1</mn> <mi>t</mi> </mfrac> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#964;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>0</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi> <mo stretchy="false">\[</mo> <msubsup> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>Q</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mtext>sum</mtext> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#964;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">\]</mo> <mo>&#60;</mo> <mi>&#8734;</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

As opposed to the system without prediction, in predictive scheduling, the system schedules the service rate ![images](images/c19-i0272.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> serving the request that has already or will arrive in the system according to a certain rate‐allocation discipline Huang et al. ([2016a](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0018)), such as FIFO, LIFO, or random discipline. We adopt a fully efficient scheduling policy for queues, which means:

(19.26)![equation](images/c19-math-0026.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <munder> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>f</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script">F</mi> </mrow> </munder> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>d</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>D</mi> <mi>u</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> </munderover> <msubsup> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>u</mi> <mi>f</mi> </mrow> <mi>d</mi> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mi>&#956;</mi> <mi>u</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>t</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

and where ![images](images/c19-i0273.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is defined in ([19.4](#c19.xhtml#c19-disp-0004)) and ![images](images/c19-i0274.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>&#956;</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math> if ![images](images/c19-i0275.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>y</mi><mrow><mi>h</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.

The problem formulation and analysis framework are the same as those with FEMOS in the previous sections. Based on this, we will show the theoretical and numerical analysis for PMOS in the following.

 

### 19.4.2 Theoretical Analysis

The term ![images](images/c19-i0276.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow><mtext>PMOS</mtext></msubsup></mrow></math> is defined as the long‐term expected average network throughput of PMOS, and ![images](images/c19-i0277.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow><mtext>PMOS</mtext></msubsup></mrow></math> is defined as the long‐term expected average queue length of users. The performance of PMOS is described in the following theorem.

The theorem shows that under the proposed PMOS algorithm, the lower bound of average network throughput increases inversely proportional to ![images](images/c19-i0282.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math>, which performs the optimality of the proposed algorithm. It also demonstrates that the upper bound of average queue length ![images](images/c19-i0283.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>Q</mi><mrow><mi>a</mi><mi>v</mi></mrow><mtext>PMOS</mtext></msubsup></mrow></math>, including the true backlog ![images](images/c19-i0284.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mrow><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and prediction queues ![images](images/c19-i0285.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msubsup><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>Q</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover></mrow><mrow><mi>u</mi><mi>f</mi></mrow><mi>d</mi></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>D</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, increases linearly with ![images](images/c19-i0286.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math>. Hence, there exists an ![images](images/c19-i0287.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> trade‐off between these two objects. Through adjusting ![images](images/c19-i0288.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math>, we can balance the network throughput and average delay.

In the following, we will show the average backlog reduction due to predictive scheduling in PMOS. To do so, we employ one theorem from Huang and Neely ([2011](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0017)), which shows that the queue vector of the network is within distance ![images](images/c19-i0289.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> from a fixed point. First, we define the following optimization problem:

(19.29)![equation](images/c19-math-0029.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mo>:</mo> <mspace width=".5em"/> <mspace width=".5em"/> <mi>g</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#8467;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>,</mo> <mspace width=".5em"/> <mspace width=".5em"/> <mspace width=".5em"/> <mspace width=".5em"/> <mtext>s.t.</mtext> <mspace width="1em"/> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#8467;</mi> <mo>&#8829;</mo> <mn>0</mn> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c19-i0290.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#8467;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is called the dual function with scaled objective (by ![images](images/c19-i0291.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math>) of the original problem that maximizes the average network throughput. The expression ![images](images/c19-i0292.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#8467;</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>l</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> U</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> is the Lagrange multiplier. The term ![images](images/c19-i0293.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#8467;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is defined as follows:

![equation](images/c19-math-0030.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#8467;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><munder><mi mathvariant="normal">inf</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></munder><mspace width=".5em"/><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mfenced open="{" close="}" separators=""><mrow><mi>V</mi><mi>&#966;</mi><mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#956;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mfenced><mo>+</mo><munder><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo><mrow><mi>u</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mi mathvariant="script">U</mi></mrow></munder><msub><mi>l</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mfenced open="\[" close="\]" separators=""><mrow><msub><mi>&#955;</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo>&#8722;</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mi>&#956;</mi><mi>u</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></mfenced></mrow></mfenced><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> 

Let ![images](images/c19-i0294.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#8467;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></math> denote the optimal solution of problem ([19.29](#c19.xhtml#c19-disp-0029)) and ![images](images/c19-i0295.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">&#8467;</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup></mrow></math> be either ![images](images/c19-i0296.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> or 0 according to Huang and Neely ([2011](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0017)). Now we have the following Theorem 3, which is listed as Theorem 1 in Huang and Neely ([2011](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0017)).

 

### 19.4.3 Numerical Analysis

The detailed simulation parameters are the same as those for the earlier FEMOS algorithm. We first evaluate the performance of PMOS under different prediction window sizes and compare it with the FEMOS algorithm in Zhao et al. ([2018](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0057)) without prediction (![images](images/c19-i0315.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>). The FIFO rate‐allocation discipline is adopted and the perfect prediction is considered, ![images](images/c19-i0316.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. The maximum network traffic arrival is set to ![images](images/c19-i0317.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>A</mi><mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow></math> kbits.

[Figure 19.5](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0005)a shows the average network throughput against ![images](images/c19-i0318.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> for PMOS with different prediction window sizes ![images](images/c19-i0319.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mn>5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>10</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>15</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math>. It can be observed from [Figure 19.5](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0005)a that the average network throughput increases and converges to the maximum value when ![images](images/c19-i0320.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> is sufficient large. In addition, [Figure 19.5](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0005)a also shows that PMOS with different prediction window sizes can achieve the same average network throughput.

[Figure 19.5](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0005)b presents the average delay per UT against ![images](images/c19-i0323.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> for PMOS. It can be observed that the average delay experienced by per UT increases linearly with the control parameter ![images](images/c19-i0324.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math>, which along with the observations in [Figure 19.5](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0005)a verifies the ![images](images/c19-i0325.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">/</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>,</mo><mi>O</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>V</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> trade‐off between average network throughput and average queue backlog derived in Theorem 1. This indicates that a proper ![images](images/c19-i0326.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>V</mi></mrow></math> should be chosen to balance these two objects. We also observe that PMOS always generates a smaller average delay than the multi‐tier operations scheduling without prediction (![images](images/c19-i0327.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>). As the predictive window size ![images](images/c19-i0328.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math> increases, the average delay per UT decreases almost linearly in ![images](images/c19-i0329.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>D</mi></mrow></math>, which is in accordance with the theoretical analysis in Theorem 4. The reason behind those observations is that the predictive information helps the operator design a better FAN assignment and bandwidth allocation strategy, which utilizes the network more efficiently.

 

## 19.5 A Multi‐tier Cost Model for User Scheduling in Fog Computing Networks

Although different aspects of user scheduling in multi‐tier fog computing networks have been widely discussed in the literature, such as Zhao et al. ([2018](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0057)), Shah‐Mansouri and Wong ([2018](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0039)), Liu et al. ([2018b,a](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0027)), the effective user scheduling scheme still faces challenges, especially when the cost model is considered. Generally, the FCN is operated by a telecom operator that signs a service contract with UTs, while the FANs belong to different individuals. To better motivate FANs to share resources and anticipate in caching, the cost model, especially for FANs, should be taken into consideration.

 

### 19.5.1 System Model and Problem Formulation

 

#### System Model

Just like [Figure 19.1](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0001), a multi‐tier fog computing network consisting of one FCN, ![images](images/c19-i0330.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math> FANs, and ![images](images/c19-i0331.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> UTs is considered. As mentioned, the FCN is operated by a telecom service provider, which provides services to ![images](images/c19-i0332.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math> UTs, i.e. service subscribers, while the FANs belong to different individual owners. To reduce service delay and improve QoS, the FCN is willing to pay money to FANs if they provide services to UTs. For ease of expression, we take caching as an example in the following context. [1](#c19.xhtml#c19-note-0001) In the fog‐enabled caching network, the FCN can allocate files to FANs during off‐peak time, i.e. file placement, and thus the UTs can be associated with proper FANs or FCN to download files during peak time, i.e. user scheduling.

M</mi></mrow></math>. Specifically, if ![images](images/c19-i0361.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, the requested file of UT ![images](images/c19-i0362.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is available at FAN ![images](images/c19-i0363.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>; otherwise, ![images](images/c19-i0364.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>b</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>. If ![images](images/c19-i0365.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, UT ![images](images/c19-i0366.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> can connect to FAN ![images](images/c19-i0367.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>; otherwise, ![images](images/c19-i0368.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>c</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></math>.

Similar to many previous works, such as Shah‐Mansouri and Wong ([2018](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0039)), Liu et al. ([2018b, 2018](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0029)), Yang et al. ([2018d](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0051)), a quasi‐static scenario, wherein the UTs remain unchanged during a user scheduling interval, is assumed.

 

#### Cost Model

 

##### *Service Delay*

If UT ![images](images/c19-i0369.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> is associated with FAN ![images](images/c19-i0370.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>, the downloading delay of a file can be expressed as

(19.33)![equation](images/c19-math-0034.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>m</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mi>L</mi> <mrow> <msub> <mi>R</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>m</mi> </mrow> </msub> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c19-i0371.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is the transmission rate from FAN ![images](images/c19-i0372.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math> to UT ![images](images/c19-i0373.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>.

If UT ![images](images/c19-i0374.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> cannot obtain the requested file from neighboring FANs or it is more cost‐effective to get the file from FCN, UT ![images](images/c19-i0375.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> will be associated with FCN. Similarly, the downloading delay of a file can be written as

##### *Payment*

Just like the payment scheme for online advertisement, i.e. cost per click Moon and Kwon ([2011](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0033)), the FANs are assumed to charge by usage amounts or downloads. To motivate more UTs to download files from them, and thus earn more revenue, the FANs set their prices as an inverse demand function Lã et al. ([2016](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0023)). Assume a linear inverse demand function, and the price for single download or the payment for downloading a file from FANs is given by

(19.35)![equation](images/c19-math-0036.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>&#945;</mi> <mi>m</mi> </msub> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>&#946;</mi> <mi>m</mi> </msub> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mi>N</mi> </munderover> <msub> <mi>a</mi> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi>m</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <mo>&#8704;</mo> <mi>m</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c19-i0378.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c19-i0379.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> are two price‐related constants set by FAN ![images](images/c19-i0380.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>m</mi></mrow></math>. It is worth noting that the FCN pays money to FANs for UTs downloading files from them.

If the UTs download files from the FCN, the FCN will pay extra for electric power consumption. Without loss of generality, a constant payment or cost ![images](images/c19-i0381.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi></mrow></math> per download is considered here.

If a UT is more sensitive to delay, or a UT subscribes to better services, ![images](images/c19-i0385.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> is higher; otherwise, ![images](images/c19-i0386.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> may be lower.

Constraints ([19.37b](#c19.xhtml#c19-disp-0039)) and ([19.37c](#c19.xhtml#c19-disp-0040)) ensure that each UT is associated with only one FAN or FCN. Constraint ([19.37d](#c19.xhtml#c19-disp-0041)) guarantees that each UT is associated with the FANs that cache its requested file. Constraint ([19.37e](#c19.xhtml#c19-disp-0042)) assures that each UT is associated with the FANs to which it can connect.

The optimization problem ([19.37a](#c19.xhtml#c19-disp-0038)) is an NP‐hard combinatorial problem, which has a high computational complexity. In the following section, we will reformulate the problem into a user scheduling game, which can be proven to be a potential game, and thus can be effectively solved by a distributed algorithm called COUS.

display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>.

As stated in Theorem 5, any asynchronous better or best response update process is guaranteed to reach a pure‐strategy NE within a finite number of iterations. By employing such a property, a distributed user scheduling algorithm called the COUS algorithm can be obtained and shown in Algorithm 2 according to Chen et al. ([2016b](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0008)).

 

#### Price of Anarchy

In game theory, price of anarchy (PoA) is most often used to evaluate the efficiency of an NE solution. It answers the question of how far the overall performance of an NE is from the socially optimal solution. To be specific, let ![images](images/c19-i0400.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#915;</mi></mrow></math> be the set of NEs of the user scheduling game ![images](images/c19-i0401.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>G</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c19-i0402.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi><mo>&#42;</mo></msup><mo>=</mo><msup><mrow><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mn>2</mn><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8943;</mi><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mi>N</mi><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo><mi>T</mi></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow><mi>T</mi></msup></mrow></math> be the centralized optimal solution that minimizes the system cost. Then, the PoA is defined as

![](images/c19-gra-0002.png)(19.42)![equation](images/c19-math-0047.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi>P</mi> <mi>o</mi> <mi>A</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mfrac> <mrow> <munder> <mi mathvariant="normal">max</mi> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#915;</mi> </mrow> </munder> <munder> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> N</mi> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mi>O</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <munder> <mo movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> <mrow> <mi>n</mi> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> N</mi> </mrow> </munder> <msub> <mi>O</mi> <mi>n</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold">A</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math>

### 19.5.3 Performance Evaluation

 

#### Simulation Setup

There are a total of ![images](images/c19-i0408.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> files, each of which is 10 Mbits, and ![images](images/c19-i0409.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> FANs, each of which can cache 4 random files. Assume that the UTs communicate with FCN and FANs via long‐term evolution (LTE). As measured in Kwak et al. ([2015](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0022)), the average data rate of LTE is 5.85 Mbps, and thus the data rate between FANs and UTs, i.e. ![images](images/c19-i0410.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, is randomly distributed in ![images](images/c19-i0411.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>5.35</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6.35</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> Mbps. Furthermore, generally, we have ![images](images/c19-i0412.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub><mo>&#60;</mo><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></math> Liu et al. ([2018a](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0027)), and thus the data rate between FCN and UTs, i.e. ![images](images/c19-i0413.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>R</mi><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>,</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></math>, is randomly selected from ![images](images/c19-i0414.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>4.35</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>5.35</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> Mbps. Set ![images](images/c19-i0415.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#947;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math>, while ![images](images/c19-i0416.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#945;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> is uniformly distributed over ![images](images/c19-i0417.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>5.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>6.5</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>. To guarantee that the revenues of FANs can increase with increasing downloads, ![images](images/c19-i0418.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#946;</mi><mi>m</mi></msub></mrow></math> is randomly chosen from ![images](images/c19-i0419.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0.05</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> in our simulation. In addition, ![images](images/c19-i0420.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c19-i0421.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow><mi>n</mi><mi>C</mi></msubsup></mrow></math> are uniformly and randomly selected from ![images](images/c19-i0422.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0.5</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c19-i0423.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mn>0.1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>0.2</mn><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math>, respectively. All numerical results are averaged over 500 simulation trials. In each simulation trial, the requested file of each UT is randomly determined.

 

#### Overall Cost

[Figure 19.6](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0006) compares our proposed COUS algorithm with the following baseline solutions in terms of the overall cost:

*   *Optimal scheduling (Optimal)*: The near‐optimal solution to the overall cost minimization is obtained, utilizing the Cross Entropy method Rubinstein and Kroese ([2004](#c19.xhtml#c19-bib-0038)).
*   *Random scheduling (Random)*: Each UT is randomly associated with FCN or one FAN.
*   *FCN scheduling (FCN)*: Each UT is associated with FCN.

As demonstrated in [Figure 19.6](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0006), the overall cost increases as the number of UTs increases, and the COUS algorithm can always offer near‐optimal performance. The COUS algorithm shows better performance than the random scheduling scheme and the FCN scheduling scheme, especially when the number of UTs is large.

#### Average Cost

[Figure 19.7](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0007) shows the average cost with different number of UTs, under different payment schemes. We compare the solution achieved by our payment scheme and algorithm with the optimal solution (Fixed) under the fixed payment scheme, where the FANs set a fixed price for a single download, regardless of downloads.

![Figure 19.8 Revenue of all FANs with different UTs.](images/c19f008.jpg)

[Figure 19.8](#c19.xhtml#R_c19-fig-0008) Revenue of all FANs with different UTs.

As shown in [Figure 19.7](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0007), the average cost of our dynamic scheme is smaller than that of the fixed scheme. And the average cost offered by the dynamic scheme decreases with the increase in UTs, while the average cost achieved by fixed scheme almost remains the same, in despite of the number of UTs.

 

#### Service Revenue

[Figure 19.8](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0008) demonstrates the revenue of all FANs with different numbers of UTs under the COUS algorithm and the fixed scheme, respectively. As demonstrated in [Figure 19.8](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0008), the revenue of all FANs offered by the dynamic scheme is larger than that offered by the fixed scheme. Moreover, the revenues of all FANs offered by the dynamic scheme and the fixed scheme increase as the number of UTs increases, while the revenue of all FANs offered by our proposed dynamic scheme shows a faster growth trend.

[Figures 19.7](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0007) and [19.8](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0008) show a win‐win outcome for the proposed cost model, or dynamic payment scheme. To be specific, the proposed dynamic payment scheme can not only offer lower average cost for FCN, but also provide higher revenues for FANs, and this advantage becomes increasingly prominent as the number of UTs increases.

 

#### Workload Distribution

[Figure 19.9](#c19.xhtml#c19-fig-0009) illustrates the number of UTs served by different FANs under different payment schemes when ![images](images/c19-i0425.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>50</mn></mrow></math>. It can be seen that our proposed dynamic payment scheme will incur unfair workload distribution among different FANs, compared with the fixed payment scheme.

 

## 19.6 Conclusion

In this chapter, we investigated online multi‐tier operations scheduling in fog‐enabled network architecture with heterogeneous node capabilities and dynamic wireless network conditions. A low‐complexity online algorithm based on Lyapunov optimization was proposed. Performance analysis, as well as simulations, explicitly characterized the trade‐offs between average network throughput and service delay, and affirmed the benefit of centralized assignment of access node and dynamic online bandwidth allocation. Following this, we investigated the proactive FAN assignment and resource management problem, given the availability of predictive information, and proposed a predictive scheduling‐based online algorithm to reduce service delay. In the end, a unified multi‐tier cost model, including the service delay and a linear inverse demand dynamic payment scheme, was proposed to motivate the FANs for resources sharing. Furthermore, the COUS algorithm, based on a potential game, was provided to show how to minimize the overall cost for the FCN.
