# 20  
Physical‐Layer Location Verification by Machine Learning

*Stefano Tomasin Alessandro Brighente Francesco Formaggio and Gabriele Ruvoletto*

*Department of Information Engineering, University of Padova, Padova, Italy*

 

Information on the position of wireless communication devices is nowadays used for a variety of services, e.g. social networking, gaming, content distribution systems, and navigation. Position‐related applications relying only on information reported by the device itself can be easily modified by a malicious user tampering with either the software or the global navigation satellite system (GNSS) receiver.

In order to be effective against these attacks, location verification systems verify the user position independently of the reported one. In particular, *in region location verification* (IRLV) aims at assessing if the user is in a specific authorized area or *region of interest* (ROI). To this end, the network examines the *features* of the physical‐layer channel over which communications occur. While in general any channel feature related to user position – such as components related to line‐of‐sight reception, reflections, scattering, and Doppler phenomena – could be exploited, this chapter focuses on the attenuation at various frequencies of a broadband channel, thus taking into account multi‐path, path loss, shadowing, and fading. Indeed, some of these characteristics (such as fading) actually act as a disturbance of the channel path‐loss, which most appropriately identifies the position.

IRLV can be seen as a hypothesis‐testing problem between the two hypotheses of the device being inside or outside the ROI. Due to the mentioned disturbances, the test outcome is affected by two types of error: false alarms (FAs), occurring when a user inside the ROI is classified as being outside; and misdetections (MDs), occurring when a user outside the ROI is classified as being inside. The optimal[1](#c20.xhtml#c20-note-0001) test is given by the Neyman‐Pearson (NP) theorem by Neyman et al. ([1933](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0008)).

In order to perform the NP test, the probability density functions (PDFs) of the channel features under both hypotheses are needed. However, closed‐form expressions of the PDFs may not be immediately available, e.g. upon deployment in a new environment or when the environment is changing over time. In this context, machine learning (ML) approaches provide a suitable solution, as discussed by Brighente et al. ([2018](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0004)): during the learning phase, the channel features for trusted devices positioned both inside and outside the ROI are estimated and suitable machines are trained in order to classify the features into the two classes. Among ML classification solutions, this chapter focuses on those using neural networks (NNs) and support vector machines (SVMs) (see Bishop ([2006](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0003)) for an introduction to these topics).

 

### Literature Survey

A number of works on IRLV assume that feature measurements are not affected by errors and are related to the device position in a deterministic way, thus giving neither FAs nor MDs. Sastry et al. ([2003](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0011)) first studied the IRLV problem, where the access points (APs) of the verification network measure the round‐trip time (related to AP–device distance) of ultrasound links with the device under test. Using an empirical approach, the location is verified if the round‐trip time is below a threshold computed according to the claimed user position. Vora and Nesterenko ([2006](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0017)) exploit radio waves, as the device sends a sequence of messages with increasing power: a user is classified as inside the ROI if APs inside the ROI detect messages earlier than APs outside it. Singelee and Preneel ([2005](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0013)) use distance bounding protocols (DBPs) run in cascade by each AP to upper‐bound the distance between the APs and the tested device, showing that with at least three APs and triangulation techniques, accurate IRLV can be obtained. Song et al. ([2008](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0014)) use DBPs in the context of vehicular ad hoc networks where IRLV protects from GNSS spoofing.

The possibility of test errors is considered by Wei and Guan ([2013](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0018)), who adopt a strategy similar to that of Vora and Nesterenko ([2006](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0017)) in a sensor network context. In this case, the user is classified inside the ROI if the probability of this event, given the observed features, is higher than a threshold, thus again the PDF of the channel features must be available. Yan et al. ([2016](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0019)) use the NP test under both a more complex model (the received power includes Gaussian spatially correlated shadowing) and more sophisticated attacks (the attacker can adjust the transmission power). In Brighente et al. ([2018](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0004)) the application of ML strategies to the IRLV problem is first introduced, and the connections of both NN and SVM classifiers to the NP test are established.

The ML approach has been already pursued in a problem closely related to IRLV, i.e. *user authentication*, aiming at verifying if a message is coming from the claimed sender by checking whether it goes through the same channel as previously authenticated messages. In this context, Pei et al. ([2014](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0009)) use three channel features (the channel impulse response, the received signal strength, and the time of arrival), and SVM or the linear Fisher's discriminant analysis algorithm (see Fukunaga ([2013](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0005))) are adopted. Abyaneh et al. ([2018](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0002)), instead, apply a NN classifier on the received signal.

 

### Chapter Objective and Outline

This chapter analyzes ML algorithms for IRLV with emphasis on multiple‐layer NN and SVM approaches. As these solutions efficiently match the performance of the NP hypothesis test (see Brighente et al. ([2018](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0004))) at convergence, they turn out to be both effective and efficient in terms of computational complexity, resource consumption, and processing latency.

The rest of the chapter is organized as follows. [Section 20.1](#c20.xhtml#c20-sec-0004) describes the IRLV system model and revises the optimal hypothesis testing framework. [Section 20.2](#c20.xhtml#c20-sec-0006) presents the ML IRLV procedure and quickly reviews the fundamentals of NNs and SVMs. We also discuss the optimality of ML‐based classification. [Section 20.3](#c20.xhtml#c20-sec-0010) reviews theoretical results on the complexity‐performance trade‐off of ML solutions, which will be used to assess performance of methods based on NNs. [Section 20.4](#c20.xhtml#c20-sec-0017) presents results obtained over a dataset of experimental data with attenuation values of a cellular system; and in the last section we make offer further discussion and conclusions.

 

## 20.1 IRLV by Wireless Channel Features

The IRLV reference scenario is shown in [Figure 20.1](#c20.xhtml#c20-fig-0001), where a set of ![images](images/c20-i0001.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>AP</mtext></msub></mrow></math> APs measure the features of AP channels to user equipment (UE), whose position must be verified by the IRLV system.

The broadband channel is described by ![images](images/c20-i0002.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math> attenuation values at different frequencies,[2](#c20.xhtml#c20-note-0002) and ![images](images/c20-i0003.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> denotes the measured attenuation at the ![images](images/c20-i0004.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mtext>th</mtext></msup></mrow></math> AP on frequency ![images](images/c20-i0005.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>. Vector ![images](images/c20-i0006.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>AP</mtext></msub></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>AP</mtext></msub></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>Q</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> collects the attenuation values at all APs in all frequencies. In a Rayleigh fading‐channel environment comprising path loss, shadowing, and fading, the channel gain (including its uniformly distributed phase ![images](images/c20-i0007.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#958;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>) ![images](images/c20-i0008.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msqrt><mrow><msubsup><mi>a</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></msqrt><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>j</mi><msubsup><mi>&#958;</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></msup></mrow></math> is a complex Gaussian‐distributed random variable. Its mean is zero, while its variance is ![images](images/c20-i0009.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>a</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></msubsup><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mtext>PL</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><msup><mi>e</mi><mi>s</mi></msup></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c20-i0010.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>P</mi><mrow><mtext>PL</mtext><mo>,</mo><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi>f</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> is the path loss coefficient; ![images](images/c20-i0011.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>s</mi></mrow></math> is the zero‐mean Gaussian distributed shadowing component, having variance ![images](images/c20-i0012.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math>, where we omitted the dependence on position and frequency for the sake of simpler notation. We first observe that various components of the attenuation are specifically related to the UE's (and APs') position. This is the case of path loss and shadowing, which are slowly time‐varying and can thus be used for IRLV of users moving in and out of the ROI over a long time.

![Figure 20.1 Typical in‐region location verification scenario.](images/c20f001.jpg)

[Figure 20.1](#c20.xhtml#R_c20-fig-0001) Typical in‐region location verification scenario.

The path loss of a wireless link is directly related to the distance between the transmitter and the receiver. In particular, let ![images](images/c20-i0013.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext>AP</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> be the position of AP ![images](images/c20-i0014.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>AP</mtext></msub></mrow></math>, and similarly let ![images](images/c20-i0015.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mtext>UE</mtext></msub></mrow></math> be the true position of the UE under verification. Finally, let ![images](images/c20-i0016.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi><mtext>UE</mtext></msub><mo>,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi></mrow><mrow><mtext>AP</mtext></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>n</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> be the distance between the UE and AP ![images](images/c20-i0017.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math>. With reference to the scenario described by 3GPP ([2018](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0001)), two types of links are considered: line of sight (LOS) and non‐LOS. For a LOS link, the path loss in dB can be modeled as

(20.1)![equation](images/c20-math-0001.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>P</mi> <mrow> <mtext>PL&#8211;LOS</mtext> <mo>,</mo> <mi>n</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mn>10</mn> <mi>&#957;</mi> <mspace width=".2em"/> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mn>10</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mn>4</mn> <mi>&#960;</mi> <mi>L</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mtext>UE</mtext> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mtext>AP</mtext> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mi>c</mi> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c20-i0018.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi></mrow></math> is the path loss coefficient and ![images](images/c20-i0019.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>c</mi></mrow></math> is the speed of light. For a non‐LOS link we have instead

(20.2)![equation](images/c20-math-0002.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>P</mi> <mrow> <mtext>PL&#8211;NLOS</mtext> <mo>,</mo> <mi>n</mi> </mrow> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <mn>40</mn> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mn>10</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mfrac> <mrow> <mi>L</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msub> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mtext>UE</mtext> </msub> <mo>,</mo> <msubsup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">x</mi> <mtext>AP</mtext> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>n</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <msup> <mn>0</mn> <mn>3</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mn>21</mn> <mspace width="0.1em"/> <msub> <mi mathvariant="normal">log</mi> <mn>10</mn> </msub> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mi>f</mi> <mi>i</mi> </msub> </mrow> <mrow> <mn>1</mn> <msup> <mn>0</mn> <mn>6</mn> </msup> </mrow> </mfrac> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>+</mo> <mn>80</mn> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Note that shadowing is only statistically related to the distance, and thus it does not provide a direct information on the position. Instead, shadowing can also be seen as noise over the path loss component of the attenuation, thus complicating IRLV. Moreover, fading and measurement noise further prevent directly mapping the attenuation values into distances. Therefore, for given positions of both UE and APs, the measured attenuation vector ![images](images/c20-i0020.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi></mrow></math> is a random vector and any IRLV solution will be in general affected by both FA and MD errors.

 

### 20.1.1 Optimal Test

The IRLV problem can be formulated as a hypothesis‐testing problem between two hypotheses: ![images](images/c20-i0021.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math>, the UE is transmitting from inside the ROI; and ![images](images/c20-i0022.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math>, the UE is transmitting from outside the ROI.

Let ![images](images/c20-i0023.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> be the decision made by the IRLV system on the two hypotheses, whereas ![images](images/c20-i0024.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mn>0</mn></msub><mo>,</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> is the ground truth, i.e. the effective location of the UE. We also denote the FA probability as ![images](images/c20-i0025.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>FA</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> and the MD probability as ![images](images/c20-i0026.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mtext>MD</mtext></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>.

Let ![images](images/c20-i0027.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>p</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo><msub><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi></mrow><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> be the PDF of attenuation vectors conditioned to the position of the UE. The log‐likelihood ratio (LLR) is defined as the ratio between the two conditioned PDFs for a certain attenuation vector ![images](images/c20-i0028.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi></mrow></math>, i.e.

[(20.3)](#c20.xhtml#c20-R_disp-0003)![equation](images/c20-math-0003.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script">&#8499;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">ln</mi> <mfrac> <mrow> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> </mrow> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>p</mi> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> </mrow> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> </mrow> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </mfrac> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

According to the NP theorem, the most powerful test on an observed attenuation vector ![images](images/c20-i0029.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi></mrow></math> is obtained by comparing ![images](images/c20-i0030.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script"> M</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> with a threshold value ![images](images/c20-i0031.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="normal">&#923;</mi></mrow></math>, obtaining the test function

(20.4)![equation](images/c20-math-0004.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> </mrow> <mo>&#770;</mo> </mover> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> </mrow> <mn>0</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mtext>if</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi mathvariant="script">&#8499;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8805;</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#923;</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> </mrow> <mn>1</mn> </msub> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mtext>if</mtext> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mi mathvariant="script">&#8499;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#60;</mo> <mi mathvariant="normal">&#923;</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> 

This procedure provides the minimum MD probability for a given FA probability.

 

## 20.2 ML Classification for IRLV

As the NP theorem requires the knowledge of the PDFs of the attenuation vectors conditioned on ![images](images/c20-i0032.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c20-i0033.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>, which can be hard to obtain, a ML approach can be adopted, operating in two phases:

1.  1\. *Learning phase*: The APs collect attenuation vectors from a trusted UE moving both inside and outside the ROI. The UE reports its position to the APs, so that the network can learn how to classify the attenuations, by means of a suitable test function, according to the provided ground truth of the hypothesis.
2.  2\. *Exploitation phase*: In order to test the location of an untrusted UE, the IRLV system collects attenuation values from the APs and gives them to the test function designed in the learning phase.

During the learning phase, the APs collect ![images](images/c20-i0034.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math> attenuation values. Since the channel is affected by fading, we consider ![images](images/c20-i0035.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></mrow></math> fading realizations for each fixed spatial position ![images](images/c20-i0036.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>s</mi></msub></mrow></math>, so that ![images](images/c20-i0037.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mi>s</mi></msub><mo>&#183;</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></msub></mrow></math>.

The details of the two phases are now described. When collecting training attenuation vectors ![images](images/c20-i0038.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c20-i0039.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>, we associate them with *labels* ![images](images/c20-i0040.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub></mrow></math>, ![images](images/c20-i0041.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>.</mo><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>, where ![images](images/c20-i0042.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> if the trusted UE is inside the ROI, and ![images](images/c20-i0043.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>&#8467;</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> if the trusted UE is outside the ROI. With these settings, the IRLV system designs the test function

(20.5)![equation](images/c20-math-0005.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8712;</mo> <mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo>,</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo> </mrow> </math> 

that provides a decision ![images](images/c20-i0044.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover></mrow></math> (![images](images/c20-i0045.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></mrow></math> for ![images](images/c20-i0046.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c20-i0047.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mo>&#770;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><msub><mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> for ![images](images/c20-i0048.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>) for each attenuation vector ![images](images/c20-i0049.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi></mrow></math>. This function is then used to make a decision in the exploitation phase. Note that this solution does not explicitly evaluate the PDF and the LLR; rather it directly implements the test function with a ML algorithm.

 

### 20.2.1 Neural Networks

A NN is a function ![images](images/c20-i0050.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> that maps an ![images](images/c20-i0051.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>‐size input vector to an ![images](images/c20-i0052.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi></mrow></math>‐size output vector, i.e. ![images](images/c20-i0053.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>N</mi></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>M</mi></msup></mrow></math>. Function ![images](images/c20-i0054.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>g</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is implemented as the cascade of multiple functions that can be represented by a graph where nodes (*neurons*) are the functions whose input and output are represented by the connecting edges (*connections*).

Neurons are organized in ![images](images/c20-i0055.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi></mrow></math> layers, the first layer being defined as the *input* layer, the last as the *output* layer, and all other layers as *hidden layers*. The neurons of layer ![images](images/c20-i0056.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi></mrow></math> are connected only to those of the two adjacent layers, and we focus on an implementation of the NN without loops, as shown in [Figure 20.2](#c20.xhtml#c20-fig-0002).

All neurons of layer ![images](images/c20-i0059.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi></mrow></math> implement the same function. In particular, at neuron ![images](images/c20-i0060.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow></math> of layer ![images](images/c20-i0061.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#8467;</mi></mrow></math>, the elements of output vector ![images](images/c20-i0062.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup></mrow></math> of the previous layer are linearly combined with weights ![images](images/c20-i0063.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, and then a scalar bias ![images](images/c20-i0064.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> is added. The result of these operations is the input of the *activation function* ![images](images/c20-i0065.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#968;</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msup><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> (the same for all neurons of the same layer). The output of the ![images](images/c20-i0066.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>n</mi><mtext>th</mtext></msup></mrow></math> neuron at the ![images](images/c20-i0067.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msup><mi>&#8467;</mi><mtext>th</mtext></msup></mrow></math> layer is therefore

(20.6)![equation](images/c20-math-0006.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi>y</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#8467;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi>&#968;</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#8467;</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mfenced open="(" close=")" separators=""> <mrow> <msubsup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#8467;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">y</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#8467;</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msup> <mo>+</mo> <msubsup> <mi>b</mi> <mi>n</mi> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#8467;</mi> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msubsup> </mrow> </mfenced> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> ![Figure 20.2 Example of a neural network architecture with five input values and images layers with images neurons in the hidden layers.](images/c20f002.jpg)

[Figure 20.2](#c20.xhtml#R_c20-fig-0002) Example of a neural network architecture with five input values and ![images](images/c20-i0057.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>L</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>4</mn></mrow></math> layers with ![images](images/c20-i0058.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>5</mn></mrow></math> neurons in the hidden layers.

During training, weights ![images](images/c20-i0068.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>n</mi></mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> and biases ![images](images/c20-i0069.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>b</mi><mi>n</mi><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>&#8467;</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> are selected in order to minimize a suitably chosen *loss function* over the *training set*. The parameters optimization is typically based on gradient algorithms. Usually the *activation functions* are sigmoids, which generate a single output.

For the IRLV problem, the input to the NN is the ![images](images/c20-i0070.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>AP</mtext></msub><mi>Q</mi></mrow></math>‐size attenuation vector ![images](images/c20-i0071.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi></mrow></math> and the output is a single (![images](images/c20-i0072.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>M</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow></math>) value ![images](images/c20-i0073.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math>, denoting the decision made. The NN output is then compared against a threshold ![images](images/c20-i0074.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math>, providing the decision[3](#c20.xhtml#c20-note-0003)

[(20.7)](#c20.xhtml#c20-R_disp-0007)![equation](images/c20-math-0007.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mfenced open="{" close="" separators=""> <mrow> <mtable columnalign="left"> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mover accent="true"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#62;</mo> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mtd> </mtr> <mtr> <mtd class="array"> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mtd> <mtd class="array"> <mover accent="true"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8804;</mo> <mi>&#955;</mi> <mo>.</mo> </mtd> </mtr> </mtable> </mrow> </mfenced> </mrow> </math> 

Collecting into vectors ![images](images/c20-i0075.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c20-i0076.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi></mrow></math> all the weights and bias factors, and using the mean square error (MSE) as loss function, the optimization problem for the NN training can be written as

[(20.8)](#c20.xhtml#c20-R_disp-0008)![equation](images/c20-math-0008.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <mo>,</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi> <mo>&#42;</mo> </msup> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mtext>argmin</mtext> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">W</mi> <mo>,</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">b</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> </mrow> </msub> <munderover> <mrow> <mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo> </mrow> <mrow> <mi>&#8467;</mi> <mo>=</mo> <mn>1</mn> </mrow> <mrow> <msub> <mi>k</mi> <mi>t</mi> </msub> </mrow> </munderover> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mover accent="true"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#94;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi>&#8467;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <msub> <mi>t</mi> <mi>&#8467;</mi> </msub> <msup> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mn>2</mn> </msup> <mspace width="0.3em"/> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math>  

### 20.2.2 Support Vector Machines

A SVM used for classification purposes is again a function that maps an ![images](images/c20-i0077.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>N</mi></mrow></math>‐dimensional input into a scalar. In particular, the operations performed by an SVM can be described as

[(20.9)](#c20.xhtml#c20-R_disp-0009)![equation](images/c20-math-0009.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <mover accent="true"> <mi>t</mi> <mo>&#732;</mo> </mover> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <msup> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi> <mi>T</mi> </msup> <mi>&#966;</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>+</mo> <mi>b</mi> <mo>,</mo> </mrow> </math> 

where ![images](images/c20-i0078.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>AP</mtext></msub></mrow></msup><mo>&#8594;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>K</mi></msup></mrow></math> is a fixed *feature‐space transformation function*, ![images](images/c20-i0079.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mo>&#8712;</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="double-struck">R</mi><mi>K</mi></msup></mrow></math> is the weight vector, and ![images](images/c20-i0080.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> is a bias parameter. As seen for NNs, in order to obtain a binary decision from the soft (continuous value) given by Eq. ([20.9](#c20.xhtml#c20-disp-0009)), we use Eq. ([20.7](#c20.xhtml#c20-disp-0007)), where now ![images](images/c20-i0081.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>y</mi><mn>1</mn><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>L</mi><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> is replaced by ![images](images/c20-i0082.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#732;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> obtained by Eq. ([20.9](#c20.xhtml#c20-disp-0009)). In Eq. ([20.9](#c20.xhtml#c20-disp-0009)), function ![images](images/c20-i0083.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mo>&#183;</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is fixed (see Goodfellow et al. ([2016](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0007))), while both vector ![images](images/c20-i0084.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi></mrow></math> and scalar ![images](images/c20-i0085.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>b</mi></mrow></math> are properly chosen according to the specific modeled problem.

The design of the SVM parameters is obtained by minimizing various objective functions. *Maximum margin* classifiers aim at maximizing the margin between the two classes, and thus the design problem is

(20.10a)![equation](images/c20-math-0010.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></munder><mspace width="1em"/><mi>&#969;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8796;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></munderover><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></math> (20.10b)![equation](images/c20-math-0011.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>&#8805;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>&#8722;</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>,</mo></mrow></math> 

where ![images](images/c20-i0086.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> is a hyper‐parameter. Inequalities in the constraints lead to a quadratic programming problem, typically solved in its dual version, where the feature function is implicitly defined by the *kernel*. In the least squares SVM (LS‐SVM) by Suykens and Vandewalle ([1999](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0015)), instead of maximizing the margin, the LS error is minimized, providing the problem

(20.11a)![equation](images/c20-math-0012.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><munder><mi>min</mi><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi></mrow></munder><mspace width="1em"/><mi>&#969;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8796;</mo><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi><mfrac><mn>1</mn><mn>2</mn></mfrac><munderover><mrow><mo stretchy="false" movablelimits="false">&#8721;</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></munderover><msubsup><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup></mrow></math> (20.11b)![equation](images/c20-math-0013.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>e</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><msub><mi>t</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><msup><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">w</mi><mi>T</mi></msup><mi>&#966;</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>i</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>+</mo><mi>b</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mspace width="1em"/><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mi>&#8230;</mi><mo>,</mo><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msub><mspace width="0.3em"/><mo>.</mo></mrow></math> 

Equality constraints in Eq. (20.11) yield a linear system of equations in the optimization values. Ye and Xiong ([2007](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0020)) have shown that both SVM and LS‐SVM are equivalent under mild conditions.

 

### 20.2.3 ML Classification Optimality

A first question to address is whether the ML approaches are somehow equivalent to the optimal NP approach. Note that the performance of the ML approaches significantly depend on (i) the complexity/configuration of the model, e.g. the neurons of the NN or the feature‐space transformation function, and (ii) the size/type, e.g. the balance between the attenuations in the two classes of the training set.

Thus, we expect to achieve the performance of NP test only for an infinite‐size training set and for sufficiently (infinite) complex models. Indeed, Brighente et al. ([2018](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0004)) have shown that under these asymptotic conditions both the NN‐ and LS‐SVM‐based tests achieve the performance of the NP test.

In order to prove this, a MSE criterion is used for NN design, which Ruck et al. ([1990](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0010)) have shown to converge to the minimum MSE approximation of the Bayes optimal discriminant function

(20.12)![equation](images/c20-math-0014.png)<math display="block" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" overflow="scroll"> <mrow> <msub> <mi>g</mi> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>=</mo> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> </mrow> <mn>0</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>&#8722;</mo> <mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi> <mo stretchy="false">(</mo> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> <mo>=</mo> <msub> <mrow> <mi mathvariant="script"> H</mi> </mrow> <mn>1</mn> </msub> <mo stretchy="false">&#124;</mo> <mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi> <mo stretchy="false">)</mo> <mo>.</mo> </mrow> </math> 

Then, by algebraic manipulations on the thresholding of ![images](images/c20-i0087.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>g</mi><mn>0</mn></msub><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#62;</mo><mi>&#955;</mi></mrow></math>, as from Eq. ([20.7](#c20.xhtml#c20-disp-0007)), we obtain a thresholding on the LLR of Eq. ([20.3](#c20.xhtml#c20-disp-0003)), as done in the NP test.

Similarly, starting from the LS optimization criterion of the SVM, it is possible to show first that it is equivalent to the MSE optimization of a parametric function similar to Eq. ([20.8](#c20.xhtml#c20-disp-0008)), from which, using the same reasoning for the MSE‐designed NN, we conclude that LS‐SVM is asymptotically equivalent to the optimal NP approach.

 

## 20.3 Learning Phase Convergence

A key issue for ML approaches is the convergence speed of the training phase: while having a larger training set yields better tuning of the machine parameters, the complexity (and time) entailed by training also increases. Here we first recall some theoretical bounds on the training set size as a function of the desired classification accuracy, and then present some numerical results for the considered IRLV scenario.

 

### 20.3.1 Fundamental Learning Theorem

The performance of a learning algorithm can be analyzed within the *probably approximately correct* (PAC) learning framework. To this end, we first recall two fundamental concepts: the PAC learnability and the Vapnik‐Chervonensky (VC) dimension.

About the PAC learnability, let ![images](images/c20-i0088.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">E</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>&#8800;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> be the error event of a wrong decision, where ![images](images/c20-i0089.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>t</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math> is the ground truth associated with the UE giving the attenuation vector ![images](images/c20-i0090.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi></mrow></math>. For a parametric test function ![images](images/c20-i0091.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></math>, the error probability ![images](images/c20-i0092.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow></msub><mo>=</mo><mi mathvariant="double-struck">P</mi><mo stretchy="false">\[</mo><mi mathvariant="script">E</mi><mo stretchy="false">\]</mo></mrow></math> obtained in the exploitation phase depends on both the test function and the specific training set, and thus ![images](images/c20-i0093.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>&#960;</mi><mrow><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover></mrow></msub></mrow></math> is itself a random variable. Note also that this theory refers generically to *errors*, while the distinction between MDs and FAs is instead relevant for the IRLV problem. Let ![images](images/c20-i0094.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow></math> be the set of possible attenuations and ![images](images/c20-i0095.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">T</mi><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mover accent="true"><mi>t</mi><mo>&#94;</mo></mover><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi mathvariant="bold-italic">a</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>:</mo><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi><mo>&#8594;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#123;</mo><mo>&#8722;</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo><mo stretchy="false">&#125;</mo></mrow></math> a set of test functions defined on ![images](images/c20-i0096.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi mathvariant="script">A</mi></mrow></math>.

The VC dimension is ![images](images/c20-i0141.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>d</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>250</mn></mrow></math>, and we set ![images](images/c20-i0142.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#948;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.01</mn></mrow></math>. Each dot represents the average value of ![images](images/c20-i0145.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#949;</mi></mrow></math> obtained over 100 realizations of the attenuation maps for a fixed value of ![images](images/c20-i0146.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi></msub></mrow></math>. We notice that the error‐performance saturation is well represented by the bound curves.

The results give a first intuition on the classification error probability, comprising both FA and MD errors, for a given size of the training set. We notice that, after a certain point, increasing the training set size ![images](images/c20-i0147.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mi>k</mi><mi>t</mi><mrow><mo>&#42;</mo></mrow></msubsup></mrow></math> does not reduce the classification error. This is due to the size of the NN (in terms of number of neurons and layers), which is not sufficient to deal with the problem complexity.

 

### 20.3.2 Simulation Results

Due to the shortcomings of the PAC learnability theory when applied to classification problems where FA and MD probabilities must be clearly distinguished, either experiments or simulations are needed to assess performance.

![Figure 20.3 images vs. images for a neural network with two hidden layers with images.](images/c20f003.jpg)

([2012](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0016)), where ![images](images/c20-i0163.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c20-i0164.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math> are the shadowing parameters at frequencies ![images](images/c20-i0165.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>1</mn></msub></mrow></math> and ![images](images/c20-i0166.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>f</mi><mn>2</mn></msub></mrow></math>, respectively. In the following results, the channel is affected by path loss with ![images](images/c20-i0167.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#957;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow></math>, Rayleigh fading and shadowing with ![images](images/c20-i0168.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msubsup><mrow><mi>&#963;</mi></mrow><mi>s</mi><mn>2</mn></msubsup><mo>=</mo><mn>3.39</mn></mrow></math>, decorrelation distance ![images](images/c20-i0169.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>d</mi><mi>c</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>75</mn></mrow></math> m, and frequency correlation coefficient ![images](images/c20-i0170.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>&#961;</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.84</mn></mrow></math>; see Van Laethem et al. ([2012](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0016)).

The NN is implemented with a single hidden layer of ![images](images/c20-i0171.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>N</mi><mi>h</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> neurons and trained with the MSE loss function. The activation functions of hidden layers are sigmoids, whereas the activation function of the output layer is a hyperbolic tangent. The SVM is designed according to the maximum margin criterion, with Gaussian kernel (see Bishop ([2006](#c20.xhtml#c20-bib-0003))) and suitably optimized ![images](images/c20-i0172.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><mi>C</mi></mrow></math> parameter and kernel scale. We consider ![images](images/c20-i0173.png)<math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline" overflow="scroll"><mrow><msub><mi>k</mi><mi>f</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mn>10</mn></mrow></math> fading realizations per spatial position.

 

##### *Performance Results*

## 20.5 Conclusions

In this chapter, we proposed a solution to IRLV formulated as a hypothesis‐testing problem. Power attenuation values gathered by multiple APs were used as input the test function, implemented by a learning machine. A key design driver for ML algorithms is the number of training samples needed for parameter tuning, which provides a trade‐off between complexity and classification accuracy. We recalled some key bounds on the training set size and applied them to ML‐based IRLV.

We evaluated the performance of ML algorithms in terms of ROC for both a simulated propagation scenario and experimental data. We explored different NN architectures by varying the number of hidden layers and numerically evaluated the impact of training size on the MD probability.

The concept algorithm we considered opens new research opportunities in the ML framework, e.g. the NN architecture can be further optimized (in the number of neurons, layer shape, and activation function type) for a better adaptation to different IRLV scenarios.
